articles.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen débarque dans Google Search, « la plus grosse mise à jour de modèle » de son histoire
articles.text:
Google déploie Gemini 4 Hydrogen dans son moteur de recherche, où il devient le modèle par défaut du mode IA. Il est aussi proposé dans l’app Gemini, y compris aux comptes gratuits, et remplace la lignée « Flash ».
Après les modèles de pointe Argon et Carbon, c’est donc la version taillée pour le grand public qui arrive, et c'est elle que la plupart des internautes croiseront. Selon Google, il s’agit de « la plus grosse mise à jour de modèle » apportée à Search jusqu’ici, avec un déploiement mondial dès le 12 novembre.
Le mode IA passe à Hydrogen, les AI Overviews aussi pour les questions ardues
Hydrogen devient le modèle par défaut du mode IA de Google et sert aussi aux « questions les plus difficiles » des AI Overviews, d’après Robby Stein, vice-président produit de Search. Google promet qu’on peut formuler une requête en plusieurs parties, avec des fautes de frappe ou des demandes très pointues, et que chaque volet recevra sa réponse.
Le moteur repose sur la technique du « query fan-out » : une question est découpée en sous-requêtes lancées en parallèle. Avec Hydrogen, ce découpage serait plus fin, ce qui doit mener vers un éventail plus large de sites, y compris des pages qu’on n’aurait pas trouvées autrement. Reste à vérifier à l’usage si les éditeurs en tirent un trafic réel, car Google ne chiffre rien à ce sujet.
Côté affichage, attendez-vous à davantage d’images, de tableaux comparatifs, de graphiques et de cartes. Google cite même une simulation interactive animée générée en réponse à une question sur la localisation d’une voiture sur une autoroute sans réseau. Les améliorations de compréhension s’appliquent à toutes les langues prises en charge par le mode IA.
Un modèle d’exécution rapide, pas un Carbon au rabais
Hydrogen succède à Gemini 3.8 Flash. Google annonce des tâches bouclées 2,5 fois plus vite, un score de 57 % contre 18,2 % sur Terminal-Bench 4.1 et plus de cinq fois moins d’affirmations inventées. Il dépasse même Argon sur l’Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (51 contre 50, et 54 au niveau « xhigh »), tandis que Carbon, à 59, reste loin devant.
Le tableau n’est pas uniformément flatteur : Hydrogen reste en retrait sur les sciences et maths, les tâches au terminal et l’utilisation d’un ordinateur face à Claude Sonnet 5.5 et GPT-6.1 Terra. Google reconnaît aussi qu’il hallucine encore, comme tous les modèles génératifs. Polyvalent, donc, mais pas dominateur.
Les développeurs le paient 1,50 dollar le million de tokens en entrée et 7,50 dollars en sortie, sur toute la fenêtre d’un million de tokens. Quatre niveaux de réflexion (low, medium, high par défaut, xhigh) permettent d’ajuster vitesse et coût.
Gratuit dans Gemini, mais sans choix manuel pour tous
Dans l’app Gemini, Hydrogen occupe la case « aide au quotidien » du sélecteur de modèles. Les utilisateurs gratuits n’ont pas la main : il leur est servi par la sélection automatique, quand Gemini juge qu’il convient à la requête. Google met en avant des brouillons d’e-mails ou des fiches de révision « prêts à l’emploi » dès le premier essai, et un meilleur recours aux applications connectées.
Dans Antigravity, réservé aux abonnés AI Pro et Ultra, l’outil Orchestrator bascule en cours de session entre Carbon et Hydrogen. Sur Terminal-Bench 4.0, Google affirme qu’il approche le taux de réussite de Carbon avec 24 % de quota en moins et 19 % de temps gagné.
Le vrai test se jouera dans la barre de recherche, pas dans les tableaux de benchmarks : c’est là que 2,5 fois plus vite devra se traduire en réponses justes.
- Multimodalité texte, voix et fichiers
- Intégration poussée aux services Google
- Applications Web, mobile et bureau

articles.title: AMD wants gamers to remember Radeon loyalty, days after declaring itself a data center-first company
articles.text:
Facepalm: AMD Gaming has just posted a message on its official X account that has left a lot of people scratching their heads. It shows someone walking along a beach appearing to hold hands with a Radeon graphics card, along with the text, "Never forget who was there for you at your lowest." There's also a catopion that reads "I know you'll always be there for me." What's strange is that this attempt to appeal to gamers comes a week after CEO Lisa Su announced that AMD was a "data center first company."
AMD's post might be a response to all that's going on at Nvidia right now. With Jensen Huang having just quit as CEO after 33 years at the helm, and questions mounting over what his departure means for the AI industry and the wider economy, perhaps Team Red thought it was a good time to suggest it has gamers' best interests at heart.
 – AMD Gaming (@AMDGaming) November 12, 2026
Except that isn't true – at all. A week ago, Su made the company's priorities clear in an interview with Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi, where she presented data centers as central to AMD's identity and growth.
"We are a data center first company, that is our profile and you know, people need more computing to power all these applications," Su said.
It's not too surprising to hear Su adopt the same "what are gamers?" attitude we've become used to seeing at Nvidia. AMD's Instinct accelerators and Epyc server processors pushed the company's Q3 revenue to a record $13.4 billion, up 45% from a year earlier. Data center revenue alone jumped 97% to $8.5 billion, accounting for almost two-thirds of the total. Meanwhile, its gaming revenue crashed 40% from a year ago to $773 million, mostly due to the AI-driven memory crisis driving up prices.
The post could also be a nod to AMD's cheaper GPU prices, but it's not like Radeon cards have escaped the hikes. Our most recent GPU pricing guide found that the RX 9060 XT 16GB was selling for roughly $200 above its $350 MSRP on average across the ten countries surveyed. That's still a smaller markup than the roughly $300 premium on Nvidia's RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, though neither is much of a reason to celebrate.
AMD hasn't exactly flooded gamers with new graphics cards this year. Its main new desktop release was July's Radeon RX 9050, an entry-level offering available with 8GB of memory in selected retail markets and just 4GB in some prebuilt systems. We gave it an abysmal score of 30. AMD also brought the previously China-exclusive RX 9070 GRE to more markets, but that was an expansion of availability rather than a new GPU.
AMD might not be able to compete with Nvidia in terms of sales, but it often found more love among gamers as the underdog that offered better value. Today, it wants to be another AI company that happens to make gaming GPUs, no matter what its social media posts imply.

articles.title: In Other News: New CISA Director Nominee, Connected Car Hacking, Baker Tilly Data Breach
articles.text:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.
This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.
Here are this week’s highlights:
Ex-FBI agent’s $2.47M crypto theft compromised bureau investigations
Patrick Steven Yaroch, a former FBI counterintelligence agent, faces up to 20 years in prison after pleading guilty to wire fraud and money laundering over the theft of roughly $2.47 million in cryptocurrency. Yaroch used wallet credentials stored on FBI systems to make about 100 fraudulent transfers tied to 35 investigations. He took funds from investigation subjects and adversarial nation-state actors, and the thefts compromised multiple investigations and FBI sources and methods.
Baker Tilly client data taken from supplier’s platform
US accounting giant Baker Tilly is informing clients that hackers stole personal information, including Social Security numbers, from a platform operated by one of its service providers. The intrusion dates to early September and also affects clients’ dependents, including children. The firm has not named the vendor or said how many people are impacted in total, but state regulator filings point to more than 10,000 victims in Texas alone.
OpenAI agents concealed unauthorized activity
OpenAI has revealed new details about a July incident in which five AI agents conducting cybersecurity evaluations gained root privileges in CI workloads on the company’s research clusters. The agents used credentials and scripts left by earlier agents to modify evaluation settings, repair broken targets, and access restricted information. Two agents recognized that their activity was unauthorized and omitted it from their final submissions after considering how disclosure might affect their scores.
Prompt injection chain could have backdoored OpenAI’s Codex npm package
Depi researchers have described an attack chain against OpenAI’s Codex repository that started with a prompt injection in a GitHub Actions workflow and could have led to a malicious Codex release on npm. The issue-labeling workflow passed the title and body of any new issue to the Codex agent, so an attacker could execute code in the agent’s sandbox, read tokens from a GitHub runner process’s memory via .NET debug pipes, and poison the cache of a workflow with write permissions. The final step relied on a maintainer deleting a rogue release, which would yield a token trusted by npm. OpenAI has fixed the issue and awarded an initial $1,000 bounty.
Siemens details security advisory policy and planned improvements
Siemens has published a policy document that sets out how its PSIRT deals with product vulnerabilities and what its security advisories contain. Planned improvements include an API for automated lookups of product and vulnerability data, wider coverage of flaws in third-party components, more explicit “not affected” declarations, and getting advisory data into commonly used third-party vulnerability databases.
VulnCheck: Glasswing fixes lag far behind findings
VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity says that seven months after Anthropic launched Project Glasswing, he has tracked 442 CVEs credited to the company (about 0.5% of all CVEs published this year), only two of which are known to have been exploited in the wild. Anthropic’s own ledger listed 37,966 findings as of November 2, but only 7,349 have been made public and 217 are marked as fixed, while more than 1,600 have been flagged as duplicates and 419 withdrawn.
Railway puts unauthorized spend from stolen AI keys at $740,000
Railway has released a detailed incident report on the October attack, in which a threat actor used an undiscovered flaw in its build infrastructure to partially escape isolation, obtained a copy of the company’s code repository, and then abused a misconfigured OIDC binding to reach credentials that let it decrypt customer environment variables. At most 1.85% of workspaces (roughly 100,000) could have had variables decrypted. Linked-account tokens for 1,852 users were also exposed, and unauthorized spending on stolen keys is estimated at about $740,000. Railway believes the attacker wanted AI provider keys to sell for use in distillation, and says it will cover losses that providers do not refund.
Exposed MS SQL servers hijacked to deliver cryptominer and Gh0st RAT
Fortinet has analyzed a campaign in which Go-based malware with the open source Naabu scanner built in looks for internet-facing Microsoft SQL Server instances, and a companion tool then brute-forces logins using a list of more than 2,700 passwords. After a successful login, T-SQL commands enable xp_cmdshell and download or drop a loader, which installs a Monero miner disguised as a Microsoft Edge update and a Gh0st RAT variant whose features include keylogging and data theft.
Microsoft urges weight audits after ‘Lazarus’ dormant neuron backdoor research
Microsoft researchers have described Lazarus, a technique that backdoors an LLM without any training by rewriting the weights of fewer than 10 dormant neurons, so that an agent built on the model behaves normally until a trigger (such as a date or an error message) makes it emit an attacker’s command. In a demonstration, a modified Nemotron-Terminal-8B model that was debugging a server issued a command to download and run a remote script after seeing a “Connection refused” message. Because the attack needs write access to the weights and can only be reliably detected by comparing them with the originals, Microsoft recommends verifying model provenance and auditing weights the way code is audited.
Connected cars exposed by flaws in automakers’ ForgeRock deployments
Researchers Sam Curry and Shubham Shah have disclosed weaknesses in the ForgeRock identity deployments of unnamed automakers that allowed them to take over customer accounts and send remote commands to connected vehicles, including unlocking doors and starting engines. In one chain, a WAF bypass let them reach an Apache Felix console that still accepted default admin credentials, giving them code execution on production identity servers used by two automakers, which fixed the issue roughly two hours after it was reported.
Palantir CISO LoSapio nominated to fill long-vacant CISA director post
President Donald Trump has nominated Michael LoSapio, Palantir’s CISO since September 2024, to lead CISA, which has not had a Senate-confirmed director since Jen Easterly left in January 2025, Nextgov reports. Should the Senate fail to act before this Congress adjourns, Trump would need to renominate him under an incoming Democratic majority whose members have questioned Palantir’s government work. Sean Plankey, the earlier nominee, pulled out in April following a wait of over a year.
Vanderbilt tells campus to power down devices amid attack claimed by BYOD group
US-based Vanderbilt University this week told everyone in its community to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi as its IT team worked on an active cybersecurity incident that it said could affect devices, systems and cloud-based services. The BYOD group has taken credit for the attack.
Related: In Other News: Trezor Implant, LLMJacking Bills Hit $1M, SAP Flaws Weaponized Within Days
Related: In Other News: Anthropic Breach Dispute, UEFI Flaw Hits Most Servers, Cloudflare AI Data Leak

articles.title: Netflix Turns Operational Data Into a Knowledge Graph for AI-Driven Observability
articles.text:
Netflix is developing an ontology-driven knowledge graph to accelerate production investigations and provide AI agents with a shared understanding of its operational environment. The platform connects information about applications, incidents, deployments, alerts, and infrastructure dependencies, addressing a problem that can leave engineers spending hours piecing together information scattered across different systems.
The company claims it handles more than 2 billion requests daily and upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. During the November 2024 Jake Paul-Mike Tyson fight, its infrastructure supported approximately 65 million concurrent streams. Yet investigating a typical application regression can take around four hours, with much of that time spent reconstructing relationships between systems rather than analysing the underlying data.
Netflix's solution is to make those relationships explicit through an operational ontology and knowledge graph, creating a foundation for automated root-cause analysis and, eventually, self-healing infrastructure.
Netflix already collects metrics, events, logs, and traces (MELT) across its applications and infrastructure. However, these signals are spread across systems such as alerting, incident management, deployment tooling, and engineering communication platforms.
An application regression might originate from a client release, an experiment, infrastructure load shedding, or a service several dependencies downstream. Although each system contains useful information, engineers must often connect the evidence manually.
Netflix identified the missing capability as a consistent way to describe not just individual components, but how they relate to one another.
Its Observability Ontology provides that common model, defining operational entities, their properties, and the relationships between them. It uses established standards including RDF, OWL, SHACL, and SPARQL, while the resulting knowledge graph is stored in QuipuDB, Netflix's distributed RDF database built on Rust's redb storage engine.
The graph is populated through a pipeline of components Netflix calls enrichers. These consume information from operational systems and transform it into structured relationships, represented as subject-predicate-object triples.
Some enrichment is deterministic, while other stages use LLMs and probabilistic techniques to interpret less structured information. Netflix constrains these outputs through strict validation rules, including consistent entity types, URI naming conventions, and checks against its software catalogue.
Netflix also captures information from incident discussions, including hypotheses, rejected explanations, and mitigation decisions. This allows human reasoning to become part of the operational knowledge base rather than disappearing when an incident conversation ends.
Its correlation engine examines 13 types of signals, including log errors, metric anomalies, traces, alerts, incidents, deployments, configuration changes, experiments, and code changes. It searches for potential causal relationships, evaluating evidence such as temporal proximity and severity to produce ranked hypotheses.
Netflix describes the process as a knowledge flywheel: Observe, Enrich, Infer, and Adapt. As investigations produce new insights, those relationships can inform future detection and analysis. The knowledge graph also underpins AutoRCA, Netflix's internal agentic AI system for root-cause analysis.
Rather than having specialist agents exchange loosely structured findings, they use the ontology as a common interface. Agents analysing traces, logs or deployments can contribute information about the same operational entities without needing to understand each other's internal implementations.
Netflix intends to use this foundation to produce ranked, evidence-backed explanations for incidents, with humans retaining approval authority over proposed changes and remediation.
Platforms such as Datadog, Dynatrace, and Splunk already correlate observability signals and increasingly incorporate AI into incident investigation. Netflix's approach emphasizes the semantic model behind those signals, making operational relationships persistent and directly accessible to both engineers and machines.
The company ultimately wants to extend this capability from automated root-cause analysis into automated remediation and self-healing infrastructure. It also plans to explore integration with its Unified Data Architecture, connecting operational information to broader business and technology domains

articles.title: Nueva preocupación en Estados Unidos sobre Nvidia: ¿es una empresa demasiado grande para caer?
articles.text:
El senador demócrata Jack Reed pidió el jueves que el Congreso de Estados Unidos evalúe si Nvidia es una empresa “demasiado grande para caer” y si su eventual quiebra afectaría al sistema bancario y a los mercados de crédito, según informó la agencia Reuters.
Reed dijo que Nvidia “ha respaldado el ecosistema de la IA mediante transacciones financieras complejas” y reclamó “total transparencia” sobre esos acuerdos, además de un análisis de cómo podrían repercutir en bancos y créditos.
El senador agregó que millones de estadounidenses tienen exposición económica a la compañía a través de sus cuentas de jubilación y fondos de pensión.
El pedido llegó el mismo día en que Nvidia anunció la renuncia inmediata de Jensen Huang como director ejecutivo, presidente y miembro del directorio. La directora financiera, Colette Kress, quedó como directora ejecutiva interina mientras el directorio busca un reemplazo permanente.
Un escándalo que ya costó USD 500.000 millones en bolsa
Huang admitió el domingo, en un mensaje interno a los empleados, que fue infiel a su esposa. Antes, el Financial Times había informado de su relación con una ejecutiva de Megaspeed, una empresa de centros de datos con sede en Singapur, a la que se sospecha de espiar para China. El gobierno chino negó las acusaciones.
El miércoles, The New York Times publicó que Huang tuvo además otra relación con una directiva de Nvidia que dependía de él. ABC News señaló que no pudo verificar ese reporte. En medio de las revelaciones, NBC News calculó que las acciones perdieron unos USD 500.000 millones de valor en la semana.
El jueves la acción llegó a caer 16% durante la jornada y cerró con una baja de 4,3%, según NBC News. La capitalización de la compañía quedó apenas por encima de los USD 4 billones.
Los compromisos que preocupan al senador
Reed no precisó en su declaración cuáles son las operaciones que le inquietan. La CNBC enumeró varios compromisos de Nvidia: compras de hasta USD 36.000 millones en servicios en la nube a proveedores de IA más pequeños y una garantía condicionada de hasta USD 105.000 millones para un proyecto de centro de datos en Ohio de OpenAI y SB Energy.
También mencionó un respaldo de hasta USD 125.000 millones para un programa de crédito de USD 500.000 millones en el que participan firmas de Wall Street. El profesor de finanzas de la Universidad de Columbia Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh estima el total en unos USD 400.000 millones, aunque las condiciones difieren y es improbable que todo se exija a la vez.
Especialistas descartan una repetición de la crisis de 2008, porque Nvidia es una empresa rentable y no un banco que recibe depósitos. Sheila Bair, ex presidenta de la agencia que garantiza los depósitos bancarios (FDIC), sostiene de todos modos que los reguladores deberían examinar esas exposiciones.
El Servicio de Investigación del Congreso recuerda que Washington no designa formalmente a las empresas como demasiado grandes para caer, en parte para no sugerir que habría un rescate garantizado.
Nvidia no hizo comentarios sobre el pedido del senador. La próxima cita es el 17 de noviembre, cuando la empresa presentará resultados trimestrales, con una proyección de ingresos de unos USD 108.000 millones que excluye ventas de centros de datos en China, según ese mismo medio.

articles.title: Screenless GPS: Slate Auto says, "Remember the road atlas"
articles.text:
Whether it’s nostalgia or a sense that technology has gotten a bit too pervasive, there’s no denying that Slate Auto appears to be tuned into the particular moment. The startup has a simple pitch: an affordable electric truck with just the basics, leaving owners to DIY and BYOD for everything else, all for a sub-$25,000 starting price.
Among the things Slate does without is an embedded infotainment system. The small digital display on the dashboard that shows your speed and range is also where the backup camera appears if you engage reverse, and there are two USB-C ports that provide power but not connectivity, and that’s that. But there is a solution to getting lost, and it’s called “Screenless GPS.” Even though we don’t have a Slate truck to test it with, the OEM sent us a unit to review.
That’s right, it’s a good old spiral-bound road atlas! “We believe you should use the devices you know and love,” Slate says, and it reckons that maps worked just fine for past generations, so they should still work now.
Upside: a bored child can stare at the maps in the back seat endlessly on long drives. Not me, obviously.
Downside: wait, this Slate doesn't have a back seat! Where's little Joey!?

articles.title: Microsoft's latest email outage turned into a full-blown global cloud crisis | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Microsoft is slowly recovering from its daylong outage after much of the company’s systems were hit by a cascading software issue.
The problems, which started Thursday, were initially flagged as affecting the company’s services in the U.S. and the Americas, but quickly spread around the world, as engineers struggled to recover downed servers.
What began as an Outlook email and Teams video conferencing outage soon developed into a full-blown meltdown affecting the company’s cloud services for both consumer and business email, files, and documents. The outage also knocked out the company’s Copilot AI tools and Defender security screening software, and prevented system administrators from accessing their internal Intune dashboards and features. Some users reportedly experienced issues with accessing their cloud-based Windows computers.
Microsoft hasn’t yet said what caused the issues, only saying the outage involved “a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable.” The company said it continues to investigate the cause.
The outage affected a broad range of industries, including TechCrunch’s own email. We’ve reached out to Microsoft for comment about the incident.
As of Friday morning on the U.S. East Coast, Microsoft’s Outlook email service had begun to recover and some emails have been trickling in. The recovery comes after engineers initially could not find the cause of the issue that was causing servers in Microsoft’s data centers to fail.
Doug Madory, the director of internet analysis at Kentik, a company that monitors internet traffic worldwide, said in a post on Bluesky that traffic was returning to Microsoft’s services after about 18 hours of downtime.
Microsoft said in its latest status update on Friday that there was “no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident,” and later noted that there was “not related to cyber or AI / agents.” That may be some solace for the millions who went without their email and online services yesterday, but the company is likely to face questions about its inability to swiftly recover from an outage of its own making.
A Microsoft spokesperson did not respond to our questions asking if the company has the technical means to detect malicious activity, such as logs, or if Microsoft has a way to check what happened.
“We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure,” said Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president for Copilot, agents, and platform, in a statement on Friday. “Our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward.”
The last major incident affecting Microsoft services was in September, when a dayslong outage hit Microsoft’s cloud services. During that outage, Microsoft blamed a “core authentication configuration” issue that prevented users from accessing the service.
This story was first published on November 12 and has been updated throughout.

articles.title: The Download: Silicon Valley’s blind spot and Nvidia’s chip-tracking plan
articles.text:
The Download: Silicon Valley’s blind spot and Nvidia’s chip-tracking plan
Plus: A major Microsoft outage has disrupted services worldwide.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
—Aaron Zamost, a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square
The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley have built careers claiming to see the future. Yet five weeks before the midterms, many gathered at the White House to pose with Trump and endorse his “Super Intelligence” agenda, despite growing opposition to AI and data centers.
Their decision to lash themselves to President Trump was a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.
Here’s why Silicon Valley’s tech leaders may be less visionary than they think.
Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
Nvidia representatives told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it was possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review on Thursday, despite an industry group claiming they were “potentially infeasible.”
Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips and prevent their smuggling to China.
The act is drawing renewed attention following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair. Find out what the proposed tracking measures would involve.
—James O'Donnell
More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can control robotic limbs and computers, and even “speak.”
The people who volunteer for trials of these devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart, who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014.
He’s been working on a set of guidelines for ethical trials to respect participants’ autonomy—and access their own brain data whenever they want.
Read the full story on the push to give volunteers in brain implant trials more rights.
—Jessica Hamzelou
This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.

Quote of the day
“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place—TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!”
—Donald Trump shares his succession plan for Nvidia on Truth Social, The Verge reports.
One more thing
Inside the world’s deepest and longest subsea road tunnel
—Niall Firth
I’m currently around 1,000 feet beneath the North Sea, in a dark, dank cave. It smells weird. And I’m increasingly aware of the pressure from millions of tons of seawater just above my head.
I’m under the iconic fjords of Norway to visit what will soon become the world’s longest and deepest subsea road tunnel—an exceptional engineering feat that will carry drivers deep beneath the North Sea.
I’m here to understand how you make a 16.6-mile highway that sits 1,280 feet below the sea at its deepest point. And also—at a time when it can feel hard to get anything done—to reassure myself that ambitious engineering is still possible. That we can still make things.
Step inside Norway’s Rogfast tunnel and see how engineers are making it happen.

articles.title: Japanese workers return to fax machines during ongoing Microsoft 365 outage — 'We're going full analog' say workers forced to ditch PDFs
articles.text:
Japanese workers return to fax machines during ongoing Microsoft 365 outage — 'We're going full analog' say workers forced to ditch PDFs
The outage has lasted nearly a full 24 hours.
Japanese workers dealing with the impacts of Microsoft's ongoing 365 outage have reportedly taken to analog measures, including using fax machines to deal with the ongoing blackout, the Japan Times reports. An outage that has now lasted nearly 24 hours was still going on Friday when employees turned up to work.
The downtime has meant businesses reliant on Microsoft 365 are unable to use Outlook, Teams, and Copilot, with workplaces hit with error messages and blank screens, forced to reschedule meetings or delay work. For some, the outage has proven a respite from Japan's notoriously workaholic culture. "I couldn’t open Outlook and panicked … I got in touch with my boss and was told to stay home," one person reported on X, while another remarked that the only task they could carry out at work was to clean the coffee machine in the production room.
But while some employees and companies are throwing in the towel and calling it an early weekend, others are taking a novel, more analog approach. "Microsoft’s server glitch has made it impossible to get any work done since this morning. I guess phones and fax machines really are unbeatable. … We’re going full analog!" one user claimed. The report cites another employee who confirmed that their company was switching to fax machines to send the regular updates the company normally sends out as PDFs. "Analog is strong," they rejoiced.
Some 78% of Japanese companies rely on Microsoft for their digital infrastructure. The outage began on Thursday, with mass disruption to Outlook, Teams, Copilot, OneDrive, and Microsoft 365 as a whole. It's a saga impacting entire sectors, including UK health care, businesses, travel, and transport.
Microsoft's latest update said it was seeing "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe, while the situation in America was improving, but warned some users may still experience intermittent issues. The company has also denied rumblings that the outage was caused by a cybersecurity breach. The outage has even caused some companies, such as Switzerland's luxury Richemont (Cartier) outfit, to delay giving their latest earnings report.
Download the Tom's Hardware app for up-to-the-minute updates on iOS and Android. Also follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.

Stephen is Tom's Hardware's News Editor with almost a decade of industry experience covering technology, having worked at TechRadar, iMore, and even Apple over the years. He has covered the world of consumer tech from nearly every angle, including supply chain rumors, patents, and litigation, and more. When he's not at work, he loves reading about history and playing video games.

articles.title: Forget Wordle, Canadian puzzle game Dayzle is my new addiction
articles.text:
I love a good puzzle, but in the era of the smartphone, I feel like few have managed to capture the feeling of sitting down with the morning paper and a coffee, and poking away at a puzzle.
Wordle came close when it took the world by storm in 2021, offering a great daily puzzle and a fun social system that made sharing your score (and competing with friends and family) an easy and fun element of the daily ritual.
But as much as I like Wordle, I keep falling off it, in part because I eventually get bored doing the same puzzle every day, and in part because one puzzle isn’t quite enough.
That’s where Dayzle comes in. This cool, made-in-Canada app offers a daily ‘set’ of five puzzles to complete, pulling from a broader list of almost 30 games.
That list spans several types of puzzles, including classics like Sudoku, word searches, and even its own Wordle clone, as well as novel puzzles like Terminus, Span, Crowns, and more. It makes for a wonderful amount of variety each day, which helps Dazyle feel fresh.
Daily set is ad-free
The daily set is the core focus for Dayzle, available for free with no ads. However, Dayzle also lets you run ‘practice’ puzzles to learn the different puzzles and improve on them without impacting your daily scores.
That’s where the ads come in, showing up every few puzzles. I found the number of ads more than fair, and they never interrupted my puzzles during testing. But for those who dislike ads, there are subscriptions (Plus for $14.99/year or Unlimited for $19.99/year) which remove ads and provide extra hints and lives. (Free users can refill hints by watching ads.)
What further helps the daily sets feel fresh is just how different some of the puzzles are. On the numbers side, Terminus and Span were among my favourites. The former has you building a route to connect a number of ‘stops’ in one line that doesn’t break or double back, while the latter has you joining islands with bridges, but you have to be smart about the connections since each island can only support so many bridges.
For word puzzles, I like Tumbler, which tasks you with transforming a word into another word, letter by letter. Loom is also interesting, offering a crossword-like puzzle with no hints. Witness is also clever, giving clues so players can rule out the suspects and find the real crook.
However, the visual puzzles are where things get really creative. Crowns has players placing crowns in colourful sections of a grid — each section has one crown, but crowns can’t touch, and there can only be one per row and column. Parcel has people dividing a board into squares and rectangles that match clues about their size, while Trailhead will have you building a trail based on simple clues.
And that’s just a handful of my favourites, with many other options available. Plus, several of the puzzles use a standard square grid, but Dayzle also offers more challenging ‘Hive’ variants that use a hexagonal grid instead.
Constantly adding new puzzles
Further, Dayzle has been steadily adding to the puzzles since I’ve been testing the app, including adding a few “relaxing” puzzles that don’t appear in the daily sets.
Finally, Dayzle offers a social aspect too, with leaderboards for the daily sets so you can see how your performance stacks up against others. Players can also earn medals and participate in events with friends. There’s also some self-improvement stuff here, with Dayzle measuring how players perform across statistics like speed, focus, or memory, highlighting improvements, and more.
All told, there’s a lot to like here, and the frequent updates are great to see. It feels like almost every time I open the app, there’s something fresh.
Part of how Dayzle pulls everything off, and at a fairly reasonable price, is through AI. The Toronto-based team of three behind the app told MobileSyrup that its sort of “core thesis” behind Dayzle was using AI to lower costs on the development side so it wouldn’t need to monetize as aggressively.
The team uses AI to help with coding, generating ad content, animating things, and more, while the human element comes more from managing the product and making decisions.
Dayzle is available for free on iOS and Android, as well as on the web if you’d rather try without downloading anything first. The free version is supported by ads, with Plus ($14.99) and Unlimited ($19.99) annual subscriptions available to remove ads and add extras like more hints and lives.
Screenshots credit: Dayzle

articles.title: Retro-Look, moderne Technik: 8 Gadgets, die den Charme der 80er und 90er zurückbringen
articles.text:
CDs, Disketten oder Klapphandys: 8 moderne Gadgets, die ganz auf Nostalgie setzen
Nein, früher war sicherlich nicht alles besser. Aber einiges eben doch. Zum Beispiel die CD-Sammlung, die man behutsam kuratiert und wertgeschätzt hat, statt unaufmerksam eine randomisierte Streaming-Playlist im Hintergrund laufen zu lassen. Oder die ersten Handys, mit denen man tatsächlich noch telefoniert hat und nicht nur stundenlang durch Social Media gescrollt ist.
Zumindest lösen diese und andere Erinnerungen bei vielen Menschen eine große Sehnsucht aus. Und wenn man die Zeit auch nicht zurückholen kann, so doch zumindest ein paar der Gegenstände, die einem damals so wichtig waren – wenn auch in moderner Form. Diese acht Gadgets setzen ganz auf Nostalgie.
KM5 Instant Disc Audio: CD-Player im Fotoformat
Mit den CD-Playern früherer Tage hat die Variante der japanischen Firma KM5 nur noch wenig gemein. Hier ist der Player kaum noch größer als die CD selbst. Das quadratische Sichtfenster ist von einem Rahmen umgeben, der an den Seiten schmal und unten größer ist. Das erinnert an das Fotoformat von Instantkameras. Das Sichtfenster lässt sich mit einem CD-Cover überdecken. Preis: 180 Euro
Commodore Callback: Das Comeback des Klapphandys
Mit dem C64 und Amiga hat Commodore die frühe PC-Landschaft geprägt. Nun versucht sich das 2025 wiederbelebte Unternehmen an einem sogenannten Dumbphone: Das Commodore Callback ist ein Klapphandy, das zwar Apps für Messaging, Musikstreaming und Navigation unterstützt. Social-Media-Apps und Browser sind aber gesperrt. Getippt wird auf einem klassischen Ziffernblock mit T9-Wörterbuch. Preis: ab 399 US-Dollar.
Reto 3D Classic: Analoge Fotografie trifft 3D-Effekt
Mit dem Aufkommen von Digitalkameras sind Kameras mit Fotofilmen praktisch verschwunden. Das Unternehmen Reto stellt sich gegen den Trend – und setzt weiterhin auf die analoge Technik. Die Reto 3D Classic hat zusätzlich einen Twist verbaut. Die drei Linsen schießen vom selben Motiv drei Hochkant-Fotos in leicht versetzter Perspektive. Auf der Filmrolle werden dafür anderthalb Plätze verbraucht. Die zugehörige App erstellt aus den drei Analogfotos, die vorher eingescannt werden müssen, ein animiertes Gif mit einem 3D-Wackel-Effekt. Preis: 79,20 Dollar.
Ollee Watch: So wird die Casio-Uhr zur Smartwatch
Casio-Uhren gelten als Designklassiker – besonders smart sind sie nach heutigen Maßstäben aber nicht. Ollee Watch möchte das ändern. Das Startup hat ein Nachrüst-Kit entwickelt, dank der die Uhren neben der Zeit auch Temperatur und Herzfrequenz sowie gegangene Schritte messen können. Dafür wird ein neuer Chip eingesetzt. Daten werden dann per Bluetooth ans Smartphone gesendet. Die Batterie der Uhr soll bis zu zehn Monate durchhalten. Preis: ab 54,99 Dollar.
Iretro Lab The Time Planet: Röhrenfernseher-Design
Die 1970 erschienene Videosphere ist ein ulkiges Produkt der Tech-Geschichte. Der kugelförmige Röhrenfernseher der Marke JVC erinnert optisch an einen Astronautenhelm. Die Firma Iretro Lab hat die Gehäuseform per 3D-Druck kopiert – setzt aber auf ein modernes Innenleben mit Retina-Displays aus iPads. Per USB-C können Computer angeschlossen werden, ein Mac Mini kann im Gehäuse verstaut werden. Im Gerätefuß ist eine mechanische Flip-Uhr verbaut. Preis: 769,99 Dollar.
Wakcas Floppy Disk MagSafe-Ständer für iPhones
Als Speichermedium haben Disketten wegen ihrer geringen Kapazität längst ausgedient, als Icon für die Speicherfunktion bei Software haben sie aber überlebt. Das Unternehmen Wakcas bedient sich an dem ikonischen Design für einen iPhone-Ständer. Das Gadget ist Mag-Safe-kompatibel und haftet an der Rückseite des iOS-Geräts. Zum Abstellen wird die Halter-Diskette in der Mitte aufgeklappt. Die Firma hat zudem optisch passende Hüllen im Programm. Preis: 35,95 Euro.
WinRar Fashion-Kollektion: Retro-Tech als Accessoire
Das Modelabel Forever Vacation hat mit in.tern.et noch einen zweiten Online-Store, der um einiges unbekannter ist. Hier tummeln sich allerlei Klamotten, Poster und Schmuck in einer Retro-Internet-Ästhetik. Zu finden ist hier etwa eine Kollaboration mit WinRar. Neben T-Shirts und Hoodies gibt es auch eine ZIP-Ordner-Tasche aus veganem Leder, die dem Logo nachempfunden ist. Preis: 115 Euro
We Are Rewind: Kassettenspieler im Retro-Design
Das Unternehmen We are Rewind hat sich zur Aufgabe gemacht, Kassettenspieler und Blaster wieder cool zu machen. Wie das klappen soll? Mit knalligen Farben und Kooperationen mit großen Namen. Mit dem US-Rapper Ab-Soul oder dem Videospiel Fortnite hat We are Rewind schon gemeinsame Kassettenspieler veröffentlicht. Momentan gibt es eine limitierte Koop mit den Markenverwertern von Elvis Presley – dazu gehört sein ´68er Comeback-Special. Preis: 179 Euro
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 20.08.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.

articles.title: BYD a trouvé la solution pour simplifier à l'extrême la charge de votre voiture électrique : vous n'aurez même plus à sortir
articles.text:
Le constructeur chinois BYD veut définitivement devenir le leader de la voiture électrique. Après sa technologie Flash Charging, qui promet des temps de recharge défiant ceux d’un plein de carburant, et le record du monde de vitesse d’une voiture homologuée, la marque présente un système de charge totalement automatisé. Vous n’aurez même plus besoin de sortir de votre voiture.
Un chargeur automatisé
On dit toujours que la recharge des voitures électriques s’accélère. C’est vrai : les chargeurs deviennent plus puissants et les voitures peuvent accepter des puissances plus importantes, réduisant inévitablement les temps de charge. Toutefois, il faut également prendre en compte le temps nécessaire à la manœuvre, à la manipulation du câble et au déclenchement de la borne, qui peut parfois être aussi long que la recharge elle-même.
BYD présente alors sa solution. La marque chinoise a dévoilé aux Émirats arabes unis un chargeur doté d’un bras automatisé permettant de brancher une voiture sans intervention humaine. Il ne serait même plus nécessaire de descendre du véhicule pour débuter la recharge. Le bras robotisé dispose d’un système de reconnaissance capable de repérer l’emplacement de la trappe de recharge et de positionner le connecteur. BYD explique que plusieurs types de connecteurs sont compatibles, comme le CCS utilisé en Europe.
Avec ce chargeur, BYD propose de faciliter le ravitaillement en énergie de sa voiture. Une opération qui reste parfois contraignante, même si faire le plein de diesel n’est pas non plus une partie de plaisir. Pour que le fonctionnement soit optimal, il faut que la voiture soit compatible avec le Plug & Charge. Cette fonctionnalité ne nécessite aucun moyen de paiement pour déclencher la recharge : les coordonnées de paiement sont enregistrées dans la voiture, qui entre directement en relation avec la borne.
BYD bientôt leader des chargeurs rapides ?
Avec cette annonce d’un chargeur automatisé, en marge du record de vitesse de la Yangwang U9 à plus de 500 km/h, BYD veut s’imposer comme un leader de la recharge rapide. La marque de Shenzhen travaille actuellement au déploiement de sa technologie Flash Charging, capable de délivrer jusqu’à 1 500 kW. Ces chargeurs ultra-rapides permettent aux modèles BYD équipés de la batterie Blade 2.0 de passer de 10 à 70 % de charge en 5 minutes et de 10 à 97 % en seulement 9 minutes. Avec cette technologie, l’argument du temps nécessaire pour recharger une voiture électrique face au ravitaillement d’un modèle thermique perd de son poids.
En Europe, la Denza Z9 GT (berline haut de gamme de BYD) est déjà prête pour le Flash Charging, avec une puissance de recharge pouvant atteindre 1 000 kW. Mais les infrastructures manquent encore. BYD espère déployer 100 bornes d’ici à la fin de l’année 2026 en Europe, puis 3 000 bornes de recharge rapide d’ici à la fin de 2027.

articles.title: How South African startup GreenBDG Africa is building the “digital brain” behind sustainable assets - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South African climate-tech startup GreenBDG Africa has developed a platform that helps businesses track energy use, reduce emissions and make better decisions about their buildings and infrastructure.
Founded in 2014 by Songo Didiza, GreenBDG Africa pulls in data that usually sits in silos – utility meters, building management systems (BMS), solar inverters and utility invoices. Using artificial intelligence, the platform checks and analyses this data, helping businesses better understand their energy use and environmental performance. It also helps organisations meet sustainability reporting requirements and make more informed financial and operational decisions.
“The output is tailored to each stakeholder. A CFO sees Rand-denominated risk, tax recovery, such as Section 12L, and fines avoided. A sustainability officer gets framework-ready disclosures. A facility manager gets actionable alerts,” Didiza told Disrupt Africa.
The Sandton-headquartered startup is also a registered Tier 1 Energy Services Company (ESCO) on the South African National Energy Development Institute database, meaning its work does not start and end with sustainability reporting.
“We design and implement energy efficiency, renewable energy and low-carbon projects. Our approach is simple: measure, understand, predict, optimise, decarbonise,” Didiza said.
Turning sustainability data into better decisions
Didiza, an ESG strategist and green building specialist with a background in computational and applied mathematics, leads the business alongside Chief Strategy Officer Sumaya Mahomed and Chief Technology Officer Ridhwaan Mayet. The team was responding to rapidly rising ESG pressure on African asset owners from investors, lenders, regulators and export markets to demonstrate their environmental performance.
“The data they need to respond is scattered across meters, spreadsheets, invoices and consultants’ reports. Sustainability reporting had become a costly annual compliance exercise rather than a source of better decisions,” she said.
Regulation has made the problem more urgent. In South Africa, building owners face requirements to assess and report how efficiently their properties use energy, with fines of up to ZAR5 million (US$300,000) for non-compliance.
Businesses also face carbon tax obligations and growing sustainability reporting requirements, while energy efficiency tax incentives can go unclaimed without verified data.
Meanwhile, exporters face carbon-related trade measures such as the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, which places a carbon-related cost on certain imported goods.
Didiza said GreenBDG Africa’s competition fell into two camps: global sustainability reporting platforms, which are not always designed for African regulations, infrastructure or energy pricing; and local engineering and sustainability consultancies, which often rely on manual reporting processes rather than continuously updated data.
“We bridge this gap: we are locally engineered, AI-enabled, and backed by a Tier 1 ESCO model that can implement the projects the data identifies,” she said.
Growing impact and expanding across Africa
The startup says it has contributed to decarbonising assets by approximately 250,000 tonnes of CO₂e, and supported more than one million square metres of building space with energy performance certificates and over 13.5 megawatts of renewable energy capacity.
The startup’s sustainability engagements have covered portfolios with a combined net asset value of more than ZAR50 billion (US$3 billion).
Flagship projects include the Bertha Solar & Digital Decarbonisation Project, a net-zero precinct pathway for industrial precincts such as the Dube TradePort Special Economic Zone, and energy performance optimisation for Eastern Cape Public Works.
“Uptake has been strongest among organisations with large, distributed portfolios, where ESG risk translates directly into financial risk,” Didiza said.
Clients include manufacturers, property funds, freight and logistics firms, ICT companies and data centre operators looking to decarbonise their portfolios.
GreenBDG Africa has set itself a public target, #1000by2030, of helping more than 1,000 assets reach decarbonisation status by 2030, and is currently a quarter of the way there.
The startup earns revenue in three ways: platform subscriptions per asset or portfolio for ongoing ESG data, analytics and reporting; advisory and certification work, including ESG strategy, green building certification and net-zero pathways; and implementation through its Tier 1 ESCO capability, often structured so that savings from one phase fund the next.
Currently operating in South Africa across six sectors – real estate, financial services, manufacturing, logistics, ICT and mining – GreenBDG Africa plans to expand in two directions – deeper into sectors beyond real estate, particularly export-oriented manufacturers facing carbon border mechanisms, and into the rest of the continent, starting with Botswana and Zimbabwe.
“ESG disclosure requirements and green finance are growing fast but local, data-driven tools are scarce. Our Special Economic Zone methodology is built to be replicable, which makes SEZs and industrial parks across Africa a natural route,” Didiza said.
Overcoming challenges and supporting women in climate tech
“The biggest challenge has been data, not technology. Many facilities still run on manual meter readings, incomplete records and invoices in different formats, so much of our early work went into building integrations with more than 15 hardware brands and AI validation that turns messy inputs into audit-ready data,” Didiza said.
Changing how businesses view sustainability has been another hurdle. It is often seen as a compliance cost rather than an investment, meaning GreenBDG Africa has had to demonstrate its financial value to business leaders before conversations move forward.
Like many African climate-tech businesses, the startup has also faced lengthy enterprise and public sector sales cycles and limited access to growth capital, while competing with well-funded global platforms.
As it navigates these challenges, GreenBDG Africa is also working to strengthen its business model and position itself for growth.
The startup participated in the Standard Chartered Foundation Women in Tech programme, implemented locally by Standard Chartered Bank in South Africa and supported globally by Village Capital across 12 markets in Africa, the Middle East and Pakistan. Through the programme, it received mentorship, investor-readiness training, market access, networking and funding.
Didiza said the programme helped the startup begin developing its own models and solutions to the challenges it faced, and she would “absolutely” recommend that other women founders apply.
“Climate tech in Africa needs more women building and leading it, and programmes like this give founders the network and confidence to scale,” she said.

articles.title: Microsoft says November security updates cause printing issues
articles.text:
Microsoft warned customers earlier this week that the November 2026 security updates may break printing for documents with complex formatting.
As the company explained in a service alert seen by BleepingComputer, this known issue affects users attempting to print documents with images that have zero height or width on server (Windows Server 2016 or later) and client (Windows 10 or later) devices.
"After installing the November 2026 Windows security update (the Originating KBs listed above), or later updates, printing might fail for documents containing images rendered with a height or width value of zero at the selected printing resolution," Microsoft said.
"These images can be used as part of certain complex document formatting, such as adding "invisible" images intended to serve as a document watermark, layout anchoring, or generation tools that may inserting images objects even when no graphic present."
The bug mainly affects users printing Microsoft Word documents via the Windows Graphics Device Interface (GDI), but it may also trigger failures when printing from other applications.
Microsoft also addressed printing issues triggered by Windows updates in March and July 2025: the first caused USB printers to print random text, and the second broke the 'Print to PDF' feature.
More recently, the company notified customers that the August 2026 .NET Framework cumulative updates broke printing and PDF export in apps that use the Windows Presentation Foundation (WPF) UI framework.
This week, Microsoft also confirmed that this month's Patch Tuesday security updates trigger Windows activation and licensing failures with 0x80041008 error codes and that Windows updates released since the October Patch Tuesday cause SQL Server performance and stability issues.
Additionally, the company warned that the November 2026 Windows 11 security updates fail to install on systems with the October 2026 preview update.

articles.title: Mittal says India must hold the satellite 'kill switch', warns against reliance on one company
articles.text:
Mittal says India must hold the satellite 'kill switch', warns against reliance on one company
The kill switch is the ability to cut off, throttle or restrict a satellite network's service, whether for a single terminal, a region or an entire country, from the operator's control systems and ground gateways.
Bharti Airtel Founder and Chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal said India must keep control of the "kill switch" for satellite communications on its own soil, as the government weighs security conditions that will decide when satellite broadband goes live.
"The kill switch, as we call it, should not be sitting somewhere else," Mittal said in an interview with PTI marking Bharti Enterprises' 50th year. "India must have control over its own space destiny."
He did not name a company in that remark.
The kill switch is the ability to cut off, throttle or restrict a satellite network's service, whether for a single terminal, a region or an entire country, from the operator's control systems and ground gateways. In satellite broadband, user terminals connect to satellites, which relay traffic to ground stations and then to the internet, so whoever runs those control and gateway systems can in principle disable users or reroute their data.
Governments see it as a security tool. It would let them shut down service quickly in a conflict, during a security threat or to enforce lawful orders, and it would let them monitor and intercept traffic.
The implications cut both ways. If the switch sits with a foreign operator or abroad, a country's military, emergency and civilian users can lose connectivity because of a decision made elsewhere, which Mittal calls losing control of "its own space destiny."
If it sits with the government, that same power can be used to cut off access in national emergencies or for strategic reasons.
It is for these reasons that security clearances, in-country gateways and monitoring requirements will shape who can launch satellite broadband in India and how fast.
Mittal pointed to Ukraine, saying that "if Ukraine is using Starlink, it's also using OneWeb now".
Last month, Ukraine accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself by cutting connectivity speeds, disrupting military operations. Those restrictions, rendered some Ukrainian strike and interceptor drones virtually unusable.
Whether the government's scrutiny of satellite operators is justified, Mittal said it is. He argued that warfare is moving to space. "Whether it's drone or it's cyber issues, or indeed guided missiles and all, they're all going to be managed from space," he said.
"Everybody in the world needs to have control over its security," he said. "There India will need to have guardrails. It'll need to secure itself."
He said India should not lean on a single provider. "Importantly, it may need to have different players. You can't just depend on one country or one company," he said. India must also ensure "the security of the apparatus, of the equipment, the communications coming down into the ground to be monitored," and "everything should be routed through India," he added.
He said Eutelsat OneWeb is building a secure European communications network, in which he said the EU is spending 14-15 billion euros, and that this has drawn attention to the company.
Mittal said OneWeb's service already works in India. "The government occasionally uses their terminals for emergency services," he said.
As an example, he said economic adviser Sanjeev Sanyal took a terminal on a boat trip to Oman.
"He was streaming all the way through," Mittal said. "It is, right now, fully available. We can just switch it on soon."
"We were the first licence given by the government. We have satisfied all their needs, and we just now wait for their signal," he said. "I still hope we'll get the first approval."
Three companies hold satellite communications licences in India: Jio, OneWeb and Starlink. The government has said all three operators hold provisional spectrum and are at a similar stage, and that final launch depends on security clearance.
On the spectrum debate, Mittal said satellite spectrum is shared. "Everybody dips into the same spectrum," he said, with operators at different orbital heights having to coordinate. He said OneWeb has "the highest priority on the KU band, and therefore others have to coordinate with us," and that the regulators understand the debate.
Mittal said satellite will not replace mobile networks. "For the foreseeable future it will remain complementary. It's very expensive. Satellites need to be replaced every five, six years," he said. "Where there is fibre, radio cannot compete with it. Where there is a radio, satellite cannot compete with it. But together all of them... will coexist."
He said the case for satellite is coverage. There are still "dark spots" in "deep rural hinterlands, in the forests, in the hills, mountains, in the high seas, in the ocean and of course in the air," he said.
Satellite links would connect a phone user in the mountains with no signal, he added.

articles.title: Gmail : ces deux fonctions IA arrivent chez tous les utilisateurs majeurs
articles.text:
Google est d’humeur généreuse : les résumés et la rédaction assistée par Gemini sont désormais ouverts à tous les utilisateurs majeurs dans Gmail.
Gmail a fait beaucoup parler de lui ces temps-ci. Google a, en effet, revu sa politique de confidentialité début novembre afin de personnaliser ses publicités. Côté fonctionnalités, le géant de Mountain View a facilité la gestion des codes de vérification et abandonné la relève POP des comptes tiers. Gemini prend aussi de plus en plus d’importance dans la messagerie.
Google étend l’accès à deux fonctions IA
On le sait, Google veut que l’IA devienne centrale dans ses produits. Au printemps, Gemini s’est invité dans la messagerie des abonnés AI Plus et Pro et cet été, le géant de la Tech a généralisé la recherche conversationnelle avec l’assistant dans sa messagerie. Cette semaine, le géant a annoncé qu’il étendait l’accès « à certaines fonctionnalités de Gemini dans Gmail à un plus grand nombre d’utilisateurs de Google Workspace âgés de 18 ans et plus. »
Les deux fonctions concernées sont les résumés de conversations AI Overview, qui affichent un bref topo en haut des conversations à rallonge, et l’aide à la rédaction IA (connue sous le nom « Help me write » en anglais), qui permet d’écrire un brouillon à partir d’une consigne ou d’améliorer un message.
Tous les clients de Google Workspace, les abonnés Workspace Individual et les propriétaires de comptes personnels peuvent accéder à ces options IA, du moment qu’ils sont majeurs.
- storage15 Go de stockage
- securityChiffrement natif en option
- alternate_emailPas de domaine personnalisé
- smartphoneApplications iOS, Android
- push_pinJurisdiction USA
Des fonctions ouvertes d’office pour certains utilisateurs
Pour être sûr que personne ne passe à côté, Google a activé par défaut les résumés de conversation et l’aide à la rédaction IA dans la messagerie. Un choix qui pourrait mal passer après la polémique de l’an passé : on se rappelle que des utilisateurs avaient critiqué la firme car certaines options intelligentes se réactivaient seules dans Gmail. Un recours collectif avait notamment été déposé en Californie.
- Multimodalité texte, voix et fichiers
- Intégration poussée aux services Google
- Applications Web, mobile et bureau
Les Européens sont un peu mieux lotis : l’aide Google précise que les paramètres des fonctionnalités intelligentes sont désactivés par défaut dans l’Espace économique européen. Une petite vérification s’impose malgré tout, si vous voulez éviter que Gemini ne mette le nez dans vos e-mails :
- Ouvrez Gmail et cliquez sur la roue crantée en haut à droite de l’écran sur Gmail, puis appuyez sur « Voir tous les paramètres » ;
- Allez dans l’onglet « Général » ;
- Rendez-vous dans la section « Fonctionnalités intelligentes » et décochez l’option « Activer les fonctionnalités intelligentes dans Gmail, Chat et Meet » ;
- Rendez-vous ensuite dans la section « Fonctionnalités intelligentes dans Google Workspace » puis cliquez sur « Gérer les paramètres des fonctionnalités intelligentes Workspace ». Désactivez l'option « Fonctionnalités intelligentes dans Google Workspace » ;
- Enregistrez vos modifications.
Si ces fonctions IA vous intéressent, il faudra patienter un peu avant de pouvoir y accéder : le déploiement a démarré le 10 novembre et devrait prendre une quinzaine de jours pour être effectif.

articles.title: Microsoft outage exposes South Africa's Big Tech dependence
articles.text:
Microsoft, the technology and software giant, has disrupted big businesses in South Africa following a global infrastructure failure, exposing the country’s dependence on a handful of technology providers to keep everyday operations running.
Eskom, South Africa’s power utility, warned that its email services had been affected by a worldwide disruption to Microsoft Exchange. Domestic airline FlySafair said it could temporarily neither send nor receive emails, while Absa, one of South Africa’s largest banks, reported intermittent difficulties accessing Microsoft’s workplace applications.
“Eskom’s email services are currently impacted due to the worldwide disruption of the Microsoft Exchange service,” the utility said in a Friday post on X, directing customers to its telephone, WhatsApp, chatbot and USSD channels for assistance.
FlySafair similarly warned customers that the disruption to Microsoft 365 was affecting its email services, leaving it temporarily unable to send or receive messages. The airline advised customers to use its call centre and WhatsApp instead.
Absa said the disruption was affecting aspects of its Microsoft environment, with some employees experiencing intermittent difficulties accessing applications including email and Copilot.
“Microsoft is actively working on a resolution, and our tech teams are monitoring the situation closely,” the bank said.
The three organisations operate in vastly different sectors, but their experiences expose a growing vulnerability in South Africa’s digital economy: businesses, financial institutions and essential service providers increasingly depend on the same global technology infrastructure to keep their operations running. When that infrastructure fails, the disruption can spread across industries, affecting everything from internal communication to customer service and business continuity.
The outage, which hit South Africa on Thursday affected Microsoft’s widely used productivity and cloud services, including Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Copilot. The disruption extended beyond South Africa, affecting businesses, government institutions and educational organisations across multiple countries.
For South African organisations, the consequences extended beyond employees being unable to access their inboxes. Eskom had to redirect customers to alternative communication channels, while FlySafair asked passengers and other customers to use its telephone and WhatsApp services. Absa warned that the disruption was affecting access to tools used by its employees.
Other South African institutions also reported problems. The City of Cape Town said its Microsoft 365 environment, including email, Teams and OneDrive, had been affected. The South African Revenue Service, the country’s national tax authority, also issued an alert about the disruption to its services.
Microsoft’s recovery efforts highlighted the complexity of restoring services that support millions of users. In updates on its service health channels, the company said it was investigating elevated server loads and unexpected server unavailability, while attempts to redirect traffic away from affected infrastructure encountered further difficulties.
By Friday, Microsoft was reporting early signs of stabilisation and improvements in capacity as it worked to restart affected infrastructure.
“To help preserve delayed mail through this event, we’ve extended email timeout to 48 hours,” the company said in an update on Friday morning.
The incident raises questions about how prepared South African businesses are for prolonged disruptions to the technology platforms underpinning their operations.
Cloud services have become central to how organisations manage communications, store documents, collaborate and deliver services
The outage forced Eskom, FlySafair and Absa to redirect customers and employees to alternative communication channels while Microsoft worked to restore its services. For businesses that rely on cloud platforms to manage communications, documents and daily operations, the disruption highlighted the need for backup systems and business continuity plans.

articles.title: Anduril's first satellite has night vision for catching rivals sneaking around in orbit
articles.text:
The big picture: Most cameras that keep watch over Earth's orbit only work when sunlight bounces off whatever they're tracking. So when a satellite slips into the planet's shadow, it effectively vanishes for a while. Anduril now says its first satellite can follow spacecraft through those dark stretches. That could let the US military catch a rival quietly changing course at night.
Anduril-216 rode a SpaceX rideshare to orbit back in July. It's roughly the size of an oven and flies about 590 km (366 miles) up, so it spends around a third of every lap in darkness.
Oddly enough, those dark passes are when it does its best work. Its long-wave infrared sensor picks up the heat other spacecraft give off rather than the sunlight bouncing off them – Anduril says the imaging tech was adapted from its autonomous weapons.
Speaking to Ars Technica, orbital systems chief Adam Thurn said the sensor finally lets the company see adversaries maneuvering during eclipse periods, "where in the past we've been fairly blind." Engineering head Gokul Subramanian went a step further, saying the US currently can't keep track of satellites through those stretches at all. The sensor is only rarely blinded by the Sun, too.
That blind spot matters because the Space Force tracks satellites both to warn operators about collisions and to catch threatening moves. China, for one, has already been spotted practicing coordinated "dogfighting" maneuvers in low Earth orbit. A stretch where optical sensors can't see could make for handy cover.
Alongside the infrared sensor, Anduril-216 carries two third-party visible-light cameras and an onboard computer that blends both feeds. That computer works out tracking solutions by itself, without waiting on analysts on the ground. According to Via Satellite, it's also beefy enough to run frontier AI models.
So far, though, the only picture the company has shared is an infrared shot of the Moon hanging over Earth's horizon. Thurn says the sensor can also capture detailed, resolved images of other satellites if it gets close enough. Still, Anduril hasn't shown an actual target maneuvering in the dark yet.
Weirdly, the company isn't really in this to sell satellites. Subramanian says it would rather sell the tracking data to the US military. It doesn't even plan to build its own satellite production line. Anduril-216's body actually came from startup Apex Space, and Anduril just supplied what's bolted onto it.
That data business already has some backup on the ground. In March, Anduril bought ExoAnalytic, a firm that runs around 400 telescopes tracking spacecraft in higher orbits. The same infrared imager is also slated to fly to geostationary orbit aboard an Impulse Space spacecraft for a planned close-inspection demo. Further out, the company says the sensor could eventually work in the space around the Moon.

articles.title: Scientists warn 1.5°C climate change threshold could arrive by 2029
articles.text:
ANTALYA, Turkey—Amid upbeat green-tech pep talks and notices for happy hours at the annual United Nations COP31 climate change conference on Thursday, two new reports offered a stark reminder of how far the world remains from containing global warming.
Climate Action Tracker, a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5° Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicus climate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement.
When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7° Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. After another decade of global climate summits, warming is now projected to cross that benchmark as soon as 2029, according to Copernicus.
“This striking change suggests that global warming has accelerated in recent years,” the EU scientists wrote. Even without understanding every aspect of the recent rapid global temperature increase, “It is clear that the ever-growing concentrations of greenhouse gases emitted by human activity in the atmosphere remain the main driver of this trend.”
The current level of warming has already triggered deadly and destructive floods, wildfires and catastrophic glacier collapses, said Swedish activist Greta Thunberg, who is attending the UN “Conferences of the Parties” climate talks, for the first time since 2021.
“The climate crisis is a matter of life and death,” she said. “The actions from those in power here are completely detached from reality. As we speak, we are losing priceless lives, ecosystems and species that we will never get back.”
Sarah Heck, a climate policy analyst with Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute, said governments have failed to meaningfully improve the outlook for end-of-century warming.
