articles.title: Sony BRAVIA 9 II et Theatre Trio : le meilleur duo home cinéma de 2026 ?
articles.text:
Sony BRAVIA 9 II et Theatre Trio : le meilleur duo home cinéma de 2026 ?
Le Sony BRAVIA 9 II, associé au BRAVIA Theatre Trio et à sa spatialisation sonore à 360°, forme un duo de choc pour transformer votre salon en véritable salle de cinéma. Aurait-on trouvé la référence du home cinéma ?
Un excellent home cinéma doit être capable de transmettre des émotions, de nous happer dès les premières secondes et de nous faire oublier, le temps d’un film, que l’on est simplement installé dans son salon.
Pour atteindre ce niveau d’immersion, il faut parfois savoir résister aux sirènes du premier prix, quitte à patienter quelques semaines, à économiser un peu plus ou à guetter la bonne promotion. Car certains équipements méritent qu’on fasse un petit effort supplémentaire pour profiter pleinement du spectacle. Et le duo Sony Bravia 9 II et Bravia Theatre Trio fait partie de ceux-là.
True RGB : une nouvelle dimension pour les couleurs
Sony et la gestion des couleurs, c’est une longue, très longue histoire d’amour. La marque japonaise a cette volonté de restituer les images avec le plus de justesse et de fidélité possible, sans en faire des tonnes pour flatter la rétine. La technologie True RGB en est la dernière illustration, et sans doute l’une des plus ambitieuses.
Plutôt que de s’appuyer sur un rétroéclairage blanc ou bleu, comme c’est souvent le cas sur les téléviseurs LCD, le BRAVIA 9 II exploite des LED rouges, vertes et bleues, pilotées indépendamment.
Cette architecture permet d’obtenir des couleurs plus pures, plus intenses et surtout plus précises, y compris à des niveaux de luminosité élevés. Sony revendique d’ailleurs le plus grand volume colorimétrique jamais atteint sur ses téléviseurs grand public.
Mais disposer d’une large palette de couleurs ne suffit pas. Encore faut-il savoir l’exploiter avec précision. C’est là qu’intervient le RGB Backlight Master Drive Pro, chargé de piloter ces LED rouges, vertes et bleues pour préserver la fidélité des teintes, optimiser le contraste et limiter le blooming.
Sony y associe également ses technologies RGB Triluminos Max, Luminance Booster Pro X-Wide Angle Pro, qui permettent d’étendre la richesse des couleurs, de maintenir leur précision à des niveaux de luminosité élevé et de préserver le rendu même lorsqu’on regarde l’écran de côté.
Le téléviseur des cinéphiles : Studio Calibrated et antireflet
S’il y a bien un domaine dans lequel Sony sait de quoi il parle, c’est le cinéma ! Entre ses caméras professionnelles et ses studios Sony Pictures, le constructeur connaît les exigences de ceux qui créent les images… et ce savoir-faire se retrouve dans le BRAVIA 9 II.
Le mode Studio Calibrated est conçu justement pour respecter au mieux les intentions des créateurs. Il est compatible avec différents services de streaming, Netflix, Prime Video et Sony Pictures Core. Les amateurs de cinéma apprécieront également la compatibilité Dolby Vision et IMAX Enhanced, qui sont des incontournables.
Sony propose par ailleurs son propre catalogue avec SONY PICTURES CORE avec une qualité de streaming comparable à celle d’un Blu-ray 4K UHD, de quoi exploiter tout le potentiel de cet écran et se faire un véritable séance home cinéma de temps à autre.
A ce sujet, puisqu’il s’agit d’un téléviseur que l’on peut regarder en pleine journée, dans une pièce baignée de lumière, Sony a non seulement mis le paquet sur la luminosité, mais aussi prévu un traitement antireflet pour limiter les reflets gênants.
Un petit détail à connaître avant de choisir : si vous craquez pour la version géante de 115 pouces, sachez qu’elle ne bénéficie pas du traitement antireflet.
Gaming 4K à 120 Hz : la PS5 va adorer ce téléviseur
Vous l’avez compris, entre Sony et le cinéma, c’est une longue histoire. Mais avec le jeu vidéo aussi ! Difficile de parler de la marque sans penser à la PlayStation. Alors, forcément, lorsqu’on souhaite la meilleure expérience pour jouer, se tourner vers un téléviseur de la marque fait sens.
Résolution 4K UHD ? C’est oui. Fréquence de rafraîchissement de 120 Hz ? Aussi ! Et la liste ne s’arrête pas là… connectique HDMI 2.1, VRR pour éviter les déchirures d’image, ALLM pour réduire automatiquement la latence, sans oublier le Dolby Vision Gaming pour profiter de belles images en jeu. Les utilisateurs de PS5 ont même droit à quelques attentions supplémentaires, comme le réglage automatique HDR, qui optimise l’image en fonction du téléviseur.
Google TV et Gemini : le petit plus au quotidien
Et quand vient le moment de poser la manette, Google TV prend le relais en apportant une interface connectée lisible et agréable, qui rassemble les principales plateformes de streaming.
La présence de Gemini est aussi appréciable. L’assistant IA peut vous aider à trouver votre prochain film ou une série que vous souhaitiez regarder mais dont vous avez oublié le titre.
BRAVIA Theatre Trio : un son modulaire étonnant !
Comment fournir une immersion sonore convaincante sur des téléviseurs toujours plus grands ? Sony a sa petite idée.
Plutôt que de tout miser sur une barre de son classique, le fabricant propose un trio composé d’une enceinte centrale et de deux haut-parleurs latéraux. L’idée derrière cette approche est d’élargir au maximum la scène sonore. Cela passe donc par des enceintes physiques, mais aussi par un traitement virtuel.
La technologie 360 Spatial Sound Mapping peut créer jusqu’à 24 enceintes virtuelles pour donner l’impression que le son surgit de toutes part (sans transformer le salon en showroom). Pour affiner le rendu, Sony propose d’ailleurs un calibrage acoustique via un micro afin d’adapter le rendu à la pièce.
Et pour compléter le tableau, le BRAVIA Theatre Trio peut accueillir un caisson de basses optionnel pour donner encore plus de profondeur et d’impact aux scènes d’action. Le système prend également en charge les formats Dolby Atmos et DTS, sans oublier la certification IMAX Enhanced.

articles.title: One stack, not three silos: How Stelcore’s leaders want Indian brands to go global
articles.text:
One stack, not three silos: How Stelcore’s leaders want Indian brands to go global
At TechSparks 2026, Stelcore’s Bharat Mandot, Percy Avari and Navin Mistry explained how brands can turn compliance, tech and supply chain into one growth engine.
Selling abroad once meant stitching together a marketplace, a freight partner, and a compliance consultant, and hoping the pieces held. For India’s next wave of brands, that patchwork is giving way to one connected commerce stack.
That shift was the focus of a session at TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s flagship event. Navin Mistry, Strategic Partner, Stelcore Commerce, was speaking with Bharat Mandot, Founder & Chairman, Stelcore Group, and Percy Avari, Co-Founder, Stelcore Supply Chain, about how technology, trade and supply chain can work as a single layer.
Mistry kept the conversation informal, with the aim of giving D2C founders a clear sense of the integration layers, process layers, and mindset needed to build a brand in India or beyond.
Why silos hold brands back
Mandot started Stelcore in 2011 as a management consultancy. The business turned to compliance in 2016, when Amazon began taking Indian sellers global and merchants needed help making their products compliant. Today the group covers compliance, trade enablement, and payments across 14 countries.
Avari, who has spent 35 years in logistics, including 29 years at Aramex, said the old model was the problem. What he saw over those decades, he said, was that “commerce, technology, and logistics were operating in silos”.
Avari added that the goal now is to bring all three into one ecosystem, so Indian brands can go cross-border in an effortless, intelligent and compliant way.
Prove demand, then fix compliance
Asked how a founder should sequence the journey, Mandot put the customer first. “Customer acceptance is the most important part,” he said. A brand can test through a marketplace or even social channels, then bring in compliance, logistics and payments once buyers keep returning.
He advised making only the top-selling products compliant at the start, since certifying an entire catalog pushes up launch costs. Mandot also pointed to inventory placement as a growth challenge. The Middle East can be served within a day, while the US is far larger, so stock must be spread across locations. His advice on scale was patient: win one country, build loyalty and healthy margins, and only then replicate the model in the next.
Avoiding the first-shipment trap
Avari said compliance has eased considerably over the past decade, but destination rules still catch new exporters out. Many first shipments, he noted, get stuck at foreign customs because founders skipped the homework.
Stelcore Supply Chain now builds this knowledge into its technology, so a seller is warned about required documents while creating a shipment. “If you don’t look at all three together, you cannot grow your brand in a profitable way,” he said.
Mandot described two tools for founders. One is a compliance assessment that shows the rules for a category across several countries in minutes. The other is an order management system linking warehouses and last-mile partners across countries, so no brand depends on a single facility.
From dropship to forward fulfillment
On when to move beyond third-party fulfillment, Avari said most brands begin with dropshipping, with 85-90 % of orders in year one. Demand data then shows which SKUs deserve forward fulfillment from regional hubs such as Dubai. By years two or three, he said, dropshipping can fall to 10-20 % of orders.
Mistry added that no single formula fits every brand: “There’s no universal answer, but it’s a mixture of both.”
The MSME opportunity
Avari called small businesses the backbone of Indian exports and said Stelcore aims to move 25,000 MSMEs from domestic to cross-border trade within five years.
Mandot expects export opportunity to grow roughly tenfold in three to five years, helped by government support. For tech founders, his advice was simple: build “the product for which we are willing to pay”.
From the audience
Audience questions covered customer acquisition and delivery economics.
Mandot said Stelcore acts as an introductory partner, connecting brands with marketplace teams to gauge market potential before they commit.
Avari said unit economics improve over two to three years as brands shift from dropshipping to regional forward fulfillment, though a long tail of SKUs will always stay on dropship. He suggested holding inventory in free trade zones across a few regions to keep costs in check.
The takeaway from Stelcore’s leaders was that cross-border growth depends less on any single tool than on aligning compliance, technology, and logistics from the first order.

articles.title: Jordi Wild pregunta por la bajada de impuestos. Feijóo, sobre las cuentas públicas: "Tengo muchas dudas"
articles.text:
La pregunta sobre los impuestos le llegó a Alberto Núñez Feijóo cuando hablaba de cómo financiar las pensiones. Jordi Wild le recordó que había defendido una rebaja fiscal y le pidió que concretara si pensaba llevarla a cabo. El presidente del Partido Popular (PP) insistió en que quería reducir los impuestos y añadió que necesitaba explicar a los españoles en qué estado estaban las cuentas públicas. Cuando Wild le preguntó si sabía cómo estaban las cuentas, Feijóo contestó en la entrevista de The Wild Project: "Tengo muchas dudas".
La repregunta de Wild. Feijóo había defendido que más inversión y más empleo permitirían sumar cotizantes y aumentar los ingresos del sistema de pensiones. Wild le puso delante las decisiones que se suelen discutir cuando esas aportaciones no bastan, entre ellas retrasar la jubilación o recaudar más. Ahí llegó el intercambio sobre si bajar los impuestos era una intención o un compromiso que el candidato podía concretar en ese momento.
Feijóo dijo que desconfiaba de los datos y que creía que se ocultaban gastos y había compromisos para varios años que desconocía. El ejemplo que dio a continuación fue el gasto en defensa. Más adelante, cuando Wild volvió a preguntarle cuánto gastaría en ese ámbito, Feijóo dijo que haría una auditoría antes de fijar la cifra.
Las cuentas que seguían en vigor. Feijóo vinculó sus dudas con la falta de nuevos presupuestos durante la legislatura. En 2026, Hacienda seguía publicando las cuentas prorrogadas, con los Presupuestos Generales del Estado de 2023 como base. El artículo 134 de la Constitución establece que, si la nueva ley de presupuestos no está aprobada al comenzar el ejercicio, se prorroga automáticamente la anterior hasta que se aprueben las nuevas cuentas.
La rebaja que ya tenía año. Antes de sentarse con Wild, Feijóo sí había puesto fecha a una medida. En octubre, anunció una rebaja para 2027 del impuesto sobre la renta de las personas físicas (IRPF). El programa electoral del PP propone elevar los mínimos personales y familiares y ajustar la tarifa a la inflación. Ajustar la tarifa, o deflactarla, implica actualizar los umbrales de los tramos para que una subida de ingresos que solo compensa el encarecimiento de la vida no aumente la carga fiscal por esa vía. En otro tramo del pódcast, Feijóo criticó que la tarifa no se hubiera ajustado a la inflación. Con la escala general del IRPF, si la base liquidable cruza un tramo, el tipo superior se aplica a la parte que supera el umbral. Cambiar esos umbrales afecta a cuánto tributa cada parte.
El programa también prevé una auditoría en los primeros cien días de un eventual Gobierno del PP, cuyas conclusiones servirían para preparar sus primeros presupuestos. En la respuesta a Wild, Feijóo mantuvo su intención de reducir los impuestos. En ese tramo de la entrevista dejó sin concretar qué rebajas aplicaría y en qué plazo.

articles.title: A wave of cyberattacks hit Nigerian banks, billions at risk
articles.text:
In early October, a wave of cyberattacks, leading to fraud losses, hit several Nigerian banks and financial institutions, potentially costing billions of naira in customer funds, according to several sources with direct knowledge of the matter.
The attacks, the sources noted, affected institutions that rely on external technology providers to run critical financial services, including core banking infrastructure. In one incident, a vendor providing core banking services to financial institutions was reportedly compromised at the system level on October 1. The vendor is one of Africa’s biggest fintech companies.
TechCabal could not immediately establish how many attacks happened, how much money was lost, or whether the incidents were connected. But according to their respective financial reports, three of the country’s biggest banks, Access Holdings Plc, Guaranty Trust Holding Company Plc (GTCO), and Zenith Bank collectively reported ₦2.74 billion ($2.03 million) in fraud losses for the first six months of 2026. GTCO recorded the sharpest year-on-year increase, with fraud losses up by 450.24%.
The Concentration of Bank Fraud
Three top-tier banks absorbed ₦2.74 billion in fraud losses in just six months, driven by an unprecedented surge at GTCO.
The Financial Institutions Training Centre (FITC) reported 19,719 fraud cases in the fourth quarter of 2025, a 34.2% increase from the previous quarter.
The attacks reflect the growing scale of security risks facing Nigeria’s financial services industry, where rising cyber threats and fraud incidents expose weaknesses in how institutions protect customer funds and critical infrastructure. In Q4, 2025, reported fraud loss surged by 575.7% to ₦5.26 billion ($3.89 million), according to FITC.
These risks are amplified by the industry’s reliance on shared technology providers to process transactions, manage customer accounts and provide lending infrastructure. A breach at one provider could expose multiple financial institutions connected to its systems.
“The Bank maintains ongoing supervisory oversight of cybersecurity incidents affecting regulated financial institutions,” a Central Bank of Nigeria spokesperson told TechCabal in an emailed response on Tuesday. “The Nigerian financial system remains resilient, and the Bank’s supervisory and cybersecurity frameworks remain in force.”
A top executive at one of the country’s payment gateways, who asked not to be named to discuss sensitive matters, described October as “Black October,” saying the attacks affected businesses across the financial services industry. Another source at an investment bank told TechCabal that staff were warned not to open external emails amid heightened cyber threats during the month.
“It eventually ends up at your door,” the payments gateway executive said.
A major microfinance bank was also among the affected institutions, according to a source familiar with the incident. The bank reportedly suffered financial losses and a system disruption that forced it to seek temporary alternatives to keep its services running. It has since hired a chief security officer, the source added.
Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS), the country’s payments switch, did not respond to a request for comments.
“Everyone has been attacked. People have lost money,” Adedeji Olowe, founder and chief executive officer of Lendsqr, a Nigerian lending technology company, told TechCabal.
In a LinkedIn post on November 4, Olowe said security testing of Lendsqr’s platform uncovered about 800 vulnerabilities and that they “spent three weeks fixing them.” He did not disclose the vulnerabilities’ severity, how many were fixed, or whether any were exploited.
Nigerian banks’ growing fraud losses
The reported attacks come against a backdrop of persistent fraud losses across Nigeria’s financial system.
Financial institutions recorded ₦25.85 billion ($19.16 million) in actual fraud losses in 2025, according to data from the Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS). This reflects a 50.55% decline from 2024, but in 2024, 60.53% of attempted frauds eventually became losses. That number jumped to 68.81% in 2025.
The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has also warned about rising fraud and money-laundering risks as more financial services move online.
“The payments ecosystem faces rising SIM swap incidents, account takeover fraud, insider collusion, and social engineering,” the CBN said in its Nigeria Payments System Vision 2028.
The apex bank has introduced measures to strengthen fraud prevention and make financial institutions more accountable. In its 2024 Risk-Based Cybersecurity Framework, the CBN asked banks and payment service banks to assess the security of third-party providers through due diligence, routine audits, and ongoing monitoring.
In March 2026, it formally recognised artificial intelligence as a tool for fighting financial crime. But the effectiveness of those measures depends partly on whether institutions report incidents promptly and share information that could help others identify similar threats.
Gaps in industry reporting
Despite the scale of fraud in Nigeria’s financial system, financial institutions have historically been reluctant to publicly disclose security breaches and fraud incidents. For an industry built on interconnected payment rails and shared technology providers, silence can become a security risk in itself.
NIBSS’s 2023 Annual Fraud Landscape found that only 60 of the 163 financial institutions it profiled reported fraud incidents that year, a 37% compliance rate. The remaining 103 institutions did not report cases. NIBSS said failure to report fraud incidents violated the CBN’s circular establishing industry fraud desks.
The CBN’s 2024 cybersecurity framework requires supervised financial institutions to report detected cyber incidents to the regulator within 24 hours. It also requires them to submit intelligence on cyber threats through a designated reporting channel by the fifth day of the following month. These requirements are intended to give the regulator visibility into emerging threats and help institutions respond to incidents across the financial system.
The reporting gap highlights a weakness in how Nigeria’s financial system coordinates its response to fraud and its missed opportunity to identify and contain attacks before they spread.
The CBN’s Payment System Vision 2028 proposes the establishment of a national Security Operations Centre (SOC) and a fraud intelligence-sharing platform. The initiative is part of a broader ambition to reduce fraud losses by 70% by 2028.
In January, the CBN directed NIBSS to debit the settlement accounts of commercial banks that receive fraud proceeds, making financial institutions tighten their fraud detection measures. The new rule was part of the regulator’s efforts to hold banks and fintechs accountable for lapses in their transaction monitoring systems.
In December 2024, TechCabal reported that First Bank, Nigeria’s oldest bank, suffered a massive fraud incident that led to the theft of ₦7 billion ($5.19 million) from customer accounts. The incident came several months after an employee fraudulently diverted ₦60 billion ($44.47 million) over two years, undetected, resulting in the dismissal of over 100 employees and reportedly connected to the bank’s CEO’s abrupt exit eight months before the end of his tenure.

articles.title: Más de 60 huesos encontrados en Murcia han permitido reconstruir al lince ibérico más antiguo conocido: vivió hace un millón de años
articles.text:
El lince ibérico es el felino más representativo de la península y, durante mucho tiempo, fue también uno de los más amenazados del planeta por su riesgo de desaparecer. Conocemos bien sus hábitos actuales, su inconfundible perfil y su estrecha dependencia del conejo, pero en su árbol genealógico más antiguo siempre hemos encontrado una cierta bruma paleontológica.
Lo que sabemos. Un equipo de paleontólogos ha confirmado el hallazgo del esqueleto más antiguo de un lince ibérico conocido hasta la fecha en el yacimiento de Quibas (Abanilla, Murcia) con 60 piezas de un mismo individuo, con costillas y vértebras, entre otros. Pero este descubrimiento no es fruto de un solo día de suerte con el pincel y la paleta, sino el resultado de años de excavaciones.
Un rompecabezas. La historia de este esqueleto comenzó a perfilarse en 2021 durante las campañas de excavación en la sierra murciana hechas por los investigadores del Instituto Catalán de Paleoecología Humana y Evolución Social, que lograron identificar una colección de huesos excepcionalmente bien conservada.
Hoy, ese trabajo se ha materializado en una réplica compuesta por más de 60 huesos que se exhibirá en el Centro de Interpretación Paleontológica Sierra de Quibas, permitiendo a los visitantes asomarse a la anatomía de un superdepredador prehistórico.
El reloj geológico. En paleontología, poner fecha a un fósil es tan complejo como encontrarlo porque no hay un sistema 100% fiable para ello. Lo que sí sabemos es que el yacimiento de la sección Quibas-Sima es una joya en sí misma, puesto que en 2020 un estudio dató esta sucesión de vertebrados terrestres entre 1,2 y 0,78 millones de años, basándose en los pequeños vertebrados que encontraron y en técnicas de magnetoestratigrafía.
Cruzando toda esta información disponible, los restos de este lince murciano se sitúan en una horquilla temporal de entre 1,07 y 0,99 millones de años. Y este marco temporal es crucial, puesto que la ciencia estimaba la aparición del lince ibérico hace entre 1 y 1,1 millones de años, proponiendo que los linces fósiles del suroeste de Europa a partir del Epivillafranquiense ya pertenecían a Lynx pardinus.
Más grande. Una de las cuestiones que más curiosidad despierta es cómo era este "tatarabuelo" del lince actual. Ahora sabemos que este lince primitivo era de un tamaño algo mayor que los ejemplares que han evolucionado. Además, han apuntado que consumían menos conejo y capturaban con más frecuencia presas de tamaño medio, como crías de gamo o cabra.
Pero el tema de la dieta todavía está entre dudas, puesto que hace falta un artículo científico publicado que analice el desgaste dental, entre otras variables, para poder confirmar qué tipos de presa tenía.
