articles.title: AI could disrupt India's outsourcing model. It could also create millions of new exporters
articles.text:
AI could disrupt India's outsourcing model. It could also create millions of new exporters
AI is letting small Indian teams win global work that once needed a big company. As AI separates capability from headcount, it could shape India’s next export story.
I recently spoke to someone running a small creative agency from a Tier II Indian city, with most of his clients outside India. When AI came up, I expected him to talk about producing more content, faster. What he described was more interesting.
Rotoscoping, repetitive edits and parts of project management were now largely automated. His tiny team now takes on projects that once needed outside freelancers.
This is usually told as a productivity story. I think something more fundamental is happening: AI is changing how big a company must become before it can sell sophisticated services to the world.
For India, that is both an opportunity and an uncomfortable question.
The model that built India's services industry is changing
India’s services exports reached $421.3 billion in FY26, up from $387.5 billion a year earlier, with IT and business services the largest contributors. For three decades, the IT services industry ran on a simple equation: win more customers, hire more people.
AI challenges that. Coding, testing, research, documentation and customer support are the backbone of Indian outsourcing, and they are exactly where AI is improving fastest.
NASSCOM estimates that India’s tech industry earned $10-12 billion from AI services in FY26, while overall revenue grew 6.1% to $315 billion. Hiring continues, but total headcount rose just 2.3%. The link between revenue and people is loosening.
That threatens a model built on selling human capacity. Seen from a five-person company, the same shift looks very different.
AI reduces the minimum scale needed to compete
Small services firms have always faced a capacity problem: winning a large project meant building the organisation to deliver it. AI is beginning to separate capability from headcount.
I saw this first-hand when I spoke to the founder of a growth-marketing firm with 15 people and 22 AI agents, serving clients across more than seven countries. Its founder sorts every task into three buckets. Manual tasks, such as discovery calls, are deliberately kept away from AI. In AI-assisted tasks, AI does 85-95% of the work and a person checks the rest. Fully automated tasks, such as market research, run end to end and the only human step is sending the report to the client. About 40% of the firm’s budget goes to AI agents and software rather than headcount. The founder says it runs at 60-70% margins, against 20-25% for a typical agency.
Even discovery has changed. One UK client told the same growth-marketing founder that he found, evaluated and signed the firm within a single Perplexity chat.
We are beginning to see this from the payment layer
Building in cross-border payments, we see thousands of Indian businesses being paid from abroad, and what stands out is how small many of them are. Over the last 12 months, 347 solo professionals each collected more than $100,000 from overseas clients, and 117 teams of two to ten people each crossed $250,000.
The base is widening too. Exporters actively billing overseas customers each quarter grew roughly fivefold over seven quarters, from about 2,800 to 13,900. Some of that growth reflects more businesses coming onto our network, not just new exporters entering the market. But the median invoice stayed near $1,500 throughout, which suggests many more people are selling, rather than a few landing bigger deals. Eighty-two per cent of these exporters have ten or fewer people.
Exporters in AI, machine learning, data or automation grew about ninefold, and their median invoice is nearly double. They are roughly 2% of volume, so this is a direction, not yet a trend. One of them, a solo AI and machine-learning consultant, billed about $266,000 to US clients in 12 months from just four buyers. That is not typical, but a decade ago that work would have needed a firm.
Selling expertise, not capacity
If India’s response to AI is simply to perform the same outsourced work with fewer people and charge customers less, we may improve productivity without fundamentally improving our position in the global value chain.
The larger opportunity is to move from selling capacity to selling expertise and outcomes.
AI can analyse 500 customer conversations. It cannot independently decide which customer problem a business should build its future around. It can generate software. Someone still has to understand what should be built, how it fits into a customer’s organisation, and take responsibility when it doesn’t work.
The value increasingly lies in asking the right questions, applying domain knowledge, exercising judgement and owning the result.
This may actually make deep expertise more valuable, not less. Consider the Indian professional who has spent 15 years understanding insurance claims, semiconductor design, pharmaceutical regulation, supply chains or financial risk. That person can now combine their domain knowledge with tools that dramatically expand what one person can execute.
India has no shortage of such people. According to the Economic Survey 2024-25, the country accounts for 28% of the world’s STEM workforce and 23% of global software engineering talent. New kinds of work are already emerging. I find this example striking: a medical professional in Kochi spends her week marking organs and flagging anomalies in foetal ultrasound scans. She isn’t treating patients directly; she’s helping train AI systems being built for hospitals in the US.
A five-person global company cannot have a 50-person back office.
There is one problem.
India’s export framework was designed for firms with finance teams. Proof-of-export documentation, GST filings, foreign exchange conversion and bank reconciliation all assume someone in the back office is handling them.
A five-person firm billing clients in California and London, in multiple currencies, has no such person. Yet it may have hundreds of thousands of dollars moving across borders every year.
If AI shrinks the team needed to deliver the work, but the founder still loses hours each month to paperwork and compliance, the bottleneck has simply moved. Regulators, banks and the wider fintech ecosystem need to make cross-border compliance as lightweight as the businesses it now serves.
India’s next services giants may not look like giants
India’s first services-export era was built by assembling millions of skilled people into large organisations. That model isn’t disappearing. But the next phase may look much less concentrated: thousands, perhaps eventually many more, of specialist Indian businesses selling their expertise to the world.
The agency I spoke to is interesting not because AI helps it edit videos faster. It is interesting because a handful of people in an Indian city can now compete for work anywhere in the world.
Twenty-five years ago, India's services-export breakthrough was partly about proving that global work could be done from India.
The AI-era opportunity may be proving that you no longer need to build a large company to do a large amount of it.
Srivatsan Sridhar is Co-Founder and CEO of Skydo.
Edited by Affirunisa Kankudti

articles.title: Mails, contacts, agenda envolés avec la panne Microsoft 365 ? Rassurez-vous, rien n'a disparu
articles.text:
Panne Microsoft 365 : vos mails, contacts et agendas Outlook ont-ils vraiment disparu ?
Boîte mail figée, agenda vide et réunions inaccessibles : la panne mondiale de Microsoft 365 donne l’impression que vos données ont disparu. Voici ce qu’il en est vraiment.
Depuis le jeudi 12 novembre, peu avant 19 heures, une panne mondiale paralyse Microsoft 365 dans 74 pays, dont la France. Devant un Outlook inaccessible et un calendrier Teams muet, de nombreux utilisateurs craignent d’avoir perdu leurs messages, leurs contacts ou leurs prochains rendez-vous. Pas de panique, aucune donnée ne s’est volatilisée : vos applications n’arrivent tout simplement plus à joindre les serveurs de l’éditeur.
Vos mails et votre agenda restent bien à l’abri sur Exchange Online, voici pourquoi
Le cœur du problème se situe du côté d’Exchange Online, le service de Microsoft qui héberge les boîtes mail et les données des comptes professionnels et scolaires. Vos courriels, vos carnets d’adresses et vos calendriers ne sont donc pas effacés, mais toujours stockés sur l’infrastructure cloud de l’éditeur.
En réalité, la panne coupe le pont entre vos appareils et ces serveurs. Que vous passiez par Outlook sur le web, le logiciel de bureau ou les applications mobiles, la connexion échoue et l’envoi des messages peut prendre des heures. D’après Microsoft, des serveurs sont devenus “indisponibles de manière inattendue”, reportant leur charge sur le reste du réseau jusqu’à saturer le processus qui établit habituellement les connexions sécurisées.
Par ricochet, tous les outils reliés à la messagerie semblent hors d’usage. Dans Teams, le calendrier, les invitations et la planification de réunions ne répondent plus, tout comme Planner, To Do ou Copilot Chat. Même les connecteurs de ChatGPT et de Claude ne peuvent plus lire vos mails et votre agenda. Charles Lamanna, vice-président exécutif de Microsoft, a toutefois écarté toute cyberattaque, tandis que l’entreprise précise avoir “commencé à annuler une modification récente de la configuration réseau, qui coïncide avec le début de l’incident”.
En attendant que les serveurs tiennent la charge sans retomber, inutile de réinstaller Outlook ou de modifier votre mot de passe. Vos données réapparaîtront d’elles-mêmes dès le retour à la normale. D’ici là, privilégiez les messages instantanés, les appels et les visioconférences de Teams, qui continuent de fonctionner, tout comme l’ouverture de vos fichiers sur SharePoint et OneDrive.

articles.title: Grosse panne Microsoft Office, Outlook, Teams et Copilot, voici ce qui se passe ce vendredi matin
articles.text:
Débutée jeudi soir, la panne d'Outlook et de Microsoft 365 n'était toujours pas résolue ce vendredi 13 novembre au matin. Microsoft assure qu'un correctif commence à porter ses fruits, sans promettre d'horaire de retour à la normale.
Pour bien des utilisateurs, la panne d'Outlook et de Microsoft 365 est probablement le premier sujet de discussion de ce vendredi 13 novembre « de malheur », diront certains. Alors qu'on pensait à un simple souci de boîtes mail jeudi soir, l'effet domino est bien ce matin, avec une vingtaine de services professionnels et grand public de Microsoft désormais perturbés, confirme l'entreprises. La seule éclaircie, à cette heure, est que l'éditeur constate une amélioration sur une partie de ses serveurs et dit, à ce stade également, d'aucune activité malveillante. On fait le point !
Quand Outlook tousse, tout Microsoft 365 s'enrhume, avec une panne géante
Les premiers signalements sont donc tombés jeudi en fin de journée. À 19h10, Microsoft reconnaissait des erreurs de connexion sur Exchange Online, le service qui héberge les boîtes mail des entreprises. Du navigateur au logiciel de bureau en passant par le téléphone, tous les accès sont potentiellement concernés. Plus tard dans la soirée, l'éditeur évoquait une surcharge de ses serveurs dans plusieurs régions. Il cherche aussi à savoir si un afflux de trafic inattendu l'a aggravée.
Ce matin, le tableau s'est nettement alourdi. Dans Teams par exemple, on sait que les appels et les conversations tiennent bon chez certains, mais que tout ce qui touche à l'agenda (planifier une réunion, envoyer une invitation) échoue. Copilot peine à répondre, les outils de sécurité Defender patinent, To Do et Planner flanchent. Chez les particuliers, Outlook, OneDrive, OneNote et Teams sont aussi touchés.
Panne Outlook : les plaintes affluent, un correctif se déploie
Forcément, chez les utilisateurs, l'agacement est palpable, et compréhensible. Sur Downdetector notamment, Outlook, Microsoft 365 et Teams sont en tête des services les plus signalés ce matin. TotalBug compte des centaines de signalements pour Outlook ces dernières heures, avec un pic jeudi vers 19 heures et une nouvelle flambée vers 8 heures. Les internautes évoquent des fenêtres qui refusent de s'ouvrir, des pièces jointes bloquées, « impossible de travailler », soupire d'ailleurs une internaute.
Microsoft, pour sauver les apparences, affiche un optimisme prudent. Son correctif vise un composant lié à l'authentification et à l'aiguillage des connexions. Déployé sur une partie de l'infrastructure, il donne déjà des résultats encourageants sur la stabilité des serveurs et doit maintenant être étendu aux autres régions. Un rapport sur l'origine exacte de la panne est promis une fois l'incident maîtrisé. On en saura plus dans la matinée.

articles.title: DeepSeek’s coding agent is too tidy for its own good — and benchmarks are punishing it
articles.text:
DeepSeek’s coding agent is too tidy for its own good — and benchmarks are punishing it
DeepSeek’s open-source coding agent is losing points on a major benchmark for a habit developers usually treat as good practice: cleaning up after itself.
The problem surfaced when Hugging Face harness optimization researcher Joël Niklaus added DeepSeek Harness to his coding-agent leaderboard, which compares ten harnesses running the same underlying models.
DeepSeek Harness is statistically tied for first across the board’s five scored evaluations, yet on Terminal-Bench alone it drops to sixth, because one built-in behavior caused it to fail tasks that competing agents completed.
DeepSeek Harness is statistically tied for first across the board’s five scored evaluations, yet on Terminal-Bench alone it drops to sixth…
“One habit explains much of that gap,” Niklaus writes on X, referring to the agent’s weaker Terminal-Bench performance.
A tidy habit backfires
DeepSeek Harness shuts down background processes when a task finishes, which is a problem for three Terminal-Bench tasks that need those processes to keep running.
Niklaus found that DeepSeek Harness passed just two of 36 attempts using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash, while OpenCode, Pi, and Nous Research’s Hermes Agent passed all 36 on those same tasks.
DeepSeek Harness passed just two of 36 attempts … while OpenCode, Pi and Nous Research’s Hermes Agent passed all 36 on those same tasks.
That behavior knocked between 1.5 and 1.7 percentage points off DeepSeek Harness’s scores. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at high reasoning effort, it was enough to account for more than the entire 1.3-point gap between DeepSeek Harness and the leader.
The leaderboard’s changelog confirms that the shutdown behavior belongs to DeepSeek Harness itself and the results were left unchanged.
DeepSeek’s engineering documentation describes its local job registry as a deliberately short-lived component. “Choose it when jobs should live in the harness process and die with it,” it states. Jobs that need to survive restarts or run across processes require a different backend.
Same model, different results
Niklaus launched his Harness Leaderboard on November 5 after running 28,849 trials across its original nine harnesses using three open models, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Flint.
He kept the model, provider, and reasoning effort constant while swapping harnesses, and the differences were substantial. Mini-swe-agent, a relatively simple bash-based agent, completed 51.4% of tasks compared with 27.3% for OpenClaw, although several other harnesses were statistically tied with the leader.
Costs varied just as dramatically. Pi achieved a 49.4% solve rate at $0.29 per solved task, while OpenCode cost $3.35 per solved task in the initial evaluation. Hugging Face co-founder Thomas Wolf sums up the findings on X as “same open model, different harness => very different results.”
The New Stack contacted DeepSeek for comment on the findings but had not received a response by publication time.
Orchestration isn’t a guarantee
Y Combinator President and CEO Garry Tan has been running separate evaluations using Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol.
“Harnesses differed more on cost than on how often they solved tasks,” the researchers write. On multi-user tasks, OpenClaw running Opus 5.5 cost roughly twice as much per solved task as the other Opus harnesses, largely because it repeatedly sent context with each request.
The project also tested Tan’s gstack workflow skills. In 46 sessions, Opus 5.5 read the instructions but never followed the prescribed steps, and the attempts cost roughly twice as much.
The researchers note that the tasks were relatively easy, so it’s unclear whether following the instructions would have improved the results. The results make a case for testing the harness just as carefully as the model.

articles.title: BYD contre Land Rover : la justice ordonne la destruction de documents saisis chez le géant chinois
articles.text:
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) pensait tenir de quoi prouver que BYD avait copié son Defender. Le constructeur va devoir faire détruire ces documents, auxquels il n’a même jamais eu accès. D’après CarNewsChina, qui reprend une dépêche de l’agence néerlandaise ANP, le tribunal de La Haye a levé ce mercredi 11 novembre 2026, en référé (la procédure d’urgence), la saisie menée en août dans les bureaux néerlandais de BYD, à Schiedam et Hoofddorp.
JLR dispose de 24 heures après la notification du jugement pour faire détruire ces fichiers. Faute de quoi, il paiera 50 000 euros par heure de retard, dans la limite de 500 000 euros. Mais revenons un peu plus sur l’objet du litige qui oppose les deux constructeurs dans cette affaire.
Trop de ressemblance avec le Defender
Le litige porte sur le BYD Ti 7, un SUV vendu en Chine sous le nom de Fang Cheng Bao Tai 7 depuis septembre 2025. Décliné en hybride rechargeable puis en électrique, il s’y est vendu à 300 000 exemplaires au 30 octobre, selon la marque. Tant que le modèle n’était commercialisé qu’en Chine, JLR n’avait pas immédiatement réagi. Mais le début de commercialisation sur le marché britannique du BYD TI 7 en juillet 2026 a changé la donne.
JLR estime que le design extérieur du Ti 7 copie celui du Defender et soupçonne BYD d’avoir fait de la rétro-ingénierie, c’est-à-dire d’avoir démonté le 4×4 britannique pour comprendre comment il est conçu et le reproduire.
Ce mardi encore, Le Figaro racontait l’offensive judiciaire de Land Rover pour protéger son célèbre Defender. Le revers tombe mal pour un constructeur qui a déjà vu ses usines mises à l’arrêt par une cyberattaque en septembre 2025, avec des pertes chiffrées début 2026.
Des fichiers jamais remis à Land Rover
Le tribunal avait autorisé la saisie sans que BYD puisse la contester au préalable. Les documents comprenaient les plans de lancement du Ti 7, des données techniques et financières, ainsi que des dossiers sur le Defender. Ils sont restés sous la garde d’un séquestre indépendant désigné par le tribunal.
BYD a ensuite contesté l’étendue de la saisie, qui aurait aussi emporté des travaux de recherche et développement sans rapport avec l’affaire. Le juge lui a donné raison : JLR n’a pas besoin de ces fichiers pour défendre son design. Il n’en a pas besoin non plus pour chiffrer un éventuel préjudice, puisque le Ti 7 n’est pas encore vendu dans l’Union européenne (seulement au Royaume-Uni).
Pire pour JLR, le tribunal a rejeté sa demande d’astreinte, une pénalité qui grossit tant qu’une décision de justice n’est pas respectée. Le Britannique réclamait 500 000 euros à BYD. Le juge a estimé, à titre provisoire, que le constructeur chinois avait respecté l’ordonnance de saisie. JLR ne peut plus s’appuyer sur cette autorisation, sous peine d’une nouvelle astreinte de 500 000 euros. Le jugement s’applique tout de suite, même si JLR fait appel.
Sur la copie, rien n’est tranché
Pour autant, BYD n’est pas blanchi. Le jugement lève la saisie sans dire si le Ti 7 viole la propriété intellectuelle de JLR. Le Britannique a lancé deux autres procédures aux Pays-Bas.
La première, à La Haye, porte sur les droits européens qui protègent l’apparence du Defender. La seconde, à Rotterdam, vise une violation du droit d’auteur et une « imitation servile », une notion du droit néerlandais qui sanctionne une copie assez proche pour tromper l’acheteur.
En 2019, JLR a gagné contre le chinois Jiangling, dont le Landwind X7 ressemblait beaucoup au Range Rover Evoque. En revanche, il n’a pas réussi à déposer comme marque la forme de l’Evoque dans l’Union européenne, ni la silhouette du Defender d’origine au Royaume-Uni.
En attendant, BYD avance. Le Ti 7 arrive ce mois-ci chez les concessionnaires du Royaume-Uni, donc hors de l’Union européenne, en une seule version sept places de 300 kW (402 ch). Les livraisons sont prévues en janvier 2027. Outre-Manche, il coûte 47 995 livres (environ 56 000 euros), soit un tiers de moins que le Defender 110 hybride rechargeable, affiché à 71 840 livres (environ 84 000 euros).

articles.title: The bank OPay hoped would open up Africa
articles.text:
OPay has built a financial services platform that moves money, extends credit, and helps millions of people save. It operates in Nigeria, Indonesia, Egypt, and Pakistan, but its business remains heavily concentrated in Nigeria, which accounts for 89.5% of its revenue.
That concentration presents a problem for a fintech seeking to become a pan-African financial services business. Expanding into new markets allows OPay to diversify its revenue, reach underserved consumers, and replicate its financial services model beyond Nigeria. But entering a new market requires more than deploying an app. It requires banking infrastructure, regulatory relationships, local partnerships, and access to payment networks.
Standard Bank, Africa’s largest bank by assets, offered a potential shortcut.
On October 9, Standard Bank Group agreed to invest approximately $185 million in OPay, with the bank’s Africa head, Lungisa Fuzile, also set to join OPay’s board of directors. The investment was conditional on the successful completion of the fintech’s planned IPO and the receipt of applicable regulatory approvals.
Beyond the investment, the parties intended to explore opportunities in African markets involving digital banking and the distribution of selected Standard Bank products and services through OPay’s consumer and merchant platform.
But on October 30, OPay withdrew its planned New York Stock Exchange listing following a reported regulatory inquiry from China.
The failed IPO has raised questions about what OPay could lose from a partnership that promised access to some of the infrastructure, relationships, and financial products it needed to expand across Africa.
The infrastructure OPay needed
When OPay enters a market, it typically identifies a specific pain point it can solve. In Nigeria, payments were fast and accessible.
“We may enter with a focused solution to a local pain point and then broaden over time. Our Nigeria playbook of serving consumers and merchants across payments, digital banking, and credit is what we will look to replicate,” the fintech said in its prospectus.
The company has also used acquisitions to establish a presence in new markets. In Nigeria, a consortium led by OPay’s founder, Zhou Yahui, acquired a controlling stake in Paycom, a mobile-money operator, in 2018. In Pakistan, OPay acquired Finja, an electronic-money institution, in 2023.
But replicating that model across Africa requires more than acquiring a local fintech or deploying the same technology. Every market has different licensing requirements, banking systems, payment networks, and regulatory relationships.
To solve this, the fintech prioritises markets where it can obtain an appropriate banking license or operate through appropriately licensed partners.
Standard Bank operates across 21 African markets and has established relationships with regulators, financial institutions, businesses, and other participants in those financial systems. Its local knowledge and banking infrastructure help OPay navigate market-entry requirements, identify potential partners, and establish operations faster than it could independently.
“We are currently evaluating opportunities in markets across Africa and believe the Standard Bank Collaboration, if implemented, could strengthen this approach by bringing complementary products, local market knowledge, regulatory expertise and banking infrastructure across its African footprint, helping us enter and scale more efficiently,” OPay said.
OPay is particularly interested in markets where digital payments remain underpenetrated, and there is room to build new consumer and merchant relationships. “We intend to expand into new markets where we see clear unmet need and a path to build the full OPay model,” the company further noted in its prospectus.
Several markets within Standard Bank’s footprint fit that description. The bank operates in countries including Angola, Botswana, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ghana, Mozambique, and Zambia.
In 2024, only 19.2% of adults in Zambia and 18.5% in Mozambique made digital merchant payments, according to GSMA, the global industry body for mobile operators. In Ghana, the figure was 27.3%. These adoption gaps point to markets where a payments platform could build transaction habits and establish relationships with consumers and merchants.
Standard Bank’s existing relationships and knowledge of these markets could have helped OPay navigate the institutional complexity of expansion while reducing the time and resources required to establish a presence.
More financial products for OPay’s customers
The proposed collaboration also offered OPay an opportunity to expand the range of financial products available through its platform without having to develop every offering independently.
OPay already has a sizeable consumer and merchant ecosystem. It has over 50.1 million monthly active users. Its services include digital payments, savings, consumer lending, and merchant financial services. Standard Bank could have complemented these offerings with selected products from its existing portfolio.
The companies specifically identify the distribution of Standard Bank products and services through OPay’s consumer and merchant platform as an area they intend to explore.
This could have given OPay’s customers access to a wider range of financial services without the fintech having to develop every product independently.
Savings and investment products, for instance, could have expanded the ways customers put their money to work. Additional lending products could have supported consumers and businesses with different financing needs. Insurance and other financial services could have offered additional distribution opportunities.
Remittances were also on the table. Nigeria received $20.93 billion in personal remittances in 2024, according to the Central Bank of Nigeria. Standard Bank’s international banking relationships and African footprint could have helped OPay develop additional cross-border payment corridors.
OPay already had a domestic wallet network through which recipients could receive and spend money. Connecting that distribution network to Standard Bank’s banking relationships could have enabled it to participate more deeply in last-mile distribution of international remittances, allowing recipients to receive funds digitally without first withdrawing cash.
Standard Bank’s presence across multiple African markets could also have given OPay access to potential cross-border payment corridors without requiring it to establish banking relationships independently in every market. This would have offered another route to extend its business beyond domestic payments.
“If implemented, we believe the collaboration could broaden the range of financial products available through [the] OPay platform, deepen consumer and merchant engagement and create additional monetisation opportunities across our ecosystem,” OPay said.
For Standard Bank, OPay’s platform offered a different kind of distribution advantage. Rather than relying solely on its own channels to reach customers, it could leverage OPay’s digital network to distribute selected products to consumers and merchants underserved by conventional banking services.
However, the proposed arrangement remained exploratory. The arrangement was non-binding and did not oblige either company to implement a specific initiative.
For OPay, the opportunity was to accelerate its transition from a Nigerian payments giant into a broader financial services platform across emerging markets. Standard Bank could have supplied some of the infrastructure to make that expansion possible. With the IPO withdrawn, that opportunity is now uncertain.

articles.title: Apify Confirms Customer Data Accessed in Cyberattack
articles.text:
Web scraping and automation company Apify has confirmed that customer data was accessed in a cyberattack that compromised internal systems and customer accounts.
The Czech company provides a cloud platform for collecting information from websites and automating online tasks. It says it has 91,000 customers worldwide.
The intrusion took place on November 9 and 10 and was discovered on November 11, when Apify blocked the attacker’s access and launched an investigation.
According to the company, the attacker used a compromised credential to obtain additional credentials and gain access to related Apify accounts.
On November 12, Apify confirmed that some customers had their personal information or stored data accessed during the attack.
The company has contacted customers whose information was exposed. Those who have not received a notification have not been identified as affected so far, although the investigation is continuing. Apify has not disclosed the number of compromised customer accounts.
According to an Apify customer who shared a breach notification on Reddit, the exposed information included names, email addresses, billing details, account activity, and IP addresses.
More importantly, the notification listed salted password hashes, 2FA recovery codes and phone numbers, and authentication tokens associated with Google and GitHub sign-ins among the compromised data.
The notification also indicated that payment card information was limited to cardholder names, expiration dates, and the last four digits of card numbers. Full card numbers and security codes were not exposed.
The company has implemented additional monitoring, changed critical internal secrets, and revoked some OAuth connections to third-party services, including GitHub.
Apify said its investigation had not found that the OAuth connections could have been used as an attack vector. Customers building Apify Actors from private GitHub repositories have been instructed to reconnect their GitHub integrations.
