articles.title: Doing The Right Thing: Accountability In The Age Of AI Coding Summary
articles.text:
In this podcast, Shane Hastie, Lead Editor for Culture & Methods, spoke to Hugo Venturini about who is accountable when AI writes the code, how AI is reshaping code review and traditional engineering roles, and how leaders build a culture of transparency and psychological safety.
Key Takeaways
- AI is a powerful tool, but humans remain accountable for the decisions it makes possible and the code it produces.
- Pull requests have been growing for years; AI didn't create the review-scale problem, and teams should apply the same trust-based judgement about what needs reviewing that worked before AI.
- Merging the software engineer and tester roles at Microsoft in 2014 raised quality by making engineers accountable for the whole product — AI risks reversing that gain if people blame the tool instead of owning outcomes.
- AI collapses traditional role boundaries (PM, architect, tester), pushing engineers to ask better questions — a skill that defines seniority and that organisations need to deliberately teach.
- Cultures of transparency — honest no-blame Q&As, anonymous questions, naming solutions rather than people — let people dare to take accountability, and this can start at any level of the organisation, not just the top.
Subscribe on:
Transcript
Shane Hastie: Good day, folks. This is Shane Hastie for the InfoQ Engineering Culture Podcast. Today I'm sitting down with Hugo Venturini. Hugo, welcome. Thank you for taking the time to talk to us.
Hugo Venturini: Thank you, Shane, for having me.
Shane Hastie: Now, we are sitting in opposite sides of the world. I'm in New Zealand and you are somewhere in Europe.
Hugo Venturini: Yes, right now I'm in Spain, in Valencia.
Shane Hastie: Nice. You've got a beautiful warm summer. I'm sitting in a pretty cold winter, but we'll get past that. My normal starting point with these conversations is, who's Hugo?
Hugo Venturini: So I'm a software engineer. I defended my PhD on the debugging of optimized code in 2008. And after that, I joined the industry as a software engineer and I climbed the ladder one step after the other. Senior then manager. I was a manager at Meta, Facebook at the time. I was accountable for the type checker and the compiler of the hack language. Eventually I decided to try to create my own company, grew it, then joined another organization, was the CTO of Qwant, the search engine, 90 people in the organization from network engineers to AI researchers. And right now, I work in a software company, startup company that deals with tooling for AI, to help AI do the right thing, so to speak.
Defining "The Right Thing" With AI [01:58]
Shane Hastie: The right thing. What do we mean when we say, "The right thing", today?
Hugo Venturini: Somebody's making a decision about what should be provided as a product to users. Somebody's about to write the code. Somebody will test it. Somebody will make the decision to release this to prod and somebody will use it. It can be all different people or it can be the same person at every step. Doing the right thing, to me, is solving the problem to a user. And then at every step, you got doing the right thing of that step. And for a code generation, it is generating the proper code to some extent.
Shane Hastie: Now, somebody made a decision, but all too often today we are seeing the addiction of, "Yeah, but the agent did this. The code generator did this".
Hugo Venturini: I think humans are in charge and humans should be accountable and are, most of the time, at least to what I can see, and that's the right thing. I'm not minimizing what it does, but AI is just another tool. It's a very powerful tool. And don't get me wrong, I still got these wow moments several times, not a day, but at least a week. And yet if it fails, the one conducting this great tool is accountable, is in charge and should answer what goes wrong. Doing the proper thing is doing what the human asks it to do. And when you want to generate code, code has to be to the colon, to the semi-colon, to the character. And if it does not, many times, the proper tooling can actually tell the AI how to loop and give the right feedback. So when it comes back to the human, a great deal of what could be automated has been automated.
Growing Pull Request Sizes [03:44]
Shane Hastie: One of the things that we are seeing, and various studies are pointing to this, the size of pull requests are getting bigger and bigger. I've heard stories of the 2000 lines, a senior engineer who's got a backlog of over 300 pull requests, each of which is hundreds of lines long waiting to be reviewed.
Hugo Venturini: First, the size of pull request is a problem which does not rise with AI. It was already existing before. And the first thing is asking yourself, "Should I review everything?" Sometimes you got all that boilerplate. We could already, before AI, automate the verification. Let me do this. If it compiles, that's already a good thing. If it passes all the tests you've created, if it behaves the way you wanted it, do you really need to review the code? That was already not the case before.
Second thing is, already before as well, and I've lived in an organization that was working like this, you don't have to go for a signature of a diff for every single diff you do. Eventually people are good enough, senior enough or do trust each other that says, "I can totally merge this diff without having anybody reviewed it. And if it goes wrong, I'm accountable for fixing it. That'd be okay, but I'm totally sure and people trust me to merge it already". And sometimes you've got the heart of the product which you want to create and you need to be able to review for two reasons. First, for quality. Second, for sharing the knowledge, of course. And sometimes it's really just boilerplate that you can totally merge it.
With AI, big reviews always, and you can still, I believe, not go for who's got the biggest review, but who's handy enough to get your AI to create the proper diff and the proper stack of diff. So you get only one to review what the heart of the product is. I think with AI, because of the wow effect, some people are playing this game of the wow effect with, "Look, I have rewritten this entire big product in only one diff", which is just for the show. Let's face it, nobody does this. And before, at the group of engineers, if anybody were doing this, we were all telling him or her, "Please, help us review your code". That's one thing. And after that, you got the number of diffs and that's another problem.
How do you review for number of diffs? I don't have any good answer and I'm really eager to have anybody telling me, "How do you do this?" Right now, what we've decided in my team is we don't review everything. We were not reviewing everything before and we trust people with our own good judgments that this needs not being reviewed and we only ask proactively, "This, I want you to review it". I give you two other reasons for that. And this, I can merge it already. And so this minimize number of diffs to be reviewed by other people. But that's an open conversation I'm sure we all want to have, like, "How do others do about this?" And please, tell me.
Rising and Stalling Quality With AI [06:41]
Shane Hastie: We'll leave that as an open question for the audience to respond. So what are the implications of this in terms of the broader elements of quality in our product? And we think of the architectural frameworks and so forth, how do we make sure that we are building the right stuff?
Hugo Venturini: I got a story about rising quality in an unexpected way, at least for some. I worked with Microsoft in 2014 when they decided to merge the software engineer branch with the testers branch. At the time, testers were doing two things. Some were not coding, some were coding, and the software engineers were writing software and handing it to the testers for testing and was going back and forth. By removing the official testing step by somebody else, it actually raised the quality of the software. And the reason I believe is because it made software engineers accountable for the final product, not one step of the chain.
Today, I got the feeling that we are removing the software and everybody's becoming a tester via your AI, because you command some software which is written and then people become software. But we are all, again, merging those two verticals as one. And the difference is, we don't see an increase of quality yet, and I believe it's because people are still blaming the AI and don't feel accountable for what the tooling is doing. And that's one thing we totally need to work on as leaders, as managers, as colleagues, as users. I've seen some software I've been using definitely lacking quality over the last month. And I read in the press that those people are massively using AI and I'm like, "Maybe I see something here". And I'd like to know what kind of feedback I can give to get them back on quality.
Collapsing Roles: PM, Architect, Tester [08:43]
Shane Hastie: So with collapsing roles, so you mentioned the engineer, the tester. What about the architect? What about the product manager? What about the security tester, the compliance elements?
Hugo Venturini: The more people you have in an org, the more narrowed focus you have for people. When you're in a startup company, you are everybody. The tester, the PM, the architect, and sometimes the users, the dogfooter and the HR and the finance, you're everybody. And the bigger the org grows and the more people you need in every single verticals, and eventually you have a PM for the front end, a technical PM for the backend. You're going to have a handful of software engineer for the front, from the back, for the queues, and the more it grows and then it becomes like an army of people working on it. And with AI, we try to shrink it back again to when the industry was growing, to when the company was growing and we face sometimes some misunderstanding of people who have never been a PM, even a bad PM, but when you have to be a PM because you're a startup company, you eventually do the job.
And when the AI comes, it really helps you. When you've never been, but you can be and you're asked to be, that's something you have to learn. I believe that we need some more trainings or help for all those people because AI really, really empowers you, but it empowers you to do things that you're not sure how to do, and that's where AI barely helps you. It always answers the question you're asking, but if you're asking the wrong questions and being a senior is asking the right questions, the good question that helps grow, that helps define, that's being a senior. Senior is, with experience and knowledge, you actually ask the question that helps move forward to a solution. And I believe we need to help people being better at asking the right questions to the AI, if you really want it to succeed.
Asking the Right Questions: Shifting Further Left [10:38]
Shane Hastie: It worries me that the software engineer who's being used to being asked to build this and given some sort of a spec, whether it's a set of user stories, a screen mock-up or just a quick conversation, we're now asking that person to think of the right questions to ask. What is the implication of that? We've spoken about shift left and shift right for the last couple of decades. We're shifting further left, but have we and how do we empower and give the people who are being now asked to do the questioning to do that left shift to know how to do that work?
Hugo Venturini: People dare to do things if they know they will be accountable but not blamed for what happens. And that's an organization, that's a human part of your organization. If you empower people, but they don't dare, you're just not doing anything. And that comes back to the human, to managers, to organizations. How do you empower your people and give them not only the tooling, but also the state of mind of stepping out of your comfort zone? I'm a software engineer and as I said, I have to also explore a broader space. What if I don't dare? What if I can't? Because even though I got all the tooling I have, I fear it. I fear the organization I work with. And that's something which is... This is a hard part. I mean, human is the hard part of the software industry, right?
Building a Culture of Transparency and Accountability [12:07]
Shane Hastie: So this is culture. This is the Engineering Culture Podcast. How do I nurture that culture?
Hugo Venturini: I'm not sure that the recipe... Sorry, I know there's no recipe. However, I got some good examples where I believe it was the right move. The first thing is transparency and honesty. If you are honest with your team, most of the time people start being honest. I eventually became the CTO of a company which had a broken culture. People would lie, hide, steal, everything was wrong. And I was asked to fix the culture, so to speak. And very quickly I decided to lead by example. So I started to have a Q&A every week. You can ask me any question. If I can answer, I answer. If I can't, you have to keep me accountable for answering the next time. And you ask me the question again, and if I don't answer, ask it again until you have the answer. No judgment about it. Of course, first Q&A, I only got easy questions.
People wouldn't dare to challenge the head of the org. And I started to come with answers such as, "I don't know. I made a mistake. This is a good thing. Congratulations, but you don't name people. You only name solutions and product. You are accountable for what you're doing and you take the load whenever. And coming back with the last time you asked me these questions and I found the answer and it is unpleasant, but you need to hear it and we are all in this together and gathering the thing". Eventually after a few sessions, people started to ask me difficult questions and eventually we started to go with even more difficult questions by allowing for an anonymous board. So I asked my managers, "What about you ask them if they have questions and if they have it on there, write it down and you ask it. Even better, you give it to another manager so I cannot even guess which team it comes from, but I want the questions. I don't care who ask it, so please dare".
And they started to organize this so I could never guess from which part of the organization the question was coming, but I got the questions and eventually people started to vote for questions and it grew like this and it becomes very interesting. Eventually people would stack questions before the Q&A. What I noticed in the org is, when I arrived, people would lie to me and I would see it. And I was like, "Okay, you can totally confront the person, 'You're lying to me, that's bad.'" I said, "No, no, no. It's a cultural thing. How do I take it as a whole and shift almost the entire culture of lying, of hiding things by being transparent and explaining things and showing them that I can be accountable and move forward and fix things?" Being exemplary is when you can totally break things as long as you've fixed them before and you learn a lesson and you don't repeat your mistakes.
Being wrong and making mistakes is totally acceptable. What is not acceptable is repeating your own mistakes because you have not learned, so you have not grown. And this cultural thing of allowing people totally shift the essence of this organization, which went much better by the time, but you also have to be patient. When you write software, you see it right away under your hands, maybe a few hours later. With humans, you need to learn patience, but eventually you see results.
Leading Culture Change at Any Level [15:29]
Shane Hastie: Beautiful story and a great example of shifting culture. What if I'm not high enough up in the organization to do this?
Hugo Venturini: Okay. First, there's nothing as just a team lead. You are a team lead. That's not just a team lead. And at every level you got something to contribute to and to help grow. I've seen it work in smaller teams. Eventually I was in a startup company, a startup. We were already at 1200 in the company, so it was scale up, you say. And I found two teams were already working like this at their level. They were already working on this transparency and we are a team, but also we also need to be accountable. And I've seen it work. It was less efficient in terms of, I would say, impact because it was at the size of the one team and not the entire org, but already very interesting. And the good thing is, managers also gather together. I mean, as a manager, you have a team, but you are part of another team which is a team of managers.
And that's the difficulty of being a manager that most people don't get. First is, you're not only manager of a team, you are now a member of two teams with sometimes different goals or opposite goals. As a manager, you need to think outside of your own team to help the org at the size of every manager. As a manager of a team, you need to help the team grow and sometimes you have to make decisions that won't please either the rest of the managers or sometimes your team, and it cannot only be one way. You have to think outside of your own team to make it grow and make it better. And that's maybe the most difficult part of being a manager. And at every level, you always have a way to influence right outside. If you start to do the right thing and you actually see benefits, you can talk about it to other managers and eventually they will follow you and do the same thing and eventually it will grow. Okay, this is wishful thinking maybe, but if you don't try, you know it won't work, right?
Shane Hastie: Yeah. If you don't even try, you're guaranteed to fail.
Hugo Venturini: The way I see it is, as a manager, I'm here to help people. So I would always, not maybe always phrase it this way, but I'd say, "Help me help you". So if you provide the right information to your manager, your manager would be able to help you. If you hide too much, if you're too secret on some part of who you are or what you do, it becomes a little harder. You're not only a machine coding or being an engineer, you're also a human. And sometimes you got ups and downs and if you provide some information to help your manager, your manager can also totally help you. And that works at every level.
As a CTO, I was at the COMEX and talking with the CEO, the CFO, and if you give them some hints that they can help you because you are in a down moment or hub moment or you are available to help them, you become a member of the team. And it's not a day by day. It's an average, it's going to be 50/50 in the end, but it doesn't have to be you always being 50% helped and being helpful every day by the hour, by the week, it's overall. But it's kind of hard thing because you don't know when it ends.
Shane Hastie: We are dealing with people.
Hugo Venturini: I like to help people. I like to see people grow. Most of the time, staff relationship in helping people, and that's all why I moved to the management and leadership roles because I believe that most of people are better than I am at what they do in their job. So if I can help them be even better, it cascades to the next person and the overall organization grows.
Shane Hastie: So the manager as amplifier.
And that's also why when you got toxic management, it's devastating for an org. The impact is easier when you got people reporting to you, but also as easier, it's easier to destroy everything or to grow better.
Influence Without a Manager Title [19:28]
Shane Hastie: We've handed a lot and given some good advice around that transparency and bringing that into culture and the culture of accountability without blame. What is the really important question that I haven't asked you?
Hugo Venturini: We've talked about management and the impact that come with the role. Is it possible to have the same kind of impact without being a manager? I've seen individuals being able to do this, and I've been always very much impressed by their level of influence, and I'm not sure I've deciphered how they were working. What I've seen is, those people were technically very strong, very humble, and the common characteristic of those people were like, they were always, always listening more than they were speaking. So yes, it is possible, but I'm also leaning towards the conclusion that it's not everybody is able to do it. There's something natural in those people, and when you ask them, they're like, "I don't know. I got it by chance. For some reason people are listening to me". I'm like, "Oh, come on, dude. You know that's wrong. You work on your skills, but also you've met the right people". Everybody's been mentored. Nobody came naturally to this kind of position.
Hugo Venturini: That's the one thing is, you can totally grow. It is possible, and it can be a north star to have this kind of influence. And if you don't reach this kind of influence, maybe you're too humble to understand that you are actually at this level of influence, and it is more probable that it's your humility that forgives you to see it than the fact that you are not at this level of influence. But yes, it is possible. It is a very tough career. Some of the best leaders I've met as ICs, many, many of them tried being manager for a while and came back. And the easiest and best seniors, staff, principal engineers I've managed knew the role of managers and knew how to help me as a manager.
So I would say give it a go. It doesn't have to last for your life. I mean, you can totally give it a try for a moment. I was an IC at Microsoft, became a manager, was hired as an IC at Facebook, became a manager, eventually created my company, was an IC, then became a manager, and then was hired as director, a CTO. I've been an IC for a bit more than a year. Going back and forth gives you all the understanding of the scope of what is it to create the product that answers a user's demand. In the end, it's just about this, I believe.
Shane Hastie: That pendulum swing across roles. You got a lot of really interesting and meaty stuff there. If people want to continue the conversation, where can they find you?
Hugo Venturini: They can find me on X/XTwitter as monsieurv. It’s French. My alias is monsieurv. And on LinkedIn, by my name, Hugo Venturini. Please, please come and discuss it all. You agree, you disagree, you have another story, you have questions, you have things to raise questions from me, because I'm very curious. Please keep this conversation going. I think it's a fascinating space, and we decided to be in this space because it is fascinating because the meeting of software and humans is an ongoing conversation that's going to be for life.
Shane Hastie: Hugo, thanks so much for taking the time.
Hugo Venturini: Thank you, Shane, for having me in your podcast. Very, very interesting conversation.
Mentioned:
- Hugo Venturini on LinkedIn
- X/Twitter as monsieurv

articles.title: Modder tricks Switch 2 into thinking a $45 laptop hub is an official Nintendo dock
articles.text:
Serving tech enthusiasts: Plug a Switch 2 into an ordinary USB-C hub and it will charge, but the TV stays dark. That's because the console won't send a picture until the hub answers a proprietary handshake. Nintendo's $125 dock knows the replies, as do third-party docks built to mimic it. Now, a hobbyist has taught a roughly $45 laptop hub the same trick by rewriting a sliver of its firmware.
The hobbyist, who goes by mkopec, explained in a blog post that Nintendo's dock is simply too bulky to travel with. A €40 ($44) Cable Matters 7-in-1 hub looked like a neat replacement, since it already takes video over USB-C. But hooked up to a Switch 2, it only charged the console.
Nintendo's handheld is far stricter about docks than the original Switch, so mkopec put a USB-C sniffer between the console and its official dock. The dock introduced itself as a Nintendo product and offered two modes: regular DisplayPort and Nintendo's own. Oddly, the Switch picks the Nintendo mode first, then fires off a string of vendor-specific messages before any picture appears.
To answer them, mkopec squeezed about 540 bytes of code into empty space on the hub's VIA Labs power-delivery chip. The patch handles Nintendo's messages and passes everything else to the stock firmware. Weirdly, just claiming to be a Nintendo device wasn't enough. TV mode only came to life on the fifth version of the patch, once the hub copied the dock's full identity.
Even so, HDR games looked washed out at first. As mkopec put it, "the pixels were fine all along, only the label was wrong." Specifically, the Realtek chip that converts the hub's video to HDMI was tagging HDR frames with a standard-range color space. So mkopec wrote a 108-byte fix for that chip and flashed it over the same USB-C cable.
Posing as the official dock also unlocked a setting the real one never gets. Nintendo's dock doesn't support variable refresh rate on TVs, yet the Switch now offers VRR through the patched hub. Sadly, the hub's display chip can't keep up with it either. Turning VRR on froze the DisplayPort picture, so mkopec suggests leaving it off.
For anyone brave enough to try it, mkopec has since published a patcher on GitHub. It only supports this one Cable Matters model with untouched stock firmware, and the patcher must be run from a Linux PC. The README also warns that a botched flash can brick the hub.
Of course, even commercial docks haven't had it easy. Nintendo's 21.0.0 update last November cut video output to plenty of them overnight, leaving their makers to rush out firmware fixes. There's nobody pushing updates for a hand-patched hub, so a future system update could just as easily turn it back into a charger.

articles.title: Build a model improvement flywheel with Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Data Capture | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Build a model improvement flywheel with Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Data Capture
Foundation models deployed on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod meet inputs that no pre-curated dataset covers: domain-specific jargon, unexpected formats, new products, and changing user behavior. Without a record of production inference data, teams can’t detect drift, find failure patterns, or use real interactions to improve the model.
Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now provides Data Capture, a built-in capability that records live inference inputs and outputs to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) at three independent tiers, with minimal latency impact and zero impact on model availability.
In this post, we walk through one complete example on a single SageMaker HyperPod cluster. A home-appliance support router captures its production traffic, Amazon Athena queries surface a new-product blind spot, a SQL policy labels the captured records, and a fine-tune on that data teaches the router the new product. We measure accuracy before and after, on data that could not have existed before the model was deployed. The inference operator serves the model on one node, and the training operator runs the fine-tuning on another.
We use synthetic data for the walkthrough. The scripts, manifests, SQL, synthetic datasets, and expected outputs are available in the accompanying GitHub repository.
Three-tier Data Capture architecture
HyperPod Data Capture provides three independent tiers, each at a different point in the request path. You can turn on any combination in the same dataCapture block.
Tier 1: SageMaker endpoint
Tier 2: Load balancer
Tier 3: Model pod
What’s captured
Full request/response payloads
Application Load Balancer (ALB) access-log fields: request line, status codes, timings, client IP, user agent
Full request/response payloads plus event metadata
Tiers 1 and 3 both store full payloads, so enabling both stores every record twice. Use Tier 1 for compliance and Model Monitor, Tier 2 when you only need traffic metadata, and Tier 3 when you intend to use the payloads. This post uses Tier 3 only. Because Tier 3 records complete payloads, which can include names, addresses, and order numbers, protect that data before it becomes training data. Use sampling, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption (kmsKeyId), S3 lifecycle rules, and personally identifiable information (PII) redaction (for example, with Amazon Comprehend).
Two available NVIDIA GPUs, one for serving and one for training. We used an ml.g6e.8xlarge for serving and an ml.g6e.xlarge for training (one 48 GB NVIDIA L40S each). The serving pod holds its GPU for the life of the endpoint, so with only one GPU the training pod stays Pending.
kubectl configured for the cluster.
An S3 bucket in the same Region.
Confirm both operators are installed. The command returns two rows:
The following diagram shows the five steps of the walkthrough on one SageMaker HyperPod cluster: capture every request and response to Amazon S3, analyze the captures with Athena, label them with a SQL policy, fine-tune with the training operator on a second GPU, and redeploy side by side with capture still on.
Figure 1: The five-step flywheel on a single SageMaker HyperPod cluster, from capture through Athena analysis, labeling, fine-tuning, and redeploy
The inference operator adds three sidecars to the model pod. Every request that passes through the NGINX proxy is copied to an OpenTelemetry collector, batched, and written to S3 through a Mountpoint-S3 volume. Athena reads those files in place. The training operator runs the fine-tune as a HyperPodPyTorchJob on a second GPU, and the new model is served by a second endpoint that also has capture on.
Step 0: Set your variables
Every later step reads these. Edit the first block, then paste the whole thing:
# --- edit these ---
export EKS_CLUSTER_NAME="my-hyperpod-eks"
export AWS_REGION="us-east-1"
export BUCKET="amzn-s3-demo-bucket"
export SERVE_INSTANCE_TYPE="ml.g6e.8xlarge" # node type for the first endpoint
export TRAIN_INSTANCE_TYPE="ml.g6e.xlarge" # node type for the fine-tuning job
# --- leave as-is ---
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="$AWS_REGION"
export ENDPOINT_NAME="appliance-router"
export MODEL_LOCATION="models/qwen2.5-3b-instruct"
export MODEL_V2_LOCATION="models/qwen2.5-3b-router-v2"
export TRAIN_SA="flywheel" # service account with S3 access via EKS Pod Identity
aws eks update-kubeconfig --name "$EKS_CLUSTER_NAME" --region "$AWS_REGION"
render() { python3 -c 'import os,sys; sys.stdout.write(os.path.expandvars(sys.stdin.read()))'; }
Step 1: Stage the base model in S3
We use Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct because it is small enough to fine-tune in about a minute and fits on a single L40S.
The Mountpoint-S3 CSI driver role. Tier 3 capture writes through a Mountpoint-S3 volume, and the driver authenticates as its own IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA) role, not as the pod’s service account. It needs s3:PutObject, s3:AbortMultipartUpload, and s3:DeleteObject on your capture bucket, plus kms:Decrypt, kms:GenerateDataKey, and kms:DescribeKey if you set kmsKeyId. If this is missing, the endpoint stays healthy and requests succeed, but no captures appear. See Mountpoint for Amazon S3 CSI driver.
The inference operator execution role. It needs s3:PutObject on your capture bucket, plus kms:Decrypt and kms:GenerateDataKey if you set kmsKeyId. The capture files themselves are written through the CSI driver role, so when no captures appear, check that role first.
The training pod’s service account ($TRAIN_SA). Read access to the base model and training data, and write access for the merged model, through EKS Pod Identity.
Athena. Read access to the capture prefix, plus a query-results location.
Enabling Data Capture
The next three steps deploy the router with Tier 3 capture on, check that the pod runs the capture sidecars, and confirm that records reach Amazon S3.
Step 3: Deploy the model with Tier 3 capture enabled
This is the whole feature: the dataCapture.modelPod.enabled: true block. Everything else is an ordinary vLLM deployment.
The preceding modelPod block sets 100% sampling and captures both input and output, which are the defaults. To tune it, add any of these optional fields under modelPod:
modelPod:
enabled: true
initialSamplingPercentage: 50 # capture 50% of requests (default 100)
bufferConfig:
batchSize: 100 # records buffered per upload batch (default 10)
flushIntervalSeconds: 60 # max seconds before a flush (default 60)
payloadConfig:
maxPayloadSizeKB: 1024 # truncate payloads larger than this (default: no limit)
kmsKeyId: "arn:aws:kms:...:key/..." # encrypt captures at rest
Step 4: Wait for the pod
A capture-enabled pod runs four containers: the model, sidecar-reverse-proxy (NGINX), otel-collector, and s3-uploader. The model container and the pod’s app label are both named after modelName.
kubectl get pods -l app=$ENDPOINT_NAME -o custom-columns=\
'NAME:.metadata.name,READY:.status.containerStatuses[*].ready,CONTAINERS:.spec.containers[*].name,NODE:.spec.nodeName'
NAME READY CONTAINERS NODE
appliance-router-849f466476-4f5v8 true,true,true,true appliance-router,s3-uploader,sidecar-reverse-proxy,otel-collector hyperpod-i-0f3fe2684afd6a583
In our run, the pod was ready about five minutes after kubectl apply, most of it spent downloading the weights.
Step 5: Send a request and confirm captures land in S3
Send an inference request through the capture proxy on port 8081, then, after the flush interval, list the capture prefix. The model itself listens on port 8000. Requests sent there bypass the proxy and are not captured.
POD=$(kubectl get pod -l app=$ENDPOINT_NAME -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl port-forward "pod/$POD" 18081:8081 >/dev/null 2>&1 &
sleep 5
curl -s http://localhost:18081/v1/chat/completions \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
-d '{"model":"'"$ENDPOINT_NAME"'","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"my fridge is not cooling"}],"max_tokens":24}'
echo "Waiting for the capture buffer to flush..."; sleep 75
aws s3 ls "s3://${BUCKET}/capture/" --recursive | grep '\.jsonl$' | head
2026-09-28 15:47:14 634356 capture/20e4425092f90c7f/pod/AllTraffic/2026/09/28/15/28-15-47-12-999-ac31d31b-5156-46ad-9ccc-e8a040ab9ab2.jsonl
You see one or more .jsonl objects under {s3Uri}/{uniqueID}/pod/{variant}/{YYYY}/{MM}/{DD}/{HH}/. The uniqueID is generated per endpoint. Each line is one inference in the SageMaker data-capture format shown next.
The captured record format
The request and response bodies are stored base64-encoded, as the encoding field shows, so reading them back requires base64-decoding and then parsing JSON:
Decoded, endpointInput.data is the request body the client sent and endpointOutput.data is the response the model returned.
The scenario: A support-ticket router meets a product launch
The deployed model is a support-ticket router for a home-appliance retailer. It uses vLLM guided JSON decoding to classify each ticket into one of six categories: ProductFridge, ProductWasher, ProductOven, ProductDishwasher, ProductMicrowave, or the catch-all Other. Guided decoding means it can only return a valid object with one of those labels:
{"category": "ProductWasher", "confidence": 1}
After the model was deployed, the retailer launched its own line of air conditioners, the Arctis series (Arctis 9K, 12K, Mini, and so on). The router has no category for them. It can’t say “this is new.” It can only pick the closest label it knows. Unless every request and response is recorded, the evidence disappears the moment the response is returned.
The synthetic traffic
We generated two synthetic datasets:
Production traffic: 900 tickets, replayed in order through the capture proxy over 15 minutes, using the router’s original six-label prompt. The first 400 come before the launch and mention no air conditioners. In the remaining 500, the share of Arctis tickets ramps from 15% to 55%.
Evaluation set: 280 labeled tickets, 40 per category, including the new ProductAC. It is held out by content: it uses symptoms, sentence templates, and Arctis model names that never appear in the traffic.
Each production request looks like this (system prompt abbreviated):
{"model": "appliance-router", "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": 40,
"messages": [{"role": "system", "content": "You are a support-ticket router for a home-appliance retailer. ... category is one of: ProductFridge, ProductWasher, ProductOven, ProductDishwasher, ProductMicrowave, Other. ..."},
{"role": "user", "content": "Hi, our Arctis 12K blows warm air since last week. Order #66759."}],
"guided_json": {"type": "object", "required": ["category", "confidence"],
"properties": {"category": {"enum": ["ProductFridge", "ProductWasher", "ProductOven",
"ProductDishwasher", "ProductMicrowave", "Other"]},
"confidence": {"type": "number"}}}}
To replay the traffic, clone the accompanying repository, generate the datasets, and send them through the capture proxy. scripts/pod.sh runs the client inside the model container, so no load balancer or DNS is needed. The client prints the three timestamps that the Athena steps use: RUN_START, LAUNCH_TS (the first post-launch ticket), and RUN_END.
git clone https://github.com/awslabs/awsome-distributed-ai.git
cd awsome-distributed-ai/examples/use-cases/sagemaker-hyperpod-data-capture-flywheel
(cd data && python3 ../scripts/gen_dataset.py)
scripts/pod.sh $ENDPOINT_NAME drive /tmp/tickets_traffic.jsonl --seconds 900
RUN_START=2026-09-28 15:52:40
sent 100/900
...
LAUNCH_TS=2026-09-28 15:59:20
...
RUN_END=2026-09-28 16:07:40
Export the three values that your run printed, and wait one flush interval:
Offline benchmarks still look unchanged after the launch, because they are frozen in the past. The shift is visible only in the captured production traffic. This section shows how a data scientist finds it with Athena, without provisioning any infrastructure.
Step 6: Set your variables and configure an Athena helper function
export ATHENA_DB="flywheel_demo"
export ATHENA_OUTPUT="s3://${BUCKET}/athena-results/"
# Each endpoint writes under its own uniqueID. Pick the prefix whose captured requests name this
# endpoint, not whichever prefix sorts first (the Step 15 endpoint adds a second one).
for id in $(aws s3 ls "s3://${BUCKET}/capture/" | awk '/PRE/{print $2}'); do
key=$(aws s3 ls "s3://${BUCKET}/capture/${id}pod/AllTraffic/" --recursive | awk '/\.jsonl$/{print $4; exit}')
[ -n "$key" ] || continue
model=$(aws s3 cp "s3://${BUCKET}/${key}" - 2>/dev/null | head -n 1 | python3 -c 'import sys, json, base64; r = json.loads(sys.stdin.readline()); print(json.loads(base64.b64decode(r["captureData"]["endpointInput"]["data"]))["model"])')
if [ "$model" = "$ENDPOINT_NAME" ]; then export CAPTURE_LOCATION="s3://${BUCKET}/capture/${id}pod/AllTraffic/"; break; fi
done
echo "$CAPTURE_LOCATION" # s3://<bucket>/capture/<uniqueID>/pod/AllTraffic/
# run_athena "<SQL>": runs one statement, prints tab-separated rows, and sets LAST_QID
run_athena() {
local qid st
qid=$(aws athena start-query-execution --query-string "$1" \
--query-execution-context "Database=$ATHENA_DB" \
--result-configuration "OutputLocation=$ATHENA_OUTPUT" \
--output text --query 'QueryExecutionId') || return 1
while :; do
st=$(aws athena get-query-execution --query-execution-id "$qid" \
--output text --query 'QueryExecution.Status.State')
case "$st" in
SUCCEEDED) break ;;
FAILED|CANCELLED) aws athena get-query-execution --query-execution-id "$qid" \
--output text --query 'QueryExecution.Status.StateChangeReason' >&2; return 1 ;;
esac
sleep 2
done
LAST_QID=$qid
aws athena get-query-results --query-execution-id "$qid" \
--output text --query 'ResultSet.Rows[*].Data[*].VarCharValue'
}
run_athena "CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS ${ATHENA_DB}"
Step 7: Declare the captures to Athena (two layers)
The first layer is the envelope. An external table describes the outer JSON of each record, and partition projection over year/month/day/hour maps the hourly S3 prefixes to partitions without a crawler or ADD PARTITION. The data fields are declared as plain strings, because they are base64 text.
The second layer is a view that decodes each record once. from_utf8(from_base64(...)) turns the payloads back into JSON. Without it, every extraction returns NULL. The ticket is the user message (messages[1], because messages[0] is the system prompt). The model’s answer is a JSON string inside the response JSON, so it needs a second extraction.
run_athena "
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW preds AS
WITH decoded AS (
SELECT CAST(from_iso8601_timestamp(eventMetadata.inferenceTime) AS timestamp) AS ts,
from_utf8(from_base64(captureData.endpointInput.data)) AS req,
from_utf8(from_base64(captureData.endpointOutput.data)) AS resp
FROM inference_captures
WHERE year = '${RUN_START:0:4}' AND month = '${RUN_START:5:2}' AND day = '${RUN_START:8:2}'
)
SELECT ts,
json_extract_scalar(req, '\$.messages[1].content') AS ticket_text,
json_extract_scalar(json_extract_scalar(resp, '\$.choices[0].message.content'), '\$.category') AS predicted_category,
CAST(json_extract_scalar(json_extract_scalar(resp, '\$.choices[0].message.content'), '\$.confidence') AS double) AS confidence
FROM decoded
WHERE ts >= timestamp '${RUN_START}' AND ts < timestamp '${RUN_END}'
"
run_athena "SELECT count(*) AS n, count_if(predicted_category IS NULL) AS unparsed FROM preds"
n unparsed
900 0
Two notes on the view:
Always filter on partitions. Athena reads raw JSON, so a query without a partition filter scans every object you have ever captured. The view filters to one day, and the time bound limits it to our traffic run: the same prefix also holds the request from Step 5.
messages[1]assumes one system message followed by one user message. Captured traffic is whatever clients actually sent, so adjust the extraction for multi-turn or few-shot requests.
(Output is tab-separated. We aligned it here for readability. Our run compressed “weeks” into 15 minutes. In production, bucket bydate_trunc('day', ts)or'week'instead.)
The following chart plots the per-minute share of tickets routed to Other as bars, and the cumulative share as a line, with the launch marked.
Figure 2: Per-minute and cumulative share of tickets routed to Other, before and after the Arctis launch
Before the launch, Other stays under 7% per minute. It jumps to 15% in the launch minute and keeps climbing, reaching 47–65% in the last three minutes. The cumulative line in the chart only reaches 22.6%, because it averages the post-launch tickets with all the traffic from before the launch. That is why the per-minute rate, not the cumulative share, is what you would put behind an alarm.
Split at the launch, the whole category mix looks like this:
run_athena "
SELECT IF(ts < timestamp '${LAUNCH_TS}', '1-before launch', '2-after launch') AS period,
predicted_category, count(*) AS n
FROM preds GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 3 DESC"
period predicted_category n
1-before launch ProductFridge 91
1-before launch ProductWasher 83
1-before launch ProductDishwasher 74
1-before launch ProductOven 74
1-before launch ProductMicrowave 59
1-before launch Other 19
2-after launch Other 184
2-after launch ProductFridge 84
2-after launch ProductOven 66
2-after launch ProductDishwasher 64
2-after launch ProductWasher 58
2-after launch ProductMicrowave 44
Other went from 4.8% of tickets before the launch (19 of 400) to 36.8% after it (184 of 500), and became the largest category.
Step 9: What is inside the Other bucket?
run_athena "
SELECT word, count(*) AS freq
FROM preds CROSS JOIN UNNEST(regexp_extract_all(lower(ticket_text), '[a-z0-9-]{4,}')) AS t(word)
WHERE predicted_category = 'Other'
AND word NOT IN ('this','that','with','from','have','since','week','help','need','again','time',
'month','second','take','look','someone','order','last','after','when','onto')
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC, 1 LIMIT 10"
word freq
arctis 141
unit 40
mini 33
cooling 30
link 30
lost 30
loudly 30
rattles 30
wi-fi 30
blows 28
The Other bucket isn’t a mix of unrelated tickets. It’s dominated by one product name, arctis, and the vocabulary of a cooling appliance, which points to a new category the router has no label for.
Step 10: How big is it, and does the model’s confidence flag it?
Search the whole traffic stream for the new product, not just the Other bucket:
run_athena "
SELECT IF(ts < timestamp '${LAUNCH_TS}', '1-before launch', '2-after launch') AS period,
predicted_category, count(*) AS n
FROM preds WHERE regexp_like(lower(ticket_text), 'arctis|air condition')
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 3 DESC"
period predicted_category n
2-after launch Other 164
2-after launch ProductFridge 14
There are 178 air-conditioner tickets, 19.8% of all traffic. None of them appeared before the launch. They fall into two groups:
164 went toOther. Under the six-label schema, that is the correct answer: Other exists for exactly this case. The router isn’t broken. The taxonomy is missing a category, so these tickets reach a generic queue instead of the team that supports the product.
14 went toProductFridge. These are true misroutes: a refrigerator team is now getting air-conditioner tickets.
Now test the model’s confidence on these known misroutes:
run_athena "
SELECT predicted_category, confidence, count(*) AS n FROM preds
WHERE regexp_like(lower(ticket_text), 'arctis|air condition')
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2 DESC"
predicted_category confidence n
Other 1.0 157
Other 0.9 7
ProductFridge 0.95 1
ProductFridge 0.9 9
ProductFridge 0.8 2
ProductFridge 0.7 1
ProductFridge 0.0 1
Of the 14 misrouted tickets, 10 reported a confidence of 0.9 or higher. A labeling rule such as “keep predictions with confidence >= 0.9” would have kept 71% of the known-wrong labels. That’s because confidence is a field we asked the model to write, not a calibrated probability. If you need a real uncertainty signal, request token logprobs from vLLM and read the probability at the category token instead of the model’s self-report. Budget for the extra payload size, because the logprobs are captured with every response.
From diagnosis to labeled training data
A data scientist doesn’t hand-label hundreds of tickets. Instead, they write the Athena finding down as a labeling policy: a SQL view that assigns a corrected label to every captured record. We relabel the misrouted air-conditioner tickets to the new class.
Step 11: The labeling policy
run_athena "
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW labeled_training_data AS
WITH t AS (SELECT ticket_text, predicted_category, lower(ticket_text) AS txt FROM preds)
SELECT ticket_text, predicted_category,
CASE
-- 1. The new class, identified by keyword evidence, not by what the model predicted
WHEN regexp_like(txt, '\\barctis\\b|air condition|\\bac unit\\b|mini split')
AND NOT regexp_like(txt, 'fridge|refrigerat|freezer|washer|\\boven\\b|\\brange\\b|dishwasher|microwave')
THEN 'ProductAC'
-- 2. Keep the production decision when nothing hints at the new product
WHEN NOT regexp_like(txt, '\\barctis\\b|air condition|\\bac\\b|mini split')
THEN predicted_category
-- 3. Mixed signals: send to human review (Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth)
ELSE NULL
END AS corrected_category
FROM t"
The doubled backslashes (\\b) are shell escaping inside the double-quoted string. Athena receives \b, a regular-expression word boundary.
Check what the policy produced:
run_athena "
SELECT coalesce(corrected_category, '(human review)') AS label, count(*) AS n,
count(DISTINCT ticket_text) AS distinct_texts,
count_if(corrected_category <> predicted_category) AS relabeled
FROM labeled_training_data GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC"
label n distinct_texts relabeled
ProductAC 178 114 178
ProductFridge 161 110 0
ProductWasher 141 96 0
ProductOven 140 97 0
ProductDishwasher 138 95 0
ProductMicrowave 103 82 0
Other 39 8 0
This heuristic works because the new category is clear-cut (keyword-identifiable). For ambiguous tickets or overlapping categories, the NULL rows would route to Ground Truth for human labeling.
Step 12: Build the training file
Export the labeled view and convert it to chat-format JSONL. The allowed category set now includes ProductAC, the same seven-label prompt clients will send after the redeploy. Save this as build_training_file.py:
cat > build_training_file.py <<'PY'
import csv, json, sys
CATS = ["ProductFridge", "ProductWasher", "ProductOven", "ProductDishwasher", "ProductMicrowave", "ProductAC", "Other"]
PROMPT = ("You are a support-ticket router for a home-appliance retailer. Route each ticket to the product it "
'concerns. Respond with ONLY a JSON object {"category": "...", "confidence": <0-1>} where category is '
"one of: " + ", ".join(CATS) + '. Use "Other" if the ticket does not clearly concern one of these products.')
n = 0
with open(sys.argv[1], newline="") as fin, open(sys.argv[2], "w") as fout:
for row in csv.DictReader(fin):
fout.write(json.dumps({"messages": [
{"role": "system", "content": PROMPT},
{"role": "user", "content": row["ticket_text"]},
{"role": "assistant", "content": json.dumps({"category": row["corrected_category"], "confidence": 1.0})},
]}) + "\n"); n += 1
print(f"wrote {n} training examples -> {sys.argv[2]}")
PY
run_athena "SELECT ticket_text, corrected_category FROM labeled_training_data
WHERE corrected_category IS NOT NULL" > /dev/null
aws s3 cp "${ATHENA_OUTPUT}${LAST_QID}.csv" labeled.csv --only-show-errors # Athena's own CSV: header + proper quoting
python3 build_training_file.py labeled.csv train.jsonl
aws s3 cp train.jsonl "s3://${BUCKET}/training/train.jsonl"
wrote 900 training examples -> train.jsonl
Fine-tuning on captured data with the HyperPod training operator
We fine-tune on the same cluster that serves the model, using the HyperPod training operator on the second GPU. The first endpoint keeps serving throughout.
Step 13: The training script
The script downloads the base model and training data from S3 and trains a low-rank adaptation (LoRA) adapter. The loss is computed only on the assistant turn, so the model learns to produce the label rather than repeat the prompt. The script then merges the adapter back into the base weights, so vLLM can serve the result unchanged, and uploads the merged model to S3. The job mounts the script into the training pod from a ConfigMap.
cat > train.py <<'PY'
import os, boto3, torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, Trainer, TrainingArguments
s3 = boto3.client("s3")
def split(uri): b, _, k = uri[5:].partition("/"); return b, k
# 1. Stage base model + training data from S3
bucket, prefix = split(os.environ["BASE_MODEL_S3"])
for page in s3.get_paginator("list_objects_v2").paginate(Bucket=bucket, Prefix=prefix):
for o in page.get("Contents", []):
dst = os.path.join("/work/base", os.path.relpath(o["Key"], prefix))
os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(dst), exist_ok=True); s3.download_file(bucket, o["Key"], dst)
s3.download_file(*split(os.environ["TRAIN_FILE_S3"]), "/work/train.jsonl")
print("[stage] base model and training data downloaded", flush=True)
# 2. LoRA SFT, loss only on the assistant turn (the label), not the prompt
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("/work/base")
def encode(ex):
full = tok.apply_chat_template(ex["messages"], tokenize=False)
prompt = tok.apply_chat_template(ex["messages"][:-1], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
ids = tok(full, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"]
n = len(tok(prompt, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"])
return {"input_ids": ids, "labels": [-100] * n + ids[n:]}
ds = load_dataset("json", data_files="/work/train.jsonl", split="train")
print(f"[data] {len(ds)} examples", flush=True)
ds = ds.map(encode, remove_columns=ds.column_names)
def collate(batch):
m = max(len(b["input_ids"]) for b in batch)
pad = lambda xs, v: [x + [v] * (m - len(x)) for x in xs]
return {"input_ids": torch.tensor(pad([b["input_ids"] for b in batch], tok.pad_token_id)),
"labels": torch.tensor(pad([b["labels"] for b in batch], -100)),
"attention_mask": torch.tensor(pad([[1] * len(b["input_ids"]) for b in batch], 0))}
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("/work/base", torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="cuda:0")
model = get_peft_model(model, LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05, task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj", "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"]))
model.print_trainable_parameters()
Trainer(model=model, train_dataset=ds, data_collator=collate, args=TrainingArguments(
output_dir="/tmp/ckpt", num_train_epochs=float(os.getenv("EPOCHS", "2")), learning_rate=1e-4,
per_device_train_batch_size=8, bf16=True, logging_steps=10, save_strategy="no", report_to=[],
warmup_ratio=0.1, lr_scheduler_type="cosine")).train()
# 3. Merge the adapter into the base weights (a plain model vLLM can serve) and upload it
model.merge_and_unload().save_pretrained("/work/out", safe_serialization=True)
tok.save_pretrained("/work/out")
bucket, prefix = split(os.environ["OUTPUT_S3"])
for f in os.listdir("/work/out"):
s3.upload_file(os.path.join("/work/out", f), bucket, f"{prefix.rstrip('/')}/{f}")
print(f"[done] merged model uploaded to {os.environ['OUTPUT_S3']}", flush=True)
PY
kubectl create configmap router-train --from-file=train.py
logMonitoringConfigurationis the training operator’s distinguishing feature. If no loss line appears within 20 minutes of start, or the log goes quiet for 10 minutes mid-run while the process is still alive, the operator restarts the job instead of letting it burn GPU hours.
The job installs three Python packages when it starts. The training node needs outbound internet access, for example through a NAT gateway, and so does pulling the vllm/vllm-openai image from Docker Hub. On a cluster without internet egress, bake the packages into a custom image in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) and drop the pip install.
Training took 60 seconds on one L40S. LoRA at rank 16 trains about 29.9 million parameters, under 1% of the 3.1-billion-parameter model. The average training loss was 0.0123, and the per-step loss reached 0.0 within the first epoch, which shows the model memorizes 900 templated examples readily. On real data, hold out a validation split and stop early. Here we rely on the held-out evaluation set.
Step 15: Deploy the fine-tuned model side by side, with capture still on
Instead of editing the running endpoint, deploy the new model as a second endpoint from the same manifest, onto the GPU the training job just released. The first endpoint keeps serving until you cut clients over, so the redeploy causes no downtime, and rolling back means pointing clients back at the first endpoint.
The new endpoint writes captures under its own uniqueID. Because ENDPOINT_NAME is now appliance-router-v2, rerunning the CAPTURE_LOCATION lookup from Step 6 finds that prefix, so you can point a second Athena table at it for the next round of analysis. When you move clients over, update the endpoint, the label set, and the guided-JSON enum in the same release.
Measuring the lift
We ran the same 280 held-out tickets against the fine-tuned endpoint:
Fine-tuning taught the router the new category and caused no regression on the five established classes. It also fixed five Other errors that existed before the launch which the launched router sent to ProductFridge.
Because our evaluation set comes from the same generator as the training data, we also wrote 24 probe tickets by hand, in styles the generator never produces. The fine-tuned model scored 20/24:
MISS ProductFridge -> ProductAC: The cooling fan in my fridge is squealing.
MISS Other -> ProductAC: When will the Arctis 12K be back in stock?
MISS Other -> ProductAC: Can I get a quote to install central air in my house?
MISS Other -> ProductAC: Do you price match the Arctis at other stores?
overall 20/24 = 83.33%
It routes all eight air-conditioner probes correctly, but it learned two shortcuts: “cooling” means air conditioner, and any mention of Arctis means ProductAC, including stock and price-match questions. Both come from the training data: the labeling policy sent every Arctis ticket to ProductAC, and the captured traffic contained no pre-sales questions. With capture on for the new endpoint, those tickets are exactly what the next round of capture collects.
How much latency does capture add?
We measured this directly: the same 400 routing requests, sent from inside the pod either to port 8000 (no capture) or to port 8081 (through the capture proxy). We ran three rounds at 8 concurrent requests, plus one serial round:
Path
Concurrency
p50
p99
Throughput
Direct to vLLM (8000), no capture
8
200.7 ms
249.4 ms
39.1 req/s
Through capture proxy (8081)
8
200.0 ms
249.8 ms
39.1 req/s
Direct to vLLM (8000), no capture
1
164.4 ms
206.9 ms
6.0 req/s
Through capture proxy (8081)
1
164.4 ms
207.0 ms
6.0 req/s
Rows at concurrency 8 are the average of three rounds. Round-to-round variation (±1 ms at p50) was larger than the difference between the two paths.
Other uses for captured data
After inference data lands in S3, the same records feed many workflows:
Improve the model: Use supervised fine-tuning (shown here), distill a large model’s outputs into a smaller model, or build preference pairs for direct preference optimization (DPO).
Understand the model: Run Athena analytics (shown here), build golden regression sets from real prompts, set drift alarms, discover emerging intents, and detect malformed outputs and refusals.
Operate and govern: Route ambiguous samples to Ground Truth for labeling, keep audit trails (Tier 1 is recommended), replay the exact input behind an incident, and analyze traffic and payloads for cost attribution.
Cost considerations
Tier
Approximate cost impact
Tier 1 (SageMaker endpoint)
Captured by SageMaker at the endpoint. You pay S3 storage and requests for the payloads
Tier 2 (ALB access logs)
S3 storage for the log files only
Tier 3 (model pod)
Three sidecars requesting 250m CPU + 640 MiB per pod in total (NGINX proxy 100m/128Mi, OTel collector 100m/256Mi, s3-uploader 50m/256Mi), plus S3 storage and requests for the payloads
Two costs scale with usage:
S3. Our records averaged about 2.3 KB each (3,955 records in 9.0 MB). Longer prompts and responses cost proportionally more. The uploader wrote one object per flush interval per pod, about 1,440 PUTs per pod per day at 60 seconds.
Athena charges by data scanned, so always filter on the partition columns, and convert the raw JSON to Parquet with a CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) query for repeated analysis.
In this post, we showed how you can use SageMaker HyperPod Data Capture to record live inference data and turn it into training data. With capture available at three independent tiers, you can:
Collect real-world training data with no measurable impact on serving latency.
Query inference patterns at scale with Amazon Athena, with no infrastructure to manage.
Turn an Athena diagnosis into a reproducible SQL labeling policy.
Fine-tune on captured production data and measure a hard before/after lift.
Integrate with the HyperPod training operator and SageMaker Ground Truth for the rest of the loop.
We ran one full turn of the loop on a home-appliance support router. Captured traffic revealed a new-product blind spot, and a SQL labeling policy turned those captures into training data. A 60-second LoRA fine-tune with the HyperPod training operator ran on the same cluster that served the model. It took the new category from 0% to full recall without a regression on any existing category. None of that training data existed before the model was deployed.
Data Capture is available today on SageMaker HyperPod clusters with the inference operator. To get started, add the dataCapture section to your InferenceEndpointConfig or JumpStartModel resource and deploy. To close the loop on the same cluster, add the amazon-sagemaker-hyperpod-training-operator EKS add-on. The complete code for this walkthrough is in the accompanying GitHub repository.

articles.title: Specialized’s Tarmac SL9 S-Level is built to wreck your Zone 2 ride
articles.text:
I love a good Zone 2 ride. There’s nothing like getting on the bike, settling into a groove, and letting the miles (and hours) flow by. But sometimes when I hopped on the Specialized Tarmac SL9 S-Level, Zone 2 would turn into a tempo ride. It was like having a little imp—the stereotype dressed in red with the pitchfork—on my left shoulder whispering into my ear: “Go fast. This bike was built to go fast. Speed is good. You can do a Zone 2 ride tomorrow.” Normally, I’d count on the good imp—the dude with the harp and wings—on my right shoulder to restrain these urges. But the Tarmac is so seductive that he would just shrug and say “he’s got a point.” And in a moment of weakness, I would drop the hammer and head into the red, just because the SL9 makes that so rewarding.
The Tarmac SL9 is Specialized’s aero road bike, with the S-Level sitting just below the S-Works in Specialized’s top tier of carbon, aero road bikes, where it replaced the Tarmac SL8 Pro. After it got an update this year, I spent several weeks riding it, putting nearly 1,000 miles on it
Specialized offers the Tarmac SL9 in four models, all available with SRAM and Shimano drivetrains (Ars tested the SRAM version). Notably, you don’t need to buy the top-of-the-line bike to get the top-of-the-line groupset. Here’s the breakdown of the Tarmac SL9 lineup (note that the Shimano versions of the Expert is 20 g lighter and Comp is 70 grams heavier than the SRAM versions):
|  | Drivetrain and price | Claimed weight (56 cm SRAM build) | Wheelset | Saddle | Cockpit | Frame and fork | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| S-Works | RED AXS: $13,999.99 Dura-Ace Di2: $13,499.99 | 6.60 kg | Roval Rapide CLX III carbon | S-Works Power with Mirror | Roval Rapide integrated bar/stem | FACT 12r / FACT 12r | 
| S-Level | RED AXS: $10,499.99 Dura-Ace Di2: $9,999.99 | 7.10 kg | Roval Rapide CL III carbon | Power Pro Mirror; hollow titanium rails | Roval Rapide integrated bar/stem | FACT 10r / FACT 12r | 
| Expert | Force AXS: $6,999.99 Ultegra Di2: $6,499.99 | 7.55 kg | Roval C38 carbon | Body Geometry Power Expert; hollow titanium rails | Specialized Expert Shallow Drop alloy bar; Roval Rapide alloy stem | FACT 10r / FACT 12r | 
| Comp | Rival AXS: $4,499.99 105 Di2: $4,199.99 | 8.14 kg | DT Swiss R470 alloy rims; Specialized hubs | Body Geometry Power Comp; chrome alloy rails | Specialized Shallow Drop 6061 alloy bar; Roval Rapide alloy stem | FACT 10r / FACT 12r | 
The $10,500 S-Level offers the top-of-the-line SRAM Red groupset and integrated cockpit, just like the $14,000 S-Works. But the frameset, wheelset, and saddle differ. The major difference is the frame: the S-Level gets the same carbon-fiber FACT 10r frame as the Expert and Comp. At 822 g for a 56 cm frame, the FACT 10r is 135 g heavier than the FACT 12r used on the S-Works. Despite the weight difference, Specialized says the FACT 10r offers the same stiffness and comfort characteristics as its lighter sibling. Along with the frame, different wheelsets and saddles make the S-Level 500 g heavier than the S-Works. With bottle cages, a Garmin mount, and my preferred Shimano XTR XC PD-M9200 MTB pedals, the S-Level I tested weighed in at 7.98 kg. By way of comparison, my own road bike—a Gen 8 Trek Madone—weighs in at 7.71 kg.

articles.title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
articles.text:
Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
Tech executives traded their reputations as visionaries for short-term political gain.
The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda.
Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision. Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers, the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor. And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs.
For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.
What were they thinking?
The people who work for them are just as confused as the rest of us. Tech workers I’ve spoken to at OpenAI, Meta, and other firms have noted an absence of commentary from their leaders post-election. Zuckerberg has yet to address the results internally, while an employee at another AI firm said that “leadership has been pretty silent on Slack.” Most employees share concern about potential anti-data-center legislation and are curious how leadership will adjust to a Democratic Washington, DC. But more than anything, they don’t understand how their bosses didn’t see what was so blindingly obvious to everyone else.
In Silicon Valley, the Gretzkyism “skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been” is a management maxim; it preaches anticipation and foresight over reactiveness to the present moment. Tech entrepreneurs love a good “pivot,” and companies that can’t change with the times get disrupted and die.
Which is why I find it so strange that Zuckerberg, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and so many of Silicon Valley’s other prominent AI leaders and venture capitalists have put themselves in a potentially inescapable political bind. In going all in on President Trump’s cultural and business agenda instead of playing both sides of the aisle as corporate America usually does, they’ve built identities they may not be able to pivot out of. Will anyone really believe that Palantir CEO Alex Karp is suddenly progressive after a year of promising “violence and death to our enemies” and telling investors that the company is “completely anti-woke”?
I believe this is less a surprise than a very public exposure of a fundamental reality: that tech’s most visible leaders are not all-knowing visionary masterminds after all. Insights about social media or artificial intelligence do not make Zuckerberg or Altman experts on politics, the economy, or much else outside of technology. The instant gratification of presidential access, subsidies, and a say in their own regulation blinded them to the basics of political math that they clearly did not understand.
There’s a reason the chief executives of Chase, Boeing, and other Fortune 500 staples don’t go on podcasts to talk about “masculine energy,” or call the president from the stage of a MAGA-friendly AI summit to label fears about AI a “hoax” and a “scam.” This is the learned wisdom of decades operating in an environment where the customer changes every four years but contracts run for 10. Most companies play to both sides of the aisle because they know that their business models and multibillion-dollar projects must outlast the current administration. Instead, Big Tech tied itself to Trump and made its most important goals and investments—many related to grid access and data center permits—immediate targets for Democrats.
In tech, you can always sunset a feature or update some code. But in politics, there is no undo button for failures that change public perception. The tech elites’ decision to visibly align their businesses with a temporary movement has left them no credible way to pivot now that the climate has changed. As one Meta employee who has worked closely with Zuckerberg put it, “Mark is a long-term thinker, but he never charts a plan of how to get there. It’s spray and pray and see what happens.” As for whether employees expect the company to do a strategic postmortem? “Facebook has never really done that.”
“Move fast and break things” might work in a startup, but it’s a terrible strategy for building reputational goodwill. Previous technological leaps, like the rollout of fiber-optic technology and wireless infrastructure, avoided partisan politics. But by kowtowing to the Trump administration, Silicon Valley made artificial intelligence a culture-war issue. Now, when citizens vote on data center proposals from California to Florida, they are no longer considering only technical or economic concerns, but political ones.
Tech leaders didn’t see this coming because they were too focused on the urgency of the AI race to understand how reputational damage could undermine the intangible goodwill—and ultimately the very tangible infrastructure—necessary to win it. The industry’s misreading of the moment has already punctured one myth Silicon Valley holds dear: that its leaders can always see what’s next.
Aaron Zamost is a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square.
