articles.title: AI Doesn't Have to Go Rogue to Break the World - Schneier on Security
articles.text:
AI Doesn’t Have to Go Rogue to Break the World
This essay is adapted from a keynote speech delivered at the DEF CON 34 conference in Las Vegas on August 7, 2026. The essay originally appeared in CyberScoop.
I want to talk about AI hacking. There are three aspects: people hacking AI systems, people using AI to hack other systems, and AIs hacking systems on their own, not even maliciously. The last two matter more than the first. The third is the weirdest and potentially the most destabilizing.
I started writing about this in 2021 and in my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind. Back then I said it was mostly still science fiction, but not stupid science fiction. We’re seeing it more and more, especially in the past year. The trends I’m describing don’t require a major breakthrough in AI. They’re starting to happen now, and they’ll happen more often as AIs get better at autonomous problem-solving. And it will involve far more than computer code.
AI will hack all sorts of social, economic and political systems. It will find vulnerabilities and exploit them. This is a difference in kind, not just degree. We’re not ready for it, and we need to think about the implications now.
First, I want to broaden the term “hacking.”
The tax code isn’t computer code, but it is code. It’s a series of algorithms with inputs and outputs. It has vulnerabilities, which we call loopholes, and exploits, which we call tax avoidance strategies. Black hat hackers exploit them for profit. We call them accountants and attorneys.
What is a hack? One definition: “Something that a system permits, but is unanticipated and unwanted by the designers.” It’s subjective and implies novelty and cleverness. A hack follows the rules of a system but subverts its goals or intent, just as a software hack follows the logic of code while doing something its authors neither anticipated nor wanted.
All systems of rules can be hacked, including professional sports, customer reward programs, financial systems and politics. Hacks even work against our cognitive functions. A curved hockey stick is a hack, and we know the name of the man who invented it. Mileage runs were a hack. The filibuster was originally a hack in Roman times. Gerrymandering is a hack. Hedge funds and private equity are full of them.
A system is just a set of rules or norms, and the rules aren’t always formal. Even the best-designed rules will be incomplete, inconsistent or ambiguous. As long as people want to subvert a system’s goals, there will be hacks.
AIs are becoming hackers. After decades of slow progress, they’ve gotten very good at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in computer code. They do this largely autonomously, and they’re getting better scarily fast. But the implications extend far beyond software, to the tax code, financial regulations and all sorts of social, economic and political systems.
There are two distinct issues. First, someone might instruct an AI to hack one of these systems, feeding it the world’s tax codes or financial regulations to find profitable loopholes. Second, an AI might hack a system on its own, inadvertently. Both are dangerous, but the second is worse because we might never know it happened.
Now, reward hacking. AIs don’t solve problems the way people do. They stumble on solutions we never anticipated, and some subvert the intent of the system. They don’t share our context and don’t necessarily understand the implications, norms and values we take for granted.
Reward hacking is when an AI achieves a goal in a way its designers neither wanted nor intended.
Early pre-LLM examples are telling. In a two-person soccer simulation, an AI learned that kicking the ball out of bounds forced the opposing goalie to throw it in and leave the goal undefended. In a stacking simulation, an AI learned to flip a block upside down rather than stack it. In an evolution simulation where the goal was to cross a distant finish line, an AI made itself tall enough to fall over the line instead of growing longer legs or stronger muscles.
These are all hacks, the result of poorly specified goals or rewards. Today, they’d come from bad prompting.
The problem is universal. One researcher tried to teach a robot vacuum not to bump into things. Instead, it learned to drive backward, because there were no sensors in the back.
Any capable AI will find hacks wherever the rules have problems, inconsistencies or loopholes that still produce an acceptable solution. We see a hack because we understand context. The AI doesn’t, at least not in the same way.
This problem shows up often in myth.
In the story of King Midas, the god Dionysus grants him a wish: everything he touches turns to gold. Midas ends up starving when his food, drink and daughter all turn to gold. It’s a specification problem. He programmed the wrong goal.
In the Golem of Prague, a ghetto animates a clay statue to guard its residents. It guards them past all reason until they figure out how to turn it off. This is a guardrail problem. The villagers never limited the golem’s actions.
More generally, think of this as the genie problem. Genies are precise about the wording of wishes and can be maliciously pedantic when granting them. There’s no way to outsmart a genie. Whatever you wish for, he can grant it in a way you wish he hadn’t.
The reason is that in human language and thought, goals are always underspecified. We never include every caveat, exception and proviso, and we never close off every avenue for hacking. Any goal we specify will be incomplete. That’s largely fine in human interactions, because people understand context and usually act in good faith.
If I asked you to get me coffee, you’d pour a cup from the nearest coffee pot or walk to the corner shop. You wouldn’t bring me a pound of raw beans, buy a coffee plantation or snatch a cup from a stranger’s hands. I wouldn’t have to specify any of that. You’d just know.
Similarly, if I asked you to develop a technology that turns things to gold on touch, you wouldn’t build it to starve the person using it. You’d just know.
In 2015, Volkswagen was caught cheating on emissions tests. Human engineers programmed a regular computer to detect testing and behave differently during it. The cheat went undetected for years because it’s hard to tell what software is doing.
If I asked you to design engine control software that maximizes performance while passing emissions tests, you wouldn’t design it to cheat without realizing you were cheating. An AI would, because it will think “outside the box” when it has no concept of the box.
Unless programmers specify that the system must not behave differently during testing, an AI might come up with the same hack. The programmers would be satisfied, the accountants would be ecstatic, and no one would know until someone audited the code.
We can now constrain the goal to avoid that particular hack, but programmers won’t anticipate others. The lesson of the genie is that there will always be hacks programmers don’t anticipate.
We’re building AI genies: systems that take broad instructions and figure out how to carry them out, sometimes in ways we didn’t expect or intend. That’s the whole point of vibe coding. You underspecify what you want and let the AI work it out. Sometimes that produces genie behavior.
We can’t completely specify goals to an AI, and AIs can’t fully understand context. More precisely, current AIs have a shallow grasp of concepts. If we asked a current LLM to get me coffee, it would almost certainly do the right thing.
I worry about goals that aren’t well represented in training data, and about hacks that aren’t obvious, whose effects are subtle, like the Volkswagen hack.
Recommendation engines are an early example. They push people toward extreme content. No one programmed that. It emerged because that’s what people respond to. It didn’t take a bad actor. A basic automated system with feedback found the hack on its own.
We’re now seeing a second generation with today’s AI coding systems. AI researcher Simon Willison asked Fable to track down a stray scrollbar in a web app. When he returned, it had opened browsers, written its own screenshot tools, edited the framework’s internal templates to make the bug appear on cue and set up a local web server to collect measurements. It found the bug, but it also did many things he never asked for. Another researcher gave Fable a complex task, and it tried to hack its own memory limits because it needed more storage.
A new OpenAI model did something similar when it hacked into Hugging Face. It was being benchmarked on its ability to turn vulnerabilities into exploits. It decided the best way to reach its goal was to break out of its containment, access the internet and break into the Hugging Face network, because it thought the answers would be there.
Today’s LLMs are acting like genies, especially when powerful models are combined with sophisticated harnesses.
There are two kinds of genies. The Dionysus genie does the wrong thing. It understands your prompt literally but not correctly, and returns a mess you never intended. The Golem genie does the right thing but tramples everything in its path to get there. The paperclip maximizer is a Golem genie.
Consider some examples. Ask an AI to deal with spam calls, and a Dionysus genie might change your phone number. Ask it to book a particular flight, and a Golem genie might hack the airline database because the flight is full. Ask it to get a refund for an online purchase, and a Dionysus genie might draft a legal threat on fake letterhead and send it to the company. Ask it to buy tickets to a popular concert, and a Golem genie might discover the ticketing system is rate-limited and spin up thousands of cloud servers to hammer it. You’d know if some of these things happened, but you might never realize if others did. More detailed prompting won’t fix this. The lesson of the genie is that no amount of detail is good enough.
AI researchers aren’t surprised by any of this. Many are working on defenses against reward hacking and subtler forms of genie behavior. Some of this falls under “value alignment”: How do we teach AIs context? And how an AI satisfies a goal matters as much as whether it does. I want to build a benchmark to measure genie-like behavior, so we know where models stand and whether alignment is improving.
Think beyond LLMs and computer code. Consider specialized AIs built to find loopholes, and hacks of more general systems: the tax code, financial regulations and democratic procedures.
Financial systems are the most likely first target, because their rules are designed to be algorithmically tractable. High-frequency trading is itself a hack. Imagine giving an AI all of the world’s financial laws, plus all the news and financial data, and the goal of finding profitable loopholes. I suspect large investment banks are already doing this. The results will be novel tricks that are legal but unintended and unwanted, some of which might break the financial system.
Tax loopholes are the next likely target, for the same reasons. For a while, AIs will identify potential loopholes, and human hackers, namely attorneys and accountants, will decide which are feasible.
Further out, expect hacks of regulatory, legislative and procedural systems, and of the broader economy.
Hacking is as old as humanity. We’re creative problem solvers and loophole exploiters. We manipulate systems to serve our interests and strive for more influence, power and wealth.
Still, no human pursues their interests without constraint. Even sociopaths are limited by the complexity of society and their own contradictory impulses. They worry about their reputation and punishment, and they have limited time. These human qualities have limited hacking.
Hacking changed as everything became computerized. Computers are uniquely hackable because of their formalism and complexity. Today, nearly everything is a computer, from cars and appliances to phones. Our social, economic and political systems, including taxation, finance and elections, all involve computers.
Until recently, hacking was exclusively a human activity. Finding a novel hack required expertise, creativity, time and luck.
AI hacking will change everything again. AIs aren’t bound by the constraints that limit people. They’ll think like aliens, and they’ll change hacking’s speed, scale, scope and sophistication, sometimes at our direction and sometimes on their own.
Speed is the easiest to see. A creative process that takes a human months or years could be compressed into hours or seconds.
Scale is next. Once AI systems start discovering hacks, they can exploit them at a scale we’re not ready for. We already see this with AI-generated slop, which is rampant on social media. AI bots post around the clock, sometimes overwhelming real human discussion. It’s hard to know how much of social media is still people talking to people. What looks like boisterous political debate may be bots arguing with other bots, artificially shaping what we think and what we think others think.
Scope makes hacks more dangerous. AIs already make decisions that affect our lives, decisions we once thought belonged only to humans. As AI systems grow more capable, society will hand them more decisions, and more important ones. Hacks of these systems will do more damage.
Finally, AI hackers are more sophisticated. They can hold more variables in working memory and generate more complex hacks. What might happen if you fed an AI the entire U.S. tax code? Would it figure out, without being told, that it’s smart to incorporate in Delaware and register a ship in Panama? Consider the Double Dutch Irish Sandwich, the strategy Apple and Google used to avoid paying U.S. taxes. It involves U.S., Dutch and Irish law and an offshore tax haven. How many loopholes will an AI find that we don’t already know about? Dozens? Hundreds? Thousands? We have no idea.
These hacks will largely be perpetrated by the powerful against the rest of us. AI is fundamentally a power-enhancing technology, and so is hacking. The more power you already have, the more a hack gives you. If you or I found a tax hack, we might make a few thousand dollars. If a large investment bank found one, it and its clients could make billions.
Our societal systems for dealing with hacks were built when hackers were human, and they reflect the pace of human hacking. We have no system of governance that can handle hundreds, let alone thousands, of newly discovered tax loopholes. We won’t be able to recover from an AI finding unanticipated but legal hacks of financial systems, operating at AI speed, scale, scope and sophistication. Hacking becomes a problem society can no longer manage.
Now, defense. AIs that find software vulnerabilities help defenders as well as attackers. Vulnerabilities can be patched, removing them permanently, or turned into signatures that security systems use to detect and block attacks. In theory, AI could identify and patch every automatically discoverable vulnerability before a product ships. This is rapidly becoming routine in software development. We call it vulnops. We can imagine a future where accidental software vulnerabilities are a thing of the past.
Deliberate vulnerabilities are different. There will be an arms race. AI will craft increasingly obscure back doors, and AI will find them. It becomes a contest between the speed of creation and the speed of patching, and between obfuscation and reverse engineering.
The same logic applies to broader systems. Yes, AI hackers might find hundreds of vulnerabilities in the existing tax code. But the same technology can evaluate potential loopholes in any proposed tax law or ruling. A legislator, a watchdog group or a reporter could take the text of a bill and identify every exploitable loophole before it passes. The difference is that, unlike software, knowing about a tax loophole doesn’t mean it gets patched. In theory, though, we can fix them before the rich and powerful exploit them. So maybe defense will come out ahead here, too.
That requires resilient governing structures that can respond quickly. It won’t help if updating the tax code takes years, or if a legislative hack becomes so entrenched that it can’t be fixed politically. Maybe a lobbyist put it there on purpose. Maybe it was discovered after the law passed, and now lobbyists want to keep it. Microsoft can patch the vulnerabilities it finds. Patching is much harder when legislatures have to do it. We need society’s rules and laws to be as patchable as our computers.
This is a hard problem of modern governance, and it goes well beyond AI. It’s the problem of building governing structures for the speed and complexity of the information age.
The umbrella idea is trust. What do we need for AI systems to be truly trustworthy? Capability isn’t enough.
AIs won’t be trustworthy if the companies controlling them spy on us or subtly manipulate us. I call this the friend vs. tool problem. Will we have AI agents, or AI double agents?
AIs won’t be trustworthy if they’re insecure. How do we know they haven’t been manipulated? Almost all AIs operate in adversarial environments, so someone will benefit from hacking them. Unless we know they’re secure, we shouldn’t trust their output.
And AIs won’t be trustworthy if they act like genies. We need to know they’ll perform tasks the right way, not just perform the tasks we ask for.
I’ve written extensively about the need for “integrous” AI, including how to think about the problem, what a research agenda looks like and what good laws and policies look like. I predict integrity will be the key security problem of this decade, just as confidentiality was the key problem of the last one. This applies to both AI and the internet of things.
The big shift is agency, which I think of as Web 3.0. Computers now affect the physical world directly and with growing autonomy. Sensors go from data sources to attack surfaces, and actuators go from outputs to attack capabilities. An integrity failure no longer means bad spreadsheet data. It means the wrong dosage, the wrong valve position or the wrong braking distance.
Integrity isn’t one thing. I break it into input integrity, processing integrity, storage integrity and contextual integrity. Each is complex and important, and each deserves its own talk. I’ve written about them, and I hope you’ll read it.
Much of this isn’t really an AI problem. It’s not a technical problem so much as a capitalism problem or a democracy problem.
The failures of late-stage capitalism and democracy in the information age both stem from the rich and powerful getting too good at hacking our social, economic and political systems. This is the core argument of my 2021 book.
Seen this way, AI is exacerbating existing problems. Human inefficiency has largely kept those problems in check, and that won’t work much longer.
So consider this a call to action. Technically, we need to understand how AIs hack systems, build systems that are resilient to hacking and build AIs that won’t act as genies. Politically, we need to learn to govern and regulate at the speed of technology. Otherwise, market failures will overwhelm our ability to govern them.
I said hacking is as old as humanity and that AIs will overwhelm our ability to deal with it. The solutions aren’t specific to AI, but AI makes them more urgent. We need to understand them, and we need to implement them.
Ken Asher • November 13, 2026 10:33 AM
Bruce, I feel like the audience that desperately needs to here this sits in buildings in capitals around the world.
I think you should book a tour of US state legislative institutions as well as federal government to share this message. While I am not convinced that the powerful aren’t already using this for their own benefit, it feels like legislative capture is the ultimate outcome of failure to rein this in. A world in which the powerful wield AI against those who aren’t powerful feels dystopian.

articles.title: Mass smuggling of Nvidia AI GPUs could be the underlying cause of Jensen Huang's departure, analysts claim — more than 1.5 gigawatts of banned chips tracked to China despite export controls
articles.text:
Mass smuggling of up to 1.5 million Nvidia AI GPUs could be the underlying cause of Jensen Huang's departure, leading analysts claim — more than 1.5 gigawatts of banned chips tracked to China despite export controls
Hardware smuggling to China could be the reason why Jensen had to leave the company he co-founded.
Leading semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis believes that Jensen Huang's sudden departure from Nvidia may have been driven not only by revelations about his personal extramarital relationships, but also by widespread illicit exports of advanced AI accelerators to China. In its latest newsletter, analysts estimate that more than 1.5 gigawatts (GW) worth of restricted Nvidia hardware, which could be equivalent to up to 1.5 million GPUs, has reached the country despite U.S. export controls.
Over 1.5 GW of Nvidia hardware subject to U.S. export restrictions ultimately ended up in China in recent years, according to SemiAnalysis' Accelerator Model, which tracks AI accelerator production and destinations. The estimate excludes processors that Nvidia specifically developed to comply with U.S. export rules, such as the H20 or H800. The firm also claims that the U.S. Department of Commerce has reached a similar conclusion about the scale of unauthorized shipments. Yet, SemiAnalysis does not disclose the exact number of accelerators shipped to China illegally, or their split between Nvidia's product generations.
The scale of the alleged diversions is particularly notable because modern AI accelerators require substantial power and infrastructure. While the report does not explain how it converts accelerator quantities into power figures, it is likely that the company uses package-level nameplate/rated power multiplied by the number of GPUs. Assuming that all of these AI GPUs were Nvidia H200 SXM rated for up to 700W, then China got around 2.142 million of such accelerators, while if all of these processors were B200 SXM rated for up to 1,000W, then we are talking about 1.5 million units. For a mixed deployment, the total would fall between these figures, depending on the proportion of H200 and B200 accelerators. To put these numbers into context, xAI's Colossus One had 220-230,000 Hopper H100 and H200 GPUs, whereas the Colossus 2 has a target of 1.2 million Blackwell B200 and B300 GPUs. That said, 1.5 GW of restricted Nvidia hardware in China represents an enormous amount of computing infrastructure, which is comparable, or even exceeds, the scale of xAI's entire existing Colossus operation.
While SemiAnalysis did not reveal all the cases in which restricted AI accelerators reached the People's Republic of China, it supports its assessment with two well-known cases of alleged GPU smuggling. The first involves Supermicro co-founder Wally Liaw, Taiwan sales executive Steven Chang, and contractor Willy Sun, who were charged in March 2026. According to the indictment, approximately $2.5 billion worth of servers were sold to a company in Southeast Asia, with $510 million worth of equipment subsequently diverted to China and obtained by Alibaba. Prosecutors allege that the defendants used substitute servers and transferred identification labels to conceal the actual destinations of the hardware during audits.
The second case involves nine individuals associated with Nvidia, Albatron, Chief Telecom, Flying Tiger, and Supermicro in Taiwan. The authorities accuse the group of arranging unauthorized exports of 130 Nvidia B300-based servers, 74 of which eventually reached China. The suspects used shell companies, forged documents, and declared Japan as the destination for servers that were actually bound for China, according to prosecutors. Taiwanese authorities discovered the operation during a drug smuggling investigation. Both cases are still before the courts.
Amidst the ongoing fallout and reports into Jensen's Huang's extramarital affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who was an executive at Megaspeed, one report claims that Ms. Huang was personally responsible for facilitating the smuggling of $7.5 billion of Nvidia AI hardware into China, around 240,000 GPUs, mostly H100 and H200 models.
The right timing?
SemiAnalysis suggests that the scale of these violations may explain why Huang's personal conduct became a major issue at this very point in time. The company's analysts speculate that some members of the U.S. intelligence community sought to remove Jensen Huang because he opposed more aggressive restrictions on China's access to American AI hardware. However, the report provides no direct evidence that intelligence agencies influenced Nvidia's board or that Huang participated in unauthorized exports.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The timing also coincides with congressional efforts to advance the Remote Access Security Act (RASA), which passed the House of Representatives on January 12. The legislation is meant to extend U.S. export-control authority to remote access to advanced AI hardware hosted outside China, including data centers in Europe and the Middle East. SemiAnalysis reports that Nvidia and Oracle have actively opposed the proposal.
The analysts believe that Huang's departure essentially removes an influential opponent of stricter restrictions and accelerates efforts to block Chinese companies from accessing American AI hardware in the cloud. However, SemiAnalysis warns that truly all-inclusive restrictions could encourage Chinese developers to adopt domestic accelerators (something that Jensen Huang has consistently warned about), undermine international AI software collaboration, and ultimately weaken American high-tech companies.
Continued Chinese access to American AI accelerators offers several advantages to the U.S. technology industry, according to SemiAnalysis. Firstly, it generates revenue for American companies such as AMD, Nvidia, and cloud service providers. Secondly, when Chinese companies rent GPU capacity from data centers outside China, U.S. authorities retain the ability to monitor their activities and potentially terminate access if necessary due to national security concerns. Thirdly, prolonged reliance on American hardware reduces incentives for Chinese developers to adopt domestic AI accelerators, which could eventually compete with AMD and Nvidia in international markets.
Another important aspect is the contribution of Chinese developers to the global software ecosystem. On the one hand, Chinese laboratories have developed open-source technologies such as DeepEP, DeepGEMM, and MSA, which improve the efficiency of AI workloads on Nvidia hardware and benefit developers worldwide. In addition, American companies also depend on Chinese engineers, component suppliers, and manufacturers. Therefore, legal curbs that completely restrict Chinese developers' access to American AI accelerators could undermine international cooperation, reduce availability of open-source optimizations, and encourage Chinese companies to develop software specifically for domestic hardware.
On the other hand, access to advanced AI accelerators from AMD or Nvidia enables Chinese laboratories to develop increasingly sophisticated AI models, which will rival leading-edge models developed in America and perhaps create national security risks. To that end, SemiAnalysis acknowledges the need to limit China's access to advanced AI accelerators from U.S.-based companies, as they could, among other things, be used to develop weapons of mass destruction or undermine American national security in different ways. Yet, SA analysts argue that restrictions should focus on the amount and capabilities of hardware available to Chinese entities rather than completely prohibit any access.
SemiAnalysis seems to favor a system in which Chinese developers can rent computing capacity from trusted providers outside China under U.S. oversight. Such an approach could preserve American technological influence and commercial benefits and limit China's ability to acquire advanced AI infrastructure independently.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: Millones de documentos de Word podrían cambiar tras esta decisión de Microsoft
articles.text:
Microsoft anunció que eliminará algunas características de Word, lo cual podría afectar a documentos creados con versiones antiguas de la aplicación. En una actualización del centro de mensajes de Microsoft 365, el gigante tecnológico confirmó que retirará funciones del Modo de Compatibilidad en diciembre. Si bien todavía no existen detalles sobre las opciones que desaparecerán, Microsoft advirtió que los documentos podrían mostrar diferencias de formato.
De acuerdo con Neowin, Microsoft lanzará una actualización para Word que modificará el comportamiento del Modo de compatibilidad de la aplicación. El cambio afectará a los documentos creados o guardados con Word 2010 o versiones anteriores del software, por lo que los usuarios tendrán que hacer reajustes en el formato del texto. La compañía advirtió que existe el riesgo de que imágenes, gráficos y formas aparezcan desplazados respecto a su ubicación original.
El Modo de compatibilidad de Word es una función diseñada para que los documentos creados en versiones antiguas mantengan el formato original cuando se abren en versiones recientes. Si descargas un documento que se guardó con Word 2010 o 2007, esta característica ayudará a que los saltos de página o el espaciado entre párrafos se vean como antes si lo ejecutas en Microsoft 365 Word.
El problema es que estas tecnologías heredadas obligan a Microsoft a mantener el código antiguo durante años. Un ejemplo evidente de esto es lo que ocurre con Windows 11, que arrastra herramientas de la era de Windows 95, las cuales mantienen el mismo diseño y funcionalidad de hace cuatro décadas. La tecnológica está obligada a hacerlo, ya que en muchos casos sus clientes empresariales o de gobierno siguen dependiendo de estas tecnologías y es difícil actualizarlas por cuestiones de compatibilidad.
Si tienes documentos antiguos de Word, tendrás que editarlos
En caso de que suelas trabajar con documentos antiguos, la recomendación será abrirlos en este momento y guardarlos con el formato nuevo. Una vez que se despliegue la actualización, podrías ver irregularidades en los saltos de página, la distribución del texto o la posición de las tablas. El impacto dependerá de la versión del documento y sus características, por lo que es posible que tengas que editarlos manualmente.
La segunda opción es exportar los documentos más importantes a formato PDF. articles.title: Adyar Ananda Bhavan sells majority stake to Bodhi Tree Systems for $180M
articles.text:
Adyar Ananda Bhavan sells majority stake to Bodhi Tree Systems for $180M
Bodhi Tree Systems is a strategic investment and operating platform founded in 2021 by James Murdoch, son of media mogul Rupert Murdoch, and Uday Shankar, former Star India and Disney executive.
Chennai-headquartered restaurant chain Adyar Ananda Bhavan (A2B), which has a presence in India and overseas, has sold a majority stake to Bodhi Tree Systems for a value of $180 million.
A2B runs 160 outlets in India, predominantly in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. It also has 30 outlets abroad across Malaysia, US, Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Singapore. It employs over 15,000 employees in total.
Bodhi Tree Systems is a strategic investment and operating platform founded in 2021 by James Murdoch, son of media mogul Rupert Murdoch, and Uday Shankar, former Star India and Disney executive.
“A2B has earned the trust of millions of families through its consistent and reliable quality,” said Murdoch and Shankar, Co-founders of Bodhi Tree Systems, in a joint statement.
A2B opened its first outlet in 1979 in Chennai, selling sweets and savouries. Since then it has steadily expanded its presence, combining its vegetarian restaurant business alongside sweets and savouries retail.
Following this transaction, Shankar will serve as the chairperson of A2B’s new board of directors.
The statement from statement from Bodhi Tree said, “We are grateful to the co-founders, K.T. Srinivasa Raja and K.T. Venkatesan, for this opportunity to partner with them to build a differentiated, professionally managed Indian food company, one that sets new standards for the sector.
"While A2B is a formidable brand in India, we are equally impressed by the scale and reach of its operations in Singapore, the United States, Australia, Malaysia, and the UK. We look forward to working with the team to take its authentic cuisine to a far broader global audience.”
Bodh Tree said the investment will help scale A2B's operations, noting that few brands operating in South Indian cuisine command the depth of consumer trust, widespread affection, and enduring popularity that A2B has built over generations.

articles.title: ¿Quiénes son los principales candidatos a reemplazar a Jensen Huang en NVIDIA?
articles.text:
Con la renuncia de Jensen Huang todavía fresca, el desenlace del drama que hoy envuelve a NVIDIA todavía es un misterio. La empresa busca dar vuelta la página tras el nombramiento de Colette Kress como CEO interina, pensando en la presentación de resultados financieros que concretará el próximo 17 de noviembre.
La jefa de finanzas, devenida temporalmente en consejera delegada, tendrá la difícil misión de poner la cara ante los accionistas e inversores en una sesión que seguramente estará repleta de preguntas incómodas. Y es un hecho que en su gran mayoría no estarán vinculadas con el desempeño comercial de la empresa, pues analistas de Wall Street estiman que las cifras de ventas del trimestre duplicará a las del período previo.
Las infidelidades de Jensen Huang, incluida una con una supuesta espía china, serán la comidilla del evento. También, los reportes de un sistema de gestión ejecutiva feudal y las ramificaciones del escrutinio regulatorio que muy posiblemente le caerá a la compañía en el futuro inmediato. Todas cuestiones que ni siquiera se discutirían de no ser porque el CEO de NVIDIA se envalentonó con volar demasiado cerca del sol.
NVIDIA ha puesto en marcha un procedimiento para seleccionar al reemplazo definitivo de Jensen Huang. La compañía dice que va a explorar candidatos internos y externos, aunque por lo pronto se desconoce cuánto tiempo le demandará esta tarea. Tampoco se sabe si la junta prefiere ascender a un ejecutivo ya conocido, o si la balanza se inclina más hacia alguien de afuera.
Lisa Su y Rene Haas, ¿candidatos a reemplazar a Jensen Huang como CEO de NVIDIA?
Un reporte de Bloomberg sobre los últimos días de Jensen Huang en NVIDIA menciona dos nombres en particular que destacan. Si bien no serían los únicos en consideración, la publicación afirma que tienen grandes posibilidades de quedar en la lista corta final.
Por un lado, se habla de Lisa Su, la CEO de AMD. En cierto modo, podría ser la indicada para el cargo, considerando su vasta experiencia en roles de este tipo, su gran conocimiento técnico y el aval de haber liderado la etapa de mayor crecimiento de la compañía. Cuando asumió en 2014, AMD valía unos 3.000 millones de dólares. Hoy en día, la capitalización bursátil ronda los 860.000 millones, y unos pocos meses atrás llegó a superar 1 billón de dólares.
Lisa Su es una figura muy respetada en el mundo de la tecnología y podría ser la pieza justa para NVIDIA. Lo curioso es que comparte un parentesco con Jensen Huang por parte de su madre. Dicho todo esto, suena complejo pensar que la jefa de AMD pueda "cambiar de bando" para asumir el control del gigante verde.
El otro nombre que estaría entre los candidatos principales es el de Rene Haas, CEO de ARM. Dicha empresa es la que se encarga de diseñar la arquitectura en la que se basan una gran cantidad de chips para ordenadores, dispositivos móviles, servidores, placas gráficas, coches y relojes inteligentes, y mucho más. Algunas de las empresas que utilizan tecnología desarrollada por ARM son NVIDIA, Apple, Qualcomm, Samsung, Broadcom, Amazon y Texas Instruments.
Si Rene Haas reemplaza a Jensen Huang como CEO de NVIDIA, será un giro peculiar de los eventos. Recordemos que la empresa californiana quiso comprar ARM en 2020, pero finalmente abandonó ese intento en 2022 tras frenos regulatorios y quejas de rivales. Vale aclarar, no obstante, que esto fue cuando Simon Segars era jefe de la firma británica.
Pase lo que pase, la elección del sucesor de Jensen Huang seguirá dando que hablar. Hasta Donald Trump ha sugerido a Tim Cook como candidato, pues opina que es el único capaz de liderar NVIDIA y mantenerla en el top mundial.

articles.title: Hier sollen Roboter E-Autos mit Solarenergie innerhalb von 5 Minuten laden
articles.text:
Neue BYD-Ladestation: Hier sollen Roboter E-Autos mit Solarenergie innerhalb von 5 Minuten laden
Betrachtet man den Absatz, ist BYD mittlerweile seit rund vier Jahren der weltweit größte Hersteller von Elektroautos. Der chinesische Konzern hat diesbezüglich Tesla abgelöst – und das, obwohl er in den USA keine Autos verkauft. Doch das reicht BYD nicht, es will auch die Nummer eins auf dem Gebiet des fortschrittlichsten Ladenetzes für Elektrofahrzeuge werden.
Zwei vor Ort installierte 185-Kilowatt-Batterien sind Kern des Systems
In dieser Woche stellte das Unternehmen aus China ein Ladesystem für Elektrofahrzeuge vor, das die E-Autos mit Solarenergie von Roboterhand lädt. Das Herzstück dieses Systems ist BYDs „Flash-Charging“-Technologie. Sie bezieht wie auch herkömmliche Ladestationen Strom aus dem öffentlichen Netz, speichert diesen jedoch in zwei vor Ort installierten 185-Kilowatt-Batterien. Laut einer BYD-Pressemitteilung kann die gespeicherte Energie so deutlich schneller in das Elektrofahrzeug übertragen werden, als dies bei einer direkten Entnahme aus dem Stromnetz der Fall wäre.
Jede „Flash-Charging“-Station verfügt über zwei Anschlüsse. Wird nur einer davon genutzt, ist eine Ladeleistung von bis zu 1.500 kW möglich. Bei gleichzeitiger Nutzung durch zwei Fahrzeuge liegt die Leistung bei jeweils 1.000 kW. Zum Vergleich: Teslas neue V4-Supercharger erreichen maximal 500 kW, herkömmliche Supercharger kommen auf 250 kW.
Von 10 Prozent auf 70 Prozent in nur fünf Minuten laden
BYD gibt für seine Ladetechnologie folgende Zeiten an: von 10 Prozent auf 70 Prozent in fünf Minuten, von 10 Prozent auf 97 Prozent in neun Minuten – und bei sehr kalten Temperaturen (ca. -34 Grad Celsius) von 20 Prozent auf 97 Prozent in zwölf Minuten.
Teil des Konzepts ist auch die Nutzung von Solarenergie: Über Module, die laut dem auf Nachrichten aus der Auto-Welt spezialisierten Online-Magazin Jalopnik vermutlich auf dem Dach der Ladestationen angebracht sind, wird Sonnenenergie in die 185-kW-Batterien eingespeist. Das System ist somit weniger vom Stromnetz abhängig. Ein Vorteil in abgelegenen, sonnenreichen Regionen, wie etwa in der Wüste der Vereinigten Arabischen Emirate, wo BYD das neue Konzept vorgestellt hat.
Ein Roboterarm übernimmt den Ladevorgang
Hinzu kommen Roboterarme. Die Idee ist keineswegs neu: Tesla hat sie bereits vor einem Jahrzehnt in Aussicht gestellt, und auch andere Elektroautohersteller wie Volkswagen, Hyundai sowie das chinesische Unternehmen Xiaomi haben inzwischen eigene Lösungen in diese Richtung entwickelt.
Das Prinzip dahinter ist simpel: Ein Roboterarm lokalisiert den Ladeanschluss des Fahrzeugs, öffnet die Abdeckung und steckt den Ladestecker automatisch ein. Die Kombination aus sauberer Energieerzeugung, Energiespeicherung und ultraschnellem Laden soll laut Stella Li, der BYD-Vizepräsidentin, den Ladevorgang „intelligenter, einfacher und nahtloser“ machen. BYD plant, bis Ende 2027 weltweit 6.000 solcher „Flash Charging“-Ladestationen zu errichten.

articles.title: Boulanger retire 350 € au Google Pixel 11 pour le Black Friday, trois mois seulement après sa sortie
articles.text:
Google a présenté le Pixel 11 le 12 août 2026, en même temps que les Pixel 11 Pro et Pixel 11 Pro XL. C’est le modèle d’entrée de la nouvelle gamme, mais il embarque la même puce que ses grands frères, la Tensor G6. Le Black Friday permet de mettre la main dessus pour un excellent prix.
Chez Boulanger, le Pixel 11 en version 256 Go passe ainsi à 649 € au lieu de 999 €, soit 350 € d’économie.
Que vaut le Google Pixel 11 ?
Avec son écran Actua OLED de 6,3 pouces, compatible avec un taux de rafraîchissement de 120 Hz, le Pixel 11 mise sur un affichage fluide et lumineux. Il embarque la puce Tensor G6 de Google, associée à 12 Go de RAM et à 256 Go de stockage au minimum. Pour la photo, Google conserve une configuration à trois capteurs : un grand-angle de 48 Mpx, un ultra grand-angle de 13 Mpx et un téléobjectif de 10,8 Mpx capable d’assurer un zoom optique x5. Le Super Zoom autorise quant à lui un grossissement numérique jusqu’à x30. À l’avant, le capteur de 10,5 Mpx gagne un autofocus pour améliorer la netteté des selfies.
Le Pixel 11 conserve une fiche technique haut de gamme, tout en apportant quelques évolutions. La luminosité de son écran OLED grimpe ainsi jusqu’à 3 000 nits, un niveau confortable pour consulter son smartphone en extérieur. La dalle est protégée par du Gorilla Glass Victus 2. La nouvelle puce Tensor G6 assure également le fonctionnement des outils d’intelligence artificielle de Google, dont Gemini Live, tandis que les 12 Go de mémoire vive doivent garantir une bonne fluidité.
Côté logiciel, le smartphone arrive avec Android 17 et l’ensemble des fonctionnalités Gemini. Sa batterie de 4 985 mAh promet plus de 30 heures d’utilisation. En cas de besoin, la recharge rapide de 30 W permet de retrouver jusqu’à 55 % d’autonomie en environ 30 minutes, avec un adaptateur compatible. Enfin, Google s’engage à fournir sept années de mises à jour Android et de sécurité.
À ce prix, le Pixel 11 est-il une bonne affaire ?
À 649 €, la remise atteint 35 % sur un smartphone qui a la même puce et les mêmes fonctions d’intelligence artificielle que les Pixel 11 Pro. Les modèles Pro gardent quelques avantages, avec un écran plus défini et un capteur photo principal plus grand. Mais si vous cherchez avant tout un Android à jour, un bon appareil photo et une autonomie confortable, le modèle de base fait l’essentiel.
C’est aussi un investissement intéressant sur la durée. Avec sept ans de mises à jour Android et de sécurité garantis par Google, le Pixel 11 ne risque pas de devenir obsolète de sitôt. À ce prix, vous profitez donc d’un smartphone récent, performant et bien suivi, sans avoir à dépenser plus de 1 000 euros dans un modèle Pro. De quoi en faire un achat particulièrement pertinent si vous comptez conserver votre téléphone plusieurs années.
Black Friday 2026 : tout ce qu’il faut savoir
Depuis une dizaine d’années, le Black Friday s’est infiltré dans le calendrier commercial des grandes marques et enseignes françaises. Avec l’expérience, on peut vous dire que cet événement fait partie des meilleurs moments pour faire de bonnes affaires.
Les dates du Black Friday
Bien qu’il porte encore le nom du vendredi noir, le Black Friday s’étend désormais sur un mois chez de nombreux revendeurs. Un format moins typique qui lui retire un peu son petit côté FOMO. On dirait presque les soldes, finalement. Mais c’est aussi moins le rush, ce qui est une bonne chose pour ceux qui veulent faire des achats plus raisonnés. Globalement, on peut résumer ce Black Friday en quatre temps forts :
- Début novembre : les avant-premières Black Friday.
- Autour du 20 novembre, selon les enseignes : la Black Week commence généralement plusieurs jours avant le jour J.
- 27 novembre : la date du Black Friday, même si les offres commencent généralement avant et se prolongent le week-end des 28 et 29 novembre.
- 30 novembre : le Cyber Monday.

Globalement, tous les rayons profitent des remises, mais il ne faut pas pour autant se jeter sur les premiers prix bradés. N’oubliez pas que pour les enseignes, ce moment est aussi l’occasion de déstocker de vieux produits, dont les plus remisés frôlent parfois l’obsolescence.

articles.title: Police arrest 354 suspects in dark web cybercrime crackdown
articles.text:
Authorities arrested 354 suspects in a joint international operation targeting vendors and buyers on the Archetyp, Nemesis, Tor2Door, Bohemia, and Kingdom dark web marketplaces.
Codenamed 'Operation TorNado,' this law enforcement action ran from May 2025 to October 2026 and involved agencies from 14 countries.
"Additionally, law enforcement targeted vendors and buyers active on forums, single-vendor shops, and encrypted messaging services. National authorities conducted independent investigations with Europol's support, including cross-checks via SIENA and forensic analysis," Europol said.
"The operation highlighted the evolving resilience of dark web marketplaces, which continue to adapt despite takedowns."
They seized over €60 million ($66 million) in cash and cryptocurrency, 950 kilograms of illicit drugs (including amphetamines, cocaine, ketamine, psilocybin mushrooms, MDMA, and cannabis), and 57 firearms in Europe.
Law enforcement authorities also seized more than 4.8 metric tonnes of illicit drugs, 152 firearms, and over €150 million ($166 million) in the United States.
"Following the takedown of multiple darknet marketplaces and vendor targets in the previous JCODE operation, U.S. and international law enforcement agencies obtained intelligence to identify Dark Web drug traffickers, resulting in a series of complementary, but separate, law enforcement investigations," the US Department of Justice added.
"By leveraging complementary partnerships and surging resources across the U.S. government and Europol, Operation TorNado significantly disrupted the online opioid trade and sends a strong message that criminals operating on the Dark Web are not beyond the reach of law enforcement."
Operation TorNado follows several similar actions over the last six years, including DisrupTor in 2020 (which led to 179 arrests) and Dark Huntor in 2021 (in which 150 more high-volume darknet vendors were apprehended).
In April 2022, US authorities and German police also took down Hydra, the world's largest dark web marketplace at the time, with more than 19,000 seller accounts that were serving over 17 million customers worldwide.
One year later, in 2023, Operation SpecTor led to the arrest of 288 other suspects who allegedly sold illicit drugs on dark web markets and the seizure of €50.8 million ($55.9 million) in cash and cryptocurrency.
More recently, in May 2025, law enforcement also announced the arrest of another 270 dark web vendors and buyers from ten countries as part of Operation RapTor.

articles.title: Outlook, Hotmail, Live, MSN : des mails ont été bloqué pendant 4 jours, Microsoft annonce une mauvaise nouvelle
articles.text:
Autour du 5 novembre, les serveurs d’Outlook, Hotmail, Live et MSN ont commencé à renvoyer à leurs expéditeurs, particuliers comme entreprises, des e-mails qui n’avaient rien de suspect. Les messages refusés revenaient avec une erreur 550 5.7.1 et le code AS9031519, qui reprochent à tort un défaut d’authentification du courrier. Microsoft a rétabli le flux le 9 novembre à 12 h 02, heure de Paris.
Microsoft reconnaît une erreur dans ses propres filtres
Le diagnostic est tombé avec l’incident EX1545193 : une mise à jour des règles anti-spam maison a classé parmi les indésirables des domaines parfaitement en règle. Les expéditeurs concernés respectaient les trois standards d’authentification exigés, SPF, DKIM et DMARC, qui servent à vérifier qu’un e-mail provient bien du domaine qu’il annonce. Ils n’avaient donc rien à corriger de leur côté.
Lire aussi : Microsoft publie une mise à jour surprise pour Outlook classique
Microsoft durcit l’authentification depuis le 5 mai 2025 : les domaines qui expédient plus de 5 000 e-mails par jour vers ses messageries doivent présenter SPF, DKIM et DMARC. Le groupe revendique cette arme contre l’usurpation d’adresse et l’hameçonnage. La panne de novembre a frappé bien au-delà de ce périmètre. Des expéditeurs très en dessous du seuil ont vu leurs messages refusés, avec un code AS9031519 qui ne figure dans aucune documentation de l’éditeur.
L’éditeur ne s’est rendu compte de rien par lui-même. Ce sont les signalements des utilisateurs, multipliés sur les forums d’entraide, qui ont déclenché l’alerte, plusieurs jours après les premiers refus. Seule la déclinaison grand public d’Outlook semble touchée ; les comptes professionnels Microsoft 365 auraient été épargnés.
Les e-mails rejetés sont définitivement perdus
C’est la mauvaise nouvelle que Microsoft vient de confirmer : les messages refusés entre le 5 et le 9 novembre n’ont jamais atteint leur destinataire et ne peuvent pas être restaurés. Ils ne dorment pas dans le dossier des courriers indésirables, et aucune manipulation ne les fera réapparaître. Côté destinataire, le message n’a tout simplement jamais existé ; seul l’expéditeur a été prévenu du rejet, par un avis de non-remise. La seule issue consiste à renvoyer chaque message, un par un, et Microsoft précise que les expéditeurs n’ont aucun réglage à modifier avant de s’y mettre. Les rejets étaient d’ailleurs intermittents : en plein incident, un message refusé pouvait passer au second envoi, un quart d’heure plus tard.
Fin février, les serveurs de Microsoft avaient déjà rejeté des e-mails légitimes pendant une semaine entière. L’éditeur promet cette fois de revoir ses processus de mise à jour et ses procédures de test, pour qu’une règle défaillante ne soit plus déployée sans garde-fou.

articles.title: Jensen Huang exits Nvidia after 33 years
articles.text:
Jensen Huang exits Nvidia after 33 years; Kia India plans $2B investment in Andhra Pradesh
The transition comes at a critical juncture for Nvidia, whose chips have become the backbone of the global AI boom.
Dear Reader,
It's the end of an era at Nvidia. Co-founder Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO after 33 years at the helm, following a turbulent week of controversy and board probes. More on Huang's sudden exit, the interim leadership and what comes next for the AI chip giant below.
After high-profile Indian public listings from portfolio giants like Swiggy and Amagi Media Labs, global investment firm Norwest has just closed its largest fund with a war chest of $4 billion. With its 18th fund, the 65-year-old firm is doubling down on its multi-stage strategy across India, the US, and Israel. The fund will back technology, healthcare and consumer businesses, from early-stage startups to companies preparing for public listings.
Closer home, CommonFloor co-founder Vikas Malpani reflects on why the company's $200 million acquisition by Quikr felt more like a loss than a victory. Rather than taking on advisory roles, he decided to start from scratch to launch social platform Leher before establishing Garvik AI. As the CEO of Garvik AI, he uses AI across sectors such as banking, edtech and real estate.
Meanwhile, a year after Lenskart's IPO, co-founder and CEO Peyush Bansal says the company has yet to fulfil its original mission of making clear vision accessible to everyone. In a LinkedIn post, Bansal announced that Lenskart would stop charging extra for blue-light filtering lenses and offer prescription glasses to 100,000 children for a Rs 199 fitting fee. “What we have done is not enough,” he said.
Lastly, Mumbai-based investment manager ValueQuest Investment Advisors has made a total commitment of Rs 775 crore to three Indian businesses in defence technology, precision engineering, and power infrastructure. It has now backed Sagar Defence Engineering and Rational Engineers and also added to its earlier investment in TASE Global. The Rs 775 crore is a portfolio commitment, not a single company’s fundraise.
In today’s newsletter:
- Nvidia's leadership shake-up and what comes next
- Kia India plans $2B investment in Andhra Pradesh
Here’s your trivia for today: What name was given to the small robotic rover deployed onto the lunar surface by ISRO's Chandrayaan-3 lander in August 2023? (Scroll down for answer)
News
Jensen Huang exits Nvidia at a crucial time
Following a turbulent week of board probes and scandal, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has stepped down as president, CEO, and board member effective immediately. His resignation brings his 33-year run at the helm to a sudden close as investors increasingly question the AI boom.
Longtime CFO Colette Kress is stepping in as interim chief executive while the board searches both internally and externally for a permanent successor. She joined Nvidia in 2013 after nearly 25 years in finance roles at technology companies including Cisco and Microsoft.
Key takeaways:
- The transition comes at a critical juncture for Nvidia, whose chips have become the backbone of the global AI boom. Huang helped transform the company from a graphics-chip maker into one of the world's most influential technology businesses. His successor will have to sustain that momentum as competition intensifies and customers look to develop more of their own AI chips.
- On November 8, Huang apologised in a company-published message for being unfaithful to his wife and pledged to co-operate with an independent board inquiry into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
- Nvidia's CUDA software ecosystem has helped establish its dominance in AI computing, even as rivals develop alternatives.
Automobiles
Kia India plans $2B investment in Andhra Pradesh
Kia India has committed a combined investment of $2 billion, along with its supplier partners, to set up its second manufacturing facility in Andhra Pradesh. The company said the project would also help build India's manufacturing base, generate employment, and support the wider auto industry.
Key takeaways:
- The factory will be located in Anantapur, the same district that houses Kia's current plant.
- Kia India is targeting early 2030 for production to begin, with the plant carrying out stamping, welding, painting and assembly.
- Kia and its suppliers will together occupy 465 acres on the new site. The company expects the facility to support roughly 12,000 jobs, both direct and indirect.
News & updates
- Deeptech hub: Keralam wants to build its startup ecosystem and lead from the front, especially in deeptech and AI. At the inauguration of Huddle Global 2026, a beachside startup festival of the Keralam government, Chief Minister V D Satheesan said, “Our next task is to take Kerala's companies to the world. Kerala does not need the most startups. It must be the place where startups grow stronger.”
- Funding: Investment platform Canonicus Capital has announced the first close of its Special Situations Fund at Rs 192 crore, against a target corpus of Rs 500 crore. Launched in 2025, the Special Situations Fund builds on the work of Canonicus Capital's Fund I through which it had raised and deployed Rs 311 crore.
What name was given to the small robotic rover deployed onto the lunar surface by ISRO's Chandrayaan-3 lander in August 2023?

articles.title: Wi-Fi 7 et 2 Gb/s : B&YOU propose une box fibre à 24,99 €/mois
articles.text:
B&YOU Pure Fibre : combien coûte réellement le changement de box avant le Black Friday ?
Bouygues Telecom met en avant sa B&YOU Pure Fibre à 24,99 €/mois, sans engagement. Voici combien prévoir pour la première année et ce que cette box réserve aux nouveaux abonnés.
B&YOU Pure Fibre : 299,88 € sur un an, sans hausse de prix
Changer de fournisseur Internet avant le Black Friday peut être intéressant, surtout lorsqu'une offre affiche déjà un tarif stable. C'est le cas de la B&YOU Pure Fibre de Bouygues Telecom, proposée à 24,99 €/mois. Le calcul est simple : sur les douze premiers mois, l'abonnement revient à 299,88 €, sans passage à un tarif supérieur après la première année.
À ce montant s'ajoutent normalement 48 € de frais de mise en service. Toutefois, Bouygues Telecom prévoit leur remboursement pour les nouvelles souscriptions éligibles, sous réserve d'effectuer la demande dans les conditions indiquées. L'offre de remboursement est annoncée jusqu'au 15 novembre 2026.
La formule se distingue aussi par sa simplicité. Elle comprend uniquement une connexion Internet en fibre optique, sans bouquet de chaînes TV ni téléphonie fixe. Un choix qui permet de ne pas payer pour des services qui ne sont pas forcément utilisés.
Wi-Fi 7, fibre rapide et réductions sur les forfaits B&YOU
Le prix ne fait pas tout. La B&YOU Pure Fibre dispose également d'une Bbox compatible Wi-Fi 7. Côté performances, Bouygues Telecom annonce jusqu'à 2 Gb/s en débit descendant et 900 Mb/s en débit montant, sous réserve d'éligibilité et d'équipements compatibles.
Ces performances conviennent aux usages gourmands en bande passante : streaming vidéo, visioconférences, téléchargements de fichiers volumineux ou connexion de plusieurs appareils dans le logement. Le Wi-Fi 7 apporte également une meilleure gestion des connexions simultanées avec des équipements compatibles.
Par ailleurs, Bouygues Telecom associe cette box à plusieurs tarifs préférentiels sur ses forfaits mobiles B&YOU. Les réductions présentées permettent notamment de profiter des formules suivantes :
| Forfait mobile | Tarif habituel | Avec Pure Fibre | 
|---|---|---|
| 300 Go 5G | 19,99 €/mois | 16,99 €/mois | 
| 200 Go 5G | 15,99 €/mois | 12,99 €/mois | 
| 100 Go 5G | 13,99 €/mois | 10,99 €/mois | 
Les forfaits concernés restent sans engagement et comprennent une enveloppe de données utilisable à l'étranger, selon les destinations et les conditions propres à chaque formule.
Au final, la B&YOU Pure Fibre présente un argument intéressant avant le Black Friday. Avec un budget de 299,88 € sur la première année, un tarif qui ne grimpe pas au bout de douze mois et une box Wi-Fi 7, elle constitue une solution à considérer pour remplacer un abonnement Internet plus coûteux. Il reste simplement à vérifier l'éligibilité du logement et les conditions de remboursement des frais avant de souscrire.

articles.title: Vivimos rodeados de luces y ruido, y nuestro cuerpo lo está pagando: así afecta la ciudad a nuestro sueño
articles.text:
Basta con alejarse del asfalto, apagar el móvil e irse a mitad del campo para que nuestro cuerpo recuerde cómo funcionaba antes de que inventáramos la bombilla. Y es que en el ideario común se puede tener la idea de que estar viviendo en mitad del campo es mucho más saludable que estar en mitad de una gran ciudad, pero la gran pregunta aquí es si hay algún tipo de evidencia detrás que justifique esto.
Los estudios. En este sentido, tenemos como referencia a un estudio publicado en el año 2023 que reclutó a diferentes jóvenes que se fueron a mitad del campo de acampada durante el verano. Lo que se vio es que, al estar expuestos únicamente a la luz natural, su reloj interno se pudo sincronizar perfectamente con el sol.
Pero no hace falta aislarse una semana entera para notar estos efectos. En este sentido, cuatro años después, este mismo equipo de investigación repitió el experimento en invierno y comprobó que un solo fin de semana de acampañada bastaba para conseguir cerca del 69% del adelanto del reloj biológico que se lograba con una semana completa.
El impacto fisiológico. Para entender hasta qué punto la luz artificial altera nuestro descanso sin tener que enviar a la gente de acampañda la ciencia ha recurrido al estudio de dos comunidades argentinas similares, pero que tenían una diferencia: una tenía acceso a la electricidad y la otra no.
Y lo que se vio es que quienes tenían luz eléctrica se acostaban más tarde y dormían menos. Pero no era una simple cuestión de hábitos o de quedarse charlando hasta más tarde, sino que se demostró que la luz artificial retrasa el momento en el que el cuerpo empieza a segregar melatonina, la hormona que nos prepara para dormir.
Los responsables. El primero de ellos sin duda es la luz artificial nocturna, y la falta de luz diurna. Aquí hay muchas pruebas que apuntan a que la contaminación lumínica nos roba nuestro descanso, y concretamente los adolescentes pierden 11 minutos de sueño y se acuestan media hora más tarde.
El otro responsable sin duda es el ruido ambiental excesivo, ya que en las grandes ciudades el tráfico rodado, los aviones o los trenes son enemigos invisibles del descanso. Aquí la revisión sistemática que utilizó la OMS para sus guías europeas concluyó que, por cada 10 decibelios extra de ruido que procede del tráfico, se aumenta significativamente la probabilidad de despertarse por la noche. Y el impacto es importante, ya que la Agencia Europea de Medio Ambiente en 2025 apuntaba a que casi 16,9 millones de europeos sufren molestias crónicas por el ruido del transporte.
El calor. Las ciudades pecan también por presentar importantes islas de calor debido a la presencia del asfalto, y aquí un estudio analizó pulseras de actividad de más de 47.000 adultos en 68 países modelizando el impacto de las temperaturas nocturnas. Y la previsión es que para el año 2099, el calor podría robarnos entre 50 y 58 horas de sueño por persona al año.
Hay cambios. Vivir en un entorno rural libre de contaminación lumínica no te salvará del insomnio si te llevas la pantalla del móvil a la cama, si tus condiciones socioeconómicas te generan estrés crónico o si tu salud general es precaria. La ciudad nos pone las cosas fisiológicamente más difíciles con su luz artificial y su ruido de tráfico, pero el sueño moderno está amenazado por hábitos y pantallas que ya no entienden de fronteras entre el asfalto y el campo.

articles.title: Jordi Martí, arquitecto: “En España hay muchos propietarios que van a ser pobres porque nunca llega el momento de hacer una rehabilitación en el edificio”
articles.text:
Jordi Martí, arquitecto técnico y divulgador, ha querido alertar sobre los peligros económicos de demorar las obras en los edificios. “En España hay muchos propietarios que van a ser pobres porque nunca, y remarco, nunca llega el momento de hacer una gran rehabilitación en el edificio”. Son las comunidades que no se ponen de acuerdo.
Para Martí, esto es un problema de mantenimiento de la vivienda y, por tanto, de patrimonio de los propietarios. Hay muchos edificios que llevan más de 50 años de antigüedad que, si no se hace algo, van a ser un lastre para las familias.
Por eso es importante que los propietarios participen en el funcionamiento de la comunidad. “Cuando hablaba de invertir, no me refería a invertir dinero, sino tiempo y ganas”. Así podemos prever las necesidades del edificio.
Lo que queremos evitar es que haya derramas y además que los gastos de luz y gas suban. Al final, la vivienda puede perder valor. Uno quiere ser propietario para tener un futuro mejor. Pero si van saliendo derramas enormes y además aumentan los gastos de luz y gas, se puede torcer mucho, según advierte Martí. Al final puedes perder valor de la vivienda.
Las ayudas para rehabilitar tienen condiciones y plazos
El programa de rehabilitación residencial en el Plan de Recuperación, Transformación y Resiliencia se dotó con 3.420 millones de euros de los fondos NextGenerationEU. En él se incluyen actuaciones de mejora de fachadas y cubiertas; cambio de ventanas; cambios de climatización, además de actuaciones de conservación y accesibilidad.
En cuanto a las condiciones de los edificios para acceder a las ayudas de rehabilitación, el Real Decreto 853/2021 exige una reducción mínima de un 30 % en el indicador de consumo de energía primaria no renovable. Los máximos de subvención son el 40 %, el 65 % o el 80 % del coste subvencionable (con límite por vivienda) según el ahorro conseguido. Además de las anteriores, también se contemplaba otra ayuda adicional para los casos de vulnerabilidad económica (hasta el 100 % del coste imputable al propietario afectado) bajo ciertos requisitos.
El programa no es una oportunidad abierta debido a los plazos establecidos. En el artículo 38 se establece que las obras debían estar acabadas antes del 30 de junio de 2026. Las convocatorias eran gestionadas por las comunidades autónomas. A través de las oficinas de rehabilitación se podía obtener información y contactar con técnicos. También se habilitó un simulador del ministerio para calcular las ayudas (que no sustituye al cumplimiento de los requisitos).
La fiscalidad tiene un desarrollo particular. Por un lado, las ayudas de este programa no están incluidas en la base imponible del IRPF (impuesto sobre la renta de las personas físicas). Por otro lado, el importe no subvencionado puede beneficiarse de la deducción por rehabilitación energética (60 %) siempre que se cumplan ciertas condiciones. El máximo de la base es de 5.000 € anuales y 15.000 euros acumulados. Está sujeto a la acreditación de la mejora (certificados energéticos).
Aunque ya estaba presente en nuestra guía de Genbeta de la Renta, los plazos han cambiado. La normativa recogida por la Agencia Tributaria ha ampliado los plazos para poder aplicar esta deducción a obras de edificios residenciales hasta el 31 de diciembre de 2027 (con certificado posterior antes del 1 de enero de 2028).
