articles.title: Run Native DLA Inference in Python on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin Using cuDLA | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
AI applications at the edge often need to run multiple neural networks within limited compute and power budgets. NVIDIA Deep Learning Accelerator (DLA) platforms provide dedicated hardware for deep learning inference. On NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, DLA executes supported neural network operations, allowing applications to offload inference work from the GPU. This can improve power efficiency and leave GPU capacity available for other application tasks.
NVIDIA cuDLA is the runtime API for managing execution on this accelerator. Applications use it to create DLA devices, load compiled networks, register memory buffers, and submit inference tasks. The cuda.bindings.cudla module exposes these APIs directly to Python, so developers can integrate DLA execution into their applications without writing C++ code to manage the runtime.
This post walks through the inference lifecycle on Jetson AGX Orin using an image classification example. It briefly covers installation and compiling a model into a DLA loadable, then follows execution from creating a device and loading the network to managing buffers, synchronizing execution, and reading the output. The example also shows how GPU and DLA stages work together in a single Python application.
How cuDLA fits within a Python application
DLA is a fixed-function accelerator. This means that it efficiently performs fixed operations, such as convolutions and pooling, that are common in modern neural network architectures. It does not have as many supported layers as the GPU, but it still supports a wide variety of layers used in many popular neural network architectures.. To learn more about when and why to use DLA, see Getting Started with the Deep Learning Accelerator on NVIDIA Jetson Orin.
Introduced in cuda-bindings 13.3.0 as part of the CUDA Python project, cuda.bindings.cudla is a thin, Cython-generated Python layer over the cuDLA C++ API for hybrid-mode workflows. It exposes thirteen functions, nine data types, eight enums for hybrid-mode workflows, where CUDA streams coordinate DLA execution with GPU work. On Jetson Orin, NVIDIA JetPack supplies the underlying libcudla.so runtime. 
The Python bindings expose that runtime directly to your application, while inference executes on DLA hardware. This complements the existing C++ workflow by allowing runtime management and inference orchestration to remain in Python. Figure 1 shows where cuda.bindings.cudla fits in the stack.
While this post focuses on Jetson, NVIDIA RTX Spark brings DLA inference to mainstream Windows AI developer laptops for the first time, extending cuDLA well beyond the embedded and robotics space. The cuda.bindings.cudla API is identical on both platforms, so everything in this post related to cuDLA APIs applies directly to RTX Spark as well.
Prerequisites and installation
If you are on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin running JetPack, libcudla.so ships with the JetPack installation and is automatically discoverable by the bindings. There is nothing additional to install for the DLA runtime itself—no separate cuDLA SDK and no extra runtime libraries.
Install the cuDLA Python bindings:
pip install "cuda-bindings>=13.3.0"
The JetPack default Python may be older than 3.10, which is the minimum required version. Install Python 3.12 from the deadsnakes PPA if needed:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y software-properties-common
sudo add-apt-repository -y ppa:deadsnakes/ppa
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y python3.12 python3.12-venv python3.12-dev
python3.12 -m venv ~/dla-env
~/dla-env/bin/pip install "cuda-bindings>=13.3.0"
You only need TensorRT to compile a trained model into a DLA loadable. To run an existing loadable, you only need libcudla.so, which ships with JetPack.
Compiling a DLA loadable
A DLA loadable is the binary artifact produced by the TensorRT trtexec tool. It encodes a trained network in a format DLA hardware can execute directly. This compilation example targets TensorRT 11.4.1 with CUDA 13.4 Update 1 on Jetson AGX Orin running JetPack 7.2.2 or later. For an FP16 CHW16 loadable, using an FP16-typed ONNX model with fixed input dimensions, use the following:
trtexec \
    --onnx=your_model_fp16.onnx \
    --useDLACore=0 \
    --inputIOFormats=chw16 \
    --outputIOFormats=chw16 \
    --memPoolSize=dlaSRAM:1 \
    --saveEngine=model.bin \
    --buildDLAStandalone
The key flags are:
- --useDLACore=0 targets the first DLA engine on Orin
- --buildDLAStandalone produces a raw DLA loadable that does not require TensorRT at inference time
- I/O format options select CHW16 layout
TensorRT 11 derives precision from the model’s tensor types; --fp16 and --int8 are no longer supported. This example assumes fixed input dimensions, so --shapes is omitted.
This reflects the sample’s current FP16 path and TensorRT 11 flag changes.
Not every network layer is DLA-compatible, and preprocessing the ONNX graph to trim DLA-incompatible head and tail layers is often necessary. The Python workflow in the next section works with any .bin or .nvdla file you produce. Figure 2 shows the split between the one-time build step and the on-device runtime.
The Python workflow
For the CUDA and cuDLA calls, three imports cover everything:
import numpy as np
from cuda.bindings import cudla
from cuda.bindings import driver, runtime
cudla is the new module. driver and runtime are the existing cuda-python bindings for the CUDA driver and runtime APIs—used here for stream management, memory allocation, and data transfers. Everything runs through a single CUDA stream, the coordination point for DLA and GPU work in hybrid mode.
Step 1: Initialize CUDA and create a DLA device
cudla.Mode.CUDA_DLA selects hybrid mode, where you submit DLA tasks through a CUDA stream. This enables GPU-DLA pipelines: preprocessing kernels, DLA inference, and postprocessing kernels can all be enqueued on the same stream and executed in order.
driver.cuInit(0)
runtime.cudaSetDevice(0)
cudla_device = cudla.create_device(0, int(cudla.Mode.CUDA_DLA))
This release does not support standalone mode (which requires the NvSci buffer and sync primitives). create_device raises CudlaError(ErrorUnsupportedOperation) if you request it.
Step 2: Load the loadable
Pass the loadable as a Python bytes object directly to module_load_from_memory. No file path or filesystem handle—just raw bytes, equally easy to load from memory-mapped files, embedded resources, or network streams.
with open("model.bin", "rb") as f:
    loadable_data = f.read()
module_handle = cudla.module_load_from_memory(
    cudla_device, loadable_data, len(loadable_data), 0
)
Step 3: Introspect the loaded module
Before allocating any memory, query the module to find out exactly what tensors it expects:
num_inputs = cudla.module_get_attributes(
    module_handle, int(cudla.ModuleAttributeType.NUM_INPUT_TENSORS)
)
num_outputs = cudla.module_get_attributes(
    module_handle, int(cudla.ModuleAttributeType.NUM_OUTPUT_TENSORS)
)
input_descs = cudla.module_get_attributes(
    module_handle, int(cudla.ModuleAttributeType.INPUT_TENSOR_DESCRIPTORS)
)
output_descs = cudla.module_get_attributes(
    module_handle, int(cudla.ModuleAttributeType.OUTPUT_TENSOR_DESCRIPTORS)
)
Each descriptor is a cudla.ModuleTensorDescriptor with properties for buffer size (size_), tensor shape (n, c, h, w), name, data format, and stride. All subsequent allocation calls are driven by desc.size_ with no hardcoded sizes anywhere in the application. This introspection step is what makes the workflow model-agnostic: the same code paths handle any loadable regardless of network architecture.
Step 4: Allocate GPU memory
input_gpu  = runtime.cudaMalloc(input_descs[0].size_)[1]
output_gpu = runtime.cudaMalloc(output_descs[0].size_)[1]
CUDA driver and runtime calls return a status code as the first element of a tuple. The full sample wraps every such call in a helper that checks the returned status and raises on failure—the snippets here elide that for readability, but error checking is essential in production code. For models with multiple inputs or outputs, iterate over input_descs and output_descs and allocate one buffer per tensor. The size_ field on each descriptor gives the exact byte count.
Step 5: Register GPU buffers with cuDLA
This is the step unique to cuDLA. GPU buffers must be registered with the DLA device before they can appear in a task. Registration returns a DLA-side handle that the hardware uses to access the buffer:
input_registered  = cudla.mem_register(
    cudla_device, int(input_gpu), input_descs[0].size_, 0
)
output_registered = cudla.mem_register(
    cudla_device, int(output_gpu), output_descs[0].size_, 0
)
The int() cast extracts the raw pointer from the CUDA memory object. cuda.bindings returns opaque handle objects, and int() is how you pass them to C-level APIs that expect a pointer.
Step 6: Prepare input data and copy to GPU
Preprocessing—normalizing values, matching the expected tensor stride and data format—is the only model-specific code in the script. The tensor descriptor stride, data_format, and data_type fields tell you exactly how to lay out the data. For a multi-input model, repeat the copy for each input buffer. Everything else before and after this block is identical regardless of what network is inside the loadable.
stream = driver.cuStreamCreate(driver.CUstream_flags.CU_STREAM_NON_BLOCKING)[1]
# Preprocess your input into a numpy array `input_cpu`
# matching the tensor layout described by input_descs[0] ...
runtime.cudaMemcpyAsync(
    input_gpu, input_cpu, input_descs[0].size_,
    runtime.cudaMemcpyKind.cudaMemcpyHostToDevice, stream
)
runtime.cudaMemsetAsync(output_gpu, 0, output_descs[0].size_, stream)
Step 7: Build the task and submit
cudla.Task wraps the cudlaTask C struct. Assigning a Python list to task.input_tensor or task.output_tensor automatically updates the corresponding count field. submit_task enqueues the inference work onto the CUDA stream, sequencing it with any GPU kernels before or after it on the same stream.
task = cudla.Task()
task.module_handle = module_handle
task.input_tensor  = [int(input_registered)]
task.output_tensor = [int(output_registered)]
task.wait_events   = 0
task.signal_events = 0
cudla.submit_task(cudla_device, int(task), 1, int(stream), 0)
Step 8: Synchronize and read back
The first sync waits for the DLA task to complete. Allocating output_cpu as a numpy array of the descriptor’s byte size gives the D2H copy a destination buffer; the second sync ensures the transfer is done before you read from it.
runtime.cudaStreamSynchronize(stream)
output_cpu = np.empty(output_descs[0].size_, dtype=np.uint8)
runtime.cudaMemcpyAsync(
    output_cpu, output_gpu, output_descs[0].size_,
    runtime.cudaMemcpyKind.cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost, stream
)
runtime.cudaStreamSynchronize(stream)
Step 9: Cleanup
Every handle created has a matching destroy call—DLA device, module, registered memory handles, GPU allocations, and stream.
cudla.mem_unregister(cudla_device, input_registered)
cudla.mem_unregister(cudla_device, output_registered)
cudla.module_unload(module_handle, 0)
cudla.destroy_device(cudla_device)
runtime.cudaFree(input_gpu)
runtime.cudaFree(output_gpu)
driver.cuStreamDestroy(stream)
Error handling is native to Python
All cuDLA API calls raise cudla.CudlaError on failure rather than returning error codes. The exception carries both the numeric status and its human-readable name:
try:
    device = cudla.create_device(0, int(cudla.Mode.CUDA_DLA))
except cudla.CudlaError as e:
    print(e)  # e.g. "ErrorInvalidDevice (8)"
DLA workflows fit naturally into standard Python exception handling. I recommend try/finally for cleanup. DLA device handles are opaque C resources and will not release themselves on garbage collection. Branch on e.status against cudla.Status enum values to handle specific failure modes, from parameter errors (ErrorInvalidParam) up to hardware-level faults (ErrorDlaErrEngineTimeout).
What is the resulting output?
After cudaStreamSynchronize returns, output_cpu holds the raw DLA output for your network as a numpy array, ready for any standard Python postprocessing. What you do with it depends entirely on the model, including class scores, feature maps, bounding box coordinates. The cuDLA Python layer hands you the bytes. Interpreting them is the same postprocessing you would write in any Python inference pipeline, and you can chain it directly with NumPy, PyTorch, or OpenCV without leaving the Python process.
To make this concrete: for a ResNet-50 backbone compiled as a DLA loadable, the sample output would look like this:
cuDLA device created: 0x55a1b2c30000
Module loaded: 0x55a5b6c70000
numInputTensors = 1
numOutputTensors = 1
Input 0:  size=..., shape=(1,64,56,56), name=resnetv17_pool0_fwd
Output 0: size=..., shape=(1,2048,7,7), name=resnetv17_stage4_activation2
SUBMIT IS DONE (task queued; completion pending)
Output tensor written to host
The sample output tells you the exact buffer sizes and tensor names the loadable expects, which your preprocessing and postprocessing code can read directly rather than hardcoding them. After synchronization, output_cpu is a flat numpy array; interpret or reshape it using the data_type, data_format, stride, and shape fields from output_descs[0] and pass it to whatever downstream stage your pipeline requires.
The workflow from create_device to cudaStreamSynchronize is the same regardless of network architecture. Only the tensor names, sizes, and postprocessing change.
Final steps
The cuda.bindings.cudla module ships in cuda-bindings 13.3.0. Install it, compile a loadable with trtexec, and the nine steps above take you from a .bin file to DLA inference results directly in Python on the same board.
pip install "cuda-bindings>=13.3.0"
The unit tests for enums, POD types, and API surface ship in the NVIDIA/cuda-python GitHub repo under cuda_bindings/tests/cudla/ and run entirely without DLA hardware—no libcudla.so required:
pytest cuda_bindings/tests/cudla/ -v
Get started with cuDLA in Python
For a complete end-to-end inference example, sample inputs, and scripts to prepare the model and compile a DLA loadable locally, refer to the Deep Learning Accelerator samples.
To learn more, visit the NVIDIA/cuda-python GitHub repo.

articles.title: Linky : comment vérifier si vos heures creuses changent dès ce 1er décembre — Frandroid
articles.text:
L’option Heures pleines/Heures creuses (HP/HC) est l’un des dispositifs permettant d’inciter les consommateurs à contribuer directement à l’équilibre du réseau électrique. Les abonnés sont encouragés à limiter leurs usages pendant les heures pleines, lorsque la demande d’électricité est généralement plus importante, et à reporter leurs consommations les plus énergivores durant les heures creuses.
Le kilowattheure y est en effet moins cher. Au tarif réglementé d’EDF (Tarif Bleu) en vigueur depuis le 1er août 2026, il coûte 0,1589 € TTC en heures creuses contre 0,2142 € en heures pleines, soit environ 26 % de moins ; chez les autres fournisseurs, l’écart dépend de l’offre souscrite.
Mais pour continuer à jouer ce rôle, les plages horaires doivent s’adapter aux évolutions du système électrique. Avec l’essor du solaire, l’électricité est désormais plus abondante en journée, surtout en milieu d’après-midi. Il devient donc nécessaire d’encourager les consommateurs à déplacer une partie de leurs usages vers ces périodes de forte production. Jusqu’ici principalement concentrées la nuit pour la majorité des abonnés, les heures creuses seront ainsi en partie repositionnées en journée à partir du 1er décembre, comme l’a annoncé ce lundi 9 novembre Enedis, le gestionnaire du réseau public de distribution d’électricité.
Quels sont les nouveaux horaires ?
Vous bénéficierez toujours de 16 heures pleines et de 8 heures creuses. C’est leur répartition qui va changer. Au moins 5 heures creuses consécutives seront maintenues durant la nuit, tandis que les heures restantes pourront être positionnées en journée (3 au maximum).
Désormais, les plages horaires varieront également selon la saison afin de tenir compte des différences de production photovoltaïque entre l’hiver et l’été. Dans les détails, les nouveaux créneaux seront répartis comme suit :
Du 10 au 30 novembre, le LUBA mini 2 AWD 1500 passe à 1 399 € au lieu de 1 899 €, support de lavage offert ! Sans fil, navigation LiDAR 360°, évitement précis des obstacles, tonte des bordures… La tonte sans effort, même pour les jardins les plus complexes.
- En hiver (du 1er novembre au 31 mars) : les heures creuses pourront être placées entre 11 h et 17 h en journée et entre 21 h et 7 h durant la nuit.
- En été (du 1er avril au 31 octobre) : elles pourront se situer entre 10 h et 18 h en journée et entre 23 h et 7 h la nuit.
Les plages exactes sont définies par Enedis en fonction des caractéristiques locales du réseau et des besoins du système électrique. Les horaires ne sont donc pas identiques pour tous les consommateurs, et ni le client ni son fournisseur ne peuvent les choisir.
Rappelons qu’un outil développé par Octopus Energy permet de connaître ses futures heures creuses.
    Pour aller plus loin
Heures creuses : on a testé l’outil gratuit qui annonce vos nouveaux horaires avant votre fournisseur
            
Comment se déroulera le changement des heures creuses ?
La modification des plages horaires sera mise en œuvre progressivement, du 1er décembre 2026 jusqu’à la fin du mois d’octobre 2027. Elle concernera 9,3 millions de clients sur les 14,5 millions abonnés à l’option HP/HC, et tous ne changeront pas d’horaires dès le 1er décembre.
Pour savoir si vous en faites partie, il suffit de vérifier vos plages horaires actuelles. Si certaines de vos heures creuses se situent entre 7 h et 11 h ou entre 17 h et 23 h, elles seront déplacées vers de nouveaux créneaux.
Les consommateurs concernés recevront une notification de leur fournisseur. Ce dernier devra leur communiquer leurs nouveaux horaires au moins un mois avant leur entrée en vigueur. Aucune démarche particulière ne sera nécessaire de la part des clients. Enedis procédera aux modifications à distance, grâce au compteur Linky, sans intervention d’un technicien.
Pour les clients dont les horaires auront changé dès cet hiver, un nouveau changement pourra intervenir au printemps, lors du passage aux plages estivales, le 1er avril 2027.
Côté pratique, le changement ne sera pas transparent pour tout le monde. Un chauffe-eau relié au contacteur heures pleines/heures creuses du compteur suivra normalement le nouveau signal tout seul ; en revanche, tout ce qui démarre à heure fixe devra être reprogrammé : lave-linge, lave-vaisselle, prise programmable, chauffage piloté à horaires fixes et, bien sûr, la borne ou le câble de recharge d’une voiture électrique.
Enedis conseille d’attendre de connaître ses nouveaux créneaux avant de toucher aux réglages, et rappelle au passage que l’intérêt de l’option dépend de la part de consommation que l’on parvient réellement à basculer en heures creuses.
Jusqu’à 1 GW déjà déplacé
Demandée par la Commission de régulation de l’énergie (CRE), la réforme des heures creuses a commencé à être déployée le 1er novembre 2025. La première phase, achevée en mai 2026, a concerné environ 1,7 million de clients, qui ont reçu de nouveaux horaires d’heures creuses identiques en été et en hiver.
Selon Enedis, cette première étape a déjà permis de déplacer jusqu’à 1 GW de consommation vers l’après-midi, avec un pic mesuré à 15 h. Au lancement de la réforme, Enedis visait dans son communiqué environ 5 GW de consommation déplacés vers les après-midi pendant les mois les plus ensoleillés. La deuxième phase, qui débutera le 1er décembre, concernera 9,3 millions de clients, soit plus de cinq fois plus que la première.
Selon Enedis, les quelque 3,5 millions d’abonnés restants ne sont pas concernés : ils disposent déjà de plages horaires compatibles avec les nouvelles règles.

articles.title: 55 000 € pour une batterie d’occasion : Mercedes propose de remplacer un pack défectueux avec 300 000 km
articles.text:
Acheter une voiture électrique d’occasion relève d’un sacré coup de poker. La tentation est forte vu la décote, certes, mais l’état de la batterie peut aussi laisser craindre le pire. Il suffit de tomber sur un exemplaire aux packs bien fatigués pour déchanter après quelques années. C’est ce qui est arrivé au propriétaire d’une Mercedes EQS qui pensait avoir flairé un bon plan. Hélas, 300 000 km passés, la batterie semble arriver en bout de course.
La personne, qui a remarqué une décharge anormalement rapide du pack, a emmené son EQS450+ dans une concession de la marque, en Croatie. Le diagnostic est implacable : la batterie est gravement endommagée. L’analyse révèle des cellules abîmées et un déséquilibre dû à l’autodécharge. Pire encore, l’accumulateur est tellement usé que chaque section ne pouvait être réparée individuellement.
55 000 € pour du reconditionné : la facture d’occasion qui passe mal
Un remplacement complet est donc nécessaire. Problème, Mercedes ne produit plus les batteries du modèle en question. Il faudra ainsi se contenter d’un pack d’occasion. Embêtant, même si on pourrait alors imaginer un prix de remplacement maîtrisé, l’ensemble n’étant pas neuf. C’est malheureusement tout le contraire qui s’est produit : le constructeur propose une batterie reconditionnée contre… 55 000 €.
Et la garantie, alors ? Comme la majorité des marques, Mercedes garantit bien ses packs pendant 8 ans ou 160 000 km. Pour ce propriétaire, l’échéance est malheureusement bien derrière. L’entreprise EV Clinic spécialisée dans l’entretien des véhicules électriques a pour sa part mené sa petite enquête. Ses membres se sont rendus au siège de CATL, le fournisseur de la batterie, pour savoir combien vaut réellement une cellule d’EQS.
12 000 € chez le fabricant : l’enquête qui pointe un énorme surcoût
Les estimations se sont chiffrées à environ 12 000 €. Bien moins que le devis proposé par Mercedes. Cas isolé ? On ne pense pas : cet écart spectaculaire concernerait très probablement tous les autres constructeurs. De fait, EV Clinic préconise plutôt de remplacer les packs défectueux par des batteries d’occasion compatibles coûtant au maximum 15 000 €. Même en rajoutant la main-d’œuvre, on restera bien en-deçà d’une batterie reconditionnée.
Rappelons que la Mercedes EQS est l’équivalent électrique de la célèbre Classe S. Dans sa version 450+, cette limousine embarque naturellement de gros accumulateurs d’une capacité nette de 107,8 kWh permettant 780 km d’autonomie. Cela pourrait en partie expliquer le coût de remplacement très élevé. Rappelons qu’après restylage, la limousine allemande retient des batteries de 122 kWh permettant jusqu’à 925 km d’autonomie. Un record qui sera très prochainement surpassé par les 960 km de la Lucid Air.

articles.title: iPhone 18 : Samsung pourrait être à l'origine du retard de lancement d'Apple
articles.text:
Apple a choisi de décaler la sortie de son prochain iPhone standard au printemps 2027, plusieurs mois après celle des modèles Pro. Si la pénurie de mémoire est déjà évoquée pour expliquer ce calendrier inhabituel, l’approvisionnement en capteurs photo fournis par Samsung pourrait également peser dans la balance.
Apple a pris une décision inhabituelle avec sa nouvelle génération de smartphones. Alors que les modèles classiques et Pro étaient jusqu’ici lancés au même moment, le constructeur a choisi de séparer les deux sorties. La pénurie de puces mémoire a d’abord été avancée pour expliquer ce décalage. Les tensions sur l’approvisionnement compliqueraient la production des prochains appareils et auraient conduit Apple à revoir son calendrier. Mais cette explication ne serait pas la seule.
Samsung pourrait fournir les capteurs photo du prochain iPhone
D’après les informations rapportées par SamMobile, le fabricant californien chercherait aussi à disposer d’un stock suffisant de capteurs photo avant de commercialiser son prochain modèle. Et c’est là que Samsung entrerait en jeu.
La Pomme aurait en effet prévu de s’approvisionner auprès de Samsung pour certains capteurs destinés à ses futurs iPhone. L’entreprise avait annoncé l’année dernière vouloir diversifier ses fournisseurs dans ce domaine, avec la possibilité d’intégrer des composants de 48 ou de 200 mégapixels. Cette collaboration doit notamment permettre de réduire la dépendance du constructeur à Sony, jusqu’ici son fournisseur de référence.
Selon le nouveau rapport, les premiers travaux de prototypage des capteurs Samsung destinés aux iPhone auraient commencé au printemps 2026. Leur production en série serait quant à elle prévue pour l’automne de la même année. Un calendrier qui pourrait expliquer pourquoi Apple préfère attendre le printemps 2027 pour lancer l’iPhone 18 standard. Le fabricant disposerait ainsi de davantage de temps pour constituer ses stocks.
Un partenariat qui élargit la base de fournisseurs
Cette collaboration ne se limiterait d’ailleurs pas aux seuls capteurs photo. En août 2025, Apple avait annoncé travailler avec Samsung sur une « nouvelle technologie innovante de fabrication de puces ». Les composants concernés doivent être produits dans l’usine de semi-conducteurs de Samsung, à Austin, au Texas. Les deux entreprises n’ont toutefois pas dévoilé leurs caractéristiques techniques.
En faisant appel à Samsung comme deuxième fournisseur de capteurs, Apple diversifierait donc ses sources d’approvisionnement tout en renforçant la production de composants aux États-Unis. Cette mise en concurrence avec Sony pourrait également lui permettre de réduire ses coûts de fabrication.
Le retard de l'iPhone 18 standard pourrait ainsi avoir plusieurs explications. Aux difficultés d'approvisionnement en mémoire s’ajouterait la nécessité de sécuriser les livraisons de capteurs photo Samsung, si les informations rapportées se confirment.
Source : SamMobile

Good morning ☀️️
Well, Jensen Huang’s week just got worse.
Yesterday, the NVIDIA co-founder resigned as chief executive officer of the chipmaker he helped build into one of the world’s most valuable companies. His departure follows reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman whom US officials suspect of having ties to Chinese intelligence.
Huang has denied knowing about any alleged intelligence links, and NVIDIA said it has no reason to believe its secrets were compromised. Yet, the revelations have triggered investigations, rattled investors, and now cost the 63-year-old his job.
NVIDIA’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, has taken over as interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent replacement.
It’s quite a turn of events. The man who spent three decades making NVIDIA central to the AI boom is suddenly out of the company he co-founded. And the chipmaker must now figure out what comes next without its most recognisable face.
Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly.
companies
Quickmart shares jump 33% after going public
Quickmart, Kenya’s second-largest supermarket chain, has finally gone public. On Thursday, its shares traded on the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE), opening at KES10 ($0.077); its price rose 33.3% from its initial public offering (IPO) debut of KES7.50 ($0.058). By midday, they were averaging KES9.26 ($0.071), with 6.32 million shares traded.
Explain like I’m new here: The supermarket first announced its intention to list on September 23, 2026. The offer opened on October 5 and closed on October 30, giving investors a little over three weeks to buy shares at KES7.50 ($0.058) each.
The listing is also a partial exit for Adenia Partners, a private equity firm, after nearly eight years of building the supermarket business. It entered Kenya in 2018 by acquiring a 55% stake in Tumaini Supermarket. In September 2019, it acquired a 51% stake in Quickmart, and the two businesses merged in 2020 under the Quickmart brand. Through the IPO, Adenia and the other shareholders are selling half their combined stake, allowing them to realise some returns while retaining exposure to the business.
Why investors are paying attention: Quickmart operates 72 stores across 16 counties and handles about five million customer transactions monthly. Its revenue has also grown from $37 million in 2018 to $389 million in 2025, increasing by over tenfold, the retailer said in its filing notice. Quickmart’s IPO also attracted international investors, including the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the UK-backed MOBILIST programme, 337 Frontier, and RWC Asset Management.
The first-day jump suggests investors were keen to own a piece of the retailer. But a strong debut is not a guarantee of future gains. Quickmart will now have to keep growing its business and delivering results to sustain investor interest.

regulation
Egypt admits two more fintech projects into regulatory sandbox
Financial services are a heavily regulated sector. Companies cannot simply roll out a new way to lend money without regulators checking that everything is above board. What if they could test those ideas before going through the full process of taking them to market? That is where regulatory sandboxes come in.
What happened? Egypt’s Financial Regulatory Authority (FRA), the government agency that regulates non-banking financial services, has granted preliminary approval for two projects to join its regulatory sandbox.
The first is from WeLend, working with Tamweely—the micro-lender Egypt’s e-finance acquired in September—which joined the sandbox to test its AI-powered credit assessment tool that uses financial and operational data to evaluate the creditworthiness of small and medium-sized businesses. The second is from Roa’ya Online, which wants to use a simulated stock market and gamified lessons to teach people aged 15–35 how investing works.
Explain like I’m new here: Egypt launched the FRA sandbox in 2025 to give companies developing new non-bank financial products a controlled environment to test their ideas before taking them to the wider market. In its first year, the sandbox received applications for about 49 projects. The latest approvals bring the total number of projects with preliminary approval to 11.
The appeal is that regulators can understand new technologies before they become widespread, and fintechs can test products without navigating every uncertainty.
stablecoins
IMF wants Kenya to relax stablecoin rules
Kenya has spent the past year trying to bring crypto companies under its watch. Since July, it has released rules for local and foreign operators to follow. Those rules came into effect on November 4.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) supports Kenya’s push to regulate crypto. It just thinks some of the rules could do more harm than good. The IMF has asked Kenya to reconsider those requirements that would force stablecoin issuers to keep part of the money backing their coins in local banks.
Explain like I’m new here: Kenya spent years watching its crypto market grow without a dedicated law to regulate it. In 2025, the country passed the Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASP) Act, bringing crypto businesses under formal oversight.
The next step was deciding how those businesses should operate. Kenya proposed rules covering everything from licences to the money companies must hold to protect their customers.
Now, the IMF is questioning some of the provisions.
What’s the problem? Stablecoins are cryptocurrencies designed to hold a steady value, often backed by US dollars or other assets. Kenya wants issuers to keep some of those reserves in the country.
But the IMF argued that foreign issuers should be allowed to hold their reserves abroad, provided they meet strict safeguards. Requiring them to move money into Kenyan banks could discourage them from entering the market. On November 5, Nigeria also followed a similar logic, requiring foreign issuers to hold stablecoin reserves locally.
Kenya requires stablecoin issuers, including foreign operators, to hold at least KES 300 million ($2.3 million) in paid-up capital and keep 30% of their stablecoin reserves in Kenyan banks, with the remaining 70% invested locally. The IMF wants Kenya to review the minimum capital required of crypto businesses, arguing that the rules should reflect each company’s risk.
Zoom out: Kenya is trying to make crypto safer without making it too expensive to operate legally. The IMF is concerned that overly demanding rules could leave Kenya with fewer licenced companies, while crypto trading continues anyway.

articles.title: Jensen Huang supo bailar las aguas entre EEUU, China y la propia Nvidia. Su sustituto no va a tenerlo nada fácil
articles.text:
Nvidia ya tiene una directora general interina. Colette Kress, la directora financiera de la compañía, va a ejercer temporalmente como directora general y sucesora de Jensen Huang. Nvidia comunicó oficialmente su nombramiento ayer, pero Kress no liderará la empresa de forma indefinida. Por el momento, compatibilizará la dirección ejecutiva interina con sus funciones de vicepresidenta ejecutiva y directora financiera a la espera de la llegada de un sucesor permanente.
Mientras tanto, el consejo ya ha iniciado la búsqueda de un director general definitivo. Ha confirmado que evaluará tanto candidatos internos como externos, aunque no ha fijado ningún plazo ni ha constituido un comité de selección. Aun así, ya está soportando la presión externa. Donald Trump, que ha mantenido una relación muy estrecha con Jensen Huang durante varios años, defiende que Tim Cook, el ex director general de Apple, es el candidato idóneo. Su experiencia en la gestión de la cadena de suministro juega a su favor, pero no hay ningún indicio que nos indique que le interese unirse a Nvidia.
Cabe la posibilidad de que si el liderazgo temporal de Kress va como la seda, finalmente se quede como directora general definitiva. No obstante, las quinielas también apuestan por Ian Buck, vicepresidente de Nvidia y arquitecto de CUDA; Chris Malachowsky, cofundador de la compañía; Rene Haas, director general de Arm y exdirectivo de Nvidia; o Johny Srouji, jefe de hardware de Apple. Incluso están sonando Lisa Su, la líder de AMD, y Sanjay Mehrotra, el director general de Micron, como posibles sucesores de Jensen Huang. Sea quien sea el futuro director general permanente de Nvidia, una cosa está clara: va a tener que lidiar con la tensión geopolítica que sostienen EEUU, China y Taiwán.
Jensen Huang hacía bien algo muy difícil: jugar a tres bandas
Más allá del escándalo en el que se ha zambullido, es justo reconocer a Jensen Huang su habilidad a la hora de pelear con la Administración de EEUU y de defender sus intereses ante el Gobierno chino. Durante la última etapa del mandato de Joe Biden luchó con el Departamento de Comercio de EEUU para poder vender sus chips para inteligencia artificial (IA) más avanzados en China. Y desde que Donald Trump regresó a la Casa Blanca ha mantenido un pulso intenso con él para proteger los intereses de Nvidia a toda costa. La persona que se sitúe definitivamente al frente de Nvidia tendrá que moverse con tanta habilidad como Huang en el fango.
Donald Trump no ha propuesto su propio candidato por casualidad. Para el actual presidente de EEUU es muy importante que la compañía más influyente del planeta en el ecosistema de la IA esté liderada por una persona de su confianza. O, al menos, con la que tenga una relación cercana y cordial. Y al consejo de Nvidia le interesa que su director general permanente maneje con destreza su relación con el Gobierno de EEUU, y también con la Administración de China. De hecho, la estabilidad de la compañía depende en gran medida de ello.
Nvidia difícilmente podrá soportar más disrupciones tan intensas como la actual
La capitalización de Nvidia es muy sensible a las sacudidas de la industria de la IA. Lo vimos cuando irrumpió DeepSeek. Y también a los escándalos en los que se ve envuelto su líder. Lo estamos viendo ahora. Con toda seguridad la persona a la que el consejo confiará la dirección general de la compañía será alguien con un perfil mediático bajo, pero con una experiencia en el sector de los semiconductores contrastada. Y, sobre todo, con mucha mano izquierda. No todos los posibles candidatos de los que hemos hablado unas líneas más arriba satisfacen estas condiciones.
Nvidia difícilmente podrá soportar más disrupciones tan intensas como la actual. En cualquier caso, la estabilidad de la compañía también está estrechamente ligada a la relación de su líder con los Gobiernos de China y Taiwán. Jensen Huang ha defendido con relativo éxito la posición de Nvidia en China a pesar de tener a la Administración liderada por Xi Jinping en su contra. Y, al mismo tiempo, ha manejado su dependencia de TSMC, la gestión de la cadena de suministro y su relación con el Gobierno de Taiwán con maestría. A su sucesor no va a resultarle fácil salir airoso simultáneamente en tantos frentes.

articles.title: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
articles.text:
Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
By treating qubits like individual molecules, scientists can now predict their behavior faster and more accurately
- Date:
- November 13, 2026
- Source:
- Princeton University
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a faster way to identify diamond-based materials that could power quantum computers and sensors at room temperature. The breakthrough has already revealed promising new quantum building blocks that could help unlock computing capabilities far beyond those of today's supercomputers.
- Share:
A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.
The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.
One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.
This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.
Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing
Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.
These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.
Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.
A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits
Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.
By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.
"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.
The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.
New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors
Light plays an important role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.
Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.
Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.
The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.
These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.
"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.
Beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.
Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.
How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research
The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.
In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.
A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.
"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched."
Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.
Martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.
"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well."
By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.
The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

articles.title: OpenAI Unveils Daybreak Red Team, Defense Factory Security Tools
articles.text:
OpenAI has introduced two new Daybreak cybersecurity products that use AI agents to test web applications for vulnerabilities and help security teams develop fixes.
The products, Daybreak Red Team and Daybreak Defense Factory, were announced at the company’s Cyber at the Frontier event on November 12. Red Team focuses on penetration testing and vulnerability validation, while Defense Factory investigates security findings and prepares patches.
Daybreak Red Team uses multiple AI agents to identify and investigate potential security weaknesses in web applications. “Agents use source code and app context to investigate attack paths and confirm vulnerabilities,” OpenAI says.
The product can examine findings from code scanners, bug bounty submissions, and vulnerability disclosure reports.
OpenAI says the agents operate in isolated environments, with Guardian review enforcing testing boundaries and controlling which applications and endpoints they can access.
Daybreak Defense Factory, meanwhile, is designed to help organizations address vulnerabilities identified by their security tools.
“Agents trace vulnerabilities through your code and develop patches. Engineers review and test proposed patches before merge,” OpenAI explains.
Defense Factory can investigate findings from Daybreak Red Team and other security products, and supports importing vulnerability information from Wiz, Snyk, and Endor Labs. The product can scan connected GitHub repositories, monitor new commits, and perform scheduled security assessments.
Engineers can examine supporting evidence, modify proposed patches using Codex, and create draft GitHub pull requests. However, patches are not deployed automatically.
OpenAI is accepting requests for early access to Daybreak Red Team. Defense Factory is offered through a preview plugin in ChatGPT for workspaces with Daybreak access.

articles.title: Outlook fora do ar: e-mails começam a voltar após horas de pane • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Outlook fora do ar: e-mails começam a voltar após horas de pane
Microsoft atribuiu apagão a uma atualização da capacidade da rede e descartou relação com sistemas de IA.
O Outlook começou a voltar a funcionar nesta sexta-feira (13/11), após uma falha global que também afetou outros serviços da Microsoft. Alguns usuários ainda enfrentam dificuldades para acessar e-mails tanto pela versão web quanto pelos aplicativos para computador e celular, mas a Microsoft afirma que o serviço está quase todo restaurado.
A instabilidade começou na tarde de ontem (12/11) e se estendeu durante a madrugada. Além do Outlook, foram registrados problemas no Microsoft Teams, Copilot 365, SharePoint, Microsoft Defender e outras ferramentas da suíte Microsoft 365.
We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure. We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us. We will continue to share more information as we have it, and for now we can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity. Our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward.
— Microsoft (@Microsoft) November 13, 2026
Segundo a Microsoft, o problema teve origem em uma falha durante uma atualização anterior da capacidade da rede, que se manifestou após uma mudança na infraestrutura e atingiu diversos serviços do Microsoft 365.
A empresa afirma ter corrigido a causa do incidente, mas continua trabalhando para restabelecer os serviços nas regiões ainda afetadas. A companhia descartou a hipótese de um ataque hacker e pediu desculpas aos clientes e parceiros.
No DownDetector, site que monitora a disponibilidade de serviços na web, o gráfico começou a acumular reclamações de usuários por volta das 14h45 de ontem.

articles.title: macOS on PC becomes possible again thanks to Apple Silicon translator for x86-64 — hackintosh revival project currently 'slow and not very stable'
articles.text:
macOS on PC becomes possible again thanks to Apple Silicon translator for x86-64 — Hackintosh revival project uses Linux-based UEFI app that translates Arm and Metal calls on the fly, currently 'slow and not very stable'
Everything old is new again.
The eternal spiral of computing gets yet another loop. Apple introduced its own Arm-based chips in 2020, surprising the world with a series of SoCs with a particularly high power-to-watt ratio, a perfect fit for the company's quality portables. As the designs improved on raw performance, Apple shifted away from Intel-based Macs. That meant that enterprising hackers who ran macOS on their PCs could no longer do so — until today, thanks to the Stela Apple Silicon translation layer.
Stela is a minty-fresh new project from Tyler Smith, and it's just gotten started, with three releases since the first 0.1 version in barely half a day. The author warns that "it is slow and not very stable," but those warnings are somehow invisible to techies trying out a new toy. For practical purposes, Stela is a Linux-based UEFI application for loading macOS 27, presenting a virtual M2 Mac Mini to the operating system.
The developer answered a couple of questions in the project's Discord server, and he remarked that the macOS image to be used is not modified at all: "Stela provides the translation and hardware behavior underneath that lets macOS go through the exact same restore process you might do on a real Mac."
The server has seen a substantial influx of users, many of them posting photos of their PCs near-booting macOS. Predictably, most of the questions were about supporting their own particular hardware, but the excitement is palpable.
To get started, all you need is to download Stela from the release pages, provide a USB stick to then boot your PC with, and, naturally, your own copy of macOS. Stela will take care of translating AArch instructions into x86-64. The translation layer uses a combination of ahead-of-time and just-in-time (JIT) compilation for the CPU, and translates Apple's Metal graphics layer calls to Mesa's NIR instructions.
The hardware requirements are basically potato-level, requiring only an x86-64-v2 — a 2008 Intel Core chip, or a 2011-vintage AMD FX processor. The author mentions that AVX2 and AVX-512 "are used when present," but woe betide you if your processor is that old to begin with. You'll need 8 GB of RAM, UEFI support, a GPT partition or entire drive, and an Nvidia card from the 16xx series to present-day 5000 models.
There's no Wi-Fi support yet, and Bluetooth is limited, but the list of working Ethernet controllers is extensive, covering models from Intel, Realtek, Broadcom, Aquantia, Atheros, and even USB Ethernet sticks. The author says that he intends for Stela to eventually support all the hardware the Linux kernel does.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Purely hypothetically, with AI automation, it's not completely insane to think that much of macOS could be pre-translated to x86-64. Yet such an endeavor has many caveats, namely the fact that a lot of code, like a browser's JIT JavaScript compilation, doesn't exist on the disk image to begin with.
There's also the fact that no matter how efficient a translation layer is, the OS still needs to cryptographically accept it and run it, perhaps requiring further modification still. But we can, in fact, dream of ditching Windows for macOS without being tied to Apple's pricey and barely-repairable hardware.

Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: The new Apple TV has a YouTube problem
articles.text:
People who received the brand new Apple TV 4k today saw some strange error messages as soon as they opened the YouTube app. As the first units arrived, the app was initially only showing a black screen with a QR code and an error message saying “YouTube is not yet available on this device.” In some cases the app was functional, but had a transparent red bar stuck at the bottom of the screen saying, “YouTube app is approved for device testing only and not for production use.”
The new Apple TV has a YouTube problem
A software update and a reboot should get YouTube working on your new Apple TV 4K.
Installing the new tvOS 27.2 update and rebooting wasn’t enough to resolve the issue for The Verge’s Tom Warren, he also had to uninstall and reinstall the app.
The Verge’s John Higgins said in his review of the new Apple TV 4K that it’s “one of the best streaming devices available,” but expensive compared to other streaming boxes.

articles.title: El PP está intentando generar su propio “perrosanxe” convirtiendo a Feijóo en Anuel con Anotop At
articles.text:
Hay un manidísimo adagio que dice que ‘toda crisis es en realidad una oportunidad’. En el PP han decidido retocarlo y convertir una de las más sonoras meteduras de pata de su líder, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, en una oportunidad para conectar con una parte de la población que será clave el 29N: los jóvenes. ¿Cómo? Rescatando el ininteligible “anotop at” pronunciado hace un año por Feijóo en el Congreso, un lapsus que entonces fue motivo de chanza entre la oposición y ahora el PP ha convertido en un imán para el votante joven.
Y aunque es pronto para saber si le funcionará o no, hay algo innegable: la estrategia está cuajando en las redes.
Del 26 de noviembre… En política 12 meses equivalen a varias vueltas al Sol, pero es probable que aun así recuerdes el episodio que protagonizó Feijóo hace justo un año en el Congreso. El líder del PP quiso tirar de sorna y espetar a Pedro Sánchez que algún día se rodaría una serie sobre su vida titulada “Anatomía de un farsante” cuando, en pleno chascarrillo, se quedó trabado y acabó pronunciando un ininteligible “Anotop At”. Ocurrió un 26 de noviembre.
El patinazo dejó a Feijóo cariacontecido mientras la bancada de la oposición estallaba en aplausos y carcajadas.
Le ha gustado 🐐 https://t.co/GCB9WHRAor
— Nuevas Generaciones de España 🇪🇸 (@NNGG_Es) November 12, 2026
…al 29 de noviembre. Ironías de la política (o no), el panorama es hoy bastante diferente. En dos semanas los españoles tendremos que acudir a los colegios electorales para escoger nuevo Gobierno y, con la campaña ya activada, en el PP han visto en aquel “Anotop At” algo más que un resbalón dialéctico en el fragor del debate parlamentario.
Al contrario. En vez de arrojar tierra sobre el lapsus han decidido rescatarlo, exprimiendo su espontaneidad para conectar con el electorado joven, al que probablemente más le cuesta llegar a Feijóo, un político de 65 años que se pasó 13 presidiendo la Xunta de Galicia y al que hasta hace no tanto era difícil ver sin corbata. No es una estrategia muy distinta a la que empleó en 2023 el PSOE con el famoso “Perro Sanxe”. La idea es básicamente la misma: convertir un ataque o un meme en un activo positivo.
“Primeras impresiones”. Ayer por la tarde, coincidiendo con el pistoletazo de salida de la campaña electoral, el PP colgó en su cuenta oficial de X un vídeo en el que se pueden ver las reacciones de Feijóo a los memes que juegan con el famoso “Anotop At” e incluso lo presentan como cantante de trap, con clarísimas alusiones al puertorriqueño Anuel AA.
La pieza dura menos de 50 segundos y en ella vemos al popular dentro de un coche, riéndose mientras ve la pantalla del móvil. De momento suma 1,3 millones de visitas (y subiendo). Nada mal para un perfil con menos de 860.000 seguidores.
No estáis preparados para lo que se viene https://t.co/5vHh7l25Lg
— Nuevas Generaciones de Madrid (@nnggmadrid) November 12, 2026
¿Es solo una anécdota? No lo parece. Más allá de la cuenta oficial del PP en X, el partido ha compartido otras piezas de tono similar en los perfiles que gestiona. En ocasiones con una apuesta aún más irreverente por la autoparodia.
El ejemplo más claro lo encontramos probablemente en TikTok, una plataforma empleada sobre todo por veinteañeros (en 2022 el 60,5% de sus usuarios tenían entre 18 y 34 años). Ayer la cuenta oficial de los populares cambió su foto de perfil, añadiendo una generada por IA en la que se ve a Feijóo emulando a Kobe Bryant en 2001 vestido con chándal y la copa de la NBA.
El perfil ya ha recuperado su foto habitual (el logo del PP con fondo azul), pero el gesto no ha pasado desapercibido a los analistas y el tono sigue replicándose en las cuentas de Nuevas Generaciones. En la de Madrid pueden verse aún el montaje con IA del Feijóo-Kobe Bryant y varias publicaciones en las que se intenta suavizar la imagen del líder popular asociándolo por ejemplo al trap. En la cuenta de NNGG España también han compartido una foto que muestra a Feijóo como un futbolista celebrando un gol: “Vaya farmeo de Aura”.
Efecto multiplicador. Si la estrategia está funcionando es porque no se limita a los perfiles oficiales vinculados al PP. Basta una búsqueda rápida en X para encontrar otras cuentas de contenido paródico que comparten vídeos, canciones e imágenes generadas con IA en las que se presenta a Feijóo como cantante de trap a lo Anuel, futbolista, acompañado de Jordi Wild o Ibai… Se repite el latiguillo de “Anotop At” y sobre todo se rejuvenece el perfil del líder popular, aproximándolo a los votantes conservadores de 20 o 30 y pocos años que todavía no hayan decidido su voto.
Hay algún caso en el que esas publicaciones se presentan como “colaboración pagada”, lo que sugiere que, más allá de la viralidad espontánea, hay cierta estrategia de fondo.

— Raul Becas y Ayudas (Goyim) (@raulbecasayudas) November 12, 2026
La clave: el contexto. Lo cierto es que el “Anotop At” no ha emergido en un momento cualquiera. Llega justo en el inicio de la campaña electoral y coincidiendo con un contexto especialmente favorable para el PP en su empeño por ‘pescar’ papeletas en el caladero de votantes próximos a Vox.
Hoy se publican las entrevistas de Jordi Wild con Pedro Sánchez, Ada Colau y Alberto Núñez Feijóo como parte de The Wild Project. Aunque las charlas son importantes para los tres candidatos (Jordi Wild ejerce una influencia muy relevante entre los votantes más jóvenes) quizás el que más puede rentabilizarla es el líder popular.
¿El motivo? Además de darle una ventana privilegiada para llegar a la Gen Z y los millennials más jóvenes, le permite marcar distancias con Santiago Abascal, el candidato con el que rivaliza por el voto conservador. El líder de Vox también estaba invitado al set de Wild, pero acabó echándose atrás por diferencias sobre el control y uso de la grabación.
Esa decisión le valió al dirigente de Vox una avalancha de críticas, en lo que se ha interpretado como un patinazo (este sí, mucho peor que el “Anoto At”) ante su electorado más joven. Es más, hay quien cree que ese error ha erosionado los puntos que se marcó este lunes en ‘La Revuelta’.
