articles.title: Microsoft’s massive Outlook outage might be over
articles.text:
Service is recovering for Microsoft Outlook and 365 after an almost two-day outage impacting millions of users around the world. While some apps and features are still running in a degraded state on Friday morning, some people (including Verge staffers) reported that access to their emails had been restored, though the flow of Outlook mail might be delayed.
Microsoft’s massive Outlook outage might be over
Nearly a day after the global email outage started, Microsoft said the issue has been addressed and that it wasn’t related to a cyberattack or AI.
Just before noon on Friday, Microsoft said it’s seeing “broad recovery,” and that the problem “was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents.”
We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.
This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.
Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.
We will provide a full post-incident report once our review is complete.
Senior Verge correspondent Tom Warren reports that according to his sources, the outage is linked to Azure VNet config changes. Microsoft has said that it hasn’t found any evidence of the outage being connected to “malicious activity,” and that a full report will be shared after the issues are mitigated. In a statement reported by Sky News tech correspondent Rowland Manthorpe, Microsoft described the outage as a “technical issue,” and says it isn’t related to “cyber, AI/agents, DDOS, etc.”
The scope of the outage also affected features in other Microsoft services, including SharePoint Online, Teams, Copilot AI, and 365 apps.
Update, November 13th, 2:15PM ET: Added the latest information from Microsoft.

articles.title: NovoGenius® MCU+ Devices Reshape the Automotive Edge Node - EE Times
articles.text:
Zonal architectures are pulling computing toward the center of the vehicle, yet the actuators, sensors, and lighting modules at its edges still need local intelligence. NOVOSENSE is meeting that need with single-chip devices defined around one application at a time.
The Edge Node Under Zonal Architecture
Automotive electrical and electronic architecture is consolidating. Zonal designs move processing into a small number of zone and central controllers, and the count of small, single-function ECUs falls as a result. For the motors, sensors and lights that sit at the end of each wiring run, that shift raises a practical question: how much intelligence should remain at the node, and in what form?
Ken Ye, Product Line Director for Signal Chain at NOVOSENSE, sees no ambiguity in the overall direction. “The trend is very clear,” he says. “Everyone is going to zone control.” Adoption timelines differ from one OEM and region to the next, but the destination is shared across the industry.
What the transition does not do is eliminate the need for capable local control. Ken points to heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) flap actuators as an example. Some new vehicle models carry as many as 12 flap motors in the cabin, and electrification has made their acoustic behavior a design requirement in its own right. “Inside the cabin of an electric car, it’s very, very quiet,” Ken explains. “Even if there is some small motor noise coming from the air conditioning flap, the driver will notice it.”
Holding that noise down requires precise control of current harmonics in every motor. Driving a dozen actuators to that standard from a centralized controller is not practical with current approaches, and much of the know-how for low-noise operation sits with the Tier 1 suppliers that build these modules rather than with zone controller designers. Ken expects that balance to shift as central processing power grows, but not quickly. “Especially over the next five to ten-year range, there are still some components that cannot be integrated into zone control,” he says. “They remain local.”
Newer in-vehicle networks such as 10BASE-T1S Ethernet and CAN XL will give zone controllers more reach. Even so, Ken expects precision functions to follow a command-and-execute model. “The zone control just gives a command to the nodes, and the nodes should have some intelligence inside,” he says. “It doesn’t need to be an MCU inside. It can be a smart digital part that controls the end load precisely.”
That edge node is the territory of NovoGenius®, NOVOSENSE’s family of application-specific automotive processors. Ken joined NOVOSENSE in 2019 as marketing director for the sensor product line and was later appointed to lead the signal chain product line, which includes the NovoGenius® MCU+ portfolio for motor control, ultrasonic and sunlight and rain sensing, and ambient lighting.
What MCU+ Means in Practice
A conventional automotive node pairs a general-purpose MCU with a set of companion chips: a voltage regulator, a bus transceiver, a gate driver or power stage, and an analog front end. NovoGenius® devices take a different starting point. Each is an application-specific processor whose analog peripherals are designed for one target function.
“The idea of MCU+ is an all-in-one IC for one kind of automotive application,” Ken says. “One IC covers a complete system.”
The motor-control devices illustrate the approach. An integrated automotive LDO runs directly from the 12 V battery and generates the internal 5 V supply for the MCU, while the same battery rail powers the motor through the bridge. A LIN transceiver, ADC, MOSFET driver, and the MOSFET bridge itself are all on-chip, so a single device can drive a stepper, brushless DC, or brushed DC motor. Apart from passive components, nothing else is needed on the board.
According to Ken, a comparable design built from a general-purpose MCU, an external LIN transceiver and discrete supporting components occupies roughly three times the PCB area. The smaller footprint has an architectural consequence: the controller board can be mounted inside the motor housing. “They can put the PCB into the motor itself, without any external ECU,” Ken says. “That makes the motor a smart motor.” NOVOSENSE applies the same concept to sensor modules and to ambient lighting.
Customization That Scales
Every NovoGenius® device begins with an analysis of the customer’s system rather than a generic feature list. Customers routinely ask for everything to be integrated, Ken notes, but integration is an engineering and economic tradeoff, not an end in itself. The wafer process sets limits on which functions can share a die, and physical constraints such as power dissipation set others.
“When we integrate everything into one IC, it does not always bring value to the customer for the system cost,” Ken says. “Sometimes it adds cost.” The deciding factor is the customer’s priority. Where cost leads, NOVOSENSE defines the device around system cost reduction. “If size is the highest priority,” Ken continues, “then we try to integrate everything into the IC.”
Customization usually raises cost and narrows volume, which raises the question of how an application-specific family remains commercially viable. Ken points to the structure of the automotive supply base. In mature markets, a handful of suppliers often dominate a given application; Ken estimates that the top three can hold around 70 percent of the market. “Even one customer, the volume is usually enough for you to generate such kind of IC for them,” he says. Leading suppliers also bring a clear view of where their applications are going. “The leading customer usually has a very clear definition of the trend,” Ken adds. “They understand what the next generation looks like.”
Development speed comes from shared intellectual property. NOVOSENSE operates several product lines, each with its own analog strengths, and NovoGenius® draws on them directly: the LIN interface IP comes from the isolation and interface product line, and the power supply IP from the power management product line. These blocks are ported into a common wafer process, which suits automotive edge nodes well because their needs overlap heavily. Almost all are powered directly from the 12 V battery, and their communication interfaces, such as LIN and CAN, are standardized.
“The unique role of this group is system integration,” Ken says, “understanding the customer’s system, bringing that knowledge in, and integrating every analog IP into one part to generate this kind of SoC.”
The effect on schedules is measurable. The first-generation NovoGenius® motor driver took two and a half years to develop. Once its building blocks had been converted into reusable IP, the second generation took 15 months, and the first-generation rain and light sensor IC was also completed in 15 months. “The first part on this platform takes a lot of time,” Ken says, “but for the second and the third one, it’s almost reduced by half.”
MCU + Driver: Motor Control From Small Actuators to 1,500 W
The motor-control devices span a wide power range. NSUC1610 and NSUC1612 integrate the power stage for small actuators in thermal management and body applications, while NSUC1602 pairs the MCU with an integrated pre-driver and external MOSFETs for motors of up to 1,500 W.
The dividing line is set by thermal management and cost. “If the power is too high, it will be very difficult to manage the power in a normal IC package, and the cost will dramatically increase,” Ken explains. “So we let the MOSFETs go outside and only integrate the MOSFET driver. The cost and the limitations of physics decide that.”
Putting power switching and sensitive analog circuitry on the same die also makes electromagnetic compatibility a first-order design concern. Because customers expect the device to be the only IC on the board, NOVOSENSE treats module-level EMC as a chip-level requirement. “When we design this IC, we do a system-level EMC simulation,” Ken says. The team gathers the EMC levels that customer modules must pass in type testing and simulates against them during IC development. The aim is to reduce the external EMC components a customer would otherwise add, and with them the cost of the module.
MCU + Sense: Ultrasonic, Rain and Light Sensing
For park assist and low-speed maneuvering, NSUC1800 integrates digital signal processing that calculates the distance between the vehicle and nearby obstacles. The device follows the physical and data link layers of DSI3, an open interface standard, so it communicates with DSI3 master devices already used in existing systems.
Ultrasonic nodes are also where the growing role of diagnostics is most visible. When ultrasonic sensing served only as a parking aid for a human driver, functional safety requirements were modest. Automated parking changes that. “There is no real person driving the car,” Ken says. “So every sensor node needs to be monitored and diagnosed.” An ultrasonic IC must now detect failures in itself and in external components, such as the capacitor in the transducer circuit, and either issue a warning or halt the automated parking function.
The NSUC183x sunlight and rain sensor ICs are offered at several levels of integration, a choice Ken describes as “really a commercial decision.” Some customers want to reduce the cost of an existing design without significant changes, so NOVOSENSE offers a pin-compatible analog-front-end-only version. For next-generation designs, the same customers want the MCU integrated. NOVOSENSE serves both with a two-die architecture, one die for the MCU and one for the analog front end. “We are using a two-die approach with one development,” Ken says, “but with different integration levels for the customer.”
The function of the rain and light sensor module itself is expanding. Where it once controlled wiper speed and headlamp activation, newer modules also measure ambient brightness at the windshield to set head-up display (HUD) brightness. The latest versions measure solar load separately on the driver and front passenger sides so the HVAC system can treat each zone differently. NSUC183x supports that consolidation with additional light-sensing channels.
MCU + LED: Ambient Lighting Becomes Interactive
Ambient lighting is moving from decoration toward cockpit interaction, and that changes the demands on the controller. NSUC1527, a multichannel ambient light controller, includes a CAN interface that provides the higher communication bandwidth needed to synchronize lighting effects with music, so the light can change as quickly as the audio does.
Brightness is the other pressure point. Automakers want brighter ambient lighting, which means higher LED drive current. Because the controller sits inside the lighting module, its power consumption and conversion efficiency become critical design parameters. Ken cites automated driving indicators in China, where a bright blue light shows that the vehicle is driving itself, as one application pushing drive current higher. The next generation of the NSUC1500 series is designed around those efficiency requirements.
Color consistency across temperature and LED aging remains a central challenge. NovoGenius® lighting devices monitor the forward voltage across each LED, which serves as an indicator of junction temperature, and run internal algorithms that compensate brightness for temperature and for aging. Because each module must also be calibrated on the production line, NOVOSENSE supplies manufacturing tools for brightness and color calibration. “We give them a complete system-level solution,” Ken says, “the algorithms for the compensation and the algorithms for manufacturing calibration, and they can use it very easily.”
NSUC1503 extends the family toward cost-sensitive programs. Ken describes it as primarily a cost-optimized version of the previous device, developed to meet demand for lower system cost.
From MCU+ Toward MCU-less
As control is redistributed between central controllers and local nodes, Ken sees two kinds of node that will keep an integrated MCU. The first performs precise local control, as in the HVAC flap example. The second delivers features that vary from vehicle to vehicle. Base configurations are increasingly controlled from the zone, but optional, value-added modules ordered by individual buyers remain at the node, and so do entirely new functions that the large zonal integration devices on the market do not yet address.
Over time, Ken expects some of these nodes to shed the MCU entirely. Automotive electronics is relentlessly cost-driven, and once an application stabilizes, fixed digital logic can replace programmable control. “Maybe after three or four years, when the application starts to be stable, the MCU functionality will be replaced by pure digital logic,” he says. “That’s going to be another approach, an MCU-less approach. But in between, it’s still the MCU+ approach.”
NOVOSENSE is already moving in that direction with field-oriented control (FOC) implemented in dedicated digital logic rather than MCU software. Ken cites the ventilation fan in a driver’s seat as a natural candidate: the zone controller sends only a simple speed command, such as off, low or high, and a hardware FOC engine can execute it without an MCU.
The engineering challenge is motor variation. Each motor model has historically required its own software tuning. To preserve that flexibility, NOVOSENSE provides configuration registers in which the motor’s characteristics are described, so the hardware logic can adapt to the specific motor. A GUI-based tool, which Ken describes as intelligent or AI-based, captures current and voltage from the running motor, derives a model of it and generates the parameters to write into the device, allowing the motor to run smoothly and quietly. “We call it MCU+,” Ken says, “but finally it’s going to be MCU-less.”
Software, Quality and Supply
Application-specific hardware shortens a customer’s development schedule only if the software that comes with it is dependable. The NovoGenius® motor-control turnkey solution supplies the low-level drivers, and it has achieved ASPICE Capability Level 2. Development follows the V-model, with testing at the software unit, module, function and system levels.
Ken stresses that this matters in every market. “The customer doesn’t want to develop everything from the very beginning,” he says. “They ask NOVOSENSE to give them the software, and the software needs to be robust.” Short program timelines, especially in China, make robust supplied software a requirement. “It’s not only for the customers outside China,” he adds. “It’s also for the customers inside China.”
For European Tier 1 suppliers evaluating a new source, quality management and supply continuity weigh as heavily as the device itself. NOVOSENSE operates an automotive-grade quality system with a dedicated quality organization and has passed supplier certifications from multiple global Tier 1 suppliers. Its packaging and test partners are selected among leading OSATs that operate under automotive quality rules. Ken describes NOVOSENSE as the leading domestic automotive IC supplier in China.
International Progress and Outlook
Outside China, NovoGenius® has gained traction in east Asia and Europe. One example is a Japanese supplier that holds the leading global share in HVAC flap actuators and for which NOVOSENSE has developed a customized IC. According to Ken, that customer achieved the best noise performance it had seen when controlling its motors with the NovoGenius® device.
The family’s next step extends the same concept beyond the vehicle. In a dexterous robotic hand, every finger needs a very small motor with its own driver, communication interface and magnetic encoder, the same combination of functions that MCU+ integrates for automotive actuators. NOVOSENSE expects to introduce a family member for robotics applications within the next two years. “We are looking at customers that need high integration, where the integration brings system-level value,” Ken says, adding that NOVOSENSE’s analog IP and system-level algorithms are its basis for differentiation.
Within the vehicle, NOVOSENSE continues to look for problems that no existing part addresses well. One area under study is cleaning automotive cameras, where water on the lens in rainy conditions degrades the image that driver assistance and the driver rely on.
For engineers evaluating NovoGenius® for an upcoming vehicle program, Ken’s advice is to start from the application. Each device is defined for a clear use case, with the aim of lowering system cost by removing external components, including EMC components, while delivering system-level performance. Where no suitable device exists, the definition process that produced the current family is open to new requirements. “When the customer has some kind of special requirement for those kinds of applications,” Ken says, “they can come to NovoGenius and talk with us about the approach.”
NovoGenius® is also one part of a broader portfolio. With analog and mixed-signal ICs spanning a wide range of automotive applications, NOVOSENSE positions itself as a practical partner for global customers looking to address multiple system requirements with a single semiconductor supplier.

articles.title: Speicher halbiert, Preis angehoben: Diese Fritzbox kann für Käufer zur Mogelpackung werden
articles.text:
Speicher halbiert, Preis angehoben: Diese Fritzbox kann für Käufer zur Mogelpackung werden
Der Routerhersteller Fritz hat im Juni 2024 die Fritzbox 5690 Pro auf den Markt gebracht. Das Gerät kann nicht nur DSL-Verbindungen, sondern auch Glasfaseranschlüsse handhaben, bietet Wi-Fi 7 und das mit bis zu theoretisch möglichen 18,4 Gigabit pro Sekunde. Diese Features haben auch ihren Preis. Aktuell ruft das Unternehmen 350 Euro für die Fritzbox 5690 Pro auf. Die UVP liegt mit 479 Euro aber deutlich höher.
Fritzbox 5690 Pro: Preissteigerung trotz Hardware-Downgrade?
Zum Marktstart der Highend-Fritzbox lag die UVP noch bei 369 Euro. Damit ist sie im Laufe der Jahre um 110 Euro angestiegen. Wie Vergleichsportale zeigen, ist in derselben Zeit aber auch der tatsächliche Straßenpreis angestiegen. Lag der Preis Anfang 2026 noch bei etwa 290 Euro, kostet die Fritzbox 5690 Pro mittlerweile rund 320 Euro. Warum diese Preisentwicklung so kurios ist, zeigt die Webseite Router FAQ.
Die Kund:innen, die heute eine Fritzbox 5690 Pro kaufen, erhalten nicht zwangsläufig den gleichen Router, den Kund:innen noch vor zwei Jahren erhalten haben. Das musste ein User herausfinden, nachdem er sich eine zweite Fritzbox 5690 Pro zugelegt hatte. Der Speicherverbrauch des zweiten Routers sei deutlich höher als beim ersten Modell. Der Grund: Fritz hat offenbar in der Zwischenzeit Änderungen an der Speicherkonfiguration des Routers vorgenommen.
Router FAQ hat knapp 30 Datensätze von Besitzer:innen einer Fritzbox 5690 Pro ausgewertet, um das herauszufinden. So gibt es viele Modelle, die tatsächlich zwei Gigabyte RAM und vier Gigabyte Flash-Speicher besitzen. Darunter würden sich aber auch Modelle mit nur halb so viel RAM mischen. Zudem gebe es sogar einige Routermodelle, bei denen sowohl RAM als auch Flash-Speicher halbiert wurden. Sie hätten lediglich einen Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher und zwei Gigabyte Flash-Speicher.
Für Kund:innen ist es vor dem Kauf demnach nicht ersichtlich, welche Version sie kaufen. Die Artikelnummer des Routers habe sich im Laufe der Zeit nicht verändert. Und obwohl die Seriennummer fortlaufend ist, gebe es aktuellere Modelle, die wieder den ursprünglichen Speicher verbaut haben. Kund:innen, die unbedingt eine Fritzbox 5690 Pro haben möchten, sollten also nach dem Kauf den Speicher überprüfen und vom Rückgaberecht Gebrauch machen, falls der Speicher nicht den Erwartungen entspricht. Wie das geht, zeigt Router FAQ auf der eigenen Webseite.

articles.title: Une étude de 1960 avait calculé la fin du monde pour aujourd'hui, le vendredi 13 novembre 2026
articles.text:
La fin du monde ne quitte jamais longtemps l’actualité. Le Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists a réglé le 27 janvier 2026 son Horloge de l’Apocalypse à 85 secondes de minuit, son niveau le plus proche de la catastrophe depuis sa création. Un site va même jusqu’à surveiller les décollages de jets privés, au cas où les milliardaires fileraient avant tout le monde, et Marvel sort en décembre Avengers : Doomsday.
Ce vendredi 13 novembre 2026 a pourtant une place à part, car c’est la date exacte de l’apocalypse calculée par trois chercheurs de l’université de l’Illinois, dans un article paru le 4 novembre 1960 dans la revue Science, remis en avant par plusieurs médias ces derniers jours, dont The Independent. Le calcul paraît absurde, mais sa méthode était sérieuse et ses chiffres ont longtemps été justes.
Comment arrive-t-on à une date aussi précise ? Le physicien autrichien Heinz von Foerster et deux de ses étudiants, Patricia Mora et Lawrence Amiot, ont rassemblé les estimations de la population mondiale de l’an 1 à 1958. Ils ont constaté que l’humanité grandissait plus vite qu’une croissance exponentielle, où la population double à intervalles réguliers : chez nous, l’intervalle raccourcissait sans cesse.
Leur explication tenait à notre capacité à coopérer : plus nous sommes nombreux, mieux nous nous organisons pour produire de quoi vivre, ce qui accélère encore la croissance. Une telle courbe, dite hyperbolique, finit par atteindre l’infini à une date précise, que leur équation plaçait fin 2026. D’où la phrase restée célèbre de l’article : « Nos arrière-arrière-petits-enfants ne mourront pas de faim. Ils mourront écrasés. »
Une équation qui a tenu jusqu’en 1993
Le plus troublant, c’est que la prédiction a longtemps collé à la réalité. L’historien Alan MacEachern, de l’université Western au Canada, rappelle dans The Conversation que les chiffres réels ont suivi la courbe de 1960 jusqu’aux alentours de 1993. La population mondiale a ensuite décroché, parce que le monde a fait ce que les auteurs recommandaient, c’est-à-dire réduire les naissances. Le taux de natalité mondial est aujourd’hui un peu inférieur à la moitié de celui de 1960.
Un commentaire publié cet automne dans Science juge d’ailleurs le modèle mathématiquement correct, mais valable seulement pour une période historique donnée.
Un tour de magicien, avec un revers
Von Foerster croyait-il à son apocalypse ? Visiblement pas. Le 14 novembre 1960, le magazine Time expliquait que le physicien, alors âgé de 48 ans, voulait surtout frapper les esprits : une population qui accélère sans arrêt finit tôt ou tard par avoir un problème. Il proposait même un « peoplo-stat », sorte de thermostat de la population, par exemple en taxant lourdement les familles de plus de deux enfants. Time précisait au passage qu’il était lui-même père de trois enfants.
Le choix de son propre anniversaire comme date de l’apocalypse relève de la même malice. Avant de devenir, selon le sociologue Serge Proulx, « le père de la seconde cybernétique », la science qui étudie comment machines et êtres vivants se régulent par des boucles de rétroaction, von Foerster avait été magicien de scène. Alan MacEachern salue donc un bon tour, qui a attiré l’attention du monde sur un sujet sérieux en passant par l’absurde.
Pourtant, un second texte de The Conversation, publié ce mercredi 11 novembre, rappelle ce qu’est devenue la solution défendue dans l’article : le contrôle massif des naissances a pris des formes brutales dans les décennies suivantes, des stérilisations forcées en Asie du Sud à la politique de l’enfant unique en Chine, abandonnée en 2015.
La planète compte environ 8 milliards d’habitants, un nombre qui augmente encore, mais de moins en moins vite. Heinz von Foerster, mort en 2002, aurait eu 115 ans aujourd’hui.

articles.title: Malgré le gel promis, le prix de l’électricité pourrait bien grimper de 4 % en février 2027
articles.text:
Le prix de l'électricité au tarif réglementé pourrait augmenter d'environ 4 % au 1er février 2027, selon une estimation de Papernest. Le gouvernement promet pourtant un gel cet hiver, qui pourrait surtout repousser la hausse.
La facture d'électricité des quelque 20 millions de foyers au tarif réglementé pourrait augmenter d'environ 4 % au 1er février 2027. C'est l'estimation publiée par Papernest jeudi, qui s'appuie sur la méthode de calcul de la Commission de régulation de l'énergie (CRE). Elle tombe alors que le gouvernement et EDF promettent des tarifs stables jusqu'à la fin de l'hiver, une promesse qui pourrait reporter la hausse sans la faire disparaître.
Les abonnés Tempo d’EDF pourraient voir leur facture d’électricité grimper de 9 % en février 2027
Concrètement, si aucun gel ne vient s'en mêler, la facture TTC des abonnés au tarif Bleu d'EDF pourrait grimper de 4 % en moyenne au 1er février 2027. Abonnement compris, le kWh reviendrait en moyenne à 25,4 centimes, contre 24,4 aujourd'hui. Un foyer en option Base 6 kVA qui consomme 4 800 kWh par an paierait ainsi environ 46 euros de plus, soit un peu moins de 4 euros par mois. En heures pleines et heures creuses, la hausse serait quasi identique à consommation égale. Elle atteindrait 88 euros pour un foyer en 9 kVA qui consomme 10 000 kWh par an. Si toute la hausse portait sur la consommation, le kWh en option Base passerait d'environ 20 à 20,8 centimes. Il resterait loin du record de 25,16 centimes de février 2024.
Qui seraient les plus touchés ? Les abonnés Tempo, probablement. Car avec cette option, le prix du kWh change selon la couleur du jour, bleu, blanc ou rouge. Elle grimperait d'environ 9 %, soit 92 euros par an pour un foyer en 6 kVA qui consomme 4 800 kWh. La CRE poursuit en effet le rattrapage du prix de Tempo, entamé en février 2026. Environ 900 000 clients sont concernés.
Et tout ça, ce n'est pas d'abord la faute des prix de gros. Début novembre, l'électricité livrée en 2027 s'échangeait autour de 113 euros le MWh sur les marchés à terme, où l'on achète aujourd'hui l'électricité qui sera livrée plus tard. Mais la CRE fait la moyenne de deux années d'achats, ce qui ramène le prix retenu à environ 66 euros, à peine plus que les 63,9 euros de 2026. La hausse vient surtout de l'hiver, la saison où l'on consomme le plus. Cette année, l'électricité livrée de janvier à mars 2027 s'est échangée en moyenne 65 % plus cher que celle livrée sur toute l'année, contre 37 % un an plus tôt.
Ce surcoût explique à lui seul plus de 40 % de la hausse. Le reste vient de corrections sur les coûts des années passées, de la fin d'un coup de pouce qui allégeait le tarif depuis février 2026, et de la part de l'ancien mécanisme de capacité pas encore facturée. C'est ce dispositif qui finance les moyens de production disponibles lors des pics de consommation.
Un gel du prix de l'électricité, et après ?
Sur le papier, les ménages n'ont pourtant rien à craindre cet hiver. Car le 7 octobre, Sébastien Lecornu a été clair : le prix de l'électricité ne doit pas augmenter. Dès le lendemain, la ministre déléguée chargée de l'Énergie, Maud Bregeon, en a fait « un engagement ». Un mois plus tard, le PDG d'EDF, Bernard Fontana, a dit s'attendre à des tarifs stables jusqu'à la fin de l'hiver. Il a toutefois rappelé que la décision revient au gouvernement, qui fixe le tarif par arrêté. En 2026, le tarif avait déjà bougé deux fois, de -0,83 % en février, puis +2,5 % en août.
Sauf qu'un gel ne fait pas disparaître les coûts, il les met, pour rester dans le jargon, au congélateur. En 2019, certain se souviennent peut-être que l'État avait déjà bloqué une hausse pendant l'hiver, et la note avait été présentée au 1er juin. Tant que le gel dure, il ferait économiser environ 3,80 euros par mois à un foyer en option Base 6 kVA, et 7,30 euros à un foyer en heures pleines / heures creuses 9 kVA. Ensuite, un rattrapage reste possible.
D'ici là, beaucoup de choses peuvent encore changer. La CRE publiera sa proposition à la mi-janvier. Papernest envisage une hausse limitée à 1,8 % si les prix de gros reculent d'ici fin décembre et que les rattrapages restent faibles. Elle pourrait atteindre 7,4 % si l'hiver s'annonce très cher et que les coûts commerciaux grimpent. Le tarif d'utilisation des réseaux électriques, lui, ne bougera pas avant août 2027. Quant à la TVA à 5,5 % votée par les députés le 2 novembre, elle est tombée avec le rejet de la partie recettes du budget, deux jours plus tard. Les sénateurs peuvent encore la réintroduire lors de leur examen, du 23 au 28 novembre. Enfin, précisons que ces chiffres viennent d'une plateforme qui permet de souscrire des offres de fournisseurs concurrents d'EDF, dont la sienne, papernest énergie. Son estimation ne tient compte ni du gel ni d'une baisse de TVA, avec une marge d'erreur de plus ou moins 1,4 point. Une projection, donc, pas un barème.
En clair, si l'État tient parole, la facture des abonnés au tarif réglementé ne bougera pas cet hiver, mais la hausse pourrait n'être que décalée de quelques mois.

articles.title: When One GPU Isn’t Enough: Serving GLM-5.3 Across Two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Running a frontier-scale model locally means keeping all its weights in GPU memory; the largest models no longer fit on one machine. Two NVIDIA DGX Stations connected over ConnectX-8 RDMA serve one model through a single endpoint, with tensor parallelism splitting the model weights and computation across both GPUs.
The NVIDIA GLM-5.3 NVFP4 model, a quantized version of Z.ai’s mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, has 753 billion parameters, with 40 billion activated per token. Sparse activation reduces computation, but all model weights still need to remain available because each token can be routed to different experts. At about 464 GB, the checkpoint exceeds the 252 GB of HBM3e on a single GB300 GPU. This tutorial uses two DGX Stations to keep the weights in GPU memory, with CPU weight offload disabled.
Before starting, connect the two Stations with the Connect Two DGX Stations playbook.
This post shows how to serve GLM-5.3 locally across two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM, send a request, and measure behavior under concurrent load. Tensor parallelism (TP=2) splits the model’s tensors across the two GB300 GPUs. Both Stations compute every request, and Station A returns the answer through one OpenAI-compatible API. By the end, you’ll have a working endpoint and a baseline for how it behaves under load.
Prerequisites
- Two GB300 DGX Stations running Linux, connected and validated with the Connect Two DGX Stations playbook, including its GPU-memory RDMA test on both rails.
- SSH and sudo access on both Stations with the same Linux username. Docker and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit come preinstalled with the DGX Station software stack. Allow outbound access to the container registry, Hugging Face, and package repositories.
- At least 464 GB of free disk space on each Station for its copy of the checkpoint, plus room for the vLLM container image and temporary files.
- Acceptance of the NVIDIA Open Model Agreement and the original GLM-5.3 license terms, listed on the model card. SPEED-Bench is governed by the NVIDIA Evaluation Dataset License Agreement.
- A Hugging Face account and read access token, with access to the gated cais/hle dataset: sign in, open its page, and select Agree and access repository. Step 5 downloads SPEED-Bench prompts from this dataset.
The companion video follows the same workflow.
Step 1. Prepare the two Stations
This tutorial uses a separate computer, such as your laptop, to manage both Stations. Start by opening an SSH session to each Station from that computer. Alternatively, work from a local terminal on each Station. Run every command in this step on both Stations unless it starts with “On A.”
The two Stations run the same container and checkpoint in different roles: Station A (rank 0) hosts the API, and Station B (rank 1) runs only a worker, with no API server.
First, check Docker access and collect the network values you’ll use later:
docker version
ibdev2netdev
ip -br addr
| Note: If the docker version output has no Server section, the client cannot reach the Docker daemon. If the error is permission denied, follow the Docker post-installation procedure: add your user to the docker group with sudo usermod -aG docker "$USER", run exit, then reconnect and rerun docker version. The docker group grants root-level privileges. | 
|---|
The ibdev2netdev output lists the two direct rails, cx8r0 and cx8r1. Pick one for serving traffic, for example cx8r1, and note two things for it on each Station:
- Its RDMA device, on the ibdev2netdev line that ends with the rail’s name. In mlx5_1 port 1 ==> cx8r1 (Up), the device is mlx5_1.
- Its IPv4 address, on the ip -br addr line that starts with the rail’s name. In cx8r1 UP 192.168.101.1/24, the address is 192.168.101.1.
The rail name and device are the same on both Stations; only the IPv4 address differs.
Next, create ~/glm53.env on each Station. This file stores the values that later commands use:
nano ~/glm53.env
Paste the following block and replace each <...> placeholder, keeping the quotes, with the values you noted.
RANK="<NODE_RANK>"                    # RANK="0" on Station A, RANK="1" on Station B 
HEAD_IP="<STATION_A_IPV4_ADDRESS>"    # IPv4 address you noted on Station A; same in both files
WORKER_IP="<STATION_B_IPV4_ADDRESS>"  # IPv4 address you noted on Station B; same in both files
RAIL_IFACE="<RAIL_NAME>"              # Rail you picked, for example cx8r1; same in both files
RAIL_HCA="<RDMA_DEVICE>"              # RDMA device you noted, for example mlx5_1; same in both files
IMG=vllm/vllm-openai:v0.30.0-aarch64
IMG+=@sha256:4864d46625cbc3307623e29ac742030655e27249feba7b97ec925ce4cc4dfb56
MODEL_REPO=nvidia/GLM-5.3-NVFP4
MODEL_REV=e3b8f9f2fad29727dfa95e766c5cac18ea1414bf
MODEL_HOST="$HOME/models/GLM-5.3-NVFP4"
CONTAINER=glm53-full
PORT=8000
if [ "$RANK" = 0 ]; then
  NODE_IP=$HEAD_IP; PEER_IP=$WORKER_IP
else
  NODE_IP=$WORKER_IP; PEER_IP=$HEAD_IP
fi
GPU_UUID=$(nvidia-smi --query-gpu=uuid,name --format=csv,noheader |
  awk -F, '$2 ~ /GB300/ {gsub(/ /,"",$1); print $1; exit}')
For example, with the default addresses on cx8r1, Station A’s file starts like this. Station B’s file is identical except for RANK="1":
RANK="0"
HEAD_IP="192.168.101.1"
WORKER_IP="192.168.101.2"
RAIL_IFACE="cx8r1"
RAIL_HCA="mlx5_1"
MODEL_HOST is built from your home directory, and Step 2 copies the checkpoint over SSH to the same path on Station B. 
| Note: Later steps start with source ~/glm53.env to load these values. Run this command again whenever you open a new SSH session. | 
|---|
On both Stations, load the values and check storage, connectivity, and baseline memory:
source ~/glm53.env
mkdir -p "$MODEL_HOST" && df -h "$MODEL_HOST"
ethtool "$RAIL_IFACE"
ip link show dev "$RAIL_IFACE"
ping -I "$RAIL_IFACE" -M do -s 8972 -c 3 "$PEER_IP"
timedatectl show -p NTPSynchronized --value
nvidia-smi
These checks catch cabling and addressing mistakes before they surface as NCCL timeouts. Expect a 400000Mb/s link, MTU 9000, successful jumbo-frame pings, and synchronized time. nvidia-smi should show no compute processes on the GB300. On a Station with a display GPU, Xorg can appear on both GPUs with a few MiB. 
| Tip: Note the GPU memory use shown by nvidia-smi; Step 4 compares it with the loaded model. | 
|---|
Step 2 copies the checkpoint from A to B over SSH, so A needs passwordless access to B. On A, create a key without a passphrase (see SSH keys for details), copy its public key to B after checking B’s host fingerprint, and confirm the login:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
ssh-copy-id "$WORKER_IP"
ssh -o BatchMode=yes "$WORKER_IP" hostname
Step 2. Download and copy the model
Tensor parallelism requires both ranks to run the same software against the same weights. Start by pulling the pinned image on both Stations:
docker pull "$IMG" &&
docker image inspect "$IMG" --format '{{.Architecture}} {{.RepoDigests}}'
The pull can take several minutes. Matching arm64 digests mean both ranks run identical software.
On A, download the pinned checkpoint. At about 464 GB, it takes roughly an hour at 1 Gb/s, or about six minutes at 10 Gb/s:
mkdir -p "$MODEL_HOST"
docker run --rm --network host -v "$MODEL_HOST:/model" \
  --entrypoint bash "$IMG" -lc \
  "exec hf download '$MODEL_REPO' --revision '$MODEL_REV' --local-dir /model"
When hf download prints Downloaded, copy the files to B. On A:
ssh "$WORKER_IP" "mkdir -p '$MODEL_HOST'" &&
rsync -aH --info=progress2 --exclude '.cache/' \
  "$MODEL_HOST/" "$WORKER_IP:$MODEL_HOST/"
Each disk keeps the full checkpoint; vLLM partitions the weights across the GPUs at load time, with no further quantization.
On A, compare both copies (the check reads B’s file list over SSH), then validate the checkpoint:
(
  set -euo pipefail
  L=$(find "$MODEL_HOST" -path '*/.cache' -prune -o \
    -type f -printf '%P %s\n' | LC_ALL=C sort | sha256sum)
  R=$(ssh "$WORKER_IP" "set -o pipefail; find '$MODEL_HOST' \
    -path '*/.cache' -prune -o -type f -printf '%P %s\\n' | \
    LC_ALL=C sort | sha256sum")
  test "$L" = "$R"
  test "$(find "$MODEL_HOST" -maxdepth 1 \
    -name 'model-*-of-00050.safetensors' | wc -l)" = 50
  python3 -c "import json; c=json.load(open('$MODEL_HOST/config.json')); \
assert c['architectures']==['GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM']; \
assert c['quantization_config']['quant_algo']=='MIXED_PRECISION'"
  echo MODEL_READY
)
MODEL_READY means both Stations hold the same file names and sizes in the expected layout. MIXED_PRECISION is expected: NVFP4 quantization targets MoE-block linear weights and activations, not every tensor.
Step 3. Launch the distributed service
This step turns two machines into one service: the same launch script runs on both Stations, reads ~/glm53.env, and starts one vLLM rank on each. Two settings matter most if you adapt it: --max-model-len 98304, the context ceiling in tokens, which covers input plus output, and --gpu-memory-utilization 0.93, which gives vLLM 93% of GPU memory. If you change other flags, change one at a time and test again.
For the latest recommended configurations, see NVIDIA’s Local AI recipe repository.
| Security note: --host 0.0.0.0 with --network host exposes the unauthenticated API on every Station A interface, including management. Firewall the port to intended clients, and add authentication and TLS before wider access. | 
|---|
On both Stations, create a file named ~/launch-glm53.sh:
nano ~/launch-glm53.sh
The script enables multi-token prediction (MTP), a form of speculative decoding: the model’s MTP layer drafts four tokens per step, and vLLM verifies them with the full model before accepting them, so each step can produce several tokens. The gain depends on how often drafts are accepted, which varies with the prompt.
FP8 KV-cache storage halves cache memory compared with 16-bit storage, leaving room for more tokens. Prefix caching is enabled to avoid reprocessing prompt prefixes the server has already seen. Paste the script below; it checks your configuration, finds the RoCE GID index for the selected rail, and starts this Station’s vLLM rank in a container:
set -euo pipefail
source "$HOME/glm53.env"
case "$RANK" in 0|1) ;; *) echo "Invalid RANK" >&2; exit 1;; esac
test -n "$GPU_UUID"
test -f "$MODEL_HOST/config.json"
GID_INDEX=$(/usr/sbin/show_gids 2>/dev/null |
  awk -v d="$RAIL_HCA" -v ip="$NODE_IP" \
  '$1==d && $5==ip && $6=="v2" {g=$3} END {if(g!="") print g}')
test -n "$GID_INDEX"
HEADLESS=
if [ "$RANK" = 1 ]; then HEADLESS=--headless; fi
SPEC_CONFIG='{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":4}'
KERNEL_CONFIG='{"enable_flashinfer_autotune":false,"moe_backend":"flashinfer_cutlass"}'
COMPILE_CONFIG='{"cudagraph_mode":"FULL_DECODE_ONLY","cudagraph_capture_sizes":[5,10,20,40,80],"pass_config":{"fuse_allreduce_rms":false}}'
docker run -d --name "$CONTAINER" \
  --gpus device="$GPU_UUID" --network host --ipc host --shm-size 32g \
  --device /dev/infiniband --cap-add IPC_LOCK \
  --ulimit memlock=-1 --ulimit stack=67108864 \
  -v "$MODEL_HOST:/model:ro" \
  -e RANK="$RANK" -e HEADLESS="$HEADLESS" \
  -e MASTER_ADDR="$HEAD_IP" -e MODEL_REPO="$MODEL_REPO" -e PORT="$PORT" \
  -e SPEC_CONFIG="$SPEC_CONFIG" -e KERNEL_CONFIG="$KERNEL_CONFIG" \
  -e COMPILE_CONFIG="$COMPILE_CONFIG" \
  -e NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=1 -e NCCL_IB_HCA="$RAIL_HCA" \
  -e NCCL_IB_GID_INDEX="$GID_INDEX" \
  -e NCCL_IB_TIMEOUT=22 -e NCCL_IB_RETRY_CNT=7 \
  -e VLLM_ALLREDUCE_USE_FLASHINFER=0 -e VLLM_ALLREDUCE_USE_SYMM_MEM=0 \
  -e NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME="$RAIL_IFACE" -e GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME="$RAIL_IFACE" \
  -e NCCL_NET_GDR_LEVEL=5 -e NCCL_DEBUG=INFO -e NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,NET \
  -e NCCL_DEBUG_FILE='/tmp/nccl_%h_%p.log' -e VLLM_HOST_IP="$NODE_IP" \
  -e VLLM_EXECUTE_MODEL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=1800 \
  -e PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True \
  -e VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 -e FLASHINFER_DISABLE_VERSION_CHECK=1 \
  --entrypoint bash "$IMG" -lc '
    set -euo pipefail  
    # Use NCCL 2.30.7 from the image: older versions can deadlock
    # cross-node CUDA graph replays over RoCE (vLLM issue #52504).
    export VLLM_NCCL_SO_PATH=$(python3 -c "import nvidia.nccl,os;
print(os.path.join(list(nvidia.nccl.__path__)[0], \"lib\", \"libnccl.so.2\"))")
    test -f "$VLLM_NCCL_SO_PATH"
    EXTRA=()
    if [ -n "$HEADLESS" ]; then EXTRA+=("$HEADLESS"); fi
    exec vllm serve /model --served-model-name "$MODEL_REPO" \
      --host 0.0.0.0 --port "$PORT" \
      --nnodes 2 --node-rank "$RANK" --master-addr "$MASTER_ADDR" \
      --master-port 29501 --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
      --speculative-config "$SPEC_CONFIG" \
      --max-model-len 98304  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
      --block-size 128 --max-num-seqs 16 \
      --trust-remote-code --disable-custom-all-reduce \
      --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --enable-prefix-caching \
      --gpu-memory-utilization 0.93 \
      --enable-prompt-tokens-details \
      --kernel-config "$KERNEL_CONFIG" --compilation-config "$COMPILE_CONFIG" \
      --distributed-timeout-seconds 1800 \
      --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser glm47 --reasoning-parser glm47 \
      "${EXTRA[@]}"
  '
Run the script on B first, then on A:
bash ~/launch-glm53.sh
Each command prints a container ID and returns immediately; the service is not ready yet. B’s worker waits for A to join, then each Station loads its share of the weights from local storage, prepares kernels, and captures CUDA graphs. This takes several minutes.
On A, follow the log to see when the service is ready (--since hides output from earlier runs):
docker logs --follow --since "$(docker inspect \
  --format '{{.State.StartedAt}}' "$CONTAINER")" "$CONTAINER"
When the log shows Application startup complete, press Ctrl+C to stop following it; the service keeps running. 
At this point one model spans two machines. Neither GPU holds a complete copy, and neither can answer a request alone: every token needs both ranks to exchange partial results over the RoCE rail.
The remaining GPU memory holds the KV cache, which stores the context of in-flight requests. The startup log reports its capacity (GPU KV cache size). All requests in flight share it, so longer prompts or more users need more of it. If you run out, lower --max-model-len or send fewer requests at once.
Step 4. Verify serving and send a request
On A, check the API (127.0.0.1 is A itself):
docker exec "$CONTAINER" curl -fsS --max-time 10 \
  "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/health" >/dev/null && echo HEALTH_OK
HEALTH_OK proves that Station A answers. Next, on both Stations, check that the ranks communicate over GPU RDMA rather than falling back to TCP sockets. The check reads the NCCL logs that the launcher writes through NCCL_DEBUG=INFO, and the same block shows the loaded memory:
docker exec "$CONTAINER" bash -lc '
  set -euo pipefail
  files=(/tmp/nccl_*.log)
  test -e "${files[0]}"
  grep -hE "NET/IB.*GDRDMA|GPU Direct RDMA Enabled" "${files[@]}" >/dev/null
  grep -hF "$NCCL_IB_HCA" "${files[@]}" >/dev/null
  if grep -hE "NET/Socket|NCCL WARN|NCCL ERROR" "${files[@]}"; then
    exit 1
  fi
  echo RDMA_CHECK_OK
'
nvidia-smi
RDMA_CHECK_OK means the check passed with no warnings. In nvidia-smi, A shows the VLLM::Worker_TP0 process and B shows VLLM::Worker_TP1, one rank per GPU. The startup log reports about 218 GiB of weights per GPU, roughly half the checkpoint, which confirms that the model is split across the two GPUs.
| Measurement | Station A | Station B | 
|---|---|---|
| GB300 GPU used (GiB) | 0.01 → 231.35 | 0.00 → 231.34 | 
On A, send a chat request through the OpenAI-compatible API:
docker exec "$CONTAINER" curl -fsS --max-time 120 \
  "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/v1/chat/completions" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"nvidia/GLM-5.3-NVFP4",
    "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Quarterly units sold: Q1 = 120; Q2 = 180; Q3 = 150. Summarize the trend in one sentence and calculate the percentage change from Q1 to Q2."}],
    "temperature":0,"max_tokens":4096,
    "chat_template_kwargs":{"reasoning_effort":"low"}}' |
python3 -c 'import json,sys; c=json.load(sys.stdin)["choices"][0];
print(c["message"]["content"]); print("finish_reason:",c["finish_reason"])'
The response should look like this:
**Trend:** Units sold rose sharply in Q2 before partially declining in Q3, remaining above the Q1 level.
**Q1 → Q2 percentage change:** (180 - 120) / 120 × 100 = **50% increase**
finish_reason: stop
finish_reason: stop means the model finished its answer instead of hitting the token limit. The request sets reasoning_effort to low in chat_template_kwargs. GLM-5.3 also accepts high and max, which let it reason longer before answering, at the cost of latency. Because the launcher enables tool calling (--enable-auto-tool-choice), agent frameworks that use the OpenAI tools API can call the same endpoint.
Step 5. Concurrency and release resources
AIPerf, the NVIDIA benchmarking tool for inference endpoints, measures throughput and latency. Installing it inside the serving container can change vLLM’s dependencies, so on A, install it in its own virtual environment:
sudo apt update &&
sudo apt install -y python3.12-venv python3.12-dev build-essential &&
python3.12 -m venv "$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0" &&
"$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/pip" install 'aiperf==0.12.0' &&
"$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/pip" check
The install should end with No broken requirements found.
AIPerf can send synthetic prompts or replay an existing dataset. This tutorial uses the 80 Coding conversations from SPEED-Bench, a set of real prompts built to evaluate speculative decoding, so MTP is measured on realistic text. SPEED-Bench’s preparation script fetches these prompts from several Hugging Face datasets, including the gated cais/hle: if you haven’t already, open its page and select Agree and access repository before you continue. Then, on A, log in to Hugging Face:
"$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/hf" auth login
Next, download and prepare the dataset. See the official AIPerf guide for details:
SPEED_BENCH_DIR="$HOME/datasets/speed-bench"
mkdir -p "$SPEED_BENCH_DIR"
curl -fLsS https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Skills/refs/heads/main/nemo_skills/dataset/speed-bench/prepare.py | \
  "$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/python" - --config qualitative --output_dir "$SPEED_BENCH_DIR"
On A, check the dataset and service. Continue when the check prints BENCHMARK_READY:
(
  set -euo pipefail
  source ~/glm53.env
  curl -fsS "http://$HEAD_IP:$PORT/health" >/dev/null
  "$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/python" - <<'PY_CHECK'
import json
from pathlib import Path
root = Path.home()
path = root / "datasets/speed-bench/qualitative.jsonl"
assert path.exists(), "Dataset missing: rerun the SPEED-Bench preparation"
rows = [json.loads(line) for line in path.read_text().splitlines() if line.strip()]
coding = [row for row in rows if row["category"] == "coding"]
assert len(coding) == 80, "Expected 80 Coding conversations"
assert sum(len(row["messages"]) for row in coding) == 89
assert all("FULL BENCHMARK DATA SHOULD BE FETCHED" not in message["content"]
           for row in coding for message in row["messages"])
print("BENCHMARK_READY: dataset has 80 Coding conversations, 89 turns in total.")
PY_CHECK
)
The full sweep covers concurrency 1, 8, 16, and 32. At each level, AIPerf sends 3×C warmup requests, then measures 10×C requests, where C is the concurrency. Some conversations are sent more than once at higher concurrency.
Benchmark requests use the model’s default reasoning effort (max) and an 8,192-token output cap; responses can finish before reaching it. Full sweeps can take several hours.
 A two-hour request timeout leaves room for long responses, --server-metrics collects server counters used to measure MTP acceptance, and --export-level raw keeps each response for inspection. 
For a quick test, run the block below on A with both containers running and no other API traffic. It tests C1 and C8 with prefix caching enabled, as in the reference measurements in Table 2, below.
(
  set -euo pipefail
  source ~/glm53.env
  CODING_DATASET="$HOME/datasets/speed-bench/qualitative.jsonl"
  test -f "$CODING_DATASET"
 export CONCURRENCIES=${CONCURRENCIES:-"1 8"} # Quick run: C1 and C8.
  # Optional full benchmark: follow the reproduction instructions below.
  # Step 3: --max-num-seqs 16 -> export CONCURRENCIES="1 8 16"
  # Step 3: --max-num-seqs 32 -> export CONCURRENCIES=32
  RUN_DIR="$HOME/aiperf-results/blog-coding-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
  for C in $CONCURRENCIES;  do
    ART="$RUN_DIR/c$C"
    env -u HF_HUB_OFFLINE -u TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE \
      "$HOME/.venvs/aiperf-0.12.0/bin/aiperf" profile \
      -m "$MODEL_REPO" --url "http://$HEAD_IP:$PORT" \
      --endpoint-type chat --streaming --tokenizer "$MODEL_HOST" \
      --custom-dataset-type speed_bench_coding --input-file "$CODING_DATASET" \
      --request-count "$((10 * C))" --warmup-request-count "$((3 * C))" \
      --osl 8192 \
      --use-server-token-count --concurrency "$C" --random-seed 42 \
      --request-timeout-seconds 7200 \
      --server-metrics "http://$HEAD_IP:$PORT/metrics" \
      --export-level raw --artifact-dir "$ART"
    printf "Results: %s\n" "$ART"
  done
  printf "Results directory: %s\n" "$RUN_DIR"
)
AIPerf saves metrics, raw responses, and logs in the results directory. Warmup requests are excluded from the reported metrics.
Optional: Reproduce Table 2. In ~/launch-glm53.sh from Step 3 on both Stations, keep --enable-prefix-caching and set --max-num-seqs to 16 or 32 for the corresponding group shown in the comments above. Before each group, stop and remove the current containers on A, then B (docker stop --timeout 60 "$CONTAINER", followed by docker rm "$CONTAINER"). Relaunch the updated script on B, then A with bash ~/launch-glm53.sh and wait for Application startup complete. On A, run the matching export CONCURRENCIES command from the comments, then rerun the AIPerf block.
To test without prefix caching, replace --enable-prefix-caching with --no-enable-prefix-caching in the Step 3 script on both Stations, then recreate the containers as above. Performance may differ from Table 2.
Figure 2 compares overall output throughput across measured requests with mean per-user throughput. Token counts include reasoning.
Table 2, below, shows how throughput and latency change as more requests share the service.
| Configured concurrency | Overall throughput (tok/s) | Mean request latency (s) | Mean TTFT (ms) | Mean inter-token latency (ms/token) | 
| 1 | 107.4 | 49.84 | 479.75 | 8.78 | 
| 8 | 386.0 | 114.17 | 433.79 | 19.01 | 
| 16 | 607.8 | 136.46 | 482.90 | 23.77 | 
| 32 | 385.0 | 453.54 | 899.36 | 77.90 | 
Table 2. SPEED-Bench Coding results with prefix caching enabled, four MTP draft tokens per step, and an FP8 KV cache. Latency metrics are means over measured requests; warmup is excluded. TTFT measures time to the first token, which may be reasoning
Overall throughput peaks at 607.8 tok/s at C16. It falls to 385.0 tok/s at C32, where mean request latency is 453.5 s. Higher concurrency also reduces mean per-user throughput, from 115.3 tok/s at C1 to 13.0 tok/s at C32.
After the requests finish, stop the vLLM container on A, then on B:
docker stop --timeout 60 "$CONTAINER"
docker inspect --format \
  'Status={{.State.Status}} Running={{.State.Running}}' "$CONTAINER"
nvidia-smi
The status should read Status=exited Running=false, with no vLLM processes in nvidia-smi; the checkpoint, containers, and results stay on disk. To resume, run docker start "$CONTAINER" on B, then A, and repeat the Step 4 checks.
Troubleshoot common blockers
- Missing variables or SSH failure: source ~/glm53.env after reconnecting; verify A-to-B key authentication and B’s fingerprint.
- SPEED-Bench preparation fails with a gated-dataset error: sign in to Hugging Face with the same account, open the cais/hle page, select Agree and access repository, then rerun the preparation.
- Startup or RDMA check failure: inspect docker logs "$CONTAINER" on both nodes; verify the checkpoint and the GID, and rerun the playbook’s validation (script 07).
- CUDA out of memory: lower --max-model-len or concurrency, then retest.
Put the endpoint to work
You now have a 753-billion-parameter model running behind one local API on two NVIDIA DGX Stations, with every weight in GPU memory. That opens up work that’s hard to do on a hosted endpoint: running inference on sensitive or proprietary data, prototyping agents locally, and iterating on prompts without per-token costs.
Connect your own application using the vLLM serving documentation, then rerun AIPerf with your prompts to find the concurrency that fits your workload. A frontier-scale model is now ready to build on, right from your desk.

articles.title: "Solo hay dos maneras de vivir la vida: como si nada fuera un milagro, o como si todo lo fuera": la frase más certera de Einstein tiene un problema
articles.text:
Hay científicos que pasan a la historia por sus descubrimientos y otros que acaban convertidos en una fuente inagotable de sabiduría popular. Albert Einstein ha conseguido probablemente ambas cosas. El problema es que, en su segunda faceta, buena parte del trabajo parece haberlo hecho otra gente.
El Einstein que nunca conocimos. Esta mañana me he encontrado una cita en X: “Solo hay dos maneras de vivir la vida: una, como si nada fuera un milagro; la otra, como si todo fuera un milagro”. Lo curioso es que la frase lleva décadas apareciendo en libros de autoayuda, calendarios, publicaciones motivacionales y redes sociales acompañada de un nombre: Albert Einstein.
De hecho, me pareció tan certera que me puse a investigar. Lo tiene todo para ser una de esas reflexiones que parecen encajar perfectamente con la imagen del científico: un hombre capaz de descubrir los secretos del universo y, al mismo tiempo, maravillarse ante ellos. Pero hay un pequeño problema. No existe ninguna prueba concluyente de que Einstein pronunciara o escribiera esas palabras. Y, a juzgar por la extraordinaria popularidad de la cita, a la gente parece darle bastante igual, porque no hay año que no se repita al menos una vez o que incluso se haga un artículo en torno a la forma en la que el científico lanzó semejante mensaje la mundo.
Un milagro anterior a Einstein. Ocurre que, para encontrar el origen de aquella reflexión, hay que retroceder hasta el siglo XIX, cuando el físico ni siquiera había nacido. En 1839, el teólogo estadounidense Andrews Norton ya recogía una discusión sobre la aparente contradicción de considerar milagroso todo cuanto sucede. Décadas después, en octubre de 1896, el periódico The New Zealand Herald publicó un sermón del sacerdote británico Basil Wilberforce en el que aparecía una formulación mucho más cercana a la cita actual: para una mente elevada, todo era un milagro o nada lo era.
La idea volvió a aparecer en 1918 en un libro del pedagogo Edward Porter St. John sobre educación religiosa infantil. El concepto, por tanto, llevaba tiempo circulando en ámbitos religiosos y filosóficos antes de que alguien decidiera ponerle la firma de un premio Nobel de Física.
El hombre que se la atribuyó. La primera referencia conocida que vincula directamente la frase con Einstein data de 1942. Su protagonista fue Gilbert Fowler White, un prestigioso geógrafo estadounidense que reflexionaba en sus notas personales sobre el azar y los acontecimientos decisivos de su vida. White atribuyó entonces al físico las palabras que conocemos hoy, aunque no explicó dónde las había escuchado o leído.
Aquellas anotaciones fueron recuperadas en 2006 por Robert E. Hinshaw en su biografía del geógrafo, Living With Nature’s Extremes. El hallazgo resulta especialmente interesante porque demuestra que la atribución ya circulaba cuando Einstein estaba vivo. Por contra, no nos permite saber si White escuchó realmente al científico o simplemente estaba repitiendo una frase que alguien le había contado.
El pequeño problema de los expertos. En 1989, la conocida periodista estadounidense Liz Smith volvió a atribuir la reflexión a Einstein en una columna publicada en The Baltimore Sun. Un año después apareció en una recopilación de consejos titulada Friendly Advice, editada por Jon Winokur. Pero en 2010 llegó una advertencia mucho más autorizada. Alice Calaprice, especialista en la obra del físico, publicó The Ultimate Quotable Einstein, una extensa recopilación de sus citas editada por Princeton University Press.
La famosa reflexión sobre los milagros terminó en un apartado cuyo nombre resultaba bastante esclarecedor: “Probablemente no son de Einstein”. Es decir, ni siquiera los investigadores que llevan décadas estudiando sus escritos han encontrado pruebas suficientes para concederle la autoría.
El "Paulo Coelho de la física". La reflexión sobre los milagros es solo una pequeña muestra de un fenómeno mucho mayor. Internet ha convertido al padre de la relatividad en una especie de gurú de la autoayuda capaz de aconsejarnos sobre el amor, la felicidad, la educación o el fracaso. Una de sus supuestas frases más populares sostiene que, si juzgamos a un pez por su capacidad para trepar a un árbol, vivirá creyéndose estúpido.
La primera atribución conocida de esta formulación a Einstein apareció en un libro de autoayuda de 2004, casi medio siglo después de su muerte. Tampoco existen pruebas de que definiera la locura como hacer siempre lo mismo esperando resultados diferentes, una reflexión que aparece en una novela de Rita Mae Brown de 1983. En 2018, de hecho, la revista Nature dedicó un artículo a este fenómeno y a las centenares de citas incorrectamente atribuidas al científico.
La autoridad de un genio. ¿Por qué Einstein? Supongo que, en parte, porque su nombre se ha convertido en sinónimo universal de inteligencia. Una reflexión anónima sobre cómo afrontar la vida adquiere una autoridad completamente diferente cuando aparece acompañada del rostro del hombre que revolucionó nuestra comprensión del espacio y el tiempo.
Y el fenómeno no se limita a las páginas de frases motivacionales. En 2013, la escritora y posteriormente aspirante a la presidencia de Estados Unidos Marianne Williamson compartió en Twitter la reflexión sobre los milagros atribuyéndosela al físico. En 2019, cuando trabajaba en Gizmodo, documentamos varias ocasiones en las que Williamson había difundido citas apócrifas de Einstein. El científico, fallecido en 1955, había acabado convertido en una celebridad de las redes sociales sin haber tenido jamás acceso a Internet.
Lo que Einstein sí dijo. Quizás lo más paradójico de todo es que no hacía falta inventarle frases. El verdadero Einstein dejó numerosas reflexiones sobre el misterio de la existencia y nuestra capacidad para maravillarnos ante el universo. En 1930, en un ensayo titulado El mundo tal como yo lo veo, escribió que la experiencia más hermosa que podemos tener es la del misterio, y situó esa emoción en el origen del arte y la ciencia.
Su pensamiento, sin embargo, era bastante más complejo que una frase motivacional de autoayudas: no concebía un Dios que premiara o castigara a los seres humanos, sino que encontraba una dimensión religiosa en la belleza y el orden de la naturaleza. La reflexión sobre los milagros resulta verosímil precisamente porque parece una versión simplificada de ese pensamiento. Pero, por supuesto, que una frase suene a Einstein no significa que sea de Einstein.
La última ironía. En 1930, Einstein escribió para un amigo una reflexión cuya autenticidad sí ha sido comprobada en los archivos del científico en Jerusalén: “Para castigarme por mi desprecio a la autoridad, el destino me ha convertido a mí mismo en una autoridad”. Difícilmente podría haber imaginado hasta qué punto acabarían cumpliéndose aquellas palabras. Casi un siglo después, su nombre sirve para otorgar credibilidad a reflexiones que posiblemente nunca se le pasaron ni rematadamente por la cabeza.
Y aunque los investigadores llevan décadas desmontando muchas de ellas, siguen circulando porque cumplen una función que poco tiene que ver con la física: nos dicen lo que queremos escuchar, pero con la firma de un genio. Einstein dedicó su vida a cuestionar nuestras certezas sobre el universo. Internet, en cambio, parece haber encontrado en él al hombre perfecto para confirmarlas.

articles.title: Patrick at Micro Center Grand Opening in Austin Texas Today
articles.text:
A few weeks ago, Patrick was at the Micro Center Columbus Ohio Grand Reopening with Jeff Geerling. Thousands of people showed up at the store near the company’s headquarters. Today, Patrick and Jeff will be at the brand-new Austin, Texas location. Sam and I were delayed by 7+ hours connecting through Philadelphia yesterday, so they will likely arrive in the early afternoon, assuming the new flight timing holds.
Patrick at Micro Center Grand Opening in Austin, Texas Today
If you are in the Austin, Texas area, the Micro Center opening should be a lot of fun. When Jeff and I did the Columbus, Ohio grand reopening, it was great to meet so many people who came out to greet us.
The plan for today is that when Sam and I arrive, we will do a video with Jeff for the STH YouTube channel and also film one for part of an upcoming video on Jeff’s channel.
We probably will not get to do a video like the walk-around inside the Columbus Micro Center, as we did a few months ago thanks to American Airlines. Still, Jeff’s video gives a good sense of what is inside a typical Micro Center, including a lot of the maker electronics gear, 3D printing gear, PC components, and even the random cables you sometimes need.
Final Words
I remember living in Austin a few years ago and wishing there was a Micro Center nearby. Now there is, though I do not live there anymore. If you are in the area, come and say hello. I wish Sam and I could make it for the ribbon cutting this morning, but unfortunately, even with a 3-hour layover and a 3-hour delay to the connecting flight, we missed the connection and sat on the tarmac yesterday. On the plus side, we filmed a world-first network deployment the day before. We are hoping to make it by 1PM or so and be there for the rest of the day.

articles.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
articles.text:
AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
Using AI to make bionic vision smarter and more precise, scientists are bringing the possibility of restoring sight to people with blindness one step closer to reality.
- Date:
- November 12, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Santa Barbara
- Summary:
- Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.
- Share:
Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.
The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.
Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.
"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab."
How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes
For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.
Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.
The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.
Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back."
The new findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.
Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man
An important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.
At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.
When researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.
Producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.
To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.
Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.
AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise
When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The new approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.
Another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.
This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.
"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler said. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation."
The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.
Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person
A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.
This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.
The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.
Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.
The AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.
By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.
"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around."
A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight
The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration."
The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.
Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.
Rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - Santa Barbara. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Pehuén Moure, Jacob Granley, Fabrizio Grani, Leili Soo, Antonio Lozano, Rocío López-Peco, Adrián Villamarín-Ortiz, Cristina Soto-Sánchez, Shih-Chii Liu, Michael Beyeler, Eduardo Fernández. Deep learning-based control of electrically evoked activity in human visual cortex. Neuron, 2026; DOI: 10.1016/j.neuron.2026.07.006

articles.title: Alerta: vazamento na Caixa expõe dados de 7,6 milhões de clientes • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Alerta: vazamento na Caixa expõe dados de 7,6 milhões de clientes
Dados como nome, CPF, e-mail e telefone de clientes vazaram em invasão à Caixa Vida e Previdência.
Nesta quinta-feira (12/11), clientes da Caixa Vida e Previdência passaram a ser avisados, por e-mail, de uma invasão aos sistemas da instituição financeira. Estima-se que informações cadastrais de pelo menos 7,6 milhões de pessoas vazaram na ação.
De acordo com o aviso, o acesso não autorizado aos sistemas da Caixa foi identificado no dia 6 de novembro de 2026 e resultou na captura de dados pessoais como nome, CPF, data de nascimento, nacionalidade, e-mail e telefone.
Na mesma mensagem, a Caixa afirma que, pelo menos até o momento, não identificou nenhuma evidência de que os dados vazados tenham sido divulgados publicamente ou usados de modo indevido. De todo modo, o alerta é importante, pois as informações poderão servir de base para golpes, a exemplo de ligações fraudulentas que se passam por funcionários do banco.
De acordo com as informações sobre o incidente enviadas pela Caixa à Comissão de Valores Mobiliários (CVM), a ação hacker levou ao vazamento de dados de 7,6 milhões de clientes da Caixa Vida e Previdência, divisão que, por sua vez, é controlada pela Caixa Seguridade. O número inclui clientes e ex-clientes.
Tal como o nome deixa claro, a Caixa Vida e Previdência oferece produtos como planos de previdência privada, seguros de vida, seguros viagem e seguros contra acidentes pessoais. Se você tem ou já teve algum desses produtos, precisa ficar atento quanto ao risco de contatos fraudulentos.
Vale destacar, porém, que a invasão não afetou os dados de clientes da Caixa Econômica Federal enquanto banco, bem como os dados de outras subsidiárias, como a Caixa Cartões ou a Caixa Loterias.
Tal como exige a legislação vigente, a Caixa já comunicou o incidente à Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD). A instituição financeira afirma também ter tomado providências para mitigar o acesso indevido a seus sistemas.
O Tecnoblog entrou em contato com a Caixa. A instituição nos enviou o seguinte posicionamento sobre o incidente:
A Caixa Vida e Previdência informa que foi vítima de ataque cibernético, que resultou no acesso não autorizado e na cópia de dados pessoais cadastrais para fora de seu ambiente tecnológico.
Não há indícios de comprometimento de dados sensíveis, como informações financeiras, bancárias, senhas ou de autenticação.
O incidente foi prontamente identificado e contido, com a adoção de medidas para reforçar a segurança de seus sistemas. As autoridades competentes e os titulares afetados estão sendo comunicados, conforme a legislação.
Até o momento, não foram identificadas evidências de divulgação pública ou utilização indevida dos dados envolvidos. O incidente não comprometeu a assistência prestada aos clientes nem a continuidade das suas operações.
A companhia reafirma seu compromisso com a segurança da informação, a proteção dos dados pessoais e a transparência.
