articles.title: Nightmare Eclipse Drops Windows Zero-Day Exploit ‘SignDrop’
articles.text:
Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri, known online as Nightmare Eclipse, this week dropped another zero-day exploit targeting Windows systems.
Dubbed SignDrop, the exploit allows a local user to elevate their privileges to System by abusing flawed logic in the Windows Common Log File System (CLFS).
CLFS parses complex log files in kernel mode and has long been an attractive target for threat actors. Last year, Microsoft introduced CLFS logfile authentication to mitigate exploitation, which relies on authentication codes to check file integrity.
SignDrop, Naceri says, exploits a vulnerability in how clfs.sys handles the creation of the authentication file ‘.cnpf’ during the creation of a log file.
The code responsible for creating/opening both container and log files will always open the container if the original log file is opened. If the container is empty, CLFS attempts to sign it regardless of whether the signature file exists.
A standard user can create a log file and specify a path to an associated container in it, and then coerce Windows Defender to open the file in the context of the antimalware engine by calling the signature update RPC interface.
This leads Defender to use the file path specified in the container to open the associated log file. If absent, a signature file is then created with System privileges.
SecurityWeek has not tested SignDrop, but understands that the proof-of-concept (PoC) code abuses the mechanism to create a signature file at an attacker-controlled location and then reopens the file to place a payload in it, resulting in the spawning of a System shell.
According to the security researcher, SignDrop has been tested on Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental, and should work on 80% of the world’s Windows installations.
“You’re generally vulnerable if your Windows installation is older than 90 days,” Naceri says.
According to cybersecurity services provider Cyderes, which successfully compiled and tested the PoC exploit, there is no evidence that the zero-day has been exploited in the wild.
SecurityWeek has emailed Microsoft for a statement on SignDrop and will update this article if the company responds.

articles.title: Anvisa alerta que vinagre e detergente não desinfetam vegetais
articles.text:
A Agência Nacional de Vigilância Sanitária (Anvisa) alerta que vinagre e detergente não possuem eficácia antimicrobiana comprovada para desinfetar frutas, legumes e verduras. O uso desses produtos também pode alterar o aroma natural dos alimentos.
No caso do detergente, há ainda o risco de deixar resíduos indesejáveis, especialmente em alimentos com superfícies porosas. Por isso, a agência recomenda utilizar produtos específicos e regularizados para a desinfecção, principalmente de alimentos consumidos crus.
Frutas, legumes e verduras podem carregar microrganismos dos ambientes onde são produzidos. A lavagem em água corrente remove sujeiras visíveis, como terra e insetos, mas não substitui a desinfecção necessária para combater esses agentes.
Embora sejam utilizados em receitas caseiras, vinagre e detergente não devem ser equiparados. O primeiro é um alimento; o segundo é um produto de limpeza, que não foi desenvolvido para aplicação direta em comida.
Os desinfetantes regularizados pela Anvisa precisam comprovar eficácia contra microrganismos como a bactéria Escherichia coli, associada a infecções, diarreia e gastroenterite, e o Enterococcus faecium, também relacionado a infecções.
Como higienizar os alimentos corretamente?
A Anvisa recomenda um procedimento que começa com a retirada de partes danificadas e termina com a secagem dos alimentos. As etapas são:
- Retirar partes estragadas: remover trechos machucados ou deteriorados, quando necessário.
- Lavar em água corrente: retirar a sujeira visível dos alimentos.
- Fazer a desinfecção: deixar de molho em uma solução própria para hortifrutícolas, respeitando a diluição e o tempo indicados no rótulo.
- Enxaguar com água potável: utilizar água limpa após o período de molho.
- Secar antes de guardar: deixar escorrer bem. Para verduras, é possível utilizar uma secadora doméstica de folhas.
Os cuidados não terminam na higienização. A professora Nathalia Cirone Silva, da Faculdade de Engenharia de Alimentos da Unicamp, aponta que guardar frutas e vegetais ainda úmidos favorece a proliferação de bactérias e outros microrganismos. Não lavar as mãos antes da manipulação e utilizar recipientes sem higienização também são erros comuns.
“Entre os alimentos que apresentam maior risco são os vegetais e frutas que a gente come cru e aqueles que já vêm cortados. Eles acabam perdendo a proteção natural da fruta e aumenta a superfície de contato para esse tipo de contaminação”, acrescenta a professora ao g1.
Quais produtos podem ser usados para desinfetar alimentos?
A Resolução da Diretoria Colegiada (RDC) 695/2022 da Anvisa estabelece regras para os desinfetantes de hortifrutícolas e permite três princípios ativos:
- Ácido dicloroisocianúrico e seus sais de sódio e potássio;
- Hipoclorito de cálcio;
- Hipoclorito de sódio, substância presente na água sanitária.
A presença de um desses componentes, porém, não significa que qualquer produto possa ser usado diretamente nos alimentos. O consumidor deve verificar se o desinfetante está regularizado pela Anvisa e se o rótulo indica expressamente a aplicação em frutas, verduras e legumes.
A consulta pode ser feita gratuitamente no sistema oficial da Anvisa. Também é necessário seguir as instruções do fabricante sobre a quantidade do produto e o tempo de contato com os alimentos.
Para comerciantes e manipuladores, a agência disponibiliza uma cartilha de boas práticas com orientações sobre higiene durante o preparo, o armazenamento e a comercialização dos alimentos.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: US company Shift4 to acquire Paramount Commerce for up to $317 million USD | BetaKit
articles.text:
One of the first participants in Canada’s new Real-Time Rail system is being purchased by a US payment processor.
The news: Allentown, Penn.-based Shift4 Payments, founded by current NASA administrator Jared Isaacman, said in an SEC filing on Nov. 5 that it has agreed to buy Toronto-based Paramount Commerce, an account-to-account payment provider.
Signed in August, the deal would see Shift4 pay approximately $143 million USD in cash, with a contingent consideration of up to $174 million USD. That’s a potential total of $317 million USD ($452 million CAD). The deal is expected to close before the end of the year, the filing said.
A spokesperson for Paramount Commerce said in an email that more details will be shared in a press release when the deal closes; Shift4 didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
From the source: Tarique Khan, a Canadian FinTech industry commentator who runs the Fintech North online community, wrote in a LinkedIn post on Friday that Paramount’s tech helps enable instant payouts flowing out from merchants, addressing a bottleneck that Shift4 says is now an expectation from enterprise merchants.
“Card processing was built for one direction. A customer pays, the processor takes a cut, the merchant gets paid a day or two later,” Khan said. “Merchants now need money to move the other way, too.”
The context: Founded in 2003, Paramount Commerce launched an early solution to allow online payments directly from a bank account. Since then, it has processed more than $100 billion in transactions and was the first payment processor to participate in Interac’s e-Transfer system.
The pending acquisition comes amid a “painful year” for Shift4’s shareholders, according to its most recent quarterly letter to investors. The New York Stock Exchange-listed company’s share price is down roughly 30 percent since the beginning of 2026, from $63 USD to roughly $44 USD on Friday afternoon. “Skepticism remains high” for the company and the sector, the letter said.
Shift4 noted that Paramount’s business clients include sports betting companies like FanDuel, DraftKings, and Bet365, as well as tech giant Lenovo and telecom Telus. The potential for gross profit growth and geographic expansion were both listed as upsides of the deal.
Final thought: Paramount Commerce is one of the first eight participants in Canada’s Real-Time Rail (RTR), a long-awaited instant payment system that launched on Monday. When this acquisition closes, it will become the second US-owned entity onboarded to the payment rail, alongside Bank of America—even as Canada’s biggest banks are only slated to participate in future phases.
Feature image courtesy Unsplash. Photo by Julio Lopez.

articles.title: The Verge’s 2026 gift guide for dads
articles.text:
Gone are the days when you could just buy your father a random tie or some leather-clad alcohol vessel or a shaving kit. Dads want — nay, deserve — something memorable. Luckily for you, it’s not that hard to find something special that he’ll approve of, and we’re here to guide you.
The Verge’s 2026 gift guide for dads
This year, why not get Dad a gift or two he won’t expect?
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
We’ve curated this year’s gift list with the modern father in mind, whether he’s a gamer, creator, chef, or simply a gadget lover. There’s a lot in here we think he’ll like, from noise-canceling headphones like the Sonos Ace Ultra and an autonomous drone to a brilliant QD-OLED monitor and a nifty light that’s perfect for illuminating his next campsite. Whatever your dad is into, we’ve got you covered.
Antigravity’s A1 is the ultimate gadget for the dad who dreams of owning the sky. The compact drone comes with specialized goggles that will make him feel like he’s in the cockpit, and it records always-on, 360-degree 8K video. It’s an exhilarating flight experience and an excellent creator’s tool in one slick package.
Dyson PencilVac Fluffycones
Cleaning gadgets like Dyson’s PencilVac FluffyCones are never cheap, but they’re often worth the cost and a pleasure to use. The lightweight, broom-replacing stick vacuum doesn’t do carpets, but its rolling bars pack incredible cleaning power for touching up hard floors, including stairs.
For those who love travel but hate the constraints of a hotel TV, Belkin’s ConnectAir is a slick solution. Plug the transmitter into any device with a USB-C video-out port and the receiver into the TV’s HDMI port, and voilà, you’re easily (and wirelessly) connected.
Sonos Ace Ultra
Sonos raised its headphones game on all fronts with the Ace Ultra, which deliver better noise canceling, improved sound, and the feature we’ve all been waiting for: Wi-Fi support. With the ability to bounce audio across your Sonos ecosystem, including from a TV via newer Sonos soundbars, Dad’s sonic sanctuary is finally complete.
Werewolf’s affordable dongle kit provides an almost magical way to power nearly any DC device from a USB-C charger or portable battery. Program it from a mobile app, connect it to your old gear, and everything from a PC monitor to an original Game Boy can accept USB-C charging.
Who would have thought a simple hook could make roaming the city with a backpack so much more convenient? After testing Peak Design’s well-designed bags, we’re convinced the clever addition is a game-changer for anyone who doesn’t want to leave their bag on the filthy ground.
WiiM’s first soundbar builds on its seamless Sonos-esque connectivity with a sleek design, detailed sound, and up-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos spatial audio. It also pairs with other speakers for surround sound through a no-fuss setup process, including ones you already own that are linked to one of WiiM’s amplifiers.
Alienware AW3426DW QD-OLED Gaming Monitor
Your dad needs an awesome monitor, but there are 10 billion options. Alienware’s 34-inch Penta Tandem QD-OLED delivers top-end picture quality, with vibrant colors and perfect blacks, plus a swift 280Hz refresh rate. Best of all, it’s not nearly as expensive as you might think.
If your dad is still reading books on his phone (or aging e-reader), it’s time for an upgrade. The latest in Amazon’s series of waterproof, auto-dimming e-readers loads books faster than the prior model and offers a slick aluminum upgrade. No matter which you choose, it’s a better way to bring the library along.
Sharge Disk Pro 2 SSD / HDMI dock
Give your father a little nostalgia and a lot of convenience in one package with this stylish USB-C dock and SSD combo gadget. The cassette-shaped Sharge Disk Pro 2 works as a hub with support for HDMI at 4K, SD and microSD card slots, USB-A and USB-C ports, along with up to 8TB of storage stored within.
Smart TVs are often pretty dumb. If your dad is always complaining about his TV, or if you want to get ahead of it, grab the latest Apple TV 4K. Although it’s not cheap, it stands out with built-in mics for Siri AI, lots of power, HomePod surround sound support, and a simple, ad-free interface.
The Switch 2 leverages the same ideas as its predecessor, only with a larger, 7.9-inch display, a faster chip, and a bevy of new social features. However, its most important trait is that it’s the newest Nintendo console, which means access to a host of weird, beautiful, family-friendly games that only Nintendo could dream up, now on a better screen.
Oura Ring 5
Oura didn’t reinvent the wheel with the Ring 5, but it did reshape it into a slimmer, thinner, more wearable design that could make all the difference. Inside are the same extensive health and fitness tracking features for charting everything from sleep to heart health, backed by long battery life.
The CS-Pro will make your dad feel like a private eye in the early ’80s. The retro-inspired digital camera serves up 16-megapixel stills and offers four filters accessible from its tactile dial, plus USB-C charging, a high-quality Xenon flash, and a 4GB SD card for plenty of vintage photo fun.
BougeRV T1 Portable Telescopic Camping Light
BougeRV’s fancy, compact lamp will spark joy for the glamper in your life, as well as everyone else. Its powerful, foldable spread of LEDs provides a blast of light anywhere plug-ins can’t reach, from the beach to the shed where that scary spider holds court, with up to 60 hours of light on low power.
The Rival Pro offers plenty of thoughtful extras, including swappable batteries and an ultra-wideband base station for a seamless, low-latency connection. The gaming mouse’s lightweight design and 8,000Hz polling rate also deliver both accurate and ergonomic performance for up to 16 hours per charge.
It’s time to help Dad ditch his collection of plastic reusable cups, which have clearly seen better days. NotNeutral’s hand-pressed, timeless tumbler offers ’70s vibes with a modern twist, making it the perfect vessel for whatever Dad twists into his favorite drink.
Give the gift that fixes past home improvement transgressions. These handy Japanese-made pliers from Vampire Tools have one fundamental purpose — to remove stripped screws — and they’re damn good at it. The best part? Watching Dad’s face light up seconds before he sprints to the garage for them.
One Piece Straw Hat Pirates Hockey Jersey
For the manga or live-action Netflix show lover on your list, this fashionable Pirates jersey, inspired by Monkey D. Luffy from the seminal pirate adventure series One Piece, will be as surprising as it is delightful.
If you’re after a cheap, useful stocking stuffer, Trond’s reliable three-prong extension cord is a practical pick that’s available in leftward or rightward configurations to fit nearly any outlet. Dad will probably say, “Oh, I’ve always wanted one of these,” and this time he’ll mean it.
Star Wars Zero Company
Zero Company, a strategy game set in the twilight of the Clone Wars, is a fun way to get lost in the Star Wars universe. The single-player, turn-based title lets players command a diverse team of characters across a gorgeous expanse of worlds, offering hours of solitary entertainment.
If your father already owns an Apple Watch, the Nomad Stratos is a foolproof upgrade idea. The refined watch band features titanium links with a rubbery interior for durable comfort, and it comes in an array of subtle color options that make it as suitable for the office as it is for the slopes.
Apple Crossbody Strap
We fell for Apple’s handy iPhone strap due to its effortless accessibility and comfy design, which uses flexible magnets to keep excess segments in check. From biking to hiking to concerts, it’s a great way to sling your iPhone 18 Pro, assuming you have a compatible phone case.
The new Fitbit Air provides the same great fitness tracking we’ve come to expect in a comfortable design that virtually disappears on your wrist. Google’s AI Coach can be overly assertive, but the tracker’s great battery life and metrics for everything from sleep to blood oxygen make it an excellent gift for anyone who needs a healthy hand.
Most of us have thousands of photos in the cloud, but if a photo never makes it into the real world, did it really happen? Existentialism aside, the Cricut StickerPix offers a new way to play with photos, providing you with everything you need to turn any picture into a pro-quality print or sticker.
SwitchBot Standing Circulator Fan
This battery-powered fan is a big upgrade over your average plug-in job. As a 3D circulator, it can tilt to push air in all directions. It can be controlled from an app and even detaches from its stand to sit on a desk or tabletop. Quiet, powerful, and versatile, it’s equipped for nearly any adventure on or off the grid.
Have you broken something fragile that seems impossible to mend? Maybe all you need is a Kintsugi Repair Kit, which provides the Japanese method and a special lacquer to repair and restore broken ceramics to good health. The resulting golden scar is merely to remind us that rebuilding is possible.
If your favorite cinephile is looking to get off the streaming carousel, the Kaleidescape Strato E is the key. The premium player lets library builders locally store and play their favorite films and TV shows in lossless 4K resolution with Dolby Atmos for sterling entertainment that’s all theirs.
Once The Great British Baking Show becomes an obsession, only a serious stand mixer will do for replicating recipes at home. This mixer’s timeless design adds new features in what KitchenAid calls its biggest upgrade since 1955, with a new half-speed setting and a control lever that lets you set speeds between its standard settings.
Instruo Pocket Scion Bio-Feedback Instrument
The Pocket Scion is unlike any musical instrument you’ve witnessed before, one that uses the “biofeedback” from plants to trigger built-in synths. The device offers MIDI-out to send digital signals to outboard synths, and it includes an app for both macOS and Windows, finally giving you a way to make your favorite fern a rockstar.
When it comes to jotting down notes, there’s nothing like a pen and paper. At least, that’s what we thought before we tried the Remarkable Paper Pure. Offering a strikingly realistic writing experience that saves everything in the digital realm, this tablet is a brilliant way to bridge the gap and save paper.
Fairphone 6 Plus
Electronics are becoming more sustainable, and Fairphone is leading the way. The Fairphone 6 Plus may seem like a regular Android phone on paper, but the ability to repair and replace its internals, from the screen to the battery, makes it anything but average.

articles.title: La caída de Microsoft afecta a la productividad en España, pero no a servicios esenciales
articles.text: Una mujer navega por la web de Microsoft 365 en su portátil. Tras más de 18 horas con los servicios de Microsoft caídos por todo el mundo, las incidencias en distintos sectores económicos empiezan a notarse, desde la banca japonesa a los juzgados australianos, en los más de 70 países desde los que los usuarios han reportado problemas. En España, la Administración no ha notificado que la caída de Microsoft haya tenido especial incidencia en el funcionamiento de los servicios públicos. Según fuentes del Ministerio de Transformación Digital y de la Función Pública, “el impacto está siendo menor” porque la mayoría de los correos electrónicos de los empleados de la Administración General del Estado (AGE) están alojados en centros propios de la Administración. Teams sí se está viendo afectado, igual que el chatbot de IA Copilot, que está alojado en la nube, pero la previsión, añaden esas mismas fuentes, es que los sistemas puedan restablecerse en las próximas horas. articles.text: Una chica mira el logo de TikTok en un iPhone 16. El Corte Inglés, Banco Santander, la energética Moeve y la cadena de supermercados Eroski han suspendido sus campañas publicitarias en TikTok. El Santander ha cancelado también toda actividad nueva en su cuenta en la plataforma: su último vídeo en TikTok, donde tiene 217.000 seguidores, fue este jueves. articles.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
articles.text:
Nvidia faces questions about security and oversight; 300mm SiC breakthrough; Siemens buys Lauterbach; chiplet standards; new memory bets; imec interposer process flow; TPUs with CPUs; 2D transistors; anti-smuggling tools for chips.
A wave of announcements this week, including several from SEMICON Europa and electronica 2026 in Munich, highlighted advances in semiconductor manufacturing, advanced packaging, automotive chips, and AI hardware.
Manufacturing
Infineon reported an industry-first milestone in 300mm silicon carbide manufacturing, fabricating functional power devices at its Villach, Austria fab using existing silicon processing equipment. The larger wafers can accommodate 2.3 times as many chips as 200mm wafers, potentially lowering manufacturing costs for automotive, industrial, and AI data center power devices.
imec completed baseline process flows for its NanoIC silicon-interposer platform, including TSVs and multiple routing layers for chiplet and 3D integration. A silicon-interposer PDK is planned for early 2027.
Chips and systems
AMD introduced its 6th-gen EPYC server and embedded processors, including models for semiconductor ATE; an AI GPU with 288GB of HBM4; and tamper-resistant FPGAs for security-critical systems.
Arm introduced the Cortex-M42 processor to bring ML and DSP capabilities to cost- and area-constrained intelligent endpoints in a compact, AHB-based design.
Google added two new 8th-gen TPU systems: TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and higher rack compute density, and TPU 8tx for secure and confidential inference. TPU 8tx pairs Google accelerators with AMD EPYC CPU hosts.
Fallout continues after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation:
Inaction questioned: President Trump authorized tougher action on suspected Nvidia chip diversion three times this year, but Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick resisted over concerns that tighter restrictions could escalate trade tensions with China, Axios reported. Separately, Nvidia general counsel Tim Tetercontacted a senior Commerce Dept. official in late summer 2025 seeking information about the Megaspeed chip-smuggling investigation, indicating Nvidia’s legal leadership was aware of the investigation before the current scandal. The company subsequently characterized its Megaspeed dealings as “normal.”
Circular financing: Nvidia’s web of financial ties across the AI industry is facing fresh scrutiny after Huang’s resignation. The Financial Times says Nvidia made more than 120 investments this year and held or committed about $124B in equity investments by July, raising questions about whether its aggressive dealmaking and financing of companies that buy its chips will continue without him.
Policy fallout: The episode has renewed debate over export-control enforcement and Chinese intelligence targeting of U.S. technology companies, with CFR highlighting enforcement gaps and CSET urging scrutiny without overreaction.
Deals and funding
Siemens plans to acquireLauterbach, a provider of hardware-assisted debugging and real-time trace tools for embedded software and complex SoCs. The deal is expected to close in H1 2027.
Mitsui Chemicals confirmed it will acquire JSR in a transaction valued at approximately ¥1.84T ($11.9B), combining two major Japanese materials suppliers, including JSR’s photoresist and advanced materials businesses.
Fractile raised $720M to develop frontier AI chips that stack DRAM directly on top of logic to speed up output token generation.
Memory
Samsung Electronics broke ground on a previously announced HBM advanced-packaging facility in Asan, South Korea, accelerating the planned start of production by a year to June 2028.
TSMC is reportedly considering 3D DRAM production at Nvidia’s request, potentially through new capacity or an acquired fab. Still, TSMC said that it remains focused on its core logic foundry business.
Counterpoint Research says soaring memory prices are driving up smartphone costs, with memory now accounting for 54% of a low-end phone’s bill of materials, up from 20% in Q3 2025. Prices are expected to keep rising through Q1 2027.
Chiplet standards and interoperability
The UCIe Consortium published UCIe 4.0, which takes the specification beyond chiplet-level interfaces to the integration of multiple chiplets into an on-package system. New features include an on-package memory link between SoCs and memory logic chiplets, co-optimized link profiles with improved energy efficiency, and enhanced manageability, security, and reliability.
Year-over-year revenue change: Applied Materials Q4 up 53%, Infineon Q4 up 19%, Onto Innovation Q3 up 88%, Silicon Labs Q3 up 22%, SMIC Q3 up 34%, and TSMC October revenue up ~60%.
Vishay and Kaynes plan to establish a back-end manufacturing joint venture in India covering post-fabrication wafer processing, assembly, test, and packaging.
Mitsui Kinzoku plans to invest ¥190B (~US$1.2B) in a new copper foil plant in Malaysia for high-frequency circuit boards.
LLNL and Diamond Quanta are collaborating to use pulsed laser annealing to reduce defects in diamond for high-power electronics, with plans for a pilot manufacturing platform in Petaluma, California.
In-Depth
Semiconductor Engineering published 2 newsletters this week, including:
Accellera published the Portable Test and Stimulus Standard (PSS) 3.1, adding enhancements that improve model reuse, constraint expressiveness, software integration, target-code generation, and coordination across increasingly complex hardware and software execution environments.
Teradyne introduced its Omnyx Edge inline board-test system for physical and edge AI applications, designed to improve test coverage and manufacturing efficiency for increasingly complex electronic assemblies.
Siemens announced a toolkit for signal and power integrity verification of boards and electronic systems that combines domain-specific AI agents for SerDes, DDR, signal integrity, and power integrity analysis with physics-based simulation.
Cadence launched a connected design environment for boards and electronic systems that unifies schematic design, component discovery, expertise, and procurement for individual engineers and small design teams.
Keysight‘s photonic design software added support for Tower Semiconductor‘s PH18 silicon photonics PDKs.
Synopsys supplied Infineon with a virtual development tool to support digital twin engineering for Infineon’s new MCUs for advanced automotive and physical AI applications.
Lithography and materials
Canon introduced a new KrF lithography scanner for memory and logic chip manufacturing. Scheduled for launch in early December, the system offers throughput of up to 400 300mm wafers per hour and 4.0 nm overlay accuracy. It also accommodates wafer warpage of up to 700 microns, addressing manufacturing challenges associated with 3D device structures and wafer bonding.
Expedera and Cadence teamed up to demonstrate an edge AI subsystem in pre-silicon simulation, pairing Expedera’s NPU and Cadence’s AI co-processor and distributing workloads for execution across both IP blocks.
MemryX AI released a new AI accelerator with a distributed dataflow architecture designed to support larger models across edge devices, industrial systems, and high-density inference infrastructure.
Automotive and power electronics
Keysight expanded its high-power ATE portfolio to support applications operating at up to 1,500V, including power-stage characterization, battery testing, charging systems, power conversion, and aerospace equipment.
NUS-led researchers developed wafer-scale, single-crystal gate dielectrics for 2D transistors, integrating titanium dioxide (TiO₂) with MoS₂ and WSe₂ channels. The devices achieved near-ideal switching, minimal hysteresis, and inverter static power consumption below 1 picowatt, potentially enabling ultra-low-power logic chips.
Tsinghua University researchers developed a room-temperature process for depositing gate dielectrics for 2D transistors using a clay-based material. The process avoids high-temperature annealing after dielectric deposition and enables MoS₂ transistors operating at 1 volt with hysteresis as low as 1 millivolt. The team also demonstrated logic gates and SRAM, suggesting a potential route to lower-temperature chip fabrication.
Researchers at UW–Madison, Texas A&M, and the U.S. Army Research Lab developed nonvolatile memory devices based on sliding ferroelectric tunnel junctions. Using atomically thin molybdenum disulfide and engineered gold contacts, the devices achieved a reported 100,000-fold improvement in memory readout contrast, potentially enabling more energy-efficient memory.
University of Rochester and Technion researchers developed a method for altering molybdenum’s crystal structure at room temperature using precisely controlled mechanical pressure. The technique creates new crystal grains without heating the metal to approximately 1,000°C, potentially enabling localized defect repair and improved materials for future semiconductor interconnects.
Security
Alerts and vulnerabilities
AI, chip and tech companies are recruiting ex-intelligence operatives to combat espionage risks in the wake of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Reuters reported.
AMD disclosed three side-channel vulnerabilities in 5th-generation EPYC processors that could expose sensitive data. Google Cloud has implemented protections between virtual machines but says customers need OS updates to address attacks within them.
AMD also issued security bulletins covering firmware, UEFI/SMM, IOMMU, and transient-execution vulnerabilities, including a RowHammer attack targeting SEV-SNP memory protections.
Google DeepMind developed an agentic formal-verification framework that proved key security properties of Signal’s cryptographic implementation down to the compiled machine code running on devices. DeepMind says the approach eventually could be applied to systems such as medical-device firmware and power-grid software.
ENISA released a new report on the state of cybersecurity in the EU, evaluating regulatory compliance, cybersecurity system maturity, and future resilience across each member state.
French security officials blame Iran for cyberphysical attacks that shut down refrigeration systems at more than 700 retail sites nationwide last month, but didn’t assign blame for the second wave of attacks that hit refrigeration systems across 11 European countries on Nov. 2.
President Trump nominated Palantir security chief Michael LoSapio to serve as the next CISA director, pending Senate confirmation.
Texas A&M researchers proposed a 5G-based location-verification system for AI accelerators to help combat chip smuggling and enforce semiconductor export controls. Called 5G CATS, the architecture would combine a 5G radio, cryptographic engine, and hardware interlock within the GPU package to verify chip locations and restrict unauthorized operation. Simulations showed improved detection of attempts to disguise a chip’s location using long-distance fiber relays.
Memory in Physical AI: LPDDR6 becomes an essential ingredient as intelligence moves into autonomous and mobile edge systems.
Cadence‘s Frank Ferro explains why data hierarchies are so critical for physical AI, what can be done on the memory side to speed up read/write times, and how to maximize performance while keeping costs down.
Quantum Hardware
IBM announced its upcoming quantum processor, which will be built to execute 10,000 quantum operations across 520 programmable qubits, with plans to link two into a single system.
Rigetti Computing reported 99.5% median two-qubit gate fidelity on its 108-qubit superconducting processor, built from 12 interconnected nine-qubit chiplets. Internal testing also showed 99.7% median fidelity across a 50-qubit subset, demonstrating progress in modular QPU performance.
Diraq deployed what it calls the first silicon-spin quantum computer in a commercial data center, installing an eight-qubit system at Equinix in Sydney, Australia. Built using conventional semiconductor manufacturing processes, the system draws less than 20 kW, with plans to scale to 256 qubits within a year.
Xanadu and HyperLight built a TFLN optical switch with an insertion loss of 7 mdB, a nearly 3× improvement over the companies’ previous effort to reduce qubit signal degradation in quantum photonics.
Workforce, Education
The SIA urged the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw proposed fees for Optional Practical Training (OPT), warning they could hurt U.S. semiconductor recruitment and manufacturing. The proposal would impose a $70K initial fee and $30K for subsequent OPT periods, including STEM extensions. SIA asked for exemptions for semiconductor and other critical-technology workers if the rule moves forward.
SEMI Foundation launched its global Chip the Future Challenge, inviting students to submit semiconductor research or develop solutions in chip design, manufacturing, AI hardware, advanced packaging and emerging technologies.
Lam Research and ASE expansions; data center shifts; CPO system architecture initiative; 2D-transistor interface solution; USENIX HW security; patent suits; image sensors; programmable AI memtransistor; Nvidia's new plan; earnings; Tier IV's L4 auto chip.

articles.title: Ohne Airpods: Wie es ist, nach Jahren wieder kabelgebundene Kopfhörer zu tragen
articles.text:
Ohne Airpods: Wie es ist, nach Jahren wieder kabelgebundene Kopfhörer zu tragen
Meine Airpods gehören zu meinen liebsten Gadgets. Das kompakte Case ist immer in der Hosentasche dabei, sie koppeln sich schnell und einfach mit iPhone, iPad oder Mac, bieten für unterwegs eine gute Geräuschunterdrückung – und verheddern kann sich auch nichts. Und doch werden sie unweigerlich kaputtgehen. Irgendwann macht selbst der beste Akku nicht mehr mit. Austauschen lässt sich die Batterie dann nicht. Es ist das größte Problem bei den allermeisten kabellosen Buds.
Nicht nur deswegen sah man in den vergangenen Monaten immer Promis und Nutzer:innen mit kabelgebundenen Kopfhörern. Wie der iPod scheinen sie aktuell ein Comeback zu feiern – und zwar auch als modisches Accessoire. Lässig baumeln sie aus den Jacken, als hätte es nie kabellose In-Ears gegeben. Außerdem ist die Bedienung einfach. Kabel rein, los hören. Kein aufladen, kein koppeln. Doch ein wichtiges Feature oft: die Geräuschunterdrückung. Selbst bei günstigen Buds ist sie mittlerweile standardmäßig an Bord. Bose löst das Problem nun mit den „Kabelgebundenen Noise-Cancelling-Earbuds“, wie das Modell etwas sperrig heißt.
Kabel-In-Ears mit USB-C und ANC
Im Karton findet ihr das, was draufsteht. Die In-Ears, Gummistöpsel in drei und Stabilitätsaufsätze in zwei Größen und ein Transportetui. Nach dem Auspacken seid ihr direkt bereit zum Loshören – zumindest am Smartphone. Schon 2016 marschierte Apple bei der Vorstellung des iPhone 7 schließlich voran und strich die Kopfhörerbuchse am iPhone 7. Den Schritt bezeichnete der damalige Marketing-Chef Phil Schiller noch mit Mut. Längst sind aber so gut wie alle Hersteller nachgeschoben. Damit ihr keinen Adapter braucht, kommen die Bose-Buds mit USB-C-Stecker. Der passt allerdings nicht in ältere iPhones oder gar in iPods.
Die Bedienung ist leicht erklärt: Am Kabel drei Tasten. Zwei regeln die Lautstärke. Der dritte funktioniert universal als Start- und Stop-Taste. Haltet ihr den Knopf gedrückt, switcht ihr zudem durch die integrierten Modi: Neben Noise-Cancelling gibt es einen Aware-Modus, der die Mikrofone quasi auf Durchzug schaltet, damit man mehr von der Umgebung mitbekommt. Als dritte Option lässt sich jede Unterstützung abschalten. Darüber hinaus nehmt ihr über den Button anrufe an oder springt (durch mehrfaches Drücken) durch die Playlist.
Eine App gibt es nicht. Es gibt also keine Möglichkeit, mit einem Equalizer herumzuspielen, wie es bei manchen Bluetooth-Modellen der Fall ist. Das ist allerdings kein Nachteil, denn ich brauche nicht für jedes Gadget eine eigene App, für die ich dann am „besten“ noch einen Account anlegen muss.
Wir suchen Bass
Beim Klang müsst ihr dann folglich nehmen, was ihr bekommt. Die In-Ears bieten klare Höhen, lassen allerdings etwas an Tiefe vermissen. Bässe deuten die Buds nur an. Für Hiphop-Fans ist das eher nichts. Wer unterwegs nur Podcast hören will, bekommt aber klare stimmen geliefert. Der Noise-Cancelling-Modus tut Seins dazu, dass man den Episoden oder eben der Musik in Ruhe folgen kann. Zwar ist die Geräuschunterdrückung nicht perfekt, um relativ ungestört in der Bahn unterwegs zu sein reicht es aber.
Natürlich kann man mit den Bose-In-Ears auch telefonieren oder an Videokonferenzen teilnehmen, ein entsprechendes Mikrofon ist in die Fernbedienung am Kabel eingebaut. Ich habe meine Kolleg:innen gebeten, den Klang zu bewerten. Die Rückmeldung: Mit dem Kabelheadset war ich im Meeting gut zu verstehen.
Das Leben mit dem Kabel
Und wie lebt es sich nun wieder zurück an der Strippe? Sicherlich ist es praktisch, nicht mehr auf den Ladestand der In-Ears achten zu müssen. Einen einzelnen Ohrhörer kann man ebenfalls nicht mehr verlieren. Aber es zeigt sich auch, dass früher eben doch nicht alles besser. Gerade bei kaltem Wetter unter der dicken Jacke artet es schnell in Fummelei aus, wenn man etwa das Ticket auf dem Smartphone im ÖPNV vorzeigen will oder aber an der Fernbedienung die Wiedergabe pausieren will.
Und natürlich funktioniert der Plug-and-Play-Gedanke hervorragend am iPhone und Macbook, nicht aber an der Apple Watch. Die hat bekanntlich gar keinen Anschluss. Beim Sport Musik hören? Zumindest für mich nicht möglich, obwohl die In-Ears dank IPX4-Zertifizierung (Spritzwasserschutz) durchaus dafür geeignet sind. Ein zweites Problem habe ich im Büro festgestellt. Der Bildschirm ist an die eine USB-C-Buchse angestöpselt, die Bose-Kopfhörer an die zweite. Will ich jetzt aber mein Smartphone am Laptop laden, sieht es finster aus. Mein Macbook Air hat nur zwei USB-C-Plätze (und einen Klinkenanschluss).
Fazit
Bose verbindet Retro-Charme mit der praktischen ANC-Funktion moderner Bluetooth-In-Ears. Eine Mischung, die durchaus gelungen ist. Wer zu gewissen Abstrichen bereit ist und vorsichtig mit dem Kabel umgeht, kann von den kabelgebundenen In-Ears durchaus länger etwas haben als von akkubetriebenen Alternativen. Für einen Preis von rund 100 Euro kein schlechter Deal.

articles.title: Une faute de frappe en cherchant ChatGPT ou Gemini peut vous mener sur un site piégé
articles.text:
Une seule lettre sépare chatlgpt.com de chatgpt.com. La société de cybersécurité Island a recensé 186 adresses de ce genre, et sur certaines d’entre elles, des pirates vous poussent à installer vous-même un logiciel malveillant sur votre ordinateur.
Vous voulez ouvrir ChatGPT, Claude ou Gemini, et vos doigts glissent sur le clavier. C'est le syndrome du Knacki, diront certaines mauvaises langues. Et les pirates comptent sur cette erreur. Ils enregistrent les adresses mal orthographiées des assistants d’IA, ce que les spécialistes appellent du typosquatting, et Island a relevé des imitations de 27 marques d’IA. Avec 25 imitations, ChatGPT est la marque la plus copiée, devant Claude et DeepSeek. Gemini a ses imitations, dont geimini.com, et la française Mistral AI a la sienne, mistrial.ai. En suivant les redirections de ces adresses, les chercheurs d’Island sont tombés sur des malwares et sur des extensions qui détournent vos recherches.
Les pirates vous font exécuter une commande PowerShell
Sur cloude.ai, fausse adresse de Claude, le propriétaire n’a mis en ligne qu’une page d’attente, dite page parking, et il peut revendre le trafic de ses visiteurs. Vous êtes ensuite transféré vers un système de distribution de trafic, chargé de choisir votre destination en fonction de votre pays, de votre système d’exploitation et de votre navigateur. Les pirates profilent alors votre navigateur et relèvent votre adresse IP. Seule une partie des visiteurs voit le piège.
Il s’agit d’une fausse page de vérification humaine aux couleurs de Cloudflare, traduite en six langues, dont le français. Sur Windows, une commande est copiée dans votre presse-papiers, puis les pirates vous demandent de la coller dans la fenêtre Exécuter. Avec cette technique, le ClickFix, c’est vous qui lancez leur programme. Les pirates téléchargent alors un script PowerShell dans un dossier temporaire et l’exécutent dans une fenêtre cachée, sans tenir compte des restrictions d’exécution de Windows. Sur Mac, les pirates affichent plutôt une fausse mise à jour de sécurité et vous demandent de coller une commande dans le Terminal.
Island a retrouvé le script de profilage sur 211 adresses d’entrée, dont de fausses adresses de banques nord-américaines, de l’opérateur Verizon ou de Microsoft Azure. Comme l’explique Oleg Zaytsev, chercheur principal en sécurité chez Island, ces sites sont des « sosies d’applications d’IA qui transforment la tentative d’ouvrir un outil familier en une invitation à vérifier, installer ou exécuter autre chose ». Aucune vraie vérification Cloudflare ne vous demande d’ouvrir la fenêtre Exécuter ou le Terminal pour coller du texte.
Les pirates détournent votre moteur de recherche
Si vous tapez ckaude.ai, deepceek.com ou copiot.com, vous risquez d’atterrir sur une fausse page de contrôle de sécurité. Les pirates vous proposent d’installer Net Guard, qu’ils font passer pour un outil d’analyse de votre Wi-Fi. Le fichier est signé par le Microsoft Store et correspond exactement à l’application publiée sur la boutique de Microsoft. Une fois Net Guard installé, les pirates peuvent changer votre moteur de recherche par défaut pendant que vous n’utilisez pas votre PC et installer des extensions dans Chrome.
Sur preplexity.ai, fausse adresse de Perplexity, les pirates vous invitent à ajouter à Chrome une extension de recherche Bing. En réalité, vos recherches transitent par le serveur d’une société tierce, sans qu’aucune autorisation vous soit demandée à l’installation. Au bureau, ce tiers peut ainsi récupérer les noms de serveurs internes, de clients ou de projets que vous tapez dans la barre d’adresse, prévient Island.
Google prépare pour Chrome une protection contre les extensions qui détournent votre moteur de recherche, mais seulement contre celles imposées à votre insu par des clés de politique locale, un réglage normalement réservé aux administrateurs. Ici, c’est vous qui installez l’extension. Island a recensé 30 extensions issues du même kit, que vous ne trouverez pas en cherchant dans le Chrome Web Store. Treize ont été retirées, et les autres comptaient 972 000 utilisateurs déclarés début novembre.
Pour ouvrir ChatGPT ou Gemini, passez plutôt par un favori ou par l’application officielle. Et si votre moteur de recherche a changé sans raison, ouvrez Paramètres puis Moteur de recherche dans Chrome, avant de passer en revue vos extensions.

articles.title: Adapt Human Motion for Robots with NVIDIA SOMA Retargeter | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Human motion offers roboticists a great starting point for teaching humanoid robots how to move. A human demonstration captures the coordination and timing behind natural movement, from everyday actions to complex tasks. But a robot cannot simply copy the same joint motion from a human. Its proportions, joint structure, and range of motion are different, so the movement needs to be adapted to fit the robot.
The open source NVIDIA SOMA Retargeter helps you adapt human motion to your robot’s proportions and range of motion. Built around the shared human-motion representation in NVIDIA SOMA-X, it provides tools to configure your robot, refine the resulting movement, and process motion data for downstream training.
This post explains the retargeting process, the tools for refining robot motion, and the connection to policy learning.
From human motion to robot joint trajectories
Human motion can come from many sources, including a motion capture session, a video, an online dataset, or a generative model. These sources often output motion with different skeletons and file formats. Representing compatible human motion on the SOMA skeleton gives the retargeter a consistent input.
SOMA Retargeter reads a Biovision Hierarchy (BVH) animation on the SOMA base skeleton. As Figure 1 below shows, it scales motion targets to the robot’s proportions, solves for joint poses, and applies configured corrections. The output is a comma-separated values (CSV) file containing the robot’s root position, orientation, and joint angles for each frame. These trajectories describe the desired movement for a downstream learning or control system.
Sources of human motion
Developers can draw on recorded performances, reconstruct motion from video, or generate new movements:
- Motion-capture data. BONES-SEED provides a collection of human motion-capture data.
- Video reconstruction. GEM-X reconstructs whole-body 3D human motion from a single video using the SOMA body model. Its demo workflow connects video reconstruction with G1 retargeting, showing how a recorded action can become a robot motion reference.
- Motion generation. Kimodo and ARDY let developers generate human movement from text and pose constraints. Kimodo supports creating motion sequences from those descriptions, while ARDY adds interactive steering as the motion unfolds. Both offer models that generate motion on the SOMA skeleton.
Adapting motion to different humanoid robots
The SOMA Retargeter v0.2 release includes sample motions supplied by Bones from the BONES-SEED dataset, along with reference retargeting results and configurations for five humanoid robots: Unitree G1, Unitree H2, Booster T1, AgiBot X2 Ultra, and AgiBot A3T3. These examples show how joint angles and foot placement change across humanoid embodiments according to their specific proportions and range of motion. The paired human motions and robot results give you a starting point for exploring the tool and comparing your own output.
For this example, use the supplied Unitree G1 configuration to retarget a forward walk from the sample motions. After installing SOMA Retargeter, open a terminal in the repository root and start the viewer:
uv run python app/bvh_to_csv_converter.py --config assets/default_bvh_to_csv_converter_config.json --viewer gl
The BVH to CSV Converter opens with unitree_g1 selected by default. In Scene Options, expand Motion, select Load on the BVH Motion row, and open the bundled file from here. The SOMA human animation appears in the viewer.
Under Scene Options → Motion, select Retarget on the BVH Motion row. The retargeter scales the source targets to G1, solves the configured inverse-kinematics objectives for each frame, and applies the configured post-processing. The viewer then displays the robot animation with the human source motion. Positioning gizmos let you separate them for inspection.
Use the playback controls to inspect the result. A recognizable forward walk and continuous motion are useful first checks; the robot’s poses will differ from the human’s because its proportions and joints are different. Under CSV Motion, select Save and give the output a new name, such as my_first_retarget.csv, to keep it separate from the supplied reference. The saved file contains the robot’s root pose and joint values over the animation.
To compare your output with the supplied G1 reference result for this walk, use the CSV Motion Load control to open each CSV in turn and inspect the same point in the motion. The reference file is located in the repository here. The results should show the same general movement, though exact values can vary with configuration and dependency versions. The first-retarget guide covers this example in more detail.
Configuring your robot and refining its motion
The supplied G1 configuration gives you a starting point for retargeting, while the included reference result provides a point of comparison as you adjust the settings to refine the motion. With the Robot Configurator, you can refine an existing robot configuration or create one for a new robot by loading its robot description and defining how human motion maps to it.
You can align human and robot reference poses, adjust scale, and map the source skeleton to robot body parts. The resulting configuration can be saved and reused across motion clips.
The retargeting solver uses inverse kinematics (IK) from Newton, built with NVIDIA Warp, to find joint poses that follow the scaled human targets. When a robot cannot match every target at once, IK weights determine which body parts take priority.
The experimental IK weight optimizer tunes these weights using a small set of motions representative of the robot’s intended tasks. It tests weight adjustments by retargeting those motions and checking how closely and smoothly the robot follows the targets. The selected weights are saved in a new retargeting configuration.
Sliding feet can introduce conflicting targets for a downstream motion-tracking policy: the reference foot moves while the intended action calls for planted contact. Foot-plant correction addresses this artifact by adjusting foot motion during detected contact intervals. You can refine contact timing and correction settings to reduce sliding in the reference motion before it enters a training pipeline.
Once you have refined a configuration on representative motions, headless batch retargeting lets you reuse it across a larger collection for your target robot, without operating the viewer for each clip.
Using retargeted motion to train robot policies
During training, a motion-tracking policy learns how to turn the retargeted reference into control actions, using both the desired motion and the robot’s current state.
The SONIC training workflow includes a SOMA CSV converter for G1. It converts retargeted trajectories into SONIC’s motion-library format for training. ProtoMotions offers another framework for physics-based motion tracking. In either case, the input representation and policy need to match the target robot.
Simulation provides the next stage of evaluation, where a trained policy can be assessed for balance, ground contact, actuator limits, and tracking accuracy.
In a separate experiment with MicroDuck, human motion from Bones was adapted for the robot and used to train a controller for each clip in physics simulation.
The three-panel comparison in Figure 4 below shows the human performance, the MicroDuck reference, and the trained controller executing the motion in simulation. The reference shows the intended movement, while the simulation shows how closely the trained controller follows it.
For more on simulation setup and policy training with MicroDuck, see the NVIDIA Technical Blog Using AI Agents to Teach Robots Like Microduck to Walk in Simulation and a Hugging Face post from NVIDIA called Train in Simulation, Deploy on a Real Robot: Microduck with Isaac Lab 3.0.
Generating motion in real time with MotionBricks
You can also generate motion with MotionBricks’ SOMA human model and use SOMA Retargeter to adapt it to your robot, expanding the motion references available for downstream training.
The MotionBricks G1 model was trained in part on BONES-SEED motions adapted to G1 with SOMA Retargeter. It generates continuous whole-body motion directly for G1 between changing target poses in real time.
The MotionBricks paper and project video demonstrate this approach on a physical Unitree G1. A G1-specific MotionBricks model supplies the motion targets, and SONIC controls their execution.
Get started with SOMA Retargeter
The SOMA Retargeter repository includes installation instructions, reference configurations, and examples for interactive and batch retargeting. The Robot Configurator guide explains how to add a humanoid embodiment, and the batch-retargeting guide covers processing motion collections for that robot.
Louis Marcoux contributed to the work in this blog.

articles.title: Engineering Overhead Electric Lines for Ice, Wind and Freezing Rain - Wiley Science and Engineering Content Hub
articles.text:
Download this complimentary White Paper today!
This White Paper explains how ice, wind and vegetation load overhead distribution lines at the same time. It shows engineers how to assess the complete line and compare resilience options.
What you will learn about:
- How freezing rain, rime ice and wet snow add weight to conductors and change their shape in the wind.
- Why a moderate wind on a heavily iced line can govern design, and how galloping and vegetation contact create outages.
- How a messenger-supported spacer cable separates the electrical function of covered conductors from the main mechanical load path.
- How monitored severe-weather test data compares tension changes in bare, covered and spacer cable systems.
- What utility records from the December 2008 Northeast ice storm show about circuit availability and restoration.
- How to compare options at corridor level, check the full load path of poles, brackets and foundations, and apply energized-line safety rules.
Click “LOOK INSIDE” to Download Now.
LOOK INSIDE
IEEE Spectrum and Wiley are proud to bring you this white paper, sponsored by Hendrix by Marmon Utility.
More Information
Ice storms cause long outages because several exposures act together. Ice adds weight to conductors, hardware and structures. Wind pushes on the larger iced surface. Trees and limbs bend into the line and add impact and uneven load. Conductors may also gallop and lose clearance. This paper explains how these loads combine and why the complete line must be assessed, not a single component. It reviews a monitored winter test of three conductor systems. It also summarizes utility records from a major regional ice storm. Finally, it outlines how to choose corridors, plan restoration and keep crews and the public safe around covered conductors.

articles.title: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
articles.text:
Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string
- Date:
- November 11, 2026
- Source:
- ETH Zurich
- Summary:
- Researchers have created a quantum computer that stores information in microscopic vibrations, potentially making quantum machines smaller, more powerful, and better at preserving information. The breakthrough successfully demonstrated advanced quantum calculations and could help overcome major barriers to practical quantum computing.
- Share:
A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.
Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.
By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.
The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.
Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers
The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.
Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.
The major difference lies in how that information is stored.
"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.
Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.
Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better
One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.
In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.
Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.
However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.
Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.
Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.
New Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests
The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.
The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.
To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.
"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.
Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.
A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers
One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.
However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.
Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.
Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.
Story Source:
Materials provided by ETH Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yu Yang, Igor Kladarić, Martynas Skrabulis, Michael Eichenberger, Stefano Marti, Simon Storz, Jonathan Esche, Raquel García Bellés, Max-Emanuel Kern, Andraz Omahen, Arianne Brooks, Marius Bild, Matteo Fadel, Yiwen Chu. Mechanical resonator–based quantum computing. Science, 2026; 392 (6801): 972 DOI: 10.1126/science.aef4139

articles.title: PHP2Shell Exploited in Destructive Check Point Gateway Attacks
articles.text:
Threat actors have been exploiting PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to hack Check Point Gateway appliances and deploy a wiper against victim organizations, Check Point reports.
The attacks unfolded in two waves. An initial, destructive round started on October 30 and targeted Israeli organizations, and a second one started on November 2, targeting organizations across multiple countries.
PHP2Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, refers to two critical vulnerabilities leading to remote code execution (RCE) and affecting all PHP versions from PHP 5 onwards. They were patched on October 21, but exploitation started days before patches and mass exploitation shortly after.
Dream has linked attacks targeting PHP2Shell to root Palo Alto Networks firewalls to Chinese hackers, and the hackers targeting Check Point gateways have left a note mentioning the cybersecurity firm.
As part of the Check Point campaign, the attackers exploited PHP2Shell for initial access, then targeted CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege escalation in the DynamicCLI process, to gain root access and deploy PHP webshells and establish persistence.
In late October, the attackers targeted Check Point Mobile Access gateways across multiple Israeli organizations. They placed PHP webshells in a directory the Mobile Access portal uses to construct login pages, allowing them to send commands and establish a stronger foothold on the environment.
Next, they deployed TSGA and TSProxy, variants of the malware framework PhiliKit previously seen (PDF) in China-linked UNC5221’s hacking into Ivanti products, for backdoor access and network function interception.
The attackers followed up with internal asset discovery, then moved laterally to a VMware ESXi host where they deployed and executed a wiper, and then deployed a note mentioning Dream Security.
According to Check Point, the hackers operated during typical Chinese working hours. Despite this and the use of China-linked malware and infrastructure, the use of a wiper and the destructive nature of the attacks do not align with known Chinese cyber operations.
“Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation. Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen,” Check Point says.
The second wave targeted Check Point Security Gateways across organizations worldwide, including some Israeli entities targeted in the first wave. No destructive activity was observed during this second wave.
“Neither wave showed a clear sector preference, suggesting opportunistic initial-access attempts rather than sector-specific targeting,” Check Point notes.
