articles.title: Kitesurf is now open source
articles.text:
Kitesurf is now open source
We introduced Kitesurf, our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to.
That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers.
A browser built for agents
Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer.
Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network.
Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation.
What is inside the repository?
Kitesurf builds on Cloudflare’s Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly:
- Blitz provides HTML parsing, the DOM, layout, and painting.
- Stylo provides CSS parsing, cascading, and computed styles.
- Boa runs JavaScript inside WebAssembly (as the last resort only when we can’t run JavaScript in Dynamic Workers).
- Linebender libraries provide text layout and 2D graphics, and Krilla generates PDF output.
These projects made Kitesurf possible. They retain their respective licenses; the repository's NOTICE documents third-party notices.
Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result.
All packages, the engine, its Rust core, DOM shims, renderer, and Kitesurf CLI live separately in folders under the repository’s packages directory where you can explore how all the pieces fit together.
Run your own Kitesurf
To run Kitesurf locally, follow the repository's build requirements, then clone the repository, install dependencies, and start the engine:
git clone https://github.com/cloudflare/kitesurf.git
cd kitesurf
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm run dev
The first build compiles the Rust core and its dependencies, so give it some time. Subsequent builds reuse the build cache. Finally wrangler starts a local development server at http://127.0.0.1:8787. Open that address to try a page in Chrome DevTools, or use it programmatically.
You can use puppeteer with a NodeJS script:
import puppeteer from "puppeteer-core";
const browser = await puppeteer.connect({
  browserWSEndpoint: "ws://127.0.0.1:8787/devtools/browser",
});
try {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.goto("https://example.com/");
  await page.screenshot({ path: "page.png" });
} finally {
  await browser.disconnect();
}
Or you can point your AI harness at the local CDP port (agents love CDP) and watch it take full control of Kitesurf.
Deploy to your Cloudflare account
When you’re done changing and testing locally, you can deploy the engine to your own account and use Kitesurf from there instead of the Browser Run managed APIs we provide. Note that a Workers Paid plan is required because Kitesurf uses Dynamic Workers to create isolated Workers for pages.
From the repository root:
pnpm run deploy
Help us make it better
As with all of our open-sourced projects, Kitesurf lives in Github and we welcome forks and contributions. However, note that Kitesurf is under heavy development and we are focusing on making the engine more compatible (check out Web Platform Test evolution), more reliable, and efficient.
Start with the contribution guidelines if you want to contribute. Open an issue with a minimal reproduction or a proposed approach, and get vouched by a maintainer before opening a pull request. Focused fixes with tests, clear evidence, and a well-defined scope are much easier to review than large rewrites or unrelated cleanup, but all contribution does not have to be code: a small page that reproduces a rendering bug, a failing automation workflow, or a clear documentation correction can help us move forward.
Stay tuned
Kitesurf is evolving quickly. Stay tuned for updates in the blog and our changelog, and keep an eye on the official landing page for the latest on standards compatibility in Web Platform Tests page and benchmarks.
And come chat with the team on Discord. We’re building a browser for agents, and we’d love your help making it better.

articles.title: EntrepreNorth secures $8-million initial close of fund for Indigenous entrepreneurs | BetaKit
articles.text:
Yellowknife-based Indigenous business accelerator EntrepreNorth has spun up its first fund in a push to help fill Northern Canada’s risk capital gap for entrepreneurs.
The organization announced today that the Sinew Impact Fund has completed a first close of $8 million CAD towards its $10-million target. It also made its first investment: a loan to EntrepreNorth Growth Program graduate Aurora Heat, a Fort Smith, NWT-based social enterprise that makes reusable, beaver fur-based hand, feet, wrist, and body warmers.
Through its Sinew Impact Fund, EntrepreNorth plans to invest in Indigenous entrepreneurs with lived experience or cultural ties to the Yukon, Northwest Territories, and Nunavut.
“I don’t think that there’s a fund like this anywhere in Canada.”
Kristin Richard,
Sinew Impact Fund
“This has been a dream of EntrepreNorth [since] long before I started, probably five [or] six years ago now,” Sinew Impact Fund co-founder and managing director Kristin Richard told BetaKit in an interview. “It came to be because the entrepreneurs coming through [our] growth program still struggled to access capital to grow and to really launch their business.”
The sector-agnostic, Indigenous-led fund will provide loans, equity, and revenue-based financing to early-stage, revenue-generating, majority Indigenous-led and owned businesses. It will cut cheques of anywhere between $50,000 and $1 million and offer post-investment support from EntrepreNorth.
“We wanted to be able to support entrepreneurs where they’re at, build financial tools that are really rooted in Indigenous values, and offer a mix of whatever is the best fit for the business at that time,” Richard said.
The Sinew Impact Fund’s investors consist of a mix of Canadian foundations, family offices, and impact investors, including the Mastercard Foundation, Dragonfly Ventures, Definity Foundation, Inspirit Foundation, Heart Lake Committed Capital, family members represented by Unit E Investments, federal government-backed Realize Capital Partners, and the Laidlaw Foundation. The fund has reserved the remaining $2 million for Indigenous wealth holders.
While the Sinew Impact Fund is open to all types of businesses, Richard said she would not be surprised if the fund made some technology-related investments. She noted that AI and data sovereignty are a big area of interest. Though the fund does not plan to support firms developing weaponry, she could potentially see it investing in dual-use tech for defence and civilian applications.
Richard said Sinew Impact Fund aims to support between 40 and 50 companies, with an average deal size that likely lands somewhere around $250,000. The impact-first fund plans to prioritize increasing access to capital over financial returns as it believes “the greater risk is leaving Northern communities under-financed.”
Richard said there are few local capital providers in the North beyond federal and territorial economic development agencies and Indigenous financial institutions, which often have a low risk tolerance and can take a long time to deploy capital. While some more southern organizations are interested in the North, many lack the local relationships that EntrepreNorth has built.
RELATED: Repeat tech entrepreneur Ryan St. Germaine joins Raven as partner
“I don’t think that there’s a fund like this anywhere in Canada,” Richard said. The closest comparable is likely Vancouver’s Raven Indigenous Capital Partners, a multi-stage, impact-driven venture capital firm that backs Indigenous-led tech and other businesses across the continent, and where Richard previously served as an investment analyst.
EntrepreNorth, which gets its funding from government and private foundations, got its start in 2018 as a project of the MakeWay Charitable Society’s northern platform. Since then, the Indigenous-led hub has supported more than 450 Indigenous entrepreneurs in or from Canada’s North with educational programming and mentorship. Earlier this year, EntrepreNorth transitioned into an autonomous, charitable, non-profit organization.
Richard said today’s Sinew Impact Fund milestone is the product of three years’ worth of groundwork, and “a lot more capital than we initially thought that we would be raising.”
All images courtesy EntrepreNorth.

articles.title: My favorite recipe app just got a big upgrade — and a subscription fee
articles.text:
Nearly 10 years after the launch of Paprika 3, the recipe-managing, pantry-organizing, grocery list-making app has gotten a big upgrade that adds more functionality to nearly every corner of the experience. I tested Paprika 4 for several weeks while it was in open beta, and the update recently launched across Android (the version I’ve been using), iOS, Windows, and macOS.
My favorite recipe app just got a big upgrade — and a subscription fee
The fee for newly launched Paprika 4 is well worth the price.
Where Paprika 3 was a one-time purchase per platform, accessing most of the new features in Paprika 4 requires an annual subscription fee of $14.99 (it can also be gifted). That said, new users who don’t want to pay can get a free, feature-light version of the app that offers the ability to save up to 50 recipes. Those who bought Paprika 3 (or previous versions) have been migrated to the “standard” free version of Paprika 4, which includes a small selection of new features, plus cloud syncing, unlimited recipes, and access to Paprika 4 on all platforms, just like subscribers.
The new features locked behind the paywall make it possible to import recipes from social media and from physical cookbooks, scan product barcodes to organize your pantry or shopping list, and connect with other cooks via the app to share notes and recipes. They’re good, for the most part, and makes the subscription feel worth it.
My favorite of the new subscription-exclusive features solves a conundrum I often find myself in: My wife sends me a lot of recipe videos on Instagram. I often take screenshots of the text to piece the recipe together. Paprika 4 can pull the pertinent info from those screenshots and build a recipe — that is, if there’s a complete enough recipe in the text to autofill in Paprika’s recipe fields.
As an alternative to feeding the app a screenshot, you can send a social media post from TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, or Facebook to Paprika 4 straight from the share sheet, and it’ll scrape the caption and convert it in a few seconds. It won’t pull info from a video (which would be convenient — and controversial), and it’ll only work if there’s caption text in the photo or video post available to scrape. It sounds limited, but it’s a nice improvement, and it keeps the link to the social media post in the recipe so I can easily go back and view it as needed.
A lot of social media accounts hide their recipes from people scrolling by, requiring an extra step like “comment with TASTYYUMYUM to get my free recipe.” I respect the hustle, even if I hate seeing this as I’m searching for recipes. Paprika unsurprisingly stumbles when recipe posts are too thin on parseable info. But for ones that have enough, it’s really easy to get them into the app.
Paprika 4 also lets you import recipes with your phone camera. I’ve used it to take pictures from cookbooks that we own, and the app converts them accurately. On the free and standard versions, you’re limited to copy-pasting website URLs into the app’s browser and having it convert them into recipes that way. It works really well, but feels rudimentary by comparison.
The updated app is stuffed with other new features, several of which are a tad superfluous (and less useful to me) but still seem good to offer when you’re hoping to attract subscribers. For instance, you can compile your recipes into your own digital cookbook (sharing them with others requires a subscription) and set up family sharing — even DMing links within the app to other Paprika users. Family sub-accounts can be added to your account for no extra cost beyond the subscription, so long as they haven’t made a Paprika account with the same email address.
Paprika 4 can guess the nutrition facts of your recipes, which is nice if you have fitness goals or just generally like to know what kind of heat your food is packing, so to speak. I wouldn’t take the results to be totally accurate, but it seems capable enough. This feature is locked behind the subscription paywall.
Another feature I could see myself using more of is the expanded pantry tool. Paprika 3 had a single “pantry,” but the paid and standard versions of Paprika 4 let you specify where items are stored, such as in a cupboard, fridge, freezer, and anywhere else (the free version still limits you to one pantry location). I was also excited about the new barcode scanning feature, a premium feature that can quickly and easily add items to your pantry. While it didn’t work for me in beta, the scanning function works well in the current version. It recognized items that I frequently purchase at Trader Joe’s, Whole Foods, and a bodega. It adds what they are in simple terms (i.e., olive oil spray instead of “Trader Joe’s Organic Extra Virgin Olive Oil Spray”).
The Cook Mode is neat, and is available on all versions of Paprika 4. When activated through a drop-down menu, the app reads the first step of the recipe out loud, waiting for you to chime in before continuing. You can ask it to repeat a step, go to the next one, double or halve the recipe, set timers, and strike steps or ingredients as you complete them, among other preset commands and questions. In this mode, the mic stays on by default, though the app won’t respond to unrelated chatter. If asking a prompt doesn’t get it to do anything, you can use the wake word “paprika” to reengage it. This feature has obvious accessibility benefits.
There’s extensive Alexa integration, too, if you pay the subscription fee. It gives Alexa access to your recipes, grocery list, pantry, and meal plan. You can manage grocery lists and pantries by voice with Echo speakers, and screen-equipped Echo devices like the Echo Show can display recipes and support hands-free cooking. The iOS version of Paprika 4 also adds widgets and an array of shortcuts for iOS and macOS, like adding items to a grocery list or pantry, showing scheduled meals in your meal plan, and more. These don’t require a subscription.
For people who are serious about staying organized in the kitchen — both in terms of their pantries and catalog of recipes — these paywalled features will likely get enough use each week to be worth paying for. Though, if you haven’t used Paprika before, the free version is a good place to start.
Even as someone who was content with the features in Paprika 3, I can see the value in paying for the subscription-exclusive features. During the beta, I landed on $2 being a figure I’d be comfortable paying each month for them, and Hindsight Labs settled on just $1.25 per month. It’s going to be getting a lot more money per user than it ever has, but like most Paprika users, I would have purchased the app multiple times over due to how useful it is for me. I guess I get to do that now.
Correction: The article now accounts for there being two tiers of free versions instead of just one, “free” for new users (with fewer features) and “standard” for those who have bought previous versions of Paprika (which has extra functionality).

articles.title: Le Salvador déploie des chiens-robots armés en Haïti pour chasser les gangs
articles.text:
L’armée du Salvador a ajouté des chiens robots armés à son arsenal en Haïti. Engagées aux côtés des forces locales pour reprendre le contrôle des infrastructures clés, à commencer par le stade Sylvio-Cator de Port-au-Prince, tenu par des gangs depuis 2024 et repris ce jeudi 12 novembre 2026, les troupes envoyées par le président salvadorien Nayib Bukele ont dégainé un nouvel outil de dissuasion : des robots quadrupèdes armés envoyés en éclaireurs sur le terrain.
Des chiens robots
Loin des prototypes futuristes ultra-intégrés développés par les grandes puissances militaires, l’engin repéré sur place repose sur un bricolage tactique aussi simple qu’efficace. Sur la vidéo publiée par Russia Today sur X, on distingue un robot quadrupède de type commercial, peint en gris et identifié par le numéro « 02 ».
Le robot porte un fusil d’assaut sur son châssis, avec deux modifications visibles :
- Une arme montée à l’envers : un fusil d’assaut de type carabine M4 est solidement arrimé sur le dos de la machine, orienté chargeur et poignée vers le haut. Ce montage inversé sert sans doute à dégager la ligne de visée et à garder le chargeur et le mécanisme accessibles. Ni Nayib Bukele ni l’armée salvadorienne n’ont détaillé ce choix.
- Un déclenchement télécommandé : une structure métallique vient enserrer le corps de l’arme directement au niveau de la détente. Ce mécanisme permettrait à un opérateur humain, resté à l’abri derrière les lignes, d’actionner le tir à distance via une télécommande tout en pilotant l’engin à travers ses caméras embarquées.
Avertissement : cette vidéo contient des images susceptibles de heurter la sensibilité du public (présence d’ossements humains).
Le Salvador exporte sa méthode forte en Haïti
Le Salvador intervient en pleine crise sécuritaire en Haïti, où les gangs contrôlent une large partie de Port-au-Prince et paralysent le pays. Fort de sa politique ultra-répressive menée sur son propre territoire contre les maras, le gouvernement salvadorien de Nayib Bukele a envoyé ses soldats épauler les forces haïtiennes en vertu d’un accord bilatéral, en marge de la force multinationale autorisée par l’ONU.
En envoyant ces chiens robots en première ligne dans le stade et les ruelles étroites qui l’entourent, l’armée salvadorienne chercherait d’abord à limiter les pertes dans ses rangs face à des gangs lourdement armés. Si la publication vidéo est avare en informations complémentaires, elle montre en revanche qu’un robot du commerce et un fusil d’assaut suffisent désormais à bricoler une arme télécommandée.

Black Friday 2026 – Les écouteurs sans fil Google Pixel Buds 2a à 79,00 € (-33%)
Les écouteurs sans fil Google Pixel Buds 2a passent sous les 80 € chez Amazon soit une baisse d'environ 33% sur le prix habituellement constaté.
Les Pixel Buds 2a sont les nouveaux écouteurs true wireless abordables de Google. Ils misent sur un format compact et une intégration soignée dans Android, tout en faisant quelques concessions sur certaines fonctions avancées pour contenir leur prix.

articles.title: Processeurs AMD Zen 6 : la mémoire GDDR7 confirmée pour RDNA 5 ? — Frandroid
articles.text:
« Siren Halo », ce nom ne vous dit rien ? C’est normal, il s’agirait de la dénomination désormais préférée, chez AMD, pour la prochaine génération de ses super puces, jusqu’à présent connues sous le nom de code « Medusa Halo ».
Si ce changement de surnom n’a encore rien d’officiel, de nouvelles informations, semble-t-il plus tangibles, suggèrent que la firme adopterait une approche intéressante en termes de mémoire vidéo avec ces nouvelles puces. Une approche potentiellement inspirée de ce qu’AMD développerait secrètement pour Microsoft et sa prochaine génération de consoles.
Vers une prise en charge conjointe des mémoires LPDDR6 et GDDR7 pour les futurs super APU d’AMD ?
On apprend en effet de VideoCardz qu’en parallèle de la mémoire vive LPDDR6 qu’on devrait trouver avec cette nouvelle génération de super puces « Siren Halo », AMD miserait aussi sur une prise en charge de modules de mémoire vidéo au format GDDR7 — un type de VRAM que l’on trouve notamment sur les dernières générations de cartes graphiques dédiées.
L’hypothèse d’une gestion de la GDDR7 par « Siren Halo » nous provient en l’occurrence du leaker Gotou_3rd sur X. L’intéressé suggère d’ailleurs, lui aussi, que cette nouvelle génération de super puces AMD reprendrait une partie des spécifications, graphiques notamment, du SoC custom « Magnus » développé par AMD pour le compte de Microsoft et sa future Xbox.
Selon de précédentes fuites, cette puce custom Xbox « Magnus » s’appuierait notamment sur une architecture en « chiplet » regroupant des cœurs CPU Zen 6 et Zen 6c, mais aussi 68 unités de calcul RDNA 5. On y trouverait enfin jusqu’à 48 Go de mémoire GDDR7 montée sur un bus 192 bits. Cette conception GPU serait donc la même sur « Siren Halo ».
L’ADN Xbox dans « Siren Halo »…
Plus spécifiquement, ces nouvelles super puces « Siren Halo » combineraient 24 cœurs Zen 6 à une partie graphique sous architecture RDNA 5, avec en prime une gestion atypique de la mémoire vive pour ce type de SoC : LPDDR6 côté CPU et GDDR7 côté GPU, comme nous l’avons dit.
Notez qu’on ignore à ce stade la configuration exacte de cette portion de mémoire vidéo ou la largeur de son contrôleur mémoire. Si cette approche LPDDR6 / GDDR7 se confirme, il se peut d’ailleurs qu’il y ait carrément deux contrôleurs mémoire sur la puce, un pour chaque type de mémoire vive employée.
Affaire à suivre, mais cette solution permettrait en tout cas à AMD de mutualiser ses coûts de développement entre plusieurs plateformes, avec la puce Xbox « Magnus » d’un côté ; et ses SoC « Siren Halo » de l’autre, voués aux mini-PC, stations de travail compactes vouées à l’IA, ou encore PC portables.

articles.title: How Microcredentials Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI
articles.text:
Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.
“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.
Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.
The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.
Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.
Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.
Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.
The benefits of microcredentials
Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.
Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.
For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.
Translating standards into microcredentials
Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.
The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.
To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit New N-central Zero-Day Hours After PoC Publication
articles.text:
Threat actors started exploiting a new zero-day vulnerability in N-able N-central hours after a disgruntled security researcher released it publicly.
Dubbed 4EverAble2Shell, the security defect could allow unauthenticated attackers to gain remote code execution (RCE) with root privileges on N-central servers running the latest patches.
The zero-day was dropped on GitHub by security researcher Sean Bales two days after N-able rolled out fixes for several other unpatched flaws he released publicly over the weekend.
4EverAble2Shell, Bales says, chains an exploit for a recent Apache Axis vulnerability (CVE-2026-90436, CVSS score: 9.8) with an exploit for an unspecified security hole in N-central deployments that have Legacy API enabled.
The exploit chain targets the Axis bug to achieve RCE, and then attempts to elevate privileges to root and run a shell script.
According to Bales, the exploit chain works against N-central servers that have been updated this week to 2026.4 HF2 (build number 2026.4.1.26), which contains fixes for the previously released Able2Shell zero-days.
N-able reacted immediately to the new zero-days and restricted certain N-central features and integrations, including Legacy API and Intune integration.
“Through our ongoing investigation today, we have identified additional indicators of compromise (IoCs) and are working closely with those specific customers to assess and mitigate any potential risks,” N-able said on November 13.
On November 12, Bales published proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit code for 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, a set of roughly a dozen zero-day flaws that could allow attackers to execute commands on managed Windows agents with System privileges.
4EverAble2Shell exploited within hours
Threat actors started using the 4EverAble2Shell PoC in attacks hours after it landed, early-warning threat intelligence platform Previdian (formerly KEVIntel) said.
“New N-able zero-days are out, and WatchTowr Intel is already seeing probes for ‘4EverAble2Shell’, which affects builds with the Legacy API enabled,” preemptive attack surface management firm WatchTowr warned.
Lupovis and Huntback observed attackers successfully compromising N-central servers roughly 5 hours after the PoC publication. They deployed an XMRig miner with systemd or cron persistence.
“Each victim’s miner is named after its IP address,” Lupovis told SecurityWeek, explaining that the attacker’s wallet showed 21 rigs linked to compromised N-central servers in the US (9), South Africa (4), Canada (4), the UK, Germany, France and Sweden.
“Our decoys never execute anything, so none of the listed rigs are ours. Every one is a real server that ran the chain to root,” Lupovis said.
In a technical write-up, Huntback notes that 19 of the victims had applied the latest patches from N-able.
“The miner is the only payload we have seen, but the escalation hands the operator root on a host that manages your customers’ endpoints. Treat a hit as a full compromise, not a cleanup job. Applying Hotfix 2 is not enough on its own,” Huntaback says.

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.text:
A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
- Date:
- November 7, 2026
- Source:
- University of Regensburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
- Share:
Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.
But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.
The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.
Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds
Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.
However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.
At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.
Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.
To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.
Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.
Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling
To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.
In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.
The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.
Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."
This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.
What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.
This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.
"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.
A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay
To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."
Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.
At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.
For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."
The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.
The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.
A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time
Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."
In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.
To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.
This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.
Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.
The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.
Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?
Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.
One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.
Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.
Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.
"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.
The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.
"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.
That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.
For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Regensburg. Original written by Karoline Stürmer. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- S. Maier, R. Spachtholz, K. Glöckl, C. M. Bustamante, S. Lingl, M. Maczejka, J. Schön, A. Riedel, K. Richter, F. J. Giessibl, F. P. Bonafé, M. A. Huber, A. Rubio, J. Repp, R. Huber. Tracking electrons at the space-time limit. Nature Photonics, 2026; 20 (8): 961 DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01932-0

articles.title: Why Fintechs Canada’s director says Real-Time Rail needs the Big Six banks to succeed | BetaKit
articles.text:
Last week, Budget 2026 revealed new information about some of the most important files for Canada’s FinTech ecosystem: the implementation of Real-Time Rail, an instant payment infrastructure that officially launched Monday, and the ongoing progress toward an open banking system that is intended to give consumers more control over their data sharing (though the government did not provide an updated timeline).
“You need the participation of the Big Six for it to be worthwhile.”
The budget also introduced a competition objective for the financial industry’s regulator, delivering on longtime asks from industry association Fintechs Canada. The group represents FinTech companies such as Borrowell, Neo Financial, Wealthsimple, and Koho.
To unpack industry reactions to the federal budget, BetaKit sat down with Adriana Vega, the executive director of Fintechs Canada, to discuss what successful execution of Real-Time Rail, open banking, and increased financial competition could look like.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
What was the FinTech industry’s broad reaction to Budget 2026?
I think it’s good momentum, good continuity from Budget 2025. I think you see that momentum, especially under the banner of competition.
That dual mandate for competition is something we have been asking for, so it’s very encouraging to see.
The budget also announced that Real-Time Rail, the long-awaited instant payments system, would launch its first phase this past Monday. That phase is now live. What was your reaction to that news?
That was great to see in the budget. It’s so encouraging; it was years in the making; it’s something that our sector and our association were very open about wanting to be expedited and happen quickly.
We’ve worked fairly closely with Payments Canada. I think one of the things that is especially encouraging for us is to see more and more FinTechs coming into the tent of Payments Canada, so they can start contributing more to the governance of the organization.
Is the job done? No, because it’s still coming in waves. Payments Canada has always been fairly transparent, and we understand that this is going to be an implementation that comes in waves. It’s a massive-scale project, but we’re quite reassured by the messaging that came out of Payments Canada on Monday. They said something like nine out of 10 accounts will be in some way touched by the rail within a year, so that signals to me the plan is in place for this rollout to have broad participation.
What would a successful RTR look like?
Success looks like broad adoption, broad participation. There’s a significant amount of payment volume that operates on the rail that really kind of incentivizes the kind of dynamism that FinTechs want to see. That cost-benefit equation makes it really worth their while to design innovative solutions and build them on the rails.
None of Canada’s Big Six banks are participants yet, as BetaKit had previously reported. Do they need to be on board for it to be a success?
A lot of the volume does reside within Big Six bank accounts. So yes, we want to make sure that everybody participates. I don’t see a scenario now where it breaks and then you have some participating and some not.
You need the participation of the Big Six for it to be worthwhile. We have to get to critical mass, where all this volume is here. There are real incentives for everybody to do something with it.
There is lots of public confusion about how RTR works and why it’s different from Interac e-Transfer. How are you thinking about that disconnect?
When I talk about Real-Time Rail and instant payments, folks will say, “Well, but I can already send my friends $20, right? We already have Interac.” But RTR is really infrastructure. I don’t expect a situation where a consumer says, “Oh, they’re doing my transfer on the rail versus this one doing it by a different rail.” Right now, people don’t look at the infrastructure side of the equation; hey want a product that’s reliable, that is bespoke, that is safe, that does what it’s intended to do.
I think the most visible advantages perhaps lie more in the small business segment. That’s a segment that is super challenged with delayed payments due to batch settlement.
Another long-delayed system that FinTechs have been advocating for is open banking. There was not much about it in the budget outside of a new pledge to expand data portability beyond the banking sector. What was your reaction to that?
As I mentioned, we’re very happy with the budget, and everybody is very supportive. If there’s one thing that people go, “what’s going on there?” That’s open banking, because it looks like it’s probably not going to roll out this year. Just looking at the calendar, there’s a regulatory path, and that has to continue, but my read is that we would like to be further ahead in implementation of the framework. I think it would have been so welcome to know that they’re pushing forward with write access.
For the everyday Canadian, what does write access mean in the context of open banking?
If you think about it, we already have open banking, right? You can direct FinTechs to read your financial statements on your behalf. That is done through screen scraping, which gives them read access. That’s where we’re at in our journey of regulating open banking. In many ways, the open banking regulations that are going to be rolled out are to meet the market where it’s at and standardize it.
Write access is sort of like the other side of the coin. You don’t just get to see it; you get to act on my permission based on all these security standards.
I suspect in the first half of next year you might start seeing some consultations around write access, potentially, because I think the ambition is to have write access legislation sometime next year.
The Logic reported that the feds are held up on selecting a technical standards body for the system because the frontrunner, Financial Data Exchange (FDX), is a US-based organization. What are your members’ thoughts on how the feds should move forward?
Most of the industry already uses one standard, which is FDX. Expediency and getting to the finish line should be the priority for all, and the industry standard that has broad adoption is the one that we would like to support and see appointed.
Feature image courtesy Nrth Festival.
