articles.title: Adapting to AI penetration testing orchestrators: The Modern Security Model
articles.text:
Adapting to AI penetration testing orchestrators: The Modern Security Model
Over the last month, the number of Large Language Model (LLM) penetration testing and orchestration frameworks has exploded. Just a few weeks ago, ARTEX — an open source agentic penetration testing system that automates offensive security workflows — was the only framework available. In just the last three days, we have seen over 50 framework families attempt to scan Cloudflare customers globally. The number of Internet Protocol (IP) addresses seen running these frameworks has grown into the thousands and continues to increase daily. The proliferation of these frameworks has significantly changed the status quo in cyber defense: defenders are struggling to keep up with the volumetric nature of these autonomously guided attacks.
ARTEX was taken down by its creator Autumn-27 on October 8. (“The malicious exploitation of this tool runs entirely counter to its original intent,” they wrote in Chinese.) But in the month since, the ecosystem has exploded with new fragmented versions of it. There are now over 12,000 repositories, with several hundred unique forks containing lineage from the original repository. Additionally, hundreds of other similar agentic orchestration frameworks have been created since October 8. Daily requests of AI penetration testing (pentesting) and exploitation tools has grown by 30x since October 1. These tools have also begun chaining stolen customer credentials in some of the more complex attacks, such as lateral movement chaining throughout an environment.
We expect these frameworks to continue to proliferate, and every organization should be prepared to address this threat. To counter LLM-based pentest frameworks, we recommend that all organizations adopt what we call the Modern Security Model, which has six key pillars:
- Fortify the front gate: Implement a Web Application Firewall (WAF) with advanced rules such as rate limits.
- Security station in the foyer: Anomaly detection on all web applications your customers access.
- Identify phony visitors: Implement Bot Defense.
- Remove the back door: Implement Identity-Gated Access for all high-risk external and internal web applications.
- Inspect deliveries: Enforce validated schemas and explicit security controls.
- Neighborhood watch: Implement Threat Intelligence to gain visibility into attacks.
What is an LLM penetration and exploitation orchestrator?
Open-source pentesting frameworks are able to orchestrate AI agents to carry out stages of the traditional Cyber Kill Chain at scale. Tools like ARTEX have the ability to quickly plug in existing Model Context Protocol (MCP) and connect traditional standalone pentesting tools in novel ways. Some even allow operator direction on what type of task to accomplish. These tools can map and enumerate environments, both from the inside and outside. ARTEX and its forks map assets and environments onto a graph, allowing multiple independent parallel agents to enumerate, verify, prototype, and attack at the speed of inference. These tools turn compromises into a hill-climbable problem, which agents are specifically good at.
The AI LLM pentesting tools that currently exist
We are currently tracking 50+ AI LLM agents. The table below shows the top five LLM penetration and exploitation orchestrators. Each is extremely popular (1k+ GitHub stars) and fully autonomous. The fully autonomous nature of these agents represents a doctrinal shift in offensive cyber capabilities:
- Human skills are no longer the limit: A harness performs every step of the OODA loop by observing the environment, orienting itself to prioritize valuable and/or vulnerable targets, decide on an action, and act autonomously.
- Speed increase: Having multiple parallel agents working towards a goal is a large shift compared to single operator or multiple operator augmented by AI.
- Scale: A single operator can target multiple organizations at the same time, greatly increasing their blast radius.
- Small mistakes are easily discovered: Autonomous frameworks relentlessly and systematically test exposed services, including their configurations.
|  | Architecture | Planning model | Built-in capabilities/execution environment | Post-exploitation capabilities | 
| ARTEX (and forks) | Planner and parallel agents | Graph of goals, leads, and findings is linked to separate asset graph of target | Directly on host or container with network/root access, can install/develop tools as needed | Nothing built-in, requires user instruction | 
| LuaN1aoAgent | Supervisor agent, planner agent, and generic executor agents | Three graphs, with goals/tasks/blockers, evidence/hypothesises/exploits, and target/local | Container with network/user access, can develop tools as needed and install user packages | Built-in SSH and Chisel for tunneling and attempted reconnection after disruption | 
| Decepticon | Orchestrator agent dispatching specialist sub-agents | Graph of objectives with prerequisites | Kali container running as root, can develop tools as needed | Dedicated post-access, Active Directory and cloud pivoting skills | 
| Cairn | Dispatcher orchestrating work to existing AI harnesses (Codex, Claude Code, Pi) | Graph of facts and leads; new nodes trigger dispatcher | Kali container with root access or directly on host, can develop tools as needed | Prompt guidance and Kali tools | 
| PentestGPT-Agent | Supervisor agent and one generic executor agent | Task list with dependencies, goals, and evidence | Run on host, can develop tools as needed | Nothing built-in, requires user instruction | 
Observations from the world's largest network
As of November 12, ARTEX and its forks make up over 60% of currently known AI penetration testing orchestrators. The charts below help us understand how adoption of these tools has changed over the past six weeks. Since the removal of the original ARTEX repository on October 8, traffic has grown more than tenfold, and has increased more than 30x since October 1.
As demonstrated above, the takedown of ARTEX on October 8 (and widespread reporting of it) likely caused a hydra effect, where the removal of the original repository led to a massive increase in the number of forks and modifications which can be seen in the steep acceleration of unique instances around October 8.
Identity-chained LLM exploitation
Over the last eight weeks, our Cloudforce One team has been called into multiple incident response investigations involving ARTEX and ARTEX-derived LLM exploitation frameworks. We’ve seen firsthand how exposed credentials are being chained with LLM-based exploitation frameworks to gain the upper hand over defenders.
We observed multiple incidents in which a threat actor gained initial access to a hyperscaler environment and pivoted directly into the customer's Cloudflare environment. Root-cause analysis revealed a common credential hygiene failure. Attackers repeatedly compromised static, non-expiring tokens running inside CI/CD pipelines, which granted broad, cross-environment access across the organization's hyperscaler infrastructure. LLM frameworks greatly expand the likelihood of a client’s API key being laterally leveraged to take over other tenant environments.
ARTEX in action
As part of one incident response investigation, our team observed ARTEX gaining access to a compromised account-level API token previously used for CI/CD with no IP restrictions or rate limiting. Available evidence indicated that the compromise most likely originated through a third-party hyperscaler.
We observed that a large number of new Worker scripts had been created with distinct names such as artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-*, and artex-do-*. The naming of each Worker script correlated to distinct behaviors and actions it was taking, and was often postfixed by an alphanumeric identifier. We observed activity in excess of 69 requests per minute across multiple unique parts of their Cloudflare infrastructure and 400 database dump requests in an hour. We also observed attempted persistence mechanisms and attempts to validate session tokens for other third-party applications. While we believe that much of this activity was lightly guided by the human operator, this is just one example of the speed and breadth that ARTEX and similar frameworks can achieve post-compromise.
Our recommendation: the Modern Security Model
Large Language Models increase the ability of a threat actor to rapidly iterate through the Cyber Kill Chain against a target. They do this by giving the actor the advantage of speed and validation. Each step of the Cyber Kill Chain can be validated and fed into the next stage of the attack. This level of orchestration is unparalleled and effectively vaporizes legacy cyber security models. A modern model must be used against these attacks.
To help explain this model further, let’s use the metaphor of protecting a house on an estate. Each section below outlines how to defend against the threat at each step.
Fortify the front gate: implement traffic control and a WAF with advanced rules
Before anyone even sets foot on your lawn, they have to reach the perimeter fence.
On an unprotected estate, an adversary can drive an endless fleet of decoy trucks straight into your driveway, completely blocking the entrance and smashing through the barriers (Layer 3/4 volumetric floods and direct IP probing).
With perimeter gate security in place, all incoming traffic is routed through massive, distributed outer gates miles away from the main house. Rogue delivery trucks are filtered out to the highway, rogue utility tunnels trying to wiretap your property are severed, and only legitimate foot traffic ever reaches your home address.
Network traffic control serves as an important role in stopping volumetric attacks.
A security station in the foyer: anomaly detection
Once visitors arrive at the main entry, they meet a strict security station at the foyer.
Automated prowlers don't just kick the door; they disguise themselves. They attempt weird ways to get in the door — stuffing paper into the lock, trying variations like //front-door//back-room/ to trick the mechanism into swinging open.
The security guard at the door enforces clear rules:
- You cannot knock 500 times in five seconds.
- You cannot disguise your path with trickery.
- You cannot attempt to roll a massive flatbed cart through the front hall to haul away the house's internal blueprints (diagnostic heap dumps). Suspicious behavior is turned away immediately.
- Implement security keys and hardware based FIDO keys.
Web Application Firewall (WAF) serves as a key defense mechanism in stopping application exploitation through rate limits and anomaly detection.
Identify phony visitors: implement Bot Defense
A sophisticated intruder rarely looks like a masked burglar; they disguise themselves as ordinary visitors. But automated agents, headless browser scrapers, and AI reconnaissance tools don't act like real people.
They don't blink, their posture is unnervingly rigid, their cadence is mechanical, and their "identification" is often a sloppy imitation of a real visitor badge.
Bot Defense and challenges act as behavioral specialists watching the crowd through one-way glass. It flags the unnatural cadence, catches the synthetic micro-behaviors, and quietly escorts the machines off the property before they can touch a single doorknob.
Remove the back door: implement Identity-Gated Access and micro-segmentation
Many homes historically were built with side doors or a cellar hatch (internal admin panels, /actuator diagnostic endpoints, and remote gateways). Even if locked, a prowler could stand on the sidewalk, shine a flashlight on the cellar door, and start picking the lock.
Zero Trust application access does something radical: it bricks up the doorway from the outside and restricts which rooms can be entered.
To anyone wandering the perimeter, the cellar door does not exist. There is no lock to pick, no handle to rattle, and no light on inside. The only way in is with an escort who checks your biometric badge, confirms your device has a clean bill of health, and steps you directly into the specific room you need — leaving the rest of the house out of view.
For those who do enter, you have to ensure they cannot breach rooms next to the room they enter. Micro-segmentation is a highly effective strategy at stopping lateral movement. It limits compromised credentials from breaching production, test, and development systems.
Inspect deliveries: enforce validated schemas and explicit security controls
You receive daily supply deliveries to your estate — groceries, mail, maintenance parts. In digital terms, this is your incoming API traffic, which must be inspected and verified.
Intruders often attempt to bypass controls by sending unvalidated payloads or forged delivery manifests meant for restricted internal systems.
The porch protocol mandates thorough inspection and schema validation for all traffic:
- Every incoming request must undergo OpenAPI schema validation to ensure it strictly conforms to expected definitions and structures.
- Drivers and couriers must present validated mutual TLS (mTLS) certificates to establish trusted, authenticated connections.
- Any request failing inspection or missing valid credentials is rejected immediately at the boundary.
- Default-Deny Posture: Every positive security implementation ends with an explicit deny-all rule at the bottom of the ruleset.
Neighborhood watch: implement threat intelligence to gain visibility into attacks
Even with ironclad walls, an isolated property can be vulnerable if a syndicate invents a brand-new infiltration technique across town.
Threat intelligence acts as your warning network with neighboring estates. When a rogue actor sets up a new command-and-control safehouse down the road or begins deploying dynamic tunneling vans in your district, you receive an early dossier. Your estate updates its watchlists, recalibrates its sensors, and slams the gate shut before the actor ever turns onto your street.
How to get real-time help
ARTEX and similar LLM-based frameworks pose a significant challenge to legacy cyber defense models. Even the historical defense-in-depth model — which emphasizes a classic network DMZ — falls short in today's complex architectures. Tomorrow's attacks will only advance as orchestration tools become the new normal.
Securing legacy equipment and on-premises devices requires an identity-gated approach that logically makes these devices impossible to reach on the Internet. Beyond identity, slowing or making lateral movement more noisy is the goal of micro-segmentation. This architecture emphasizes a containment-first approach to security, which is essential when users are consistently losing their keys. When combined, the elements of the Modern Security Model are the answer to this vexing problem.
If you are facing an active security incident and need the Cloudforce One team on the ground to help respond to the incident or require threat intelligence support, please contact us immediately. If you need help implementing the Modern Security Model outlined here, please contact our Solutions Engineering team.

articles.title: How Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia impacts China’s AI supply chain
articles.text:
Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday, days after he admitted to having an affair with a Chinese data center executive, whom the U.S. intelligence agency believed to be a Chinese government agent. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive.
Nvidia’s board said that chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as the company’s interim chief executive until a permanent successor has been named.
Huang’s exit has triggered worries about Nvidia’s future as the world’s top chipmaker, and about the entire AI industry where Nvidia has been a hardware provider, an investor, and a community leader. Repercussions from the saga will impact China, which has yet to replace Nvidia chips with domestic alternatives, as well as Taiwan and South Korea, which host a vast network of Nvidia suppliers.
Here are the key questions emerging from Huang’s dramatic downfall.
How does Huang’s exit affect China’s chip access?
Jensen Huang had been the biggest advocate for selling chips to China, which he argued helps America maintain its market dominance.
Despite the U.S. banning the export of advanced Nvidia chips to China, Chinese companies have been trying to access chips remotely by working with data centers in Southeast Asia.
Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang had an affair, served as the executive of Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia. The Information reported that Alice Huang helped move about 240,000 H100, H200 and some A100 chips into China. Her companies also invested in DeepSeek, promising to supply Nvidia chips.
The Nvidia scandal will likely lead the U.S. government to tighten chip controls. Anticipating a crackdown, Chinese AI labs are trying to lock in overseas supplies of Nvidia chips, while traders in China are stockpiling restricted chips, Reuters reported.
Can China do without Nvidia chips?
Chinese chips are catching up in performance, but Nvidia chips are still essential to the AI industry.
In the first half of the year, Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China, down 44% from a year earlier and making up 34% of the market, according to a Reuters report, citing IDC data. In the same period, leading Chinese chipmaker HuaweiHuaweiHuawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions.READ MORE shipped 572,000 AI accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, accounting for 28% of the market,
AlibabaAlibabaAlibaba, founded in 1999 by Chinese entrepreneur Jack Ma, is one of the most prominent global e-commerce companies that operates platforms like AliExpress, Taobao, and Tmall.READ MORE’s chip unit T-Head had 7% of the market, followed by Cambricon’s 5%. BaiduBaiduBaidu is a Chinese technology company that operates the country’s biggest search engine and video-streaming service iQiyi.READ MORE subsidiary Kunlunxin held 4% and Hygon had 3%.
Although AI labs are increasingly working with chipmakers to make sure their models can run on domestic infrastructure, most AI developers still train new models on Nvidia chips. Nvidia’s B300 delivers 6.75 times the arithmetic performance of Huawei’s best Ascend 950 chip, according to research firm Epoch AI. Huawei also lags behind Nvidia in production volume.
What do people in Asia think about Jensen Huang’s downfall?
Jensen Huang enjoys rock star status across Asia, especially in his birth country Taiwan, where he would visit night markets, share snacks with fans, and host banquets with executives of Taiwanese suppliers. He said the company planned to invest $150 billion a year in Taiwan.
Many internet users expressed disappointment that they lost a role model in tech. Some wrote that the spy allegations and the criticisms of Huang would add to the discrimination of Asians working in America’s tech industry.
Huang’s departure is also creating uncertainty around Nvidia’s supply chain relationship with Asian companies. But several executives at Nvidia’s Taiwanese suppliers said they still expected steady orders from Nvidia in the coming years because of the sustained demand from the AI industry, according to Taiwan’s Central News Agency.

articles.title: GitHub availability report: October 2026
articles.text:
GitHub availability report: October 2026
In October, we experienced eight incidents that resulted in degraded performance across GitHub services.
We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.
The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.
As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.
That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.
We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.
We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.
Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in users. More details on these and other incidents follow.
The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind plan. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.
The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.
October 05 19:11 UTC (lasting 3 hours and 38 minutes)
Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.
Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.
What went wrong and why?
Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.
Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.
How did we respond?
- A partial networking failure began, and actions jobs started backing up.
- Alerts flagged errors and slow job assignment, and we declared an incident.
- We redeployed the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners, but it did not recover. We traced the failures to the networking issue.
- We failed over the affected databases and storage to healthy regions, one service at a time, and added capacity. Actions recovered, but some other affected services kept failing even after failover.
- We worked with our cloud provider to resolve the networking failure. The remaining services recovered, and we resolved the incident.
How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?
- We are making the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners better able to handle sudden increases in load, so it keeps up when another region shifts extra jobs to it.
- We now have expanded prioritization of runner assignment based on customer profile when available runner capacity is degraded.
- We are changing the behavior of GitHub-hosted runners to reduce recovery time when job assignment services are degraded for a period of time.
- We are improving how quickly we detect and locate partial network failures between our datacenters and the cloud-hosted services they depend on.
October 06 19:57 UTC (lasting 3 hours and 43 minutes)
Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.
Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.
Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.
What went wrong and why?
A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.
The importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.
To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.
How did we respond?
- A surge of migration work overloaded a shared database, causing requests across github.com to fail or slow down.
- Automated monitoring detected the failures and paged our on-call engineers.
- The errors stopped on their own within minutes.
- We declared an incident and paused enterprise migrations to prevent a recurrence while we investigated the cause.
- Once a mitigation was deployed, we resumed migrations and resolved the incident.
How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?
- We optimized the query GitHub Enterprise Importer sends to the database so that each one stays small and fixed in size.
- We are automating importer backoff when the database is under strain, easing load before it can affect other GitHub services.
- We are adding database alerts that flag queries doing much more work than usual and identify which query is responsible, so we can find and fix problems like this one faster.
October 07 15:14 and 17:17 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 11 minutes, and 47 minutes, respectively)
Duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.
Customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or issues, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.
Web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.
What went wrong and why?
During regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One new machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.
How did we respond?
- Automated monitoring alerted us to failing writes, and we declared an incident.
- Writes recovered when an established machine with correct records became leader and published correct settings.
- We traced the cause to the new machine, resolved the first incident, and paused automated maintenance to prevent a repeat.
- When a maintenance task did not honor the pause and the outage repeated, we declared a second incident.
- Writes recovered when an established machine became leader again. We removed the new machine and resolved the second incident.
How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?
- We improved how we retire database servers, so outdated records aren’t left behind.
- We tightened controls on adding new machines that manage database routing, and making sure automated maintenance honors a pause.
- We strengthened validation of database routing settings, so incorrect settings are caught before they take effect.
October 19 15:49 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 7 minutes)
Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.
Customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.
What went wrong and why?
An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.
How did we respond?
- Automated alerts detected the failures, we declared an incident, and we traced the problem to the shared network link.
- We routed the actions service away from some of its cache servers in that region, but the link was still over capacity.
- We routed it away from the rest of those cache servers, and the link recovered.
- We raised processing limits to clear the actions backlog, and we resolved the incident once all affected services had recovered.
How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?
- We have limited how quickly this actions service can open new connections to its cache servers.
- We are alerting on spikes in new connections from this service to identify and address the source sooner.
October 21 14:52 UTC (lasting 4 hours and 30 minutes)
Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.
Customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, new commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.
Audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.
Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.
What went wrong and why?
Some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, new connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.
We took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the issue.
Audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.
How did we respond?
- We declared an incident and moved some traffic off an overloaded server, but more servers became overloaded soon after.
- We split the busiest traffic into more partitions and moved it to less-loaded servers. All affected features except audit logs gradually recovered.
- Once the audit log service stopped restarting, we raised the rate at which it could write events so the backlog would clear faster.
- We resolved the incident once audit log delays were back within the healthy range, and the remaining backlog cleared afterward.
How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?
- We added randomized delays to reconnects after a failed request, so servers that are already slow don’t get hit with a burst of new connections.
- We are alerting earlier on server memory use, so we can move traffic before a server slows down.
- We are adding a second destination for webhook delivery data that we can switch to, so we can keep webhook deliveries moving if our event streaming platform slows down.
- We have improved our playbooks to move hot partitions for similar situations in the future
October 28 14:12 UTC (lasting 1 hour and 16 minutes)
Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.
Customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.
Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.
What went wrong and why?
Copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.
How did we respond?
- A credential we use with an upstream model provider stopped working, and requests to the affected models began to fail.
- Alerts flagged rising errors on the affected models, and we declared an incident.
- We posted a public status update and recommended choosing another model in the meantime.
- We traced the errors to our own credential and created a replacement.
- We began deploying the new credential, and requests started to recover once the first environment was updated.
- We completed the deployment in the remaining environments, confirmed that requests to the affected models had recovered, and resolved the incident.
How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?
- We improved how our service handles authentication failures from upstream model providers, so requests can be retried instead of failing.
- We are strengthening how we manage credentials for upstream model providers.
- We are adding alerts for authentication failures from upstream model providers, so we can identify and address this kind of problem faster.
October 30 14:31 UTC (lasting 31 minutes)
Duration: approximately 9 minutes.
Customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Issues, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.
What went wrong and why?
A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. New requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.
The pool was already running near capacity when some update requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.
How did we respond?
- Requests used up every connection in the shared database pool, and requests across github.com began to fail.
- We declared an incident after seeing failures, and on-call engineers for the affected services were paged.
- The pool drained and error rates returned to normal. Shortly after, we confirmed that the full connection pool had caused the errors and posted a public status update.
- We verified that database connections were back to normal and resolved the incident after monitoring for stability.
How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?
- We are now running the slow lookup before these update requests start writing a change, so they no longer hold a database connection while they wait.
- We are evaluating limits on how long a pooled database connection can be held, so a slow request pattern is less likely to tie up the pool.
Follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.text:
A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
Scientists have developed a promising new method that could read quantum information with 99.85% accuracy while barely disturbing the qubit itself.
- Date:
- November 4, 2026
- Source:
- Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo
- Summary:
- Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.
- Share:
One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.
Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.
The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.
Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult
Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.
This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.
"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.
To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.
The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.
Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.
"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.
A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal
The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.
Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.
These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.
"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.
The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.
The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.
Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.
"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.
How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information
To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.
One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.
The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.
According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.
"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.
This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.
A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage
Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.
Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."
The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.
"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.
This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.
That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.
Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor
The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.
Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.
Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.
The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.
Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.
"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."
The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.
Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance
In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.
This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.
The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.
"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.
The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.
This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.
Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy
To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.
These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.
The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.
According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.
The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.
However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.
Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?
Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.
The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.
What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.
"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.
This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.
The research offers two potentially significant advances.
From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.
From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.
If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.
More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

articles.title: Introducing Spend Management: Spending limits and alerts for Cloudflare
articles.text:
Introducing Spend Management: Spending limits and alerts for Cloudflare
Spend controls have been at the top of the list of most requested features from developers building on our developer platform for quite some time now. With more than 10 million developers now building on Cloudflare, this matters more than ever.
Although we’ve had usage notifications and budget alerts available to paid plans for a while, this doesn’t solve the problem completely; informing is not the same as controlling.
You can now set spending thresholds and choose to have Cloudflare pause activity when those limits are reached, thus avoiding unexpected bills from unplanned usage. Today, we're introducing Spend Management in Beta, for any pay-as-you-go (PayGo) customer, starting with Workers and Durable Objects.
Use Spend Management alongside AI Gateway spend limits to manage compute and AI inference costs across your application. AI Gateway already supports per-user and per-model budgets for Workers AI and other AI providers, applied to requests routed through your gateway.
How it works
You can start using Spend Management using the dashboard, cf CLI, or REST API.
In the dashboard, head over to Manage Account > Billing > Spend limits and enable the products for which you want to control spending.
When you enable controls on a product, you can define a spending limit, specify a recipient email for notifications, and set one or more alert thresholds.
If you configure a recipient email, Cloudflare will send notifications when the evaluated spend reaches one of the thresholds or your spending limit. When the limit is reached, a blocking policy is enforced and your product is paused automatically.
If you go to the dashboard, you can see the current billing cycle costs for each supported product in near real time (under 10 minutes), and manage your settings and thresholds from there. The overview panel tells you which products have thresholds and limits configured. In this example, you can see that Workers triggered two alerts before hitting the hard limit.
Note that the billing cycle starts when the paid subscription begins, not when you deploy a Worker or create a spending cap; a subscription starting October 10 generally has a cycle of October 10-November 10 — not a calendar month.
The dashboard also shows an audit log, so you can see who changed a limit and when, or when a cap was reached.
As with most Cloudflare services, Spend Management is also an API that you can use programmatically; the documentation can be found in our Developer Documentation. Here’s an example, but using the API:
curl --fail-with-body --request POST \
  "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/${CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID}/billing/spend-policies" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN}" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "name": "Workers spending cap",
    "product_id": "workers",
    "enabled": true,
    "threshold_cents": 10000,
    "action": "usage_block",
    "notification_email": "me@example.com"
  }'
And, of course, you can use cf, the CLI for the entire Cloudflare API:
cf billing spend-policies list
cf billing spend-policies create
cf billing spend-policies get
cf billing spend-policies update
cf billing spend-policies delete
cf billing spend-policies audit list
cf billing spend-policies activity list
cf billing spend-policies create --body '{
  "name": "Workers spending cap",
  "product_id": "workers",
  "enabled": true,
  "threshold_cents": 10000,
  "action": "usage_block",
  "notification_email": "me@example.com"
}'
Once a cap is enforced, new invocations of that product are rejected. Note that we only pause customer-code invocations that incur costs — in Workers, for example, Cron Triggers and Queue consumer invocations are paused, but static assets continue to be served.
To resume service, you can:
- Raise the limit above the current cycle’s accumulated spend.
- Disable or delete the blocking policy.
- Wait until the next billing cycle, when the existing block expires.
That’s it. You can start using Spend Management for Workers and Durable Objects today, and other products will follow soon.
Read on to learn how we built the system, and what’s going to happen next.
How we built Spend Management
As easy and straightforward as it seems on the surface, building a system like this at Cloudflare scale was no small feat. From an invocation anywhere on our distributed network to a blocking decision that we need to apply globally, building Spend Management required working with multiple teams, changing code in existing systems, and creating new systems from scratch.
Let’s start by looking at the bird's-eye view of a capped billable event:
Now let's dig deeper.
Collecting and aggregating close to the source
Each invocation produces usage measurements: requests, CPU time, execution duration, or storage operations, depending on the product. But transporting and processing this volume of raw data all the way from the sources down to the rating engine would not scale or be efficient.
So what we do is we collect and aggregate the measurements as close to the source as possible using a two-stage metering pipeline that combines events into usage aggregates, so the engine sees accumulated usage rather than having to process all the events one by one.
Let's look at a diagram.
The first stage reduces raw-event volume close to parsing down to one-minute windows. Each metering parser converts raw events into usage measurements, then combines matching measurements into typically one-minute buckets. Still, several records can describe the same account and time window.
In the second stage, a separate service merges those first-stage partial aggregates using the same grouping rules, but over typically five-minute windows, and further reduces the volume before downstream processing by the Usage Engine. Here we also archive the consolidated aggregates; this gives us a durable dataset for later analytics and reconciliation.
The nice thing about this two-stage pipeline is that it reduces the raw event volume early, so the downstream engines process only the aggregated usage they need to calculate spend and act on it. That’s what makes this practical at Cloudflare’s scale.
Usage Engine: account-partitioned processing
The Usage Engine translates aggregated measurements into usage records, which are standardized records containing the account, usage window, metric, quantity, and relevant dimensions. In other words, it maps product-specific meters into supported usage metrics.
We partition processing by account, so an account’s usage and subscription information meet in the same place. That lets us maintain its accumulated usage and apply included allowances without coordinating across pricing processors on every update.
As you can see, we run different partitions in parallel, giving us a way to spread the work across accounts while keeping each account’s pricing state together. Also note that each partition keeps both a local state for fast access, and also a durable write-ahead logging (WAL) changelog on disk. This buys us:
- Less cross-partition coordination: each account’s usage and subscription state stay together.
- Consistent pricing: usage updates share the same allowance and accumulated-spend state.
- Parallel processing: different partitions calculate spend independently.
- Recoverability: durable state lets replacement processors rebuild and resume after failures, if necessary.
Then, finally, the usage metrics are fed into the Rating Engine.
The Rating Engine
The Rating Engine is the most important block of Spend Management; it turns usage into monetary value and it’s what’s able to answer the question: “Given what this account has consumed, its subscription, and its pricing, how much has it spent so far?”
Here’s how it works.
In essence, the Rating Engine brings together three things:
- Usage records: quantities such as requests and CPU milliseconds.
- Subscription information: the account’s billing period and plan changes.
- Pricing rules: rates, included allowances, and billing rounding.
Usage data and subscriptions are independent streams
Usage and subscription updates arrive as independent streams, so we can’t assume they reach the Rating Engine in order. Furthermore, we have to be able to recover from a data processing failure or missing subscription information from, say, a failed webhook.
If usage arrives before the subscription information needed to price it, we retain it as pending and revisit it when that information becomes available. This lets us tolerate temporary delays without treating unpriced usage as free.
Tracking accumulated spend
Finally, we calculate and track accumulated spend. The Rating Engine uses a product catalog database that defines usage metrics, including allowances, rates, and rounding rules, alongside the account’s subscription information. One million CPU milliseconds doesn’t necessarily mean an extra charge: the engine first applies the account’s included CPU allowance, then prices any excess. It prices accumulated usage rather than rounding and charging for each request independently.
Once the accumulated spend is calculated, two steps follow:
- Policy evaluation: decide whether one or more warning or blocking thresholds have been reached.
- Reporting: we show estimated usage charges in the dashboard via our APIs, and we send out email alerts (via Cloudflare Email Service) if necessary.
Asynchronous cap enforcement
The Rating Engine doesn’t sit in the request path or directly reject requests. Instead, the policy service sends the cap to our runtime configuration service and Quicksilver, our internal key-value store developed to enable fast global replication and low-latency access at planet scale. This propagates it to all our nodes asynchronously.
Once the cap reaches Quicksilver, the runtime picks it up during its periodic refresh and starts rejecting capped invocations or operations.
In other words, enforcement uses local state, so requests never have to wait on the Rating Engine. By reusing our existing runtime account-limit architecture, we keep rating out of the request path while distributing caps across the global network.
What’s next
Any pay-as-you-go customer can start using Spend Management today. While this is a major milestone in our roadmap, it’s also just the start. Let us share some of our plans for the next few weeks and months ahead.
More products
We are starting with caps for Workers and Durable Objects, but you’ll be able to measure and cap many other Cloudflare products and primitives in the near future. We’ve built the system in a way that makes it easy and familiar for our products to onboard, so expect the catalog to grow.
Closer to real time
While near real time under 10 minutes is a great benchmark, we’re not satisfied with it, and being the stubborn engineers we are, we have pretty good ideas on how to reduce that time even further. Expect us to shorten the gap between measurement and enforcement over time, hopefully to under a minute.
Agent and application-based budgets
Right now, we measure spend by products and primitives, but there are other useful dimensions to explore when controlling costs. For example, a developer might want to monitor the costs of a specific application — such as a Worker script that uses other primitives like R2 or Workers AI. How can we measure the aggregated cost of an entire application and pause that application, rather than disabling the underlying primitives across all customer applications?
Another compelling use case for cost controls is AI agents. We’ve all read horror stories about rogue agents entering unconstrained recursive reasoning loops to brute-force a problem — generating thousands of dollars in costs from high-frequency, expensive API calls, not to mention causing denial-of-service (DoS) issues on databases and other services. AI Gateway already lets you give an agent a budget for AI requests routed through it. A task can also consume compute, database, and storage resources. We want to make it possible to budget for that broader resource use across products.
You’ll be able to tag the calls from your agents and our pipeline will carry that metadata from the runtime through to the Rating Engine. That will let us attribute spend and pause an application or an agentic task across products, without interrupting other unrelated applications.
Get started
This launch is a first step toward making spend controls a normal part of building on Cloudflare, alongside deploying code and monitoring your applications.
Check out the billing developer documentation for more information. Start using Spend Management and tell us what works, what’s missing, or where more granular budgets would help.
Join us on Discord or our socials. We’re listening!

articles.title: How AI Is Helping Care Teams Get Patients the Right Care, Sooner
articles.text:
From pediatric research to smart hospitals, AI is helping care teams spend less time on routine tasks and more time with patients.
Health systems and startups are putting it to work across healthcare, from matching patients to clinical trials to supporting radiologists, hospital teams and patients at home. Clinicians stay at the center, reviewing AI outputs and guiding decisions, while NVIDIA technologies provide the compute behind the applications.
Read on to learn how healthcare teams are using AI to improve and speed patient care.
Friday, Nov. 13, 5:00 a.m. PT 🔗
Dyania Health Uses AI to Turn Decades of Patient Records Into Better Care
Hospitals hold decades of patient history, most of it written in free text, as physicians’ notes, operative reports, imaging and pathology reads and discharge summaries. To understand one patient’s full story, a clinician would need to read through years of charts.
Dyania Health, a New Jersey-based clinical AI company, built Synapsis AI to do just that. Synapsis AI is a clinical reasoning engine: It works across every note, report and lab result in a patient’s record, connecting findings that may be years apart to answer clinical questions the way a specialist reviewing the chart would.
The output is a set of clinical signals, each traceable to its source in the record, that tells care teams which patients need attention and why. Clinicians review the evidence and make every decision.
Keeping Patient Data Inside the Hospital Walls
Synapsis AI runs on NVIDIA-accelerated computing inside a health system’s own firewall. The entire health system’s patient records can be processed onsite, so patient data is never shared and never leaves the hospital.
Processing records this way takes chart review off the desks of clinical teams and lets them spend that time with patients. But Synapsis AI still requires clinician input — it’s an assistive tool that surfaces evidence from medical records that a clinician must still confirm and act on.
Dyania builds and trains its clinical models with NVIDIA NeMo open libraries, then uses NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM to optimize them to run faster and more efficiently on the hospital’s own GPU servers.
Synapsis AI in the Real World
Cleveland Clinic used Synapsis AI to support a study of more than 7,800 aortic valve replacement patients between 2005 and 2021.
Synapsis AI reasoned across each patient’s record, including every echocardiogram added in the years after surgery, and used this information to build a predictive model of valve deterioration and reintervention risk at the three-, five- and ten-year mark after a patient undergoes an aortic valve replacement procedure. The AI platform completed chart review across the full cohort that would have taken clinicians years to complete by hand.
“Using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help us predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients,” said Dr. Lars Svensson, chief of the Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute at Cleveland Clinic.
The same approach can be applied to any healthcare challenge where the answer sits inside the medical record, such as identifying patients eligible for clinical trials, closing care gaps in cardiology and oncology, and populating clinical registries.
Learn more about Dyania Health.

articles.title: Apple announces release dates for the first Apple Home Collection smart devices
articles.text:
The first few smart home devices and accessories that Apple co-developed with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric for its new Apple Home Collection are now available for preorder through the company’s online store, with delivery expected in mid-December. Apple announced the collection a month ago as part of a stronger push into the smart home space that’s led by its new Siri AI-powered HomeView smart display which is also now available starting today.
Apple announces release dates for the first Apple Home Collection smart devices
You can preorder several of the devices today, with shipping expected to start in mid-December.
Of all the Apple Home Collection devices currently listed on its online store, only a handful of LG accessories are available for preorder. These include the $299.95 LG Outdoor Cam and $199.95 Indoor Cam, plus the $249.95 LG Video Doorbell, which all show an estimated shipping timeline of December 11th to December 17th. The rest of the collection, including the $399.95 LG Floodlight Cam, $349.95 LG Smart Deadbolt Lock, $199.95 LG Smart Thermostat, $199.95 Schneider Home Smart Thermostat, and $39.95 Schneider Home Room Sensor, aren’t yet available for preorder and don’t have an estimated ship date.
The devices in the Apple Home Collection don’t include exclusive features or functionality, but through the partnership, Apple has streamlined the setup process so it’s as easy as tapping them with your iPhone to get them running. The devices in the collection also use Thread to remain connected should they lose access to the internet or your Wi-Fi network, and they can automatically update their network credentials if you make changes to your wireless network.
